A single administrator editing copies, or only one operator keeping a copy, contradicts a ledger **not owned by any single entity**; records are **immutable**, never deleted.
xa: Notes: records are visible to relevant stakeholders **without risk of alteration**; database copies sit with participants (UPSC **2020**, **2026**).
**Hash**: changing data changes the hash, so **tampering shows**.
**Distributed ledger**: a **single source of truth** with no central validator.

19.s:
Consider the following statements about Proof of Work and Proof of Stake:
1. In Proof of Work, miners race to solve complex puzzles.
2. In Proof of Stake, validators are chosen by coins staked.
3. Proof of Work generally uses far less energy than Proof of Stake.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
19.x: Proof of Work uses puzzle-solving miners, while Proof of Stake selects validators based on staked coins. Proof of Work has very high energy use, so statement 3 is false.
19.tq: Catch the reversed energy comparison after identifying the two mechanisms.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: in **Proof of Work**, **miners race to solve complex puzzles**.
Statement 2 is correct: in **Proof of Stake**, validators are chosen by **coins staked**.
Statement 3 is wrong: PoW has **very high energy use**; PoS uses far less — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: **Bitcoin** uses **PoW**; **Ethereum** moved PoW → PoS in **Sep 2022** (**The Merge**).
**PoW energy use** is one of the main criticisms of blockchain, along with scalability and interoperability.

19.s: Which one of the following correctly identifies the consensus mechanism associated with Bitcoin?
19.x: Bitcoin is associated with Proof of Work, in which miners solve complex computational puzzles.
19.tq: Direct association of a well-known blockchain with its consensus mechanism.
xs: **Bitcoin** uses **Proof of Work** — option **(2)**: miners race to solve complex puzzles.
**Proof of Stake** is used by **Ethereum** since **Sep 2022**, not Bitcoin.
xa: ⚠ Bitcoin = **public** + **PoW**; AP DigiVerify = **permissioned**.
In Bitcoin, **mining** validates transactions; users have **public/private keys** and wallets.
PoW has **very high energy use** — a standing criticism.

19.s: Ethereum's transition from Proof of Work to Proof of Stake in September 2022 was known as:
19.x: Ethereum's move to Proof of Stake in September 2022 was called 'The Merge'.
19.tq: Pair the event name with the specific month and year.
xs: Ethereum's move from **PoW to PoS** in **Sep 2022** is called **The Merge** — option **(3)**.
In PoS, validators are chosen by **coins staked**, cutting energy use sharply.
xa: **Bitcoin** still runs on **Proof of Work** (miners solve complex puzzles).
PoW = **very high energy use**; PoS = far lower energy use.
Bitcoin is a **public/permissionless** blockchain.

19.s: Bitcoin, first introduced in 2009, was created by:
19.x: Bitcoin was introduced in 2009 by the pseudonymous creator Satoshi Nakamoto.
19.tq: Direct recall of the creator-year association.
xs: **Bitcoin (2009)** was created by the pseudonymous **Satoshi Nakamoto** — option **(2)**.
It was the **first cryptocurrency** and the **first use of blockchain**.
xa: Bitcoin features: **decentralised, peer-to-peer**; **public/private keys** and wallets; **mining** validates transactions.
Bitcoin = **public** blockchain using **Proof of Work**.
In India, crypto is **not legal tender**.

19.s:
Consider the following statements about cryptocurrency:
1. It is decentralised and peer-to-peer.
2. It uses public and private keys and wallets.
3. Mining can validate transactions.
4. It is legal tender in India.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
19.x: Cryptocurrency is decentralised and peer-to-peer, uses keys and wallets, and may use mining for validation. It is not legal tender in India.
19.tq: Find the false legal-status statement among otherwise functional characteristics.
xs: Statements 1–3 are correct: crypto (e.g. **Bitcoin**) is **decentralised, peer-to-peer**, uses **public/private keys and wallets**, and **mining validates transactions**.
Statement 4 is wrong: in **India**, crypto is **not legal tender** — so **1, 2 and 3 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: Virtual digital asset service providers were brought under **PMLA in March 2023**.
**Turkmenistan** legalised crypto mining using **gas-based power** (**2026**).
**Stablecoins** are pegged to fiat, commodities or crypto.

19.s: Stablecoins are cryptocurrencies generally pegged to:
19.x: Stablecoins are pegged to fiat, commodities or crypto-assets in an attempt to provide relative price stability.
19.tq: Direct recall of the collateral or reference-asset relationship.
xs: **Stablecoins** are pegged to **fiat currencies, commodities or crypto-assets** — option **(4)**.
Nodes, inflation alone or miners' voting strength are not what they are pegged to.
xa: **NFTs**: unique cryptographic tokens; **non-fungible**, so not exchangeable at equivalency.
**DeFi**: lending and trading via **smart contracts** without banks.
**Tokenisation**: ownership rights in an asset turned into a blockchain token.

19.s: Virtual digital asset service providers in India were brought under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act in:
19.x: Virtual digital asset service providers were brought under the PMLA in March 2023.
19.tq: Use the date-specific legal-regulation fact and compare adjacent years.
xs: Virtual digital asset service providers were brought under the **PMLA** in **March 2023** — option **(4)**.
In India, crypto remains **not legal tender**.
xa: **National Strategy on Blockchain**: **MeitY**, **Dec 2021**.
**Turkmenistan** legalised crypto mining using gas-based power (**2026**).
**Vishvasya**: MeitY's Blockchain-as-a-Service stack (**2024**).

19.s:
Which of the following statements regarding NFTs is correct?
1. They are unique cryptographic tokens on a blockchain.
2. They can digitally represent physical assets.
3. They are exchangeable at equivalency like fungible units.
Select the correct answer using the code below.
19.x: NFTs are unique tokens and can represent physical assets digitally. Because they are non-fungible, they are not exchangeable at equivalency.
19.tq: Use the meaning of 'non-fungible' to reject the reversed exchangeability statement.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: **NFTs** are **unique cryptographic tokens** on a blockchain and can **represent physical assets digitally**.
Statement 3 is wrong: being **non-fungible**, NFTs are **not exchangeable at equivalency** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: UPSC **2022** asked this; key: **1 and 2 only**.
**Stablecoins** are pegged to fiat, commodities or crypto.
**Tokenisation**: ownership rights in an asset → blockchain token.

19.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Smart contracts are self-executing code on a blockchain that cut out intermediaries.
2. Web 3.0 refers to the first-generation, centralised web.
3. DeFi offers lending and trading through smart contracts without banks.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
19.x: Statement 1 is correct: smart contracts are self-executing code that cut intermediaries. Statement 2 is wrong: Web 3.0 is the third-generation, decentralised web. Statement 3 is correct: DeFi runs lending and trading via smart contracts without banks. So B; A misses statement 3, C and D accept statement 2.
19.tq: Web 3.0 = third generation, decentralised.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **smart contracts** are **self-executing code** on a blockchain that **cut intermediaries**.
Statement 2 is wrong: **Web 3.0** is the **third-generation, decentralised** web.
Statement 3 is correct: **DeFi** = lending and trading via smart contracts **without banks** — so **1 and 3 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: Smart contracts also **monitor supply chains**.
**NFTs**: unique cryptographic tokens that can represent physical assets digitally.
**Tokenisation**: ownership rights in an asset → blockchain token.

19.s: Which of the following is a stated application of smart contracts?
o: Replacing all blockchain nodes with one server
Converting every cryptocurrency into legal tender
19.x: Smart contracts can reduce intermediaries and monitor supply chains.
19.tq: Select the practical use that follows from automated blockchain code.
xs: Smart contracts **cut intermediaries** and **monitor supply chains** — option **(4)**.
They are **self-executing code on a blockchain**; they do not replace nodes with one server or make crypto legal tender (crypto is **not legal tender** in India).
xa: **DeFi** uses smart contracts for lending and trading **without banks**.
Governance uses of blockchain include a **pharma supply chain**, land records and e-Notary.
**Web 3.0**: third-generation, **decentralised** web.

19.s: The process of converting ownership rights in an asset into a blockchain token is called:
19.x: Tokenisation converts ownership rights in an asset into a blockchain token.
19.tq: Distinguish an ownership-representation term from consensus and security terms.
xs: Converting ownership rights in an asset into a blockchain token is **tokenisation** — option **(3)**.
**Mining** validates transactions (Bitcoin); **hashing** creates a cryptographic fingerprint of data.
xa: **NFTs**: unique tokens that can represent **physical assets** digitally.
**Stablecoins**: pegged to fiat, commodities or crypto.
**Smart contracts**: self-executing code that cuts intermediaries.

19.s: Which of the following is NOT included among the listed applications of blockchain technology?
19.x: The listed applications include land records, electronic health records and SHG microfinance. Unregulated creation of sovereign currency is not one of them.
19.tq: Find the outsider by checking the stated application list.
xs: **Unregulated creation of sovereign currency** is not a listed blockchain application — option **(4)**.
Listed uses include **land records**, **electronic health records** and **SHG microfinance**, so options (1)–(3) are on the list.
xa: Other listed uses: **digital certificates**, **pharma supply chain**, **e-Notary**, farm insurance, identity, **e-voting**, digital evidence.
In India, crypto is **not legal tender**.
AP examples: **Mee Bhoomi-Blockchain** (land records) and **AP DigiVerify** (certificates).

19.s:
Consider the following statements regarding MeitY's Distributed Centre of Excellence in Blockchain:
1. It includes C-DAC, IDRBT Hyderabad and VJTI Mumbai.
2. It produced a property-registration pilot in Shamshabad, Andhra Pradesh.
3. It produced a Proof-of-Existence framework for certificates.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
19.x: Statement 1 is correct: the CoE comprises C-DAC, IDRBT Hyderabad and VJTI Mumbai. Statement 2 is wrong: Shamshabad is in Telangana, not Andhra Pradesh. Statement 3 is correct: it built a Proof-of-Existence framework for certificates. So B; A misses statement 3, C and D accept statement 2.
19.tq: Shamshabad (Hyderabad airport area) = Telangana.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: the CoE comprises **C-DAC**, **IDRBT Hyderabad** and **VJTI Mumbai**.
Statement 2 is wrong: the property-registration pilot was in **Shamshabad**, which is in **Telangana**, not AP.
Statement 3 is correct: it built a **Proof-of-Existence** framework for certificates — so **1 and 3 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: **National Strategy on Blockchain**: **MeitY**, **Dec 2021**; **NeGD** had earlier released an approach paper.
**Vishvasya** (MeitY, **2024**): Blockchain-as-a-Service stack hosted across **NIC** data centres.

19.s:
Consider the following statements about NPCI's Drunix:
1. It is an open-source private blockchain.
2. It was built by re-engineering Hyperledger Fabric.
3. It was NPCI's first open-source blockchain release.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
19.x: Drunix is an open-source private blockchain re-engineered from Hyperledger Fabric. It was NPCI's second, not first, open-source blockchain release, after Falcon.
19.tq: Use the ordinal trap in the statement about the release sequence.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: **Drunix** is an open-source **private** blockchain re-engineered from **Hyperledger Fabric**.
Statement 3 is wrong: it is NPCI's **2nd** open-source blockchain release; the 1st was **Falcon** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: Drunix was released by **NPCI** on **19 Jun 2026**.
**Vishvasya** (MeitY, **2024**) builds on the **National Blockchain Framework (NBF)**.
Private/permissioned blockchains admit **only authorised entities**.

19.s: The National Strategy on Blockchain was published by MeitY in:
19.x: The National Strategy on Blockchain was published by the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology in December 2021.
19.tq: Pair the publisher with the precise year and month.
xs: **MeitY** released the **National Strategy on Blockchain** in **December 2021** — option **(2)**.
**NeGD** had earlier released an **approach paper**.
xa: MeitY's **Distributed CoE in Blockchain**: C-DAC, **IDRBT Hyderabad**, VJTI Mumbai.
**Vishvasya** (MeitY, **2024**): Blockchain-as-a-Service, built on the **National Blockchain Framework (NBF)**.
VDA service providers came under **PMLA** in **March 2023**.

19.s: Which organisation had earlier released an approach paper before the National Strategy on Blockchain?
19.x: NeGD had earlier released an approach paper related to blockchain before the National Strategy was published.
19.tq: Distinguish the earlier approach-paper issuer from the later strategy publisher.
xs: **NeGD** had earlier released an **approach paper** before MeitY's National Strategy on Blockchain (**Dec 2021**) — option **(4)**.
**C-DAC** is a member of MeitY's Distributed CoE in Blockchain; **NPCI** released Drunix and Falcon.
xa: CoE output: **Shamshabad (Telangana)** property-registration pilot and a **Proof-of-Existence** framework.
**Vishvasya** is hosted across **NIC** data centres.
**Drunix** = NPCI's 2nd open-source blockchain; 1st = **Falcon**.

19.s: Vishvasya is best described as:
o: A private cryptocurrency issued by NIC
19.x: Vishvasya is MeitY's Blockchain-as-a-Service technology stack, introduced in 2024.
19.tq: Match the named platform with its ministry and service model.
xs: **Vishvasya** is **MeitY's Blockchain-as-a-Service technology stack** (**2024**) — option **(2)**.
It is hosted across **NIC data centres** and builds on the **National Blockchain Framework (NBF)** for shared blockchain infrastructure.
It is not a cryptocurrency; NPCI's blockchain releases are **Drunix** and **Falcon**.
xa: **National Strategy on Blockchain**: MeitY, **Dec 2021**.
MeitY's Distributed CoE: **C-DAC**, **IDRBT Hyderabad**, **VJTI Mumbai**.
Drunix (**19 Jun 2026**) is re-engineered from **Hyperledger Fabric**.

19.s: Mee Bhoomi-Blockchain pilot in Andhra Pradesh was launched by whom and on which date?
o: The Chief Secretary of Andhra Pradesh on 10 April 2026
The Governor of Andhra Pradesh on 1 January 2026
19.x: The Mee Bhoomi-Blockchain pilot was launched by Chief Minister Naidu on 23 July 2026.
19.tq: Match the office-holder with the exact date rather than relying on a nearby date.
xs: The **Mee Bhoomi-Blockchain** pilot was launched by CM **Naidu** on **23 Jul 2026** — option **(2)**.
**10 Apr 2026** belongs to **Mee Bhoomi-Mee Hakku** (pattadar passbooks); **November** is when the statewide rollout is planned.
xa: It unifies **Revenue, Survey and Registration** records, earlier kept separately (with **Webland**).
**AP DigiVerify**: permissioned-blockchain PaaS holding **9.85 crore** records.
SC suggested exploring **blockchain for tamper-proof land records**; AP's earlier pilot reportedly **halved land disputes**.

19.s: AP DigiVerify is best described as which one of the following?
o: A land survey application operating without blockchain technology
A central-bank system for issuing digital currency
A public cryptocurrency exchange for government departments
A permissioned-blockchain platform-as-a-service for tamper-proof certificate verification
19.x: AP DigiVerify is a permissioned-blockchain PaaS designed for tamper-proof certificate verification.
19.tq: Use the exact functional description and reject nearby but different blockchain applications.
xs: **AP DigiVerify** is a **permissioned-blockchain PaaS** for **tamper-proof certificate verification** — option **(4)**.
It is not public or a crypto exchange — it is the notes' example of a **permissioned** blockchain.
xa: It holds **9.85 crore** records (AP SES 2025-26 analysis).
Earlier figures: AP Seva **5.70 crore**, MeeSeva **5.01 crore**.
With **Mee Bhoomi-Blockchain**, it makes AP a **front-runner** in government blockchain.

19.s: Mee Bhoomi-Mee Hakku is associated with the issue of which of the following?
19.x: Mee Bhoomi-Mee Hakku issues tamper-proof pattadar passbooks.
19.tq: Identify the scheme by its specific administrative output rather than by a general digital-governance function.
xs: **Mee Bhoomi-Mee Hakku** issues **tamper-proof pattadar passbooks** (**10 Apr 2026**) — option **(3)**.
It is a land-records initiative, not voter IDs, crypto wallets or licences.
xa: **Mee Bhoomi-Blockchain** pilot: launched by CM Naidu on **23 Jul 2026**; statewide rollout from **November**.
It unifies **Revenue, Survey and Registration** records.
**AP DigiVerify**: permissioned-blockchain PaaS for certificates.

19.s:
Assertion (A): The Supreme Court suggested exploring blockchain for tamper-proof land records.
Reason (R): An earlier Andhra Pradesh pilot was reportedly associated with halving land disputes.

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
19.x: Both statements are true. However, the reported reduction in Andhra Pradesh land disputes does not constitute the stated reason for the Supreme Court's suggestion.
19.tq: Check whether the Reason explains the Assertion, not merely whether both statements are true.
xs: Both are true: the **SC** suggested exploring **blockchain for tamper-proof land records**, and AP's earlier pilot reportedly **halved land disputes** (**1 Jan 2026**).
But R is not given as the reason for the SC's suggestion — so **both true, R not the correct explanation**, option **(2)**.
xa: AP's **Mee Bhoomi-Blockchain** pilot (**23 Jul 2026**) unifies Revenue, Survey and Registration records.
**Mee Bhoomi-Mee Hakku**: tamper-proof pattadar passbooks.
Criticisms: **scalability**, PoW energy use, **interoperability**, regulatory uncertainty.

19.s: Which one of the following is NOT identified as a criticism or debate associated with blockchain?
19.x: The identified concerns are scalability, proof-of-work energy use, interoperability and regulatory uncertainty. Guaranteed regulatory clarity is not listed as a criticism or debate.
19.tq: Find the option that reverses the direction of the stated concern by replacing uncertainty with certainty.
xs: **Guaranteed regulatory clarity** is not a criticism — the notes list **regulatory uncertainty** — option **(2)**.
The listed criticisms are **scalability**, **PoW energy use**, **interoperability** and **regulatory uncertainty**.
xa: PoW has **very high energy use**; PoS far lower.
**AP angle**: Mee Bhoomi-Blockchain + AP DigiVerify make AP a **front-runner**.
In India, crypto is **not legal tender**.

19.s: Which of the following correctly presents the first cryptocurrency, the year associated with it, and its significance in blockchain history?
o: Bitcoin, 2009, first cryptocurrency and first use of blockchain
Mee Bhoomi-Blockchain, 2026, first use of blockchain
19.x: Bitcoin, in 2009, was identified as the first cryptocurrency and the first use of blockchain.
19.tq: Link the earliest item with both its year and its stated historical significance.
xs: **Bitcoin (2009)** = **first cryptocurrency** and **first use of blockchain** — option **(1)**.
**AP DigiVerify** is a certificate-verification PaaS and **Mee Bhoomi-Blockchain** an AP land-records pilot (**2026**) — neither was first.
xa: Bitcoin was created by the pseudonymous **Satoshi Nakamoto**.
Bitcoin = **public** blockchain using **Proof of Work**.
Blockchain definition (APPSC **2018**): time-stamped series of **immutable records** managed by computers not owned by any single entity.

20.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: TRAI — Regulation of telecom and broadcasting
TDSAT — Settlement of disputes and appeals against TRAI
TEC — Collection of Universal Service Obligation Fund
Department of Telecommunications — Telecom policy and licensing
20.x: TEC is DoT’s technical body for telecom standards and equipment testing. Collection of USOF is not its stated role.
20.tq: Find the body-role mismatch by distinguishing policy, regulation, adjudication and technical functions.
xs: **TEC — Collection of USOF** is wrongly matched — option **(3)**: TEC is **DoT's technical body for telecom standards and equipment testing**.
**TRAI** regulates **telecom and broadcasting**, and **TDSAT** settles disputes and hears **appeals against TRAI** — both correctly matched.
**NOFN** was the scheme **funded by USOF**, not a TEC function.
xa: **TRAI** was set up in **1997** under the TRAI Act; **TDSAT** was created by the **2000** amendment.
**C-DOT** is the government telecom R&D centre, set up in **1984**.
**DoT** was created in **1985** when Posts and Telecom split.

20.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. TRAI was set up in 1997 under the TRAI Act.
2. TDSAT, created by the 2000 amendment, settles disputes and hears appeals against TRAI.
3. TRAI regulates telecom but has no role in broadcasting.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
20.x: Statement 1 is correct: TRAI was set up in 1997 under the TRAI Act. Statement 2 is correct: TDSAT was created by the 2000 amendment to settle disputes and hear appeals against TRAI. Statement 3 is wrong: TRAI regulates both telecom and broadcasting. So A misses statement 2, while C and D wrongly include statement 3.
20.tq: TRAI 1997 (telecom + broadcasting); TDSAT 2000 amendment (appeals).
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **TRAI** was set up in **1997** under the **TRAI Act**.
Statement 2 is correct: **TDSAT**, created by the **2000 amendment**, settles disputes and hears **appeals against TRAI**.
Statement 3 is wrong: TRAI regulates **telecom and broadcasting** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: ⚠ TDSAT hears appeals **against TRAI**; TRAI is the regulator, not the appellate body.
**TEC**: DoT's technical body for telecom standards and equipment testing.
**C-DOT** (**1984**): government telecom R&D centre.

20.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: C-DOT — Government telecom research and development centre
20.x: C-DOT is the government telecom research and development centre. TEC is associated with technical standards and equipment testing, TRAI with regulation, and TDSAT with dispute settlement.
20.tq: Start from the sure institutional pair and reject swapped organisational roles.
xs: **C-DOT** is the **government telecom research and development centre** (set up **1984**) — option **(1)**.
**TEC** is DoT's body for **standards and equipment testing**, not a broadcasting regulator; **TRAI** is the **regulator**, not a testing body; **TDSAT** settles **disputes**, not research.
xa: **TRAI** regulates **telecom and broadcasting** (**1997**, TRAI Act).
**TDSAT** was created by the **2000** amendment.
**MTNL and VSNL** came in **1986**, part of the 1980s reforms.

20.s:
Arrange the following developments in the telecommunications sector in chronological order:
A. Establishment of C-DOT
B. Creation of the Department of Telecommunications after the split of Posts and Telecom
C. Establishment of MTNL and VSNL
D. Establishment of TRAI
20.x: C-DOT was set up in 1984, DoT was created in 1985, MTNL and VSNL were established in 1986, and TRAI was set up in 1997.
20.tq: Fix the sequence using the stated years and then place the later regulatory reform.
xs: DoT was created in **1985** when **Posts and Telecom split**, between C-DOT and MTNL/VSNL.
xa: India's first experimental **satellite telecom** came in **1975**.
**TDSAT** followed TRAI via the **2000** amendment.
India's **5G launch**: **1 October 2022** at India Mobile Congress.

20.s: At 1800 MHz, which of the following correctly states the EMF values referred to for India and ICNIRP respectively?
20.x: At 1800 MHz, the Indian limit is 0.92 W/m², while the ICNIRP value is 9.2 W/m².
20.tq: Compare the paired values carefully and avoid reversing the authority-specific limits.
xs: At **1800 MHz**, India's limit is **0.92 W/m²** and ICNIRP's is **9.2 W/m²** — option **(1)**.
India's EMF limits for towers (since **2012**) are **one-tenth** of ICNIRP limits, so the Indian figure is ten times smaller.
xa: ⚠ Trap: the **APPSC 2021** key gave **9.2 W/m²**, which is the **ICNIRP** value, not India's.
ITU rules: orbital slots **first-come, first-served**; de-orbit within **25 years** of mission end.
The **Telecommunications Act 2023** moved licensing → **authorisation**.

20.s:
Consider the following statements about mobile generations:
1. 1G (1980s) carried analog voice using FDMA.
2. 2G was digital, used GSM (TDMA) and CDMA, and supported SMS.
3. 3G was based on LTE and VoLTE.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
20.x: Statement 1 is correct: 1G was analog voice with FDMA. Statement 2 is correct: 2G was digital with GSM (TDMA) and CDMA and SMS. Statement 3 is wrong: 3G was CDMA-based (WCDMA/CDMA2000); LTE and VoLTE belong to 4G. So A misses statement 2, and C and D wrongly include statement 3.
20.tq: 1G analog-FDMA, 2G GSM/CDMA-SMS, 3G WCDMA, 4G LTE.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **1G** (1980s) = **analog voice**, **FDMA**.
Statement 2 is correct: **2G** = digital; **GSM (TDMA)** and **CDMA**; **SMS**.
Statement 3 is wrong: **3G** was **CDMA-based (WCDMA/CDMA2000)**; LTE and VoLTE belong to **4G** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: **2.5G / 2.75G** = **GPRS / EDGE** (faster GSM data).
⚠ **4G and 5G** = **OFDMA**; 1G = FDMA.
**6G** is expected in the **early 2030s**.

20.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched with the intermediate GSM data technology?
20.x: GPRS is associated with 2.5G and EDGE with 2.75G, both representing faster GSM data developments.
20.tq: Discriminate between closely named intermediate generations using their associated technologies.
xs: **2.5G = GPRS** and **2.75G = EDGE** (faster GSM data) — option **(1)**.
**LTE/VoLTE/OFDMA** belong to **4G**; **CDMA2000/WCDMA** belong to **3G**; **FDMA** to **1G**.
xa: **2G**: digital, **GSM (TDMA)** and **CDMA**, **SMS**.
**5G**: OFDMA, latency as low as **1 ms**.
**1G** (1980s): analog voice.

20.s:
With reference to 4G mobile technology, consider the following statements:
1. LTE is associated with 4G.
2. OFDMA is used in 4G.
3. VoLTE means voice over the LTE data network.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
20.x: LTE and OFDMA are associated with 4G, and VoLTE denotes voice carried over the LTE data network.
20.tq: Check the generation, access method and precise expansion together.
xs: All three are correct: **4G** = **LTE**, uses **OFDMA**, and **VoLTE** = voice over the LTE data network — **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)**.
⚠ **4G and 5G** both use **OFDMA**; 3G was **CDMA-based**.
xa: **5G** offers very high speed and latency as low as **1 ms**.
**1G** = analog, **FDMA**.
**2.75G** = **EDGE** (faster GSM data).

20.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. 5G uses OFDMA and can offer latency as low as 1 ms.
2. 6G is expected in the early 2030s.
3. The phrase "omnipresent wireless intelligence" describes 5G.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
20.x: Statement 1 is correct: 5G uses OFDMA with latency as low as 1 ms. Statement 2 is correct: 6G is expected in the early 2030s. Statement 3 is wrong: "omnipresent wireless intelligence" describes 6G, not 5G. So A misses statement 2, and C and D wrongly include statement 3.
20.tq: 6G = early 2030s + omnipresent wireless intelligence; 5G = 1 ms latency.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **5G** uses **OFDMA**, latency as low as **1 ms**.
Statement 2 is correct: **6G** is expected in the **early 2030s**.
Statement 3 is wrong: **"omnipresent wireless intelligence"** describes **6G**, not 5G — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: **Bharat 6G Vision** (March **2023**): India to lead 6G by **2030**.
5G uses: **eMBB**, **IoT**, **AR/VR**, remote surgery, autonomous vehicles.
World's first 5G: **South Korea (April 2019)**.

20.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: WiMAX — Wireless Local Loop replacing the copper last mile
20.x: WiMAX is IEEE 802.16 wireless broadband. WLL refers to a radio link that replaces the copper last mile.
20.tq: Separate two similar wireless terms by matching each with its exact technical description.
xs: **WiMAX** is **IEEE 802.16 wireless broadband** — option **(2)**.
**WLL** (Wireless Local Loop) is a **radio link replacing the copper last mile** — so options (1), (3) and (4) mismatch it.
xa: **GMPCS** = DoT licence for satcom operators.
**NFC** has a range of a **few cm**.

20.s: Which of the following correctly describes the spectrum-band characteristics of 5G?
o: mmWave is used only for satellite television and not for 5G.
Sub-6 GHz offers wider coverage and better penetration, whereas mmWave offers very high data rates over short ranges.
Sub-6 GHz is restricted to short-range communication, whereas mmWave offers the widest coverage.
Both sub-6 GHz and mmWave have identical coverage and penetration characteristics.
20.x: Sub-6 GHz bands provide wider coverage and better penetration, while mmWave bands provide very high data rates but have short range.
20.tq: Test the reversed coverage, penetration and data-rate comparison between 5G bands.
xs: **Sub-6 GHz** gives **wider coverage and better penetration**; **mmWave** gives **very high data rates over short range** — option **(2)**.
Options (3) and (4) reverse or equate the two; mmWave is a 5G band, not just satellite TV.
xa: ⚠ sub-6 GHz = **coverage**; mmWave = **speed, short range**.
**Network slicing**: one network split into **virtual slices** for different services.
**5G SA** runs **without a 4G core** → lower latency + better slicing.

20.s: Network slicing in 5G refers to which of the following?
o: Restricting one network to a single application
Dividing one network into virtual slices for different services
Splitting an optical fibre into copper segments
Dividing a physical tower into separate buildings
20.x: Network slicing creates virtual network slices from one physical network, allowing different services to receive suitably configured resources.
20.tq: Apply the abstract networking concept to its service-differentiation meaning.
xs: **Network slicing** = **dividing one network into virtual slices for different services** — option **(2)**.
It is not restricting a network to one application, nor about fibre or towers.
xa: **5G Standalone (SA)** runs without a **4G core**, giving **lower latency** and **better slicing**.
**mmWave**: very high data rates, short range.
**sub-6 GHz**: wider coverage, better penetration.

20.s:
Which of the following are recognised uses or application areas of 5G?
1. Enhanced mobile broadband
2. Internet of Things
3. Augmented and virtual reality
4. Remote surgery and autonomous vehicles
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
20.x: 5G applications include eMBB, IoT, AR/VR, remote surgery and autonomous vehicles.
20.tq: Recognise the broad application set and use the complete combination option.
xs: 5G uses: **eMBB**, **IoT**, **AR/VR**, **remote surgery** and **autonomous vehicles** — all four, option **(4)**.
These are the notes' listed **5G uses**, made possible by very high speed and low latency.
xa: For vehicle communication, TRAI prefers **C-V2X**.
5G latency can be as low as **1 ms**.
**100 5G Use Case Labs**: **IIITDM Kurnool** ranked **1st** in DoT's gradation.

20.s: For vehicle communication, which technology does TRAI prefer over 4G/5G-based alternatives?
20.x: TRAI prefers Cellular Vehicle-to-Everything (C-V2X) for vehicle communication over the stated 4G/5G alternatives.
20.tq: Match the regulatory preference with the specialised vehicle-communication term.
xs: TRAI prefers **C-V2X** (over 4G/5G) for **vehicle communication** — option **(1)**.
**FDMA** is the **1G** access technology, **GPON** is used in **NOFN**, and **FSO** sends data by laser/light beams without fibre.
xa: 5G uses include **autonomous vehicles** and **remote surgery**.
**RFID** example: **Kavach** track tags.
5G latency as low as **1 ms**.

20.s: Which of the following correctly states the first 5G launch locations and dates mentioned for global and Indian deployment?
o: South Korea in April 2019; India on 1 October 2022 at India Mobile Congress
Japan in April 2019; India on 1 January 2022 at Digital India Week
South Korea in October 2022; India on 1 April 2019 at India Mobile Congress
United States in 2018; India on 15 August 2021 at the World Mobile Congress
20.x: The world’s first 5G launch was in South Korea in April 2019. India launched 5G on 1 October 2022 at India Mobile Congress.
20.tq: Lock the answer through the paired country-date-event sequence.
xs: World's first 5G: **South Korea (April 2019)**; India: **1 October 2022** at **India Mobile Congress** — option **(1)**.
Japan, the USA, **January 2022** or **15 August 2021** do not appear as launch points — **South Korea** was first, India followed in **2022**.
xa: 5G uses **OFDMA** with latency as low as **1 ms**.
**Bharat 6G Vision** (March **2023**) aims to lead 6G **by 2030**.
**TTDF (2022)** funded the **India 5G Stack**.

20.s:
Consider the following statements about the Telecom Technology Development Fund (TTDF):
1. It was introduced in 2022.
2. It receives 5% of Digital Bharat Nidhi collections.
3. It receives approximately Rs 500 crore per year.
4. It has funded India 5G Stack, 6G and quantum-encryption projects.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
20.x: TTDF was introduced in 2022, receives 5% of Digital Bharat Nidhi collections—about Rs 500 crore annually—and has funded 5G Stack, 6G and quantum-encryption projects.
20.tq: Check the fund’s year, revenue share, annual amount and funded technologies as one factual cluster.
xs: All four are correct: **TTDF (2022)** gets **5%** of **Digital Bharat Nidhi** collections (**~Rs 500 cr/yr**) and funded the **India 5G Stack**, **6G** and **quantum-encryption** projects — option **(4)**.
Its money funded the indigenous **India 5G Stack** as well as **6G** and **quantum-encryption** projects (**2026**).
xa: **Open-RAN 5G**: **Airtel-Tata** partnership.
**5G & Beyond Hackathon 2023** was run by **DoT**, not DST.
**Bharat 6G Alliance** launched in **2023** with **seven Working Groups**.

20.s: The Open-RAN 5G partnership mentioned in the context of India is between which of the following?
20.x: The indigenous Open-RAN 5G partnership is between Airtel and Tata.
20.tq: Identify the private-sector partnership rather than substituting telecom authorities or public-sector entities.
xs: The **Open-RAN 5G** partnership is between **Airtel and Tata** — option **(4)**.
**TRAI/TDSAT** are regulator and tribunal; **BSNL, RailTel** are PSUs whose fibre carries **NOFN**.
xa: **TTDF (2022)** funded the **India 5G Stack**.
India's 5G launch: **1 October 2022**.
⚠ 5G hackathon = **DoT**, not **DST**.

20.s: Which institution ranked first in the Department of Telecommunications’ gradation of 100 5G Use Case Labs for January–June 2026 in all four categories?
20.x: IIITDM Kurnool ranked first in DoT’s January–June 2026 gradation in all four categories.
20.tq: Match the institution with the specific ranking and evaluation period.
xs: **IIITDM Kurnool** ranked **1st** in DoT's gradation of **100 5G Use Case Labs** (Jan-Jun **2026**) in all four categories — option **(4)**.
Its lab, set up in **2023**, has built **18 products**.
xa: **5G & Beyond Hackathon 2023**: run by **DoT**; open to individuals, students, start-ups and academics.
**TTDF** gets **5%** of Digital Bharat Nidhi collections.
**C-DOT** is the government telecom R&D centre.

20.s:
Consider the following statements about the 5G & Beyond Hackathon 2023:
1. It was run by the Department of Science and Technology (DST).
2. It was open to individuals, students, start-ups and academics.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
20.x: Statement 1 is wrong: the hackathon was run by the Department of Telecommunications (DoT), not DST. Statement 2 is correct: it was open to individuals, students, start-ups and academics. Hence only 2 is correct; A, C and D are wrong.
20.tq: APPSC 2022 trap: DoT, not DST.
xs: Statement 1 is wrong: the **5G & Beyond Hackathon 2023** was run by **DoT**, not **DST**.
Statement 2 is correct: it was open to **individuals, students, start-ups and academics** — so **2 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: **APPSC 2022** asked about this hackathon.
**IIITDM Kurnool** ranked **1st** among **100 5G Use Case Labs**.
**Open-RAN 5G**: **Airtel-Tata**.

20.s: In the context of 5G, Standalone (SA) architecture means that the network
20.x: 5G SA runs without a 4G core. It does not mean that the network has no core network at all.
20.tq: Distinguish standalone 5G from a network with no core network.
xs: **5G Standalone (SA)** **runs without a 4G core** — option **(3)**.
It gives **lower latency** and **better slicing**, so (2) is wrong; it still has a core of its own, so (4) is wrong.
xa: **Network slicing**: one network divided into virtual slices.
**sub-6 GHz** = coverage; **mmWave** = speed, short range.
5G latency as low as **1 ms**.

20.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Bharat 6G Vision document:
1. It seeks to enable India to lead the design, development and deployment of 6G.
2. The target year for this objective is 2030.
3. The document was released in March 2023.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
20.x: The Bharat 6G Vision document was released in March 2023 and aims for India to lead the design, development and deployment of 6G by 2030.
20.tq: Combine objective, target year and release date in a coded statement question.
xs: All correct: **Bharat 6G Vision** aims for India to **lead design, development and deployment of 6G** by **2030**, released **March 2023** — option **(4)**.
The goal is for India to **lead design, development and deployment** of 6G **by 2030**.
xa: **Bharat 6G Alliance (B6GA)** launched **2023**, with **seven Working Groups** and MoUs with global 6G alliances.
**6G** expected in the **early 2030s** — "omnipresent wireless intelligence".
**TTDF** funded **6G** and quantum-encryption projects.

20.s: Which one of the following is NOT included among the participants brought together by the Bharat 6G Alliance?
20.x: The Bharat 6G Alliance brings together public and private firms, academia and standards bodies. It is not constituted exclusively of foreign military organisations.
20.tq: Find the option that violates the stated composition of the institution.
xs: B6GA brings together **public and private firms**, **academia** and **standards bodies** — **"only foreign military organisations"** is not listed, option **(3)**.
The alliance is a mix of **industry, academia and standards bodies** — nothing restricts it to military organisations.
xa: B6GA was launched in **2023** and has **seven Working Groups**.
It has signed **MoUs with global 6G alliances**.
**Bharat 6G Vision** (March **2023**): lead 6G **by 2030**.

20.s:
Consider the following statements about the Bharat 6G Alliance (B6GA):
1. It was launched in 2025.
2. It has seven Working Groups.
3. It has signed MoUs with global 6G alliances.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
20.x: Statement 1 is wrong: B6GA was launched in 2023. Statement 2 is correct: it has seven Working Groups. Statement 3 is correct: it has MoUs with global 6G alliances. So only 2 and 3 are correct; A, C and D include the wrong statement 1.
20.tq: Bharat 6G Vision and B6GA both 2023; target 2030.
xs: Statement 1 is wrong: **B6GA** was launched in **2023**, not 2025.
Statements 2 and 3 are correct: it has **seven Working Groups** and **MoUs with global 6G alliances** — so **2 and 3 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: Members: **public and private firms + academia + standards bodies**.
**Bharat 6G Vision**: released **March 2023**, target **2030**.
**6G** is expected in the **early 2030s**.

20.s: Which of the following combinations is correct regarding the TRAI recommendations of February 2026?
o: Auction of all available spectrum across nine bands; uniform 35% spectrum cap; new-entrant net worth reduced from Rs 100 crore to Rs 50 crore per service area
Auction across nine bands; no spectrum cap; net worth reduced to Rs 25 crore
Auction across five bands; uniform 50% cap; net worth increased to Rs 200 crore
Administrative assignment across nine bands; uniform 35% cap; net worth retained at Rs 100 crore
20.x: TRAI recommended auctioning all available spectrum across nine bands, a uniform 35% spectrum cap, and reducing the new-entrant net-worth requirement from Rs 100 crore to Rs 50 crore per service area.
20.tq: Check all components of a multi-part policy recommendation together.
xs: TRAI (**Feb 2026**) recommended auctioning **all available spectrum across nine bands**, a uniform **35% spectrum cap**, and halving new-entrant net worth **Rs 100 cr → Rs 50 cr** per service area — option **(1)**.
Option (4) is wrong: **administrative assignment** applies to **satellite** spectrum; (2) and (3) misstate the cap and the net-worth figure.
xa: At reserve price the spectrum is worth **≈ Rs 81,000 cr** (**25 Feb 2026**).
⚠ Terrestrial spectrum is **auctioned**; satellite spectrum is **assigned administratively**.
**SC (Feb 2026)**: telecom companies **do not own spectrum**.

20.s:
With reference to the Supreme Court decision of February 2026, consider the following statements:
1. Telecom companies do not own spectrum.
2. The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code can restructure spectrum rights in the Aircel case.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
20.x: The Supreme Court held that telecom companies do not own spectrum. It also held that the IBC cannot restructure spectrum rights in the Aircel case, making statement 2 false.
20.tq: Use the negative legal conclusion to identify the reversed statement.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: the **SC (Feb 2026)** held that telecom companies **do not own spectrum**.
Statement 2 is wrong: the **IBC cannot restructure spectrum rights** (**Aircel** case) — so **1 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: Ruling dated **14 Feb 2026**.
TRAI (**Feb 2026**) recommended auctioning spectrum across **nine bands** with a **35%** cap.
Satellite spectrum is **assigned administratively** under the **Telecommunications Act 2023**.

20.s: The Telecommunications Act, 2023 represents a shift from:
20.x: The Telecommunications Act, 2023 moves from a licensing framework to a light-touch authorisation framework.
20.tq: Discriminate between two closely related regulatory terms.
xs: The **Telecommunications Act 2023** moved from **licensing to authorisation** (light-touch) — option **(3)**.
Option (4) reverses the direction.
xa: Under it, satellite spectrum is **assigned administratively** (First Schedule), not auctioned.
DoT's July **2026** rule: infrastructure providers must store all telecom data and logs **in India**.
**GMPCS** is the DoT licence for satcom operators.

20.s: Under the July 2026 rule of the Department of Telecommunications for infrastructure providers, telecom data and logs must be stored:
o: Only in the country of the equipment manufacturer
20.x: The Department of Telecommunications rule requires all telecom data and logs of infrastructure providers to be stored in India.
20.tq: Identify the authority and location attached to a data-localisation requirement.
xs: DoT's July **2026** rule for **infrastructure providers**: all telecom data and logs **stored in India** — option **(2)**.
It was issued under the **Telecommunications Act 2023** (licensing → authorisation).
xa: Rule dated **25 Jul 2026**.
GMPCS conditions include **geofencing** and **lawful surveillance**.
Satellite spectrum is **assigned administratively**.

20.s: How is satellite spectrum assigned under the First Schedule of the Telecommunications Act, 2023?
o: Through allocation by private satellite companies
Through first-come, first-served auctions conducted by the ITU
20.x: Satellite spectrum is assigned administratively under the First Schedule of the Telecommunications Act, 2023, rather than being auctioned.
20.tq: Distinguish administrative assignment from auction-based allocation.
xs: Satellite spectrum is **assigned administratively, not auctioned**, under the **First Schedule** of the Telecommunications Act 2023 — option **(2)**.
⚠ Terrestrial spectrum is **auctioned**; first-come, first-served is the **ITU** rule for **orbital slots**, not spectrum auctions.
xa: TRAI (**Feb 2026**): auction all spectrum across **nine bands**, **35%** cap.
ITU: de-orbit within **25 years** of mission end.
**Starlink** got its **GMPCS licence** in **2025**.

20.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes GEO satellites from LEO satellites?
o: GEO satellites are about 35,786 km above Earth and have higher latency, whereas LEO satellites are below about 2,000 km and have lower latency
GEO satellites always have lower latency than LEO satellites because they remain fixed over one spot
GEO satellites orbit below 2,000 km, whereas LEO satellites orbit at about 35,786 km
Both GEO and LEO satellites operate at the same altitude and have identical latency
20.x: GEO satellites are approximately 35,786 km above Earth, remain fixed over one spot and have higher latency. LEO satellites are below about 2,000 km and generally provide lower latency.
20.tq: Compare altitude, apparent position and latency in a single table-based question.
xs: **GEO** ≈ **35,786 km**, fixed over one spot, **higher latency**; **LEO** below **~2,000 km**, large constellations, **low latency** — option **(1)**.
Options (2)–(4) reverse or equate the altitude and latency.
xa: GEO example: **GSAT series** (**GSAT-7/7A** for defence).
LEO examples: **Starlink**, **Eutelsat OneWeb**, **Amazon Kuiper**.
**Starlink** has **8,000+ LEO satellites**.

20.s: Which of the following is an example of a GEO satellite series, with GSAT-7 and GSAT-7A being associated with defence?
20.x: The GSAT series is cited as an example of GEO satellites, and GSAT-7 and GSAT-7A are associated with defence applications.
20.tq: Match the satellite series with its orbital category and use.
xs: **GSAT series** is the GEO example; **GSAT-7/7A** serve **defence** — option **(4)**.
**OneWeb**, **Starlink** and **Kuiper** are **LEO** constellations.
xa: GEO ≈ **35,786 km**, higher latency; LEO below **~2,000 km**.
India's first experimental satellite telecom: **1975**.
~**20-25%** of Indians live where terrestrial networks are hard to reach.

20.s: Which of the following groups consists entirely of LEO satellite constellations?
o: Starlink, Eutelsat OneWeb and Amazon Kuiper
20.x: Starlink, Eutelsat OneWeb and Amazon Kuiper are identified as LEO constellations. The GSAT examples listed are GEO satellites.
20.tq: Separate the LEO group from the nearby GEO examples.
xs: **Starlink**, **Eutelsat OneWeb** and **Amazon Kuiper** are all **LEO** constellations — option **(1)**.
**GSAT** satellites (incl. **GSAT-7/7A**) are **GEO**, so options (2)–(4) mix in GEO.
xa: **Starlink**: **8,000+ LEO satellites**, **GMPCS licence** in India in **2025**.
**OneWeb (Bharti)** earlier received an **LoI**.
⚠ LEO = **low latency**; GEO = **higher latency**.

20.s: Which of the following statements is correct regarding Starlink and OneWeb in India?
o: Starlink has more than 8,000 LEO satellites and obtained its GMPCS licence in India in 2025, while OneWeb earlier received an LoI
Starlink operates only GEO satellites and OneWeb obtained its licence after 2025
OneWeb has more than 8,000 GEO satellites and Starlink received only an LoI
Both companies received their Indian GMPCS licences in 2023
20.x: Starlink has more than 8,000 LEO satellites and received its GMPCS licence in India in 2025. Eutelsat OneWeb, associated with Bharti, had earlier received a letter of intent.
20.tq: Track company, constellation type, licence status and sequence of regulatory approval.
xs: **Starlink** has **8,000+ LEO satellites**, got its **GMPCS licence** in **2025**, and **OneWeb (Bharti)** earlier got an **LoI** — option **(1)**.
Starlink is **LEO**, not GEO, so (2) and (3) fail.
xa: GMPCS conditions: **geofencing**, no cross-border spillover, lawful surveillance, **terminals made in India within 5 years**.
LEO orbits below **~2,000 km** with **low latency**.
~**20-25%** of Indians live where terrestrial networks are hard to reach.

20.s: GMPCS stands for:
o: Global Mobile Personal Communication by Satellite
Global Microwave and Private Communication System
20.x: GMPCS means Global Mobile Personal Communication by Satellite. It is the Department of Telecommunications licence required for satellite communication operators.
20.tq: Expand the exact acronym without substituting a similar satellite term.
xs: **GMPCS** = **Global Mobile Personal Communication by Satellite** — option **(2)**.
It is the **DoT licence for satcom operators**.
xa: Conditions: **geofencing**, no cross-border spillover, lawful surveillance, **terminals made in India within 5 years**.
**Starlink** got its GMPCS licence in **2025**.
Satellite spectrum is **assigned administratively**.

20.s: Which of the following is NOT a condition associated with the GMPCS licence for satellite communication operators?
o: Mandatory manufacture of all satellites in India within five years
20.x: The conditions include geofencing, no cross-border spillover, lawful surveillance and terminals made in India within five years. The requirement concerns terminals, not mandatory manufacture of all satellites in India.
20.tq: Find the option that changes the exact object of a regulatory condition.
xs: The condition is **terminals made in India within 5 years**, not **manufacture of all satellites** — option **(2)**.
**Geofencing**, **no cross-border spillover** and **lawful surveillance** are genuine GMPCS conditions.
xa: **GMPCS** = Global Mobile Personal Communication by Satellite (DoT licence).
**Starlink** received its GMPCS licence in **2025**.
ITU: orbital slots **first-come, first-served**.

20.s:
With reference to ITU rules for satellites, consider the following statements:
1. Orbital slots are given on a first-come, first-served basis.
2. Satellites must be de-orbited within 50 years of the end of their mission.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
20.x: Statement 1 is correct: ITU gives orbital slots first-come, first-served. Statement 2 is wrong: the de-orbit limit is 25 years after mission end, not 50. Hence only 1 is correct; B, C and D are wrong.
20.tq: ITU: first-come first-served slots; 25-year de-orbit rule.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **ITU** gives **orbital slots first-come, first-served**.
Statement 2 is wrong: satellites must be de-orbited within **25 years** of mission end, not 50 — so **1 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: Satellite spectrum in India is **assigned administratively** (Telecommunications Act **2023**).
GMPCS requires **geofencing** and **lawful surveillance**.

20.s: India's first experimental satellite telecommunication activity took place in:
20.x: India's first experimental satellite telecommunication activity was conducted in 1975.
20.tq: Distinguish the first experimental milestone from later satellite developments.
xs: India's first experimental **satellite telecom** took place in **1975** — option **(3)**.
It predates the **1980s reforms** — **C-DOT (1984)**, DoT (**1985**), MTNL and VSNL (**1986**).
xa: **C-DOT (1984)**, **DoT (1985)**, **MTNL and VSNL (1986)** were the 1980s reforms.
**CANI** submarine OFC was inaugurated in **August 2020**.
India's 5G launch: **1 October 2022**.

20.s: Which of the following is the fastest data-transmission medium among the listed communication media?
20.x: Optical fibre provides faster data transmission than copper cable, radio waves and satellite signals.
20.tq: Use the direct comparative fact and eliminate the slower neighbouring media.
xs: **Optical fibre** is the **fastest** data-transmission medium vs **copper cable**, **radio waves** and **satellite signals** — option **(3)** (APPSC **2025**).
It works on **total internal reflection**, carrying signals as **pulses of light**.
xa: **Single-mode** fibre = long distances; **multi-mode** = short runs.
Undersea cables carry nearly **99%** of international internet and telecom traffic.
Main use of optical fibre: **communication**.

20.s:
With reference to optical fibre communication, consider the following statements:
1. Single-mode fibre is suitable for long-distance signal transmission.
2. Multi-mode fibre is generally used for short-distance runs.
3. Single-mode fibre is designed only for satellite communication.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
20.x: Single-mode fibre carries signals over long distances and multi-mode fibre is used over short runs. The claim that single-mode fibre is designed only for satellite communication is false.
20.tq: Identify the two correct application statements and reject the extreme word 'only'.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: **single-mode** fibre = **long distances**; **multi-mode** = **short runs**.
Statement 3 is wrong: optical fibre's **main use is communication**, not satellite-only — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: Principle: **total internal reflection**; signals travel as **pulses of light**.
Fibre is the **fastest** medium vs copper, radio and satellite (APPSC **2025**).
Exam angle: statement sets on **TIR**, light signals and single-mode fibre.

20.s:
Consider the following statements regarding undersea communication cables:
1. They are fibre-optic lines laid on the seabed.
2. Optical repeaters are generally placed at intervals of about 60–80 km.
3. They carry nearly 99% of international Internet and telecommunications traffic.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
20.x: All three statements correctly describe undersea fibre-optic cables, their repeater spacing and their dominant share in international Internet and telecom traffic.
20.tq: Test a compact cluster of quantitative and definitional statements together.
xs: All correct: undersea cables are **fibre-optic lines on the seabed**, with **optical repeaters every 60-80 km**, carrying nearly **99%** of international traffic — option **(4)**.
They are **cheaper and lower-latency** than satellites, which is why they dominate international traffic.
xa: The global network runs ~**1.5 million km** (Sep **2025**).
They are **cheaper and lower-latency** than satellites.
**CANI**: Chennai-Andaman & Nicobar submarine OFC, ~**2,300 km**.

20.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes undersea fibre-optic cables from satellite communication for international connectivity?
o: Undersea cables are more expensive and have higher latency than satellites.
Undersea cables cannot carry international telecommunications traffic.
Satellite communication uses fibre-optic lines laid on the seabed.
Undersea cables are generally cheaper and have lower latency than satellites.
20.x: Undersea fibre-optic cables are cheaper and offer lower latency than satellite communication for international connectivity.
20.tq: Use the reversed-comparison trap by checking both cost and latency.
xs: Undersea cables are **cheaper and lower-latency than satellites** — option **(4)**.
They carry nearly **99%** of international internet and telecom traffic, so (2) is wrong; seabed fibre is cable, not satellite, so (3) is wrong.
xa: Network length ~**1.5 million km**; repeaters every **60-80 km**.
GEO satellites (~**35,786 km**) have **higher latency**.
**CANI** was laid by **BSNL**.

20.s:
Consider the following statements about the CANI submarine optical-fibre project:
1. It is about 2,300 km long.
2. It was laid by BSNL.
3. It was inaugurated in August 2020.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
20.x: The CANI cable is approximately 2,300 km long, was laid by BSNL and was inaugurated in August 2020.
20.tq: Combine the project’s length, implementing organisation and inauguration date in a coded statement question.
xs: All correct: **CANI** (Chennai-Andaman & Nicobar Islands) is ~**2,300 km**, laid by **BSNL**, inaugurated **August 2020** — option **(4)**.
**CANI** = **Chennai-Andaman & Nicobar Islands** submarine OFC.
xa: Undersea cables carry nearly **99%** of international traffic.
**NOFN** later became **BharatNet**.
Repeaters sit every **60-80 km**.

20.s:
Consider the following statements about the National Optical Fibre Network (NOFN):
1. It was planned to link all 2,50,000 Gram Panchayats using existing PSU fibre of BSNL, RailTel and Power Grid.
2. It is funded by the National Investment and Infrastructure Fund.
3. It uses GPON technology.
4. It was later renamed BharatNet.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
20.x: Statements 1, 3 and 4 are correct: NOFN was planned to link all 2,50,000 Gram Panchayats over existing PSU fibre (BSNL, RailTel, Power Grid), uses GPON and was later renamed BharatNet. Statement 2 is wrong: NOFN is funded by USOF (Universal Service Obligation Fund), not NIIF. Hence options A, C and D, which include statement 2, are wrong.
20.tq: NOFN = USOF money + GPON tech + GP target; renamed BharatNet.
xs: Statements 1, 3 and 4 are correct: **NOFN** was to link all **2,50,000 Gram Panchayats** over PSU fibre (**BSNL, RailTel, Power Grid**), uses **GPON**, and was later renamed **BharatNet**.
Statement 2 is wrong: NOFN is funded by **USOF**, not NIIF — so **1, 3 and 4 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: Estimated cost: **Rs 20,000 cr**.
**PM Gati Shakti NMP** (**2026**): ~**13.5 lakh route km** PSU OFC, **8.26 lakh towers**, **30.15 lakh BTSs**.
**PM-WANI**: **3.15 lakh** hotspots mapped on Gati Shakti NMP.

20.s:
Consider the following statements about optical fibre:
1. It works on the principle of total internal reflection.
2. Signals travel through it as pulses of light.
3. Its main use is in communication.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
20.x: All three are correct: optical fibre works by total internal reflection, carries signals as pulses of light and is mainly used for communication. Options A, B and C each leave out a true statement.
20.tq: Fibre = TIR + light pulses; 'All of the above' type.
xs: All correct: optical fibre works on **total internal reflection**, signals travel as **pulses of light**, and its **main use is communication** — option **(4)**.
These are the classic **statement-set** points the exam tests on optical fibre (**TIR**, light signals).
xa: **Single-mode** = long distances; **multi-mode** = short runs.
It is the **fastest** medium vs copper, radio and satellite (APPSC **2025**).
**Li-Fi** also uses light — from **LEDs** — but wirelessly.

20.s:
Consider the following statements about Li-Fi:
1. It is a form of wireless optical networking.
2. It transmits data using LEDs.
3. It was coined as a term by Harald Haas in 2011.
4. It generally offers more bandwidth, efficiency and security than Wi-Fi.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
20.x: All four statements correctly describe Li-Fi, including its LED-based optical transmission, the origin of the term and its stated advantages over Wi-Fi.
20.tq: Use a complete set of technical characteristics and identify the all-correct combination.
xs: All four are correct: **Li-Fi** is **wireless optical networking** sending data via **LEDs**, the term coined by **Harald Haas (2011)**, with **more bandwidth, efficiency and security** than Wi-Fi — option **(4)**.
Li-Fi uses **visible light** from LEDs, whereas **Wi-Fi** uses **radio waves**.
xa: ⚠ Li-Fi **does not pass through walls**; Wi-Fi does and has **longer range**.
**FSO**: data by laser/light beams without fibre; first **2 Tbit/s** FSO link (**2026**).

20.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched in the comparison of Li-Fi and Wi-Fi?
o: Wi-Fi — Suitable for wireless local area networks
Li-Fi — Generally longer range than Wi-Fi
20.x: Wi-Fi has longer range than Li-Fi. Li-Fi is associated with visible light, while Wi-Fi uses radio waves and supports wireless LANs.
20.tq: Detect the reversed comparison in the range characteristic.
xs: **Li-Fi — longer range than Wi-Fi** is wrong — option **(4)**: **Wi-Fi** has the **longer range**.
Li-Fi uses **visible light from LEDs**; Wi-Fi uses **radio waves** and serves **wireless LANs** — options (1)–(3) are correct.
xa: Li-Fi offers **more bandwidth, efficiency, security**; it **does not pass through walls**.
Term coined by **Harald Haas** (**2011**).
**PM-WANI**: public Wi-Fi hotspots — **3.15 lakh** mapped on Gati Shakti NMP.

20.s: Free-Space Optical (FSO) communication transmits data primarily through which medium?
o: Laser or light beams without fibre
20.x: FSO communication sends data through laser or light beams without using fibre cables.
20.tq: Distinguish free-space optical transmission from fibre-guided optical transmission.
xs: **Free-Space Optical (FSO)** sends data by **laser or light beams without fibre** — option **(1)**.
It needs no copper wire or undersea cable; it is optical, not low-frequency radio.
xa: World's first **2 Tbit/s** FSO link used **small terminals for satellites and HAPS** (**2026**).
**Li-Fi** is also optical: wireless networking via **LEDs** (visible light).
Optical fibre works on **total internal reflection**, carrying **pulses of light**.

20.s: Which of the following statements regarding the reported high-speed FSO link is correct?
o: It was a 2 Mbit/s link using Wi-Fi routers.
It was the world’s first 2 Tbit/s FSO link using small terminals for satellites and HAPS.
It was a 2 Tbit/s copper link between mobile towers.
It was a 2 Gbit/s link using undersea fibre cables only.
20.x: The reported link was the world’s first 2 Tbit/s free-space optical link, using small terminals for satellites and high-altitude platform stations.
20.tq: Preserve the unit scale and application context while rejecting altered figures.
xs: It was the **world's first 2 Tbit/s FSO link** using **small terminals for satellites and HAPS** — option **(2)**.
FSO uses **laser/light beams without fibre**, so a copper link (3) or undersea fibre (4) is wrong; Wi-Fi routers (1) use radio waves.
xa: **Project Loon** (Google/Alphabet): internet from **high-altitude balloons**; shut down **2021**.
**PM-WANI**: public Wi-Fi hotspots, **3.15 lakh** mapped on Gati Shakti NMP.
**Li-Fi**: data via **LEDs**; term coined by **Harald Haas** (**2011**).

20.s: Which of the following correctly describes WLAN/Wi-Fi communication?
o: It operates exclusively through geostationary satellites
It uses radio waves over a short range
It requires a wired backbone between every pair of devices
It uses only infrared waves over a long range
20.x: WLAN or Wi-Fi uses radio waves for short-range wireless communication. It does not require every communicating device to have a separate wired connection.
20.tq: Identify the defining medium and range of the technology.
xs: **WLAN / Wi-Fi** uses **radio waves over a short range** — option **(2)**.
It is wireless, so no wired backbone between devices is needed; it does not run through GEO satellites or infrared.
xa: Compared with **Li-Fi**, Wi-Fi has **longer range** and **passes through walls**.
**PM-WANI** provides public Wi-Fi hotspots.

20.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Wi-Fi 6 — IEEE 802.11ax
2. Wi-Fi 7 — IEEE 802.11be
3. Wi-Fi Direct — IEEE 802.11be
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
20.x: Wi-Fi 6 corresponds to IEEE 802.11ax and Wi-Fi 7 to IEEE 802.11be. Wi-Fi Direct is a device-to-device connectivity feature, not the designation of IEEE 802.11be.
20.tq: Use precise standard-number matching and eliminate the swapped technology.
xs: **Wi-Fi 6 = 802.11ax** and **Wi-Fi 7 = 802.11be** are correct; **802.11be** is Wi-Fi 7, not Wi-Fi Direct — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(2)**.
⚠ The notes pair **802.11be** only with **Wi-Fi 7**, so pair 3 is wrong.
xa: **WiMAX** = IEEE **802.16** wireless broadband.
Wi-Fi uses **radio waves**; Li-Fi uses **visible light from LEDs**.
**WLL** = radio link replacing the copper last mile.

20.s: Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) technology is based on:
o: Reading tags only through optical fibre
Using high-altitude balloons as signal repeaters
Transmitting data exclusively through visible light
20.x: RFID identifies objects by wirelessly reading radio-frequency tags. It does not require direct optical-fibre transmission.
20.tq: Distinguish the operating principle of a named access technology.
xs: **RFID** works by **reading radio tags wirelessly** — option **(4)**.
Visible light is **Li-Fi**; high-altitude balloons are **Project Loon**; RFID does not need optical fibre.
xa: Example: **Kavach** track tags (Mar **2026**).
**NFC** works within a **few cm**.
**GMPCS**: DoT licence for satcom operators.

20.s: Near Field Communication (NFC) generally operates over a range of:
20.x: NFC is a very short-range wireless communication technology, generally operating over a distance of a few centimetres.
20.tq: Recall the characteristic range rather than confusing it with satellite distances.
xs: **NFC** has a range of **a few centimetres** — option **(2)**.
**35,786 km** is the **GEO** altitude and **2,000 km** the **LEO** ceiling — not communication ranges.
xa: **RFID**: radio tags read wirelessly, e.g. **Kavach** track tags.
**Li-Fi**: wireless optical networking via **LEDs**.
**mmWave**: very high data rates, **short range**.

20.s: Project Loon, developed by Google/Alphabet, sought to provide internet connectivity through:
20.x: Project Loon attempted to deliver internet connectivity using high-altitude balloons. The project was shut down in 2021.
20.tq: Match the project with its distinctive infrastructure.
xs: **Project Loon** (Google/Alphabet) delivered internet from **high-altitude balloons** — option **(1)**; it was **shut down in 2021**.
LEO constellations are **Starlink**, **OneWeb** and **Kuiper**; undersea fibre is a different medium.
xa: **FSO**: world's first **2 Tbit/s** link with small terminals for satellites and **HAPS** (**2026**).
**PM-WANI**: **3.15 lakh** public Wi-Fi hotspots mapped on Gati Shakti NMP.
~**20-25%** of Indians live where terrestrial networks are hard to reach.

20.s: On 30 June 2026, Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu directed telecom operators to:
o: Stop expanding telecom infrastructure in Amaravati
Replace all mobile towers with satellites within 25 years
Complete all spectrum auctions within 30 days
20.x: The Chief Minister directed telecom operators to complete new towers within 100 days. He also reviewed a fibre-optic network for Amaravati.
20.tq: Identify the action and deadline in a current-affairs directive.
xs: CM **Naidu** (**30 Jun 2026**) told operators to **finish new towers within 100 days** — option **(1)**.
He also reviewed a **fibre-optic network for Amaravati** (**1 Jul 2026**), so stopping expansion (2) is the opposite.
xa: **PM Gati Shakti NMP** assets: **8.26 lakh towers** and **30.15 lakh BTSs** (**2026**).
India rose to **49th** in the **Network Readiness Index 2024**.
**IIITDM Kurnool** ranked **1st** among **100 5G Use Case Labs**.

20.s: India's position in the Network Readiness Index 2024 was:
20.x: India rose to 49th in the Network Readiness Index 2024 from 60th earlier.
20.tq: Track both the current rank and the direction of change.
xs: India stood **49th**, **improving from 60th**, in the **Network Readiness Index 2024** — option **(4)**.
Option (3) reverses the movement; (1) and (2) give wrong ranks.
xa: CM **Naidu** (**30 Jun 2026**): new towers **within 100 days**.
**NOFN** (later **BharatNet**) was to link all **2,50,000 Gram Panchayats**.
India launched 5G on **1 October 2022**.

21.s: Which one of the following sets of technologies is most closely associated with the Fourth Industrial Revolution?
o: Steam engines, railways and coal mining
Electricity, assembly lines and mass production
Artificial intelligence, robotics, IoT and quantum computing
21.x: Artificial intelligence, robotics, the Internet of Things and quantum computing are identified with the Fourth Industrial Revolution.
21.tq: Identify the option containing the complete contemporary technology cluster.
xs: **IR4** is the convergence of digital, physical and biological tech — **AI, robotics, IoT, quantum computing** — option **(3)**.
**Steam/mechanisation** was **IR1**, **electricity/mass production** was **IR2**.
xa: Term coined by **Klaus Schwab** (WEF) in **2016**.
IR4 = **cyber-physical systems** — "smart factories".
WEF's **C4IR centre in AP** is India's **3rd** after Mumbai and Telangana.

21.s: ‘Smart factories’ associated with the Fourth Industrial Revolution are based on:
21.x: Smart factories use cyber-physical systems that integrate physical production processes with digital technologies.
21.tq: Match the descriptive term with its underlying system.
xs: 4IR **"smart factories"** rest on **cyber-physical systems** — option **(3)**.
**Steam/mechanisation** belongs to **IR1**; manual or standalone mechanical systems are pre-digital.
xa: IR4 merges **digital + physical + biological** technologies.
**IR3** = electronics/IT; **IR2** = electricity/mass production.
**IIoT** monitors production and **equipment health**.

21.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Industrial Revolutions:
1. The First Industrial Revolution was associated with steam and mechanisation.
2. The Second Industrial Revolution was associated with electricity and mass production.
3. The Third Industrial Revolution was associated with electronics and information technology.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
21.x: All three statements correctly describe the principal technological bases of the First, Second and Third Industrial Revolutions.
21.tq: Check each revolution against its defining technological combination.
xs: All three are correct: **IR1** = **steam/mechanisation**, **IR2** = **electricity/mass production**, **IR3** = **electronics/IT** — option **(4)**.
**IR4** adds **cyber-physical systems** (digital + physical + biological).
xa: "Fourth Industrial Revolution" was coined by **Klaus Schwab** (WEF) in **2016**.
IR4 technologies: **AI**, **robotics**, **IoT**, **quantum computing**.
AP got a WEF **C4IR centre** — India's **3rd**.

21.s: The term 'Fourth Industrial Revolution' was coined by:
o: Klaus Schwab of the World Economic Forum in 2016
21.x: Klaus Schwab, founder of the World Economic Forum (WEF), coined the term in 2016. Toffler wrote of the 'Third Wave', Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web, and Nilekani led UIDAI; none coined 4IR.
21.tq: 4IR = Schwab, WEF, 2016.
xs: **Klaus Schwab** of the **WEF** coined "Fourth Industrial Revolution" in **2016** — option **(1)**.
It describes convergence of digital, physical and biological tech — **AI, robotics, IoT, quantum computing**.
xa: WEF announced a **C4IR centre in Andhra Pradesh** — India's **3rd** after **Mumbai** and **Telangana** (**2026**).
IR4 = **cyber-physical systems** ("smart factories").
IR1 = steam; IR2 = electricity; IR3 = electronics/IT.

21.s: The World Economic Forum's Centre for the Fourth Industrial Revolution (C4IR) announced for Andhra Pradesh is India's:
o: Fourth, after Mumbai, Telangana and Karnataka
21.x: The WEF C4IR centre in Andhra Pradesh is India's third, after Mumbai and Telangana. So it is neither the first nor the second, and no fourth (Karnataka) centre precedes it.
21.tq: C4IR India: Mumbai → Telangana → AP (3rd).
xs: The WEF **C4IR centre in AP** is India's **3rd**, **after Mumbai and Telangana** — option **(3)**.
So it is neither first nor second, and no Karnataka centre is listed.
xa: C4IR = Centre for the **Fourth Industrial Revolution**, a term coined by **Klaus Schwab** (**2016**).
AP angle also includes an **AP-Google AI/cloud task force** (June **2026**).
IR4 = **cyber-physical systems**.

21.s: Which one of the following correctly explains the term IIoT?
21.x: IIoT stands for Industrial Internet of Things and is associated with production processes and equipment-health monitoring.
21.tq: Test the exact expansion of a confusable technology acronym.
xs: **IIoT** = **Industrial Internet of Things** — option **(2)**, used for **production** and **equipment health**.
**IoT** itself = **Internet of Things** (asked in APPSC **2023**, **2024**).
xa: **SaaS / PaaS / IaaS** = Software / Platform / Infrastructure as a Service.
**DLT** = Distributed Ledger Technology.
IoT architecture: **perception → network → application**.

21.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. NFT — Non-Fungible Token, a unique blockchain token
2. DLT — Distributed Ledger Technology
3. 5G NR — 5G Network Relay
4. Web 3.0 — Decentralised, blockchain-based internet
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
21.x: Pairs 1, 2 and 4 are correct: NFT is a Non-Fungible Token (unique blockchain token), DLT is Distributed Ledger Technology, and Web 3.0 is the decentralised, blockchain-based internet. Pair 3 is wrong: 5G NR means 5G New Radio, the air-interface standard. So A misses pair 4, and C and D wrongly include pair 3.
21.tq: NR = New Radio (air interface), not relay.
xs: Pairs 1, 2 and 4 are correct: **NFT** = Non-Fungible Token, **DLT** = Distributed Ledger Technology, **Web 3.0** = decentralised, blockchain-based internet.
Pair 3 is wrong: **5G NR** = **5G New Radio** (air interface standard) — so **1, 2 and 4 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: **RFID** = Radio Frequency Identification.
**Li-Fi** = Light Fidelity; **NFC** = Near-Field Communication.
**Tokenization**: NFTs and **real-world asset tokens** (land, bonds).

21.s: RFID is best described as a technology involving
o: communication within a few centimetres using magnetic induction only
tags and readers communicating through radio waves
21.x: RFID stands for Radio Frequency Identification and uses tags and readers communicating through radio waves.
21.tq: Identify the defining hardware pair and transmission medium.
xs: **RFID** (Radio Frequency Identification) uses **tags and readers communicating through radio waves** — option **(3)**.
**A few centimetres** describes **NFC**; data through **LEDs** describes **Li-Fi**.
xa: **Active tags**: own battery, longer range; **passive tags**: powered by the reader's signal.
**DLT** = Distributed Ledger Technology.
IoT: devices networked **without human intervention**.

21.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Li-Fi stands for Light Fidelity.
2. Li-Fi transmits data through LEDs.
3. Li-Fi can offer better bandwidth and security than Wi-Fi.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
21.x: All three statements are correct. Li-Fi means Light Fidelity, uses LEDs for data transmission and is noted for better bandwidth and security than Wi-Fi.
21.tq: Use the meaning, medium and comparative advantage together.
xs: All three are correct: **Li-Fi** = **Light Fidelity**, sends data via **LEDs**, with **better bandwidth and security than Wi-Fi** — option **(4)**.
Li-Fi uses visible light while **Wi-Fi** uses radio waves.
xa: **Wi-Fi 7** = IEEE **802.11be**, up to **46 Gbps**.
**NFC** works within a **few centimetres**.
**5G NR** = 5G New Radio.

21.s: Wi-Fi 7 is associated with which of the following specifications?
o: IEEE 802.11ax and a maximum speed of 1 Gbps
21.x: Wi-Fi 7 is based on IEEE 802.11be, supports Multi-Link Operation and is specified with speeds up to 46 Gbps.
21.tq: Match the latest standard with its identifying technical feature.
xs: **Wi-Fi 7** = IEEE **802.11be** with **Multi-Link Operation** — option **(1)**.
It runs **up to 46 Gbps**, so "1 Gbps" in (2) is wrong; that option also gives Wi-Fi 7 the wrong standard.
xa: **TP-Link** began manufacturing Wi-Fi 7 in India (**27 May 2026**).
**Li-Fi**: data via LEDs; better bandwidth and security than Wi-Fi.
**NFC**: within a few centimetres.

21.s: In cloud computing, the abbreviations SaaS, PaaS and IaaS respectively stand for:
o: Software as a Service, Platform as a Service, Infrastructure as a Service
Security as a Service, Programs as a Service, Internet as a Service
Storage as a Service, Platform as a Service, Integration as a Service
Software as a Service, Payments as a Service, Information as a Service
21.x: SaaS, PaaS and IaaS are Software, Platform and Infrastructure as a Service. The other options swap in look-alike words (Security, Storage, Programs, Payments, Internet, Integration, Information) that are not the standard expansions.
21.tq: S-P-I: Software, Platform, Infrastructure.
xs: **SaaS / PaaS / IaaS** = **Software / Platform / Infrastructure as a Service** — option **(1)**.
Look-alikes such as Security, Storage, Payments or Internet as a Service are not the expansions.
xa: **Edge computing** processes data **near the source**; **fog computing** sits between edge and **cloud**.
AP has an **AP-Google AI/cloud task force** (June **2026**).
**DLT** = Distributed Ledger Technology.

21.s: Which of the following is the correct sequence of the three-layer IoT architecture from the physical level to the user-service level?
21.x: The three layers are perception, which uses sensors; network, which transmits data; and application, which provides user services.
21.tq: Arrange the layers from sensing to transmission to service delivery.
xs: IoT's three layers run **perception** (sensors) → **network** (transmission) → **application** (user services) — option **(2)**.
⚠ Option (1) reverses the order; (3) and (4) scramble it.
xa: IoT pillars: **device, data, analytics, connectivity**.
IoT = devices networked **without human intervention**.
IoT uses: **smart city**, **smart agriculture**, **wearables**, smart grids.

21.s:
Consider the following pairs of IoT uses and examples:
1. Smart city — Traffic, air-quality monitoring and waste collection
2. Smart agriculture — Public safety and traffic control
3. Wearables — Fitness trackers and health monitors
Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched?
21.x: Pair 1 is correct: traffic, air-quality monitoring and waste collection are smart-city uses. Pair 2 is wrong: smart agriculture covers precision farming, soil monitoring, livestock and yields; public safety and traffic are smart-city uses. Pair 3 is correct: fitness trackers and health monitors are wearables. So A misses pair 3, and C and D wrongly include pair 2.
21.tq: Sort each example by where it lives: city streets, farms, or the body.
xs: Pair 1 is correct: **smart city** = traffic, air-quality monitoring, waste collection (and public safety).
Pair 2 is wrong: **smart agriculture** = **precision farming, soil monitoring, livestock, yields**; public safety and traffic are smart-city uses.
Pair 3 is correct: **wearables** = fitness trackers and health monitors — so **1 and 3 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: Other IoT uses: **smart grids**, **logistics tracking**, **smart buildings (HVAC)**.
Architecture: **perception → network → application**.

21.s: Which of the following combinations consists only of other IoT applications listed apart from smart cities, smart agriculture and wearables?
o: Smart grids, logistics tracking and smart buildings
Cloud storage, search engines and email
21.x: Smart grids, logistics tracking and smart buildings, including HVAC systems, are additional IoT applications.
