29.x: All four pairs are correctly matched: BOSS Linux is associated with C-DAC, Maya OS with Chakravyuh with the Ministry of Defence, M-Kavach with C-DAC Hyderabad, and CERT-In with CVE numbering for products made in India.
29.tq: Start with the sure developer pair and verify each institutional association.
xs: All four pairs match — so option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4** is correct.
**BOSS Linux** = **C-DAC**; **Maya OS** with **Chakravyuh** = **Ministry of Defence** (**2023**).
**M-Kavach** = **C-DAC Hyderabad**; **CERT-In** = **CVE Numbering Authority** for products made in India.
xa: CERT-In data: **29.44 lakh** incidents in **2025** (**20.41** lakh in **2024**).
CERT-In flags (**2014**): **Hikti, Dyreza Trojan, Shellshock**.

29.s: Virtual keyboards are particularly useful in defeating which of the following?
29.x: Virtual keyboards help protect against keyloggers by reducing the usefulness of recording physical keyboard keystrokes.
29.tq: Match a protective measure with the specific attack mechanism it addresses.
xs: **Virtual keyboards** defeat **keyloggers** — so option **(2)** is correct.
A keylogger **records every keystroke** (passwords, PINs, OTPs, card numbers).
xa: Keylogger example: **DarkHotel**.
⚠ **Rootkit** = hides other malware; **Keylogger** = records keystrokes.

29.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the mode of operation of a computer virus?
o: It automatically spreads across networks without any user interaction
It attaches itself to files or programmes and generally requires the user to execute the infected file
It disguises itself as legitimate software and never modifies files
It records every keystroke without attaching to any file
29.x: A virus attaches to files or programmes and usually requires the user to execute the infected file. It may corrupt or delete data.
29.tq: Distinguish malware by its precise mechanism rather than by its general harmful effect.
xs: A virus **attaches itself to files or programmes and generally requires the user to execute the infected file** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Spreading **without user interaction** is a **worm**; disguised software is a **trojan**; recording keystrokes is a **keylogger**.
xa: A virus **corrupts/deletes data**.
⚠ **Virus** = user must run it; **Worm** = spreads without user interaction.
APPSC **2024** key gave **Virus** for the malware definition.

29.s:
Consider the following statements about computer worms:
1. They can self-replicate across networks.
2. They require the user to execute an infected file before spreading.
3. They may consume network bandwidth.
4. They are regarded as the fastest-spreading type of malware.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
29.x: Statements 1, 3 and 4 are correct. Statement 2 describes a typical virus; a worm spreads automatically without user interaction.
29.tq: Separate the closely related virus and worm mechanisms by checking the user-interaction condition.
xs: Statements 1, 3 and 4 are correct: worms **self-replicate** across networks, **eat bandwidth** and are the **fastest spreading** — so option **(2) 1, 3 and 4 only** is correct.
Statement 2 is wrong: a worm spreads **without user interaction**; needing the user to run it is a **virus**.
xa: Example worm: **WannaCry** (ransomware that spreads as a worm).
Exam angle: "self-replicating without user action" = **worm**.

29.s: A malicious programme is disguised as legitimate software, does not self-replicate and opens a backdoor into a system. It is best classified as a:
29.x: A Trojan is disguised as legitimate software, does not self-replicate and may open a backdoor for unauthorised access.
29.tq: Apply the three-part distinction of disguise, self-replication and backdoor access.
xs: Disguised as legitimate software, **no self-replication**, opens **backdoors** = **Trojan** — so option **(4)** is correct.
A **worm** self-replicates; a **virus** attaches to files; a **rootkit** hides other malware.
xa: Example: **Zeus Trojan**; CERT-In flagged the **Dyreza Trojan** (**2014**).
Exam angle: "no self-replication, disguised" = **trojan**.

29.s: The AIIMS Delhi cyber incident of 2022 is associated with which type of malware?
29.x: The AIIMS Delhi attack of 2022 is cited as an example of ransomware, which encrypts files or systems and demands payment for restoration.
29.tq: Use the named incident as the anchor for identifying the malware category.
xs: The **AIIMS Delhi (2022)** attack was **ransomware** — so option **(4)** is correct.
Ransomware **encrypts** files/systems and demands a ransom (often **crypto**) for the key.
xa: Ransomware spreads via **phishing** and **malicious downloads**.
**Petya** and **WannaCry** are also ransomware (APPSC-G2 **2025** PYQ).

29.s:
Consider the following pairs (Malware : Feature):
1. Spyware : Secretly monitors the user and steals passwords or banking data
2. Adware : Encrypts files and demands a ransom for the key
3. Keylogger : Records every keystroke, including PINs and OTPs
Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched?
29.x: Pair 1 is correct: spyware does secret surveillance and steals passwords/banking data. Pair 2 is wrong: adware shows unwanted ads bundled with free/pirated software; encrypting files for ransom is ransomware. Pair 3 is correct: a keylogger records every keystroke. So 1 and 3 only.
29.tq: Adware = ads; encryption + ransom = ransomware.
xs: Pair 1 is correct: **spyware** secretly monitors the user and steals passwords/banking data.
Pair 2 is wrong: **adware** shows unwanted ads; encrypting files for ransom is **ransomware**.
Pair 3 is correct: a **keylogger** records every keystroke — so option **(3) 1 and 3 only** is correct.
xa: Examples: spyware **Pegasus**, adware **Fireball**, keylogger **DarkHotel**.
Adware comes bundled with **free/pirated software**.

29.s: Which of the following is the principal feature of a rootkit?
o: It spreads only through infected removable files
It sends repeated advertising messages to users
It demands ransom in cryptocurrency after encrypting files
It obtains administrator-level access and hides other malware
29.x: A rootkit gains deep administrator-level access and conceals other malicious components, making it particularly difficult to detect.
29.tq: Identify the defining privilege and concealment feature of the malware.
xs: A rootkit **obtains administrator-level access and hides other malware** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It is the **hardest to detect** malware type.
Ads = **adware**; ransom for encrypted files = **ransomware**.
xa: Example: **Stuxnet** components.
⚠ **Rootkit** = hides other malware; **Keylogger** = records keystrokes.

29.s: A botnet is best described as:
o: A legitimate software package containing advertisements
A network of infected devices remotely controlled for activities such as DDoS attacks
A collection of encrypted files held for ransom
A virus that can operate only after a user opens an attachment
29.x: A botnet consists of infected ‘zombie’ devices controlled remotely and may be used for DDoS attacks, spam or crypto-mining.
29.tq: Identify the network-level concept from the words ‘infected devices’ and ‘remote control’.
xs: A botnet is **a network of infected devices remotely controlled for activities such as DDoS attacks** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The infected devices are called "**zombie**" devices; uses include **DDoS, spam, crypto-mining**.
xa: Example: **Mirai**, which hijacked **IoT devices**.
**Crypto-jacking** secretly uses a victim's device to mine cryptocurrency.

29.s: 'Software designed to disrupt, damage or gain unauthorised access to a computer system.' In APPSC 2024, the key answer for this definition was:
29.x: The APPSC 2024 key gave Virus for this definition of malicious software. A firewall prevents unauthorised network access, a cookie is a small browser data file, and a patch fixes software flaws; none of them is designed to damage a system.
29.tq: Disrupt/damage/unauthorised access -> virus (malware).
xs: The APPSC **2024** key for this malware definition was **Virus** — so option **(1)** is correct.
A **firewall** prevents unauthorised network access, so it is the defence, not the threat.
xa: Malware = software designed to **disrupt, damage or gain unauthorised access**.
A virus **attaches to files/programs** and needs the user to run it.
⚠ **Creeper** = first virus; **Brain** = first IBM-PC virus.

29.s: The Creeper programme, associated with the year 1971, was developed in connection with which network?
29.x: Creeper appeared on ARPANET in 1971 and is recognised as the first self-replicating programme or virus. It was associated with Bob Thomas of BBN.
29.tq: Link the historical malware name with its year and network of origin.
xs: **Creeper** (**1971**) ran on **ARPANET** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It was the **first** self-replicating program/virus, by **Bob Thomas, BBN**.
**Windows SMB** is the flaw used by **EternalBlue**.
xa: **Reaper** removed Creeper.
⚠ **Creeper** = first virus; **Elk Cloner** = first "in the wild"; **Brain** = first IBM-PC virus.

29.s: Which one of the following is correctly associated with Elk Cloner?
o: A ransomware worm that used the EternalBlue exploit in 2017
The first virus in the wild, affecting Apple II computers in 1982
The first IBM-PC boot-sector virus, created in Lahore in 1986
A worm that sabotaged uranium centrifuges in Iran
29.x: Elk Cloner, created by Rich Skrenta, is regarded as the first virus in the wild and affected Apple II computers in 1982.
29.tq: Use the platform and historical status together to distinguish early named viruses.
xs: **Elk Cloner** was **the first virus in the wild, affecting Apple II computers in 1982** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It was written by **Rich Skrenta**.
EternalBlue ransomware worm = **WannaCry**; Lahore boot-sector = **Brain**; Iran centrifuges = **Stuxnet**.
xa: **Creeper** (**1971**) = first self-replicating program.
**Brain** (**1986**) = first IBM-PC boot-sector virus.

29.s:
With reference to the Brain virus, consider the following statements:
1. It was an IBM-PC boot-sector virus.
2. It was associated with MS-DOS.
3. It originated in Lahore, Pakistan.
4. It was created in 1971 on ARPANET.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
29.x: Brain was the first IBM-PC MS-DOS boot-sector virus and was created by the Alvi brothers in Lahore, Pakistan, in 1986. Statement 4 refers to Creeper.
29.tq: Use platform, operating system and place to separate Brain from other early viruses.
xs: Statements 1-3 are correct: **Brain** was an **IBM-PC (MS-DOS) boot-sector virus** from **Lahore, Pakistan**, by the **Alvi brothers**.
Statement 4 is wrong: **1971, ARPANET** is **Creeper**; Brain came in **1986** — so option **(2) 1, 2 and 3 only** is correct.
xa: **Elk Cloner** (**1982**) = first virus "in the wild" (Apple II).
FIRST/LAST: Brain = first PC virus (**Pakistan**).

29.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. WannaCry (2017) was a ransomware that spread as a worm.
2. EternalBlue, the exploit used by WannaCry, was a Windows SMB exploit developed by Israel's NSO Group.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
29.x: Statement 1 is correct: WannaCry was a ransomware worm (2017). Statement 2 is wrong: EternalBlue was developed by the US NSA and leaked; NSO Group (Israel) made Pegasus spyware. So 1 only.
29.tq: EternalBlue = US NSA (leaked); NSO = Pegasus.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **WannaCry** (**2017**) was **ransomware that spread as a worm**.
Statement 2 is wrong: **EternalBlue** was developed by the **US NSA** and leaked by **Shadow Brokers**; **NSO Group** made **Pegasus** — so option **(1) 1 only** is correct.
xa: WannaCry is attributed to **North Korea's Lazarus group**.
EternalBlue exploits a **Windows SMB** flaw.

29.s: Which of the following statements regarding Petya is correct?
o: It is a botnet made up of hijacked IoT devices.
It is a spyware programme requiring no user interaction.
It is an adware programme bundled with pirated software.
It is a ransomware that encrypts disk boot records.
29.x: Petya is ransomware that encrypts the master boot record or disk boot records. NotPetya, its later variant, notably affected Ukraine in 2017.
29.tq: Distinguish a named ransomware by the specific system component it encrypts.
xs: **Petya** (**2016**) is **ransomware that encrypts disk boot records** (master boot record) — so option **(4)** is correct.
IoT botnet = **Mirai**; zero-click spyware = **Pegasus**; pirated-software adware = **Fireball**.
xa: **NotPetya** (**2017**) hit **Ukraine**.
**Petya + WannaCry** = **ransomware** (APPSC-G2 **2025** PYQ).

29.s: Stuxnet was notable primarily because it:
o: Hijacked IoT devices to conduct DDoS attacks
Encrypted files on the computers of AIIMS Delhi
Targeted Iran’s Natanz uranium centrifuges using a worm with rootkit components
Affected Apple II computers as the first virus in the wild
29.x: Stuxnet was a worm containing rootkit components that sabotaged Siemens PLC-controlled uranium centrifuges at Iran’s Natanz facility.
29.tq: Connect the named malware with its distinctive target and industrial-control context.
xs: **Stuxnet** (**2010**) **targeted Iran's Natanz uranium centrifuges using a worm with rootkit components** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It attacked **Siemens PLCs** to sabotage **Iran's nuclear programme**.
IoT DDoS = **Mirai**; AIIMS Delhi = **ransomware**; Apple II = **Elk Cloner**.
xa: Rootkit = deep admin-level access, **hides** other malware.
Cyber espionage is **often state-sponsored** and uses **zero-days**.

29.s: Which one of the following correctly describes Pegasus?
o: An Android vulnerability discovered by a Norwegian firm
A boot-sector virus created in Lahore
A ransomware worm developed by the United States NSA
A zero-click spyware associated with NSO Group of Israel
29.x: Pegasus is state-grade zero-click spyware associated with Israel’s NSO Group and can exploit zero-days without requiring user interaction.
29.tq: Separate spyware identity, developer and zero-click capability from other named threats.
xs: **Pegasus** is **a zero-click spyware** from the **NSO Group of Israel** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It exploits **zero-days**, with **no user interaction** needed.
Norwegian Android flaw = **StrandHogg**; Lahore boot virus = **Brain**; NSA exploit = **EternalBlue**.
xa: **Spyware** secretly monitors users and steals passwords/banking data.
**Zero-day** = flaw developers have had "zero days" to fix.

29.s: StrandHogg is associated with which of the following?
o: An Android vulnerability that allows malware to pose as genuine applications
A Windows SMB exploit leaked by the Shadow Brokers
A worm targeting Siemens industrial controllers
A ransomware programme that encrypts master boot records
29.x: StrandHogg is an Android vulnerability that allows malware to impersonate genuine applications and steal user data. It was found by the Norwegian firm Promon in 2019.
29.tq: Use the operating system and impersonation behaviour to identify the vulnerability.
xs: **StrandHogg** (**2019**) is **an Android vulnerability that allows malware to pose as genuine applications** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It was found by the **Norwegian firm Promon**.
SMB exploit leaked by Shadow Brokers = **EternalBlue**; Siemens worm = **Stuxnet**; MBR ransomware = **Petya**.
xa: **M-Kavach** (C-DAC Hyderabad) = mobile security.
**Trojan** = disguised as legitimate software.

29.s: Mirai is correctly matched with which of the following?
o: Botnet — hijacked Internet of Things devices used for massive DDoS attacks
Trojan — disguised software opening a backdoor
Adware — displaying advertisements through pirated software
29.x: Mirai is a botnet that hijacked IoT devices and used them to launch large-scale DDoS attacks.
29.tq: Match the named malware with its distinctive device class and attack method.
xs: **Mirai** is a **botnet** of hijacked **IoT devices** used for **massive DDoS attacks** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Botnets are networks of **"zombie"** devices controlled remotely.
xa: **DDoS** floods a server from many machines so genuine users are denied service.
Botnets are also used for **spam** and **crypto-mining**.

29.s:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
A. Appearance of Creeper on ARPANET
B. Appearance of Brain virus
C. Appearance of Stuxnet
D. Appearance of WannaCry
Which one of the following is the correct sequence?
29.x: Creeper appeared in 1971, Brain in 1986, Stuxnet in 2010 and WannaCry in 2017. Therefore, the sequence is A, B, C, D.
29.tq: Place the earliest and latest events first, then order the middle events by year.
xs: Order **A, B, C, D** — so option **(1)** is correct.
xa: **Elk Cloner** (**1982**) falls between Creeper and Brain.
**Petya** (**2016**) came just before WannaCry.

29.s: 'Petya' and 'WannaCry', which caused worldwide disruption in 2016-17, are related to:
29.x: Petya and WannaCry are ransomware (APPSC-G2 2025): Petya encrypts the master boot record and WannaCry spread as a worm through EternalBlue, demanding ransom. Spyware (e.g. Pegasus) secretly monitors users, adware shows unwanted ads, and a rootkit hides other malware with admin-level access.
29.tq: Petya + WannaCry = ransomware.
xs: **Petya** and **WannaCry** are **ransomware** — so option **(2)** is correct (APPSC-G2 **2025** PYQ).
Petya encrypts the **master boot record**; WannaCry spread as a worm via **EternalBlue**.
**Spyware** (e.g. Pegasus) monitors users; **adware** shows ads; a **rootkit** hides other malware.
xa: ⚠ Trap: the scanned key is **garbled** — the correct answer is **ransomware**.
Indian ransomware case: **AIIMS Delhi (2022)**.

29.s: Which cyber threat exploits a previously unknown and unpatched software flaw, thereby giving developers no prior opportunity to prepare a patch?
29.x: A zero-day exploit targets an unknown, unpatched vulnerability; developers have had effectively zero days to fix it.
29.tq: Use the exact technical definition rather than matching a general attack category.
xs: An exploit of an **unknown, unpatched flaw** is a **zero-day exploit** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Developers have had "**zero days**" to fix it; **Pegasus** is an example.
**Supply-chain attack** compromises a trusted vendor; **SQL injection** uses website input fields.
xa: **Man-in-the-middle** = secretly intercepts/alters communication between two parties.
Cyber espionage uses **spear-phishing**, advanced malware and **zero-days**.

29.s: The SolarWinds incident of 2020 is commonly cited as an example of which of the following?
29.x: In a supply-chain attack, a trusted vendor or supplier is compromised to reach the ultimate target; SolarWinds is a cited example from 2020.
29.tq: Identify the attack from its named real-world example.
xs: **SolarWinds (2020)** is a **supply-chain attack** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It means compromising a **trusted vendor** to reach the target.
xa: MeitY's **2nd Digital Threat Report 2025-26**: attacks shifting to social engineering, credential theft, **supply-chain** and cloud exploitation.
**Zero-day** exploits target unpatched flaws, e.g. **Pegasus**.

29.s: Which one of the following best describes social engineering in cyber security?
o: Flooding a server with requests from a botnet
Encrypting traffic through a public network
Manipulating people through trust, urgency or curiosity to obtain an intended action
Injecting malicious database commands through a website input field
29.x: Social engineering targets human behaviour rather than merely exploiting a technical system. Trust, urgency and curiosity are commonly manipulated, and such methods can also be AI-enabled.
29.tq: Distinguish a human-targeting method from system-based attacks.
xs: Social engineering is **manipulating people through trust, urgency or curiosity** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It targets **people rather than systems** and is now **AI-enabled**.
Botnet flooding = **DDoS**; encrypted tunnel = **VPN**; database code via input fields = **SQL injection**.
xa: **Phishing** and **digital arrest** scams rely on social engineering.
Current: **AI-enabled phishing** on Instagram accounts.

29.s:
With reference to denial-of-service attacks, consider the following statements:
1. A DoS attack seeks to deny genuine users access to a service.
2. A DDoS attack generally uses multiple machines, often organised as a botnet.
3. Mirai is an example of a botnet associated with DDoS attacks.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
29.x: All three statements are correct. DoS/DDoS attacks overwhelm a system, while DDoS traffic originates from multiple machines such as a Mirai-linked botnet.
29.tq: Combine the general definition with the distinguishing feature and example.
xs: All three statements are correct: **DoS** denies genuine users service; **DDoS** uses many machines via a **botnet**; **Mirai** is such a botnet — so option **(4) 1, 2 and 3** is correct.
DoS/DDoS works by **flooding a server/system** until genuine users are shut out.
xa: Mirai hijacked **IoT devices**.
Worms **eat bandwidth** and are the fastest spreading.

29.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Threat)
a. Spam
b. E-mail bombing
c. Man-in-the-middle
d. SQL injection
List-II (Description)
i. Malicious database code entered through a website's input fields
ii. Unsolicited bulk messages
iii. Flooding an inbox with huge volumes of mail to crash it
iv. Secretly intercepting or altering communication between two parties
Select the correct answer:
29.x: Spam = unsolicited bulk messages (ii); e-mail bombing = flooding an inbox to crash it (iii); man-in-the-middle = secret interception/alteration (iv); SQL injection = malicious database code via input fields (i). Option B swaps spam and e-mail bombing; C swaps MITM and SQL injection; D swaps spam and MITM.
29.tq: Bulk = spam; crash the inbox = bombing.
xs: **a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Spam** = unsolicited bulk messages; **e-mail bombing** = flooding an inbox to crash it.
**Man-in-the-middle** = secret interception/alteration; **SQL injection** = malicious database code via input fields.
xa: **Spoofing** = faking a sender identity (email ID, caller ID, IP address).
**Vishing** = phishing by voice calls.

29.s:
Match the following cyber threats with their descriptions:
a. Phishing
b. Vishing
c. Spoofing
d. SQL injection
i. Phishing carried out through voice calls
ii. Faking a sender identity such as an e-mail ID, caller ID or IP address
iii. Deceptive messages posing as a legitimate source to extract passwords or financial details
iv. Malicious database code entered through a website's input fields
29.x: Phishing = deceptive messages posing as a legitimate source (iii); vishing = phishing by voice calls (i); spoofing = faking a sender identity (ii); SQL injection = malicious database code through input fields (iv). Option B swaps phishing and vishing; C swaps vishing and spoofing; D swaps phishing and spoofing.
29.tq: V-ishing = voice; spoofing = fake identity.
xs: **a-iii, b-i, c-ii, d-iv** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Phishing** = deceptive messages posing as a legitimate source; **vishing** = by voice calls.
**Spoofing** = faked sender identity; **SQL injection** = malicious database code via input fields.
xa: ⚠ **Phishing** = deceptive emails/messages; **Vishing** = voice calls; **Spoofing** = faked sender identity.
**SIM swap** frauds combine **voice phishing** with OTP diversion.

29.s: Which of the following most accurately describes ‘digital arrest’ in the context of cyber crime?
o: A cyber criminal’s use of fake police or agency officials on a video call to frighten a victim and extort money
A court-ordered arrest carried out entirely through an online warrant
Police surveillance of cyber criminals through digital devices
Temporary suspension of a person’s digital identity by an internet service provider
29.x: Digital arrest is a criminal intimidation technique in which impostors claim that the victim is under arrest and demand money, often while keeping the victim on a video call.
29.tq: Reject the official-sounding but incorrect meaning and identify the criminal modus operandi.
xs: "Digital arrest" is **a cyber criminal's use of fake police or agency officials on a video call to frighten a victim and extort money** — so option **(1)** is correct (APPSC-G2 **2025** key).
⚠ Some notes describe it as **police tracking of criminals** digitally — that contradicts the exam key.
xa: SC ordered **SOPs, zero FIRs** and restoring victims' money.

29.s:
The Supreme Court directions concerning digital-arrest cases included which of the following?
1. Framing standard operating procedures by the Centre, States, RBI and telecom authorities.
2. Use of zero FIRs.
3. Restoration of victims’ money.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
29.x: The directions covered SOPs by the specified authorities, the use of zero FIRs and restoration of money to victims.
29.tq: Treat each stated component of an institutional direction as a separate proposition.
xs: The SC told the **Centre, States, RBI and telecom authorities** to frame **SOPs**, use **zero FIRs** and **restore victims' money** — so option **(4) 1, 2 and 3** is correct.
These target **digital arrest** scams.
xa: NCRP digital-arrest complaints fell from **1,23,672 (2024)** to **58,249 (2025)**.
Current relevance mentions **time-bound refunds**.

29.s: Which one of the following correctly describes cyber slavery?
o: Trafficking people and forcing them to conduct cyber fraud, often in scam centres
Using a VPN to conceal a victim’s browsing history
Stealing a person’s identity to obtain a duplicate SIM
Selling stolen data only through encrypted e-mail
29.x: Cyber slavery involves trafficking victims and coercing them to operate cyber-fraud schemes, frequently from scam centres.
29.tq: Identify the crime from its coercion-and-trafficking element.
xs: Cyber slavery is **trafficking people and forcing them to conduct cyber fraud, often in scam centres** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Duplicate SIM is **SIM swap** fraud, not cyber slavery.
xa: **Telangana** police registered one of India's first such cases (per **INTERPOL**; APPSC-G2 **2023** PYQ).
Scam centres linked to **Myanmar and Laos** (MEA **2025**).

29.s:
Consider the following statements regarding cyber slavery and scam centres:
1. Telangana Police registered one of India’s first cases involving human trafficking to force victims to commit cyber fraud.
2. Scam centres connected with this phenomenon have been linked to Myanmar and Laos.
3. FIU-India flagged Rs 800 crore in cross-border laundering linked to the issue.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
29.x: All three statements are correct: the Telangana case involved trafficking for cyber fraud, scam centres were linked to Myanmar and Laos, and FIU-India flagged Rs 800 crore in cross-border laundering.
29.tq: Check the institution, locations and quantified financial detail separately.
xs: All three are correct: **Telangana** police case, scam centres in **Myanmar and Laos**, and **FIU-India** flagged **Rs 800 crore** laundering — so option **(4) 1, 2 and 3** is correct.
The Telangana case is cited per **INTERPOL** (APPSC-G2 **2023** PYQ).
xa: **Crime-as-a-service**: syndicates rent out ransomware and fraud infrastructure.
SIM-swap racket: Cyberabad police arrested **6** from West Bengal (Rs **77.75 lakh**).

29.s: Which of the following is a characteristic of the dark web?
o: It is a secure government-only network used exclusively for defence communication.
It is a hidden part of the internet, reachable through tools such as Tor, and may host illicit marketplaces and data dumps.
It is the publicly indexed portion of the internet accessible through ordinary search engines.
It is a type of antivirus database maintained by CERT-In.
29.x: The dark web is a hidden part of the internet commonly accessed through tools such as Tor. It may contain illicit marketplaces, hacking tools and data dumps.
29.tq: Separate a hidden network from the ordinary publicly indexed web.
xs: The dark web is **a hidden part of the internet, reachable through tools such as Tor**, hosting **illicit marketplaces and data dumps** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It also hosts **hacking tools**; it is not the indexed web.
xa: Stolen data — **personal, medical, IP** — is sold on the dark web.
CERT-In is a **CVE Numbering Authority**, not a dark-web database.

29.s: Identity theft and sextortion are correctly distinguished by which of the following statements?
o: Identity theft uses stolen personal data for impersonation, whereas sextortion involves blackmail using intimate images or material.
Identity theft means flooding an inbox, whereas sextortion means forging a caller ID.
Identity theft is committed only on the dark web, whereas sextortion is committed only through e-mail.
Identity theft always involves ransomware, whereas sextortion always involves DDoS traffic.
29.x: Identity theft involves using stolen personal information to impersonate a person. Sextortion involves blackmail or extortion using intimate images or similar material.
29.tq: Discriminate between two crimes by their distinct modus operandi.
xs: **Identity theft uses stolen personal data for impersonation**, while **sextortion** is **blackmail using intimate images** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Inbox flooding is **e-mail bombing** and a forged caller ID is **spoofing**.
xa: IT Act Sec. **66C** = identity theft; **66E/67A** also apply.
**Loan-app fraud** harvests contacts/photos and extorts borrowers.

29.s: Which of the following statutory provisions is associated with identity theft under the Information Technology Act?
29.x: Section 66C of the Information Technology Act is associated with identity theft. Sections 66E and 67A are relevant to offences involving privacy violations and sexually explicit material respectively.
29.tq: Use the offence-to-section association while avoiding neighbouring provisions.
xs: IT Act **Section 66C** deals with **identity theft** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**66E/67A** apply to **sextortion** cases with intimate images.
xa: Identity theft = stolen personal data used to **impersonate**.
**SIM swap** frauds use a duplicate SIM to **intercept OTPs**.

29.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the rule associated with QR-code fraud?
o: Scanning any QR code automatically verifies the identity of the recipient
A QR code is scanned only to make a payment, not to receive money
A QR code must be scanned to receive money into a bank account
QR codes can be used only for international transfers
29.x: A QR code is used to initiate a payment. It is not required for receiving money, and fraudsters may misuse this misconception.
29.tq: Test the reversed action in a common payment-fraud misconception.
xs: **A QR code is scanned only to make a payment, not to receive money** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Fraudsters trick victims with QR codes to "receive" money amid **rising UPI fraud attempts**.
xa: **SIM swap / OTP diversion** = duplicate SIM to intercept OTPs.
**Loan-app fraud**: illegal instant-loan apps extort borrowers.

29.s: In a SIM-swap and OTP-diversion racket, fraudsters primarily seek to obtain control over which facility?
o: The victim's mobile number and authentication messages
29.x: SIM manipulation allows fraudsters to control the victim's mobile connection and divert OTPs, often after posing as bank officials through voice phishing.
29.tq: Infer the fraud objective from the mechanism used to divert OTPs.
xs: SIM-swap fraudsters seek control of **the victim's mobile number and authentication messages** — so option **(4)** is correct.
They obtain a **duplicate SIM** to **intercept OTPs**, often by posing as **bank officials** (voice phishing).
xa: Cyberabad police arrested **6** from West Bengal for a Rs **77.75 lakh** SIM-swap racket.
**2FA/MFA** uses two independent proofs such as password + **OTP**.

29.s: Illegal instant-loan applications commonly commit fraud by:
o: Mining cryptocurrency without accessing the device
Harvesting contacts and photographs and then extorting borrowers
Using only hardware encryption to protect borrowers
Providing interest-free loans through public banks
29.x: Illegal loan apps may harvest contacts and photographs and use the collected information to extort borrowers.
29.tq: Identify the distinctive harm associated with a named fraud model.
xs: Illegal instant-loan apps work by **harvesting contacts and photographs and then extorting borrowers** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Secret crypto-mining on a device is **crypto-jacking**, a different fraud.
xa: **Crime-as-a-service**: syndicates rent out ransomware and fraud infrastructure.
**UPI/QR fraud**: a QR code is scanned only to **pay**, never to receive.
**SIM swap / OTP diversion**: duplicate SIM to intercept **OTPs**.

29.s: What is meant by crypto-jacking?
o: Encrypting a wallet with a public key
Stealing a cryptocurrency exchange's physical building
Scanning a QR code to receive cryptocurrency
Using a victim's device secretly to mine cryptocurrency
29.x: Crypto-jacking is the unauthorised and concealed use of a victim's computing device to mine cryptocurrency; botnets may also be used for this purpose.
29.tq: Use the action-object relationship to distinguish a malware-related term.
xs: Crypto-jacking is **using a victim's device secretly to mine cryptocurrency** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Botnets** are also used to mine crypto.
Scanning a QR code is never needed to **receive** money — that is the **QR fraud** trick.
xa: Botnet = "**zombie**" devices controlled remotely; also used for **DDoS** and **spam**.
**Ransomware** demands ransom, often in **crypto**.

29.s:
Consider the following statements regarding recent digital-payment threats:
1. Attacks are shifting towards social engineering and credential theft.
2. Supply-chain and cloud exploitation are among the reported areas of concern.
3. The four-layer 'Anatomy of Cyber Failure' and an 18-month roadmap were included in the Digital Threat Report framework.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
29.x: All three statements reflect the framework and threat directions described in the MeitY Digital Threat Report 2025–26 for BFSI and digital payments.
29.tq: Combine multiple components of a named report without confusing its threat areas and roadmap.
xs: All three are correct: attacks shifting to **social engineering, credential theft**, **supply-chain and cloud exploitation**, with a four-layer **"Anatomy of Cyber Failure"** and an **18-month roadmap** — so option **(4) 1, 2 and 3** is correct.
Source: **MeitY 2nd Digital Threat Report 2025-26** on **BFSI and digital payments**.
xa: **6** of **7** predictions of the 2024-25 edition came true.
**SolarWinds (2020)** = classic supply-chain attack.
Social engineering manipulates **trust, urgency, curiosity**; now **AI-enabled**.

29.s: Which of the following best describes 'crime-as-a-service'?
o: Syndicates renting out ransomware and fraud infrastructure
Banks refunding small fraud losses without court approval
A process for verifying digital signatures
Government agencies providing free malware-cleaning tools
29.x: Crime-as-a-service refers to criminal syndicates renting ransomware and fraud infrastructure to other offenders.
29.tq: Decode a service-model term through the actor and activity involved.
xs: Crime-as-a-service means **syndicates renting out ransomware and fraud infrastructure** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Free malware-cleaning or signature checks are defences, not crimes.
xa: **AI-powered malware** adapts to evade anti-virus; plus **deepfakes**.
**Ransomware** encrypts files/systems and demands a ransom.

29.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Cyber incident)
 a. e-Nagarpalika portal attack
 b. AIIMS Delhi attack
 c. Kudankulam NPP incident
 d. Cosmos Bank incident

List-II (Description)
 i. ATM/SWIFT fraud of about Rs 94 crore
 ii. Malware on an administrative network
 iii. Ransomware disrupting hospital services
 iv. Attack on an online civic tax payment portal

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
29.x: The e-Nagarpalika portal was attacked as an online civic tax payment system; AIIMS Delhi suffered ransomware; Kudankulam's administrative network was affected by malware; Cosmos Bank faced ATM/SWIFT fraud of about Rs 94 crore.
29.tq: Start from the sure incident-description pair and eliminate incompatible codes.
xs: **a-iv, b-iii, c-ii, d-i** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**e-Nagarpalika** (**Dec 2023**) = civic tax portal, **Madhya Pradesh**; **AIIMS Delhi** (**2022**) = **ransomware**.
**Kudankulam NPP** (**2019**) = malware on the admin network, **Tamil Nadu**; **Cosmos Bank** (**2018**) = ATM/SWIFT fraud of about **Rs 94 crore**, Pune.
xa: Other cases: **2016** breach of **3.2 million debit cards**; **2017 Zomato** data theft.
e-Nagarpalika was asked in **APPSC-G1 2024**.

29.s: The Critical Government Infrastructure of Andhra Pradesh is monitored through APCSOC by which organisation?
29.x: APTS (Andhra Pradesh Technology Services) monitors the State's Critical Government Infrastructure through APCSOC and has audited 270 GoAP applications. CERT-In, I4C and MeitY are national bodies.
29.tq: Identify the responsible state-level agency from the institutional relationship.
xs: **APTS** monitors AP's Critical Government Infrastructure through **APCSOC** — so option **(3)** is correct.
APTS has audited **270 GoAP applications**.
**CERT-In** and **MeitY** are national bodies; **I4C** is under MHA.
xa: **AP Cyber Security Policy 2017**.
AP Police-**IIT Tirupati** MoU for a **Cyber Crime Investigation and Training Academy**.

29.s: CERT-In recorded how many cyber-security incidents in 2025, and how many in 2024?
29.x: CERT-In recorded 29.44 lakh incidents in 2025 compared with 20.41 lakh in 2024; 2025 was the highest level in five years.
29.tq: Check both the year-wise figures and the lakh unit.
xs: CERT-In recorded **29.44 lakh** incidents in **2025** and **20.41 lakh** in **2024** — so option **(2)** is correct.
2025 was the **highest in five years**; option (3) reverses the years.
xa: Most incidents were reported from **Delhi**.
CERT-In is a **CVE Numbering Authority** for products made in India.

29.s: In 2025, the highest number of cyber-security incidents recorded by CERT-In was reported from:
29.x: Delhi was reported as the source of the highest number of cyber-security incidents in 2025.
29.tq: Identify the leading location rather than the locations of specific historical attacks.
xs: Most CERT-In incidents in 2025 were reported from **Delhi** — so option **(3)** is correct.
⚠ **Madhya Pradesh** = e-Nagarpalika; **Tamil Nadu** = Kudankulam; **Maharashtra** = Cosmos Bank.
xa: **AIIMS Delhi** (**2022**) ransomware disrupted hospital services.

29.s: The e-Nagarpalika portal, an online civic tax payment portal hit by a cyber attack in December 2023, belongs to which State?
29.x: The e-Nagarpalika portal attack (Dec 2023) hit Madhya Pradesh's online civic tax payment portal (APPSC-G1 2024). Maharashtra is linked to the Cosmos Bank fraud (2018), Tamil Nadu to the Kudankulam NPP malware (2019), and Delhi to the AIIMS ransomware attack (2022).
29.tq: e-Nagarpalika = MP.
xs: The **e-Nagarpalika** portal belongs to **Madhya Pradesh** — so option **(3)** is correct (APPSC-G1 **2024** PYQ).
**Maharashtra** = Cosmos Bank (**2018**); **Tamil Nadu** = Kudankulam (**2019**); **Delhi** = AIIMS (**2022**).
xa: e-Nagarpalika was hit in **Dec 2023**.
Stolen data (personal, medical, IP) is sold on the **dark web**.

29.s: DRDO-led Exercise Cyber Suraksha is associated with which of the following?
o: Developing a national antivirus for private companies
Training bank customers in digital payments over 12 months
Testing satellite navigation systems for civilian transport
Training the armed forces in cyber preparedness over 12 days
29.x: Exercise Cyber Suraksha is a DRDO-led 12-day exercise intended to train the armed forces in cyber security and preparedness.
29.tq: Use the organiser, duration and target group together to identify the exercise.
xs: Exercise Cyber Suraksha is **DRDO-led**, runs **12 days** and **trains the armed forces** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It is a **12-day** exercise, not a 12-month bank-customer programme.
xa: MeitY **2nd Digital Threat Report 2025-26** gives an **18-month roadmap**.
**Maya OS** with **Chakravyuh** endpoint protection: **Ministry of Defence** (**2023**).

29.s:
Consider the following statements about cyber terrorism:
1. It primarily aims at disrupting critical infrastructure.
2. Its attribution is difficult because attackers may use VPNs, proxies and botnets.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
29.x: Statement 1 is correct: cyber terrorism seeks to disrupt critical infrastructure. Statement 2 is correct: VPNs, proxies and botnets hide the true source, making attribution hard. So both.
29.tq: Target = critical infrastructure; hard to trace.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: cyber terrorism aims at **disrupting critical infrastructure**.
Statement 2 is correct: **attribution is hard** because of **VPNs, proxies, botnets** — so option **(3) Both 1 and 2** is correct.
xa: **Cyber espionage** is often **state-sponsored** and uses zero-days.
State-linked operations cost projected **$10.5 trillion** in 2025.

29.s:
Consider the following statements regarding state-linked cyber operations:
1. China, Russia, Iran and North Korea together sponsor 77% of state-linked operations.
2. China alone accounts for 33% of such operations.
3. The United States, Ukraine, Israel and India are among the most targeted countries.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
29.x: All three statements are correct according to the cited assessment of state-linked operations and targeting patterns.
29.tq: Check both the percentages and the membership of the named country groups.
xs: All three are correct: **China, Russia, Iran, North Korea** sponsor **77%**; **China** alone **33%**; most targeted are **US, Ukraine, Israel, India** — so option **(4) 1, 2 and 3** is correct.
⚠ The **77%** is the four sponsors together; **33%** is China alone.
xa: Cost projected **$10.5 trillion** in **2025**.
**WannaCry** is attributed to **North Korea's Lazarus group**.
**Stuxnet** sabotaged **Iran's** nuclear programme.

29.s: The projected global cost of cybercrime in 2025 was stated as approximately:
29.x: The projected cost was approximately $10.5 trillion in 2025.
29.tq: Distinguish the exact scale and unit of a large projected figure.
xs: The projected cost was **$10.5 trillion** in **2025** — so option **(3)** is correct.
⚠ **Rs 94 crore** = Cosmos Bank fraud; **Rs 77.75 lakh** = Cyberabad SIM-swap racket — distractor numbers.
xa: State-linked: **77%** by China, Russia, Iran, North Korea; China **33%**.
India is among the **most targeted** countries.

29.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Cyber espionage is often state-sponsored.
2. Spear-phishing and zero-day exploits may be used in cyber espionage.
3. Cyber espionage necessarily involves flooding a server with traffic.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
29.x: Cyber espionage is often state-sponsored and may employ spear-phishing and zero-days. Server flooding describes a denial-of-service attack, not a necessary feature of espionage.
29.tq: Find the one overbroad statement that confuses espionage with denial of service.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: espionage is **often state-sponsored** and uses **spear-phishing, advanced malware, zero-days**.
Statement 3 is wrong: **flooding a server** is **DoS/DDoS**, not espionage — so option **(1) 1 and 2 only** is correct.
xa: **Pegasus** (NSO Group) is a **zero-click** spyware exploiting zero-days.
Cyber terrorism disrupts **critical infrastructure**.

29.s: Which of the following correctly describes the cyber security initiative involving Andhra Pradesh Police and IIT Tirupati?
o: A Cyber Crime Investigation and Training Academy established through a Memorandum of Understanding, focusing on digital forensics and blockchain tracing
A Cyber Crime Investigation Academy established by the ITU for monitoring global cyber rankings
A National Malware Research Centre established under the Andhra Pradesh Cyber Security Policy 2017
A Blockchain Training Academy established by the Supreme Court for processing zero FIRs
29.x: A is correct: AP Police signed an MoU with IIT Tirupati for a Cyber Crime Investigation and Training Academy focused on digital forensics and blockchain tracing. It was not set up by the ITU or the Supreme Court, and it is not a malware research centre under the AP Cyber Security Policy 2017.
29.tq: Identify the correct institution-purpose combination and reject swapped authorities.
xs: AP Police and **IIT Tirupati** signed an MoU for **a Cyber Crime Investigation and Training Academy**, focusing on **digital forensics and blockchain tracing** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It was not set up by the ITU or the Supreme Court, nor under the **2017** policy.
xa: AP Cyber Security Policy **2017**.
**APTS** monitors infrastructure via **APCSOC**; audited **270 GoAP applications**.

29.s: The Andhra Pradesh Cyber Security Policy referred to in the context of cybercrime prevention was introduced in:
29.x: The Andhra Pradesh Cyber Security Policy was introduced in 2017.
29.tq: Check the year against the nearby current initiatives and avoid confusing policy and MoU dates.
xs: The **AP Cyber Security Policy** came in **2017** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It is part of the AP angle along with the **IIT Tirupati** academy MoU.
xa: **APTS** monitors Critical Government Infrastructure through **APCSOC**.
**Telangana** police registered one of India's first cyber-trafficking cases.

29.s:
Consider the following statements about the significance of cyber security:
1. Cyber security is important for national security.
2. Cyber threats can affect the economy and public services.
3. Cyber incidents can weaken trust in e-governance.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
29.x: All three statements are correct. Cyber threats have implications for national security, the economy, public services and public trust in e-governance.
29.tq: Recognise the common significance theme and test whether each listed consequence belongs to it.
xs: Cyber threats hit **national security, economy, public services and trust in e-governance** — so option **(3) 1, 2 and 3** is correct.
Each statement is listed in the topic's **significance**.
xa: **CIA triad**: confidentiality, integrity, availability.
CERT-In: **29.44 lakh** incidents in **2025**.

30.s: Which of the following is the primary law governing cyber crime and e-commerce in India?
30.x: The Information Technology Act, 2000 is regarded as the primary law on cyber crime and e-commerce in India.
30.tq: Use the direct identification method for the principal statute.
xs: The **Information Technology Act, 2000** is the primary law on **cyber crime and e-commerce** in India — so option **(4)** is correct.
It gives legal recognition to **electronic records and e-commerce** transactions and prevents computer-based crimes.
xa: Amended in **2008**.
It is a **special Act** that overrides **IPC** provisions where the crime is squarely covered.
Statutory bodies under it: **Controller of Certifying Authorities** and **CERT-In**.

30.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Information Technology Act, 2000:
1. It provides legal recognition to electronic records.
2. It provides legal recognition to electronic and e-commerce transactions.
3. It establishes a framework for preventing computer-based crimes.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
30.x: The Act recognises electronic records and transactions and provides a framework for preventing computer-based crimes.
30.tq: Check whether all three statements describe the core purposes of the Act.
xs: The IT Act recognises **electronic records**, **e-commerce transactions** and prevents **computer-based crimes** — so option **(4) 1, 2 and 3** is correct.
APPSC **2018** PYQ: it gives legal recognition to transactions by **electronic data interchange** ("electronic commerce").
xa: It also covers **security of sensitive personal data** and **due diligence by intermediaries**.
Defines cyber contraventions and crimes with an **adjudication framework**.

30.s: Which statutory authority regulates electronic signatures under the Information Technology Act, 2000?
o: National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre
30.x: The Controller of Certifying Authorities, or CCA, is the statutory regulator of electronic signatures.
30.tq: Apply the “who regulates this function?” method.
xs: The **Controller of Certifying Authorities** is the statutory regulator of **electronic signatures** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**CERT-In** is the incident response body (**Sec. 70B**); **NCIIPC** protects critical infrastructure (**Sec. 70A**).
The **Examiner of Electronic Evidence** (**Sec. 79A**) is a forensic lab notified by the Centre.
xa: **Certifying Authorities** licensed by the CCA issue **Digital Signature Certificates**.
⚠ **CERT-In** = MeitY (Sec. 70B); **NCIIPC** = NTRO (Sec. 70A).

30.s: Where an offence is squarely covered by the Information Technology Act, 2000, the Act may override the corresponding provisions of which law?
30.x: The Information Technology Act operates as a special law and may override IPC provisions where the offence is squarely covered by it.
30.tq: Identify the general law displaced by a special law.
xs: As a **special Act**, the IT Act overrides **Indian Penal Code** provisions where the crime is squarely covered — so option **(4)** is correct.
It is India's **primary law** on cyber crime and e-commerce.
xa: Framework: **adjudication** of cyber contraventions, security of sensitive personal data, **intermediary due diligence**.
Amended in **2008**.

30.s:
Which of the following concepts were introduced by the Information Technology Act, 2000?
1. Electronic record
2. Digital signature
3. Certifying Authority
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
30.x: The IT Act, 2000 introduced all three concepts: electronic record (legally recognised under Sec. 4), digital signature (Sec. 3 and 5) and Certifying Authority (licensed by the Controller of Certifying Authorities to issue Digital Signature Certificates). Options leaving out any one of them are wrong (MPPSC 2021 PYQ: 'all of the above').
30.tq: IT Act 2000 concepts = e-record + digital signature + CA (all three).
xs: The IT Act introduced **electronic record, digital signature and certifying authority** — so option **(4) 1, 2 and 3** is correct ("all of the above", MPPSC **2021** PYQ).
**Sec. 4** = legal recognition of electronic records; **Sec. 5** = electronic signatures.
xa: Certifying Authorities are licensed by the **Controller of Certifying Authorities**.
The **2008** amendment made the signature technology-neutral as "**electronic signature**".

30.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Section of the Information Technology Act, 2000)
A. Section 3
B. Section 4
C. Section 5
D. Section 6

List-II (Subject)
1. Legal recognition of electronic records
2. Use of electronic records and signatures in Government and its agencies
3. Authentication of electronic records by digital signature
4. Legal recognition of electronic signatures

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
30.x: Section 3 concerns authentication by digital signature; Section 4 legal recognition of electronic records; Section 5 legal recognition of electronic signatures; and Section 6 their use in government agencies.
30.tq: Start with the sure section-number pairs and eliminate codes containing swapped legal subjects.
xs: **A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Sec. 3** = authentication by digital signature; **Sec. 4** = recognition of electronic records.
**Sec. 5** = recognition of electronic signatures; **Sec. 6** = use in Government and its agencies.
xa: **Sec. 7** = **retention of electronic records**.
Exam angle: **Section 4 = e-records, Section 5 = e-signatures** (CGPSC **2022** match).

30.s:
Match List-I with List-II regarding provisions of the Information Technology Act, 2000.

List-I (Section)
a. Section 4
b. Section 5
c. Section 43A
d. Section 66F

List-II (Subject)
i. Cyber terrorism
ii. Legal recognition of electronic records
iii. Legal recognition of electronic signatures
iv. Compensation for failure to protect sensitive personal data

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
30.x: Section 4 concerns electronic records, Section 5 electronic signatures, Section 43A protection of sensitive personal data, and Section 66F cyber terrorism.
30.tq: Start from the sure section–subject pairs and eliminate the codes.
xs: **a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Sec. 4** = e-records; **Sec. 5** = e-signatures; **Sec. 43A** = compensation for failure to protect **sensitive personal data**; **Sec. 66F** = **cyber terrorism**.
xa: ⚠ Trap: some notes call 43A "tampering" — the Act says **data-protection compensation**.
43A is **to be omitted by DPDP Act s.44(2)**.
66F carries **up to life imprisonment**.

30.s: Section 43 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 primarily deals with which of the following?
o: Blocking public access to online content
Penalty for unauthorised access and damage
30.x: Section 43 provides for penalties relating to unauthorised access and damage to computer systems or data.
30.tq: Separate neighbouring sections by their operative subject.
xs: **Sec. 43** gives **penalty for unauthorised access and damage** to computer systems — so option **(4)** is correct.
Blocking = **69A**; cyber terrorism = **66F**; safe harbour = **79**.
xa: **Sec. 66** makes the dishonest/fraudulent acts of Sec. 43 an offence (**hacking**).
**43A** = compensation for failure to protect sensitive personal data.

30.s: Under the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, failure to undertake due diligence may result in loss of:
30.x: Intermediaries may lose safe-harbour protection if they fail to comply with due-diligence requirements.
30.tq: Apply the legal consequence to the compliance failure.
xs: Under the **IT Rules 2021**, failing due diligence means loss of **safe harbour** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Safe harbour comes from **Sec. 79**; it is lost if intermediaries fail to act on "**actual knowledge**".
xa: The Rules also require a **grievance officer**.
Takedown now within **three hours** of a court order or government intimation (MeitY, **27 Mar 2026**).

30.s: After a court order or government intimation, the revised time for content takedown under the applicable intermediary rules is:
30.x: Content takedown is required within three hours of a court order or government intimation.
30.tq: Distinguish the shortened takedown period from the six-hour incident-reporting period.
xs: Content must now be taken down within **three hours** of a court order or government intimation — so option **(3)** is correct.
Announced by **MeitY** on **27 Mar 2026**.
xa: ⚠ **6 hours** is the CERT-In **incident-reporting** deadline, not takedown.
Criticism: the **3-hour** rule and **290** MHA notices a day.

30.s:
Consider the following statements about the IT Act, 2000:
1. Section 66 deals with computer-related offences, i.e., dishonest or fraudulent acts under Section 43 (hacking).
2. Section 66F deals with cyber terrorism, punishable up to life imprisonment.
3. Under Section 79A, State Governments notify Examiners of Electronic Evidence.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
30.x: Statement 1 is correct: Sec 66 covers computer-related offences (hacking). Statement 2 is correct: Sec 66F cyber terrorism, up to life imprisonment. Statement 3 is wrong: under Sec 79A the Centre notifies Examiners of Electronic Evidence. So 1 and 2 only.
30.tq: 79A = Centre notifies forensic labs.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **Sec. 66** = computer-related offences under Sec. 43 (**hacking**).
Statement 2 is correct: **Sec. 66F** = **cyber terrorism**, up to **life imprisonment**.
Statement 3 is wrong: under **Sec. 79A** the **Centre** notifies Examiners of Electronic Evidence — so option **(1) 1 and 2 only** is correct.
xa: Examiners of Electronic Evidence are **forensic labs**.
**66C** = identity theft; **66D** = cheating by personation.

30.s:
Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
1. Section 66C — Identity theft
2. Section 66D — Cheating by personation using a computer
3. Section 66E — Violation of privacy
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
30.x: Sections 66C, 66D and 66E respectively deal with identity theft, cheating by personation using a computer, and violation of privacy.
30.tq: Keep the adjacent section numbers paired with their exact offences.
xs: **66C** = identity theft and **66D** = cheating by personation using a computer.
**66E** = violation of privacy — all three match, so option **(4) 1, 2 and 3** is correct.
xa: 66C covers theft of a **password** or **digital signature**.
66E covers capturing/publishing **private images**.
⚠ Trap: some notes say **66C = hacking** — hacking is **Sec. 66**.

30.s: Sections 67 and 67A of the Information Technology Act relate respectively to:
o: Obscene material and sexually explicit material in electronic form
30.x: Section 67 concerns obscene material in electronic form, while Section 67A concerns sexually explicit material in electronic form.
30.tq: Discriminate between two neighbouring content-related provisions.
xs: **Sec. 67** = **obscene material** and **67A** = **sexually explicit material in electronic form** — so option **(4)** is correct.
Identity theft is **66C**; cyber terrorism **66F**; interception/blocking **69/69A**.
xa: The **2008 amendment** added the offence on sexually explicit material and **video voyeurism**.
**66E** = violation of privacy.

30.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: Section 69 — Blocking of public access to content
30.x: Section 69 deals with interception and decryption, whereas Section 69A deals with blocking public access to content.
30.tq: Test the reversed-section trap between interception and blocking powers.
xs: **Section 69** = **interception and decryption** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**69A** = **blocking** of public access to content, not identity theft or interception.
xa: **69A** blocking was **upheld** in **Shreya Singhal (2015)**.
Debate: surveillance and takedown powers vs **free speech** (66A, 69A).

30.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
30.x: Section 70A relates to NCIIPC, while Section 70B provides the statutory basis for CERT-In.
30.tq: Use the adjacent-section distinction between NCIIPC and CERT-In.
xs: **Section 70A — NCIIPC; Section 70B — CERT-In** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Sec. 70** deals with **protected systems**.
xa: NCIIPC functions under **NTRO**; CERT-In under **MeitY**.
Sec. 70B was **inserted in 2008**.
⚠ **I4C** = MHA and **not statutory**.

30.s: The safe-harbour protection for intermediaries is primarily associated with Section 79 of the Information Technology Act. It may be lost when an intermediary fails to act on:
o: Actual knowledge in the legally recognised form
30.x: Section 79 gives intermediaries safe harbour, lost if they fail to act on 'actual knowledge'. After Shreya Singhal (2015), actual knowledge means a court order or a government notice, not a private complaint, a service delay or an advertisement.
30.tq: Apply the condition attached to statutory safe harbour.
xs: Safe harbour is lost if the intermediary fails to act on **actual knowledge in the legally recognised form** — so option **(1)** is correct.
After **Shreya Singhal (2015)**, actual knowledge = **court order or government notice**.
A private complaint, service delay or advertisement does not trigger loss of safe harbour.
xa: **79A** = Examiner of Electronic Evidence.
⚠ **66A** struck down; **69A** upheld; **79** read down.

30.s: The Information Technology (Amendment) Act, 2008 added provisions relating to all of the following EXCEPT:
o: Creation of the National Cyber Coordination Centre
30.x: The 2008 amendment added offences relating to sexually explicit material, video voyeurism, data leakage by intermediaries and e-commerce fraud; it did not create the NCCC.
30.tq: Find the item outside the amendment’s listed offence categories.
xs: The 2008 amendment did not **create the National Cyber Coordination Centre** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It added offences on **sexually explicit material, video voyeurism, data leakage by intermediaries** and **e-commerce fraud**.
xa: It also inserted **Sec. 70B** for CERT-In.
It made the signature technology-neutral as "**electronic signature**".
**NCCC** gives **situational awareness** of threats.

30.s: In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, the Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the Information Technology Act primarily for violating:
30.x: The Supreme Court struck down Section 66A for violating freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a), and held that it was not saved by Article 19(2).
30.tq: Match the judicial decision with the constitutional provision directly involved.
xs: **Section 66A** was struck down for violating **Article 19(1)(a)** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It was **not saved by Art. 19(2)**.
xa: 66A covered **offensive messages** via a communication service.
The same case **read down Sec. 79** and **upheld Sec. 69A**.

30.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the decision in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India:
1. Section 66A was struck down.
2. Section 79 was read down.
3. Section 69A was upheld.
4. Section 66A was held to be saved by Article 19(2).
Which of the statements given above are correct?
30.x: The Court struck down Section 66A, read down Section 79 and upheld Section 69A. Section 66A was not saved by Article 19(2), making statement 4 false.
30.tq: Separate the provisions struck down, read down and upheld; reject the reversed constitutional conclusion.
xs: Statements 1-3 are correct: **66A struck down**, **79 read down**, **69A upheld**.
Statement 4 is wrong: 66A was **not saved by Art. 19(2)** — so option **(2) 1, 2 and 3 only** is correct.
xa: Case year: **2015**; ground: **Art. 19(1)(a)**.
Sec. 79 "**actual knowledge**" = court order or government notice.

30.s: In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015), the Supreme Court read down Section 79 of the IT Act. As a result, 'actual knowledge' that obliges an intermediary to take down content means:
o: Any complaint received from a private user
A court order or a notice from the appropriate Government
Knowledge gained through the intermediary's own monitoring
An advisory issued by CERT-In alone
30.x: The Court read down Sec. 79 so that 'actual knowledge' means a court order or a government notice. A private user complaint does not by itself trigger loss of safe harbour; intermediaries are not expected to judge content on their own monitoring; a CERT-In advisory is not the stated trigger. The same judgment struck down Sec. 66A and upheld Sec. 69A.
30.tq: Sec 79 actual knowledge = court order or govt notice (Shreya Singhal).
xs: After Shreya Singhal, "actual knowledge" means **a court order or a notice from the appropriate Government** — so option **(2)** is correct.
So a private user's complaint or the intermediary's own monitoring does not count.
xa: The same ruling struck down **Sec. 66A** and upheld **Sec. 69A**.
IT Rules **2021**: due diligence or loss of **safe harbour**.

30.s: The Information Technology Act, 2000 was amended in which year to make the framework technology-neutral by recognising the term “electronic signature”?
30.x: The 2008 amendment introduced a technology-neutral approach by using the broader term “electronic signature.”
30.tq: Distinguish the amendment year from nearby legal milestones.
xs: The **2008** amendment made the law technology-neutral as "**electronic signature**" — so option **(2)** is correct.
It also added offences on **video voyeurism** and **data leakage by intermediaries**.
xa: Secs. **4-5** legally recognise electronic records and signatures.
**CERT-In** got statutory backing under **Sec. 70B** (inserted 2008).

30.s: Which statement correctly explains the roles of the keys in a digital-signature system based on asymmetric cryptography?
o: The private key signs and the public key verifies.
A single shared key performs both signing and verification.
The public key signs and the private key verifies.
Both keys are publicly disclosed before signing.
30.x: In asymmetric cryptography, the private key is used for signing and the corresponding public key is used for verification.
30.tq: Apply the sign-versus-verify role distinction in a practical scenario.
xs: **The private key signs and the public key verifies** — so option **(1)** is correct.
This is **PKI** key-pair logic; a single shared key is **symmetric** cryptography.
xa: Digital signature uses an **asymmetric crypto system and hash function**.
Functions: **authentication, integrity, non-repudiation**.

30.s: A digital signature primarily uses which combination of technologies under the Information Technology Act framework?
o: An asymmetric cryptographic system and a hash function
A firewall and a domain-name server
Symmetric encryption and a barcode reader
A password database and biometric scanning only
30.x: A digital signature uses asymmetric cryptography together with a hash function to support verification of the signed electronic document.
30.tq: Identify the exact technical pair rather than a broader cybersecurity tool.
xs: A digital signature uses **an asymmetric cryptographic system and a hash function** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Firewalls, barcode readers and passwords are not its technology.
xa: **Certifying Authorities** licensed by the **CCA** issue Digital Signature Certificates.
Private key **signs**, public key **verifies**.

30.s: Which of the following is NOT normally an assurance provided by a digital signature?
o: Guaranteed secrecy of the document’s contents
30.x: Digital signatures provide authentication, integrity and non-repudiation, but a signature by itself does not guarantee confidentiality or secrecy of the document.
30.tq: Separate authenticity and integrity assurances from confidentiality.
xs: **Guaranteed secrecy of the document's contents** is not a digital-signature function — so option **(3)** is correct.
Its functions are **authentication, integrity, non-repudiation**.
xa: UPSC **2019** key: a digital signature is an **electronic method of signing** that ensures the **original content is unchanged**.
PKI is used for **digital security infrastructure** (UPSC **2020**).

30.s: Who issues Digital Signature Certificates when authorised under the Public Key Infrastructure framework?
o: Certifying Authorities licensed by the Controller of Certifying Authorities
The Examiner of Electronic Evidence directly
Any internet service provider without licensing
The National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre alone
30.x: Digital Signature Certificates are issued by Certifying Authorities licensed by the Controller of Certifying Authorities.
30.tq: Trace the issuing authority through the licensing hierarchy.
xs: Digital Signature Certificates are issued by **Certifying Authorities licensed by the Controller of Certifying Authorities** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The **Examiner of Electronic Evidence** is a forensic lab; **NCIIPC** protects critical infrastructure.
xa: The CCA is the **statutory regulator** of electronic signatures.
A **digital certificate** identifies the issuing certifying authority.

30.s:
Consider the following statements about a digital signature:
1. It is an electronic method of signing an electronic document.
2. It helps establish that the original content has not been altered.
3. A record identifying the issuing certifying authority is itself the digital signature.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
30.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. A record identifying the issuing Certifying Authority is associated with a digital certificate, not the digital signature itself.
30.tq: Distinguish a digital signature from the certificate that identifies its issuer.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: a digital signature is an **electronic method of signing** that ensures the **original content is unchanged**.
Statement 3 is wrong: a record identifying the issuing CA is a **digital certificate** — so option **(1) 1 and 2 only** is correct.
xa: ⚠ Trap (PYQ): CA record + **ID proof for server access** = **digital certificate**, not the signature.
UPSC **2019** key: only the signing-method statement was correct.

30.s: The term 'Public Key Infrastructure' is used in the context of:
30.x: Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) is the framework of key pairs, Certifying Authorities and digital certificates for digital security: the private key signs and the public key verifies. It has nothing to do with food security, roads or land reforms (UPSC 2020 PYQ).
30.tq: PKI = digital security (key pairs + CAs + certificates).
xs: **Public Key Infrastructure** is used in **digital security infrastructure** — so option **(1)** is correct (UPSC **2020** PYQ).
In PKI, the **private key signs** and the **public key verifies**.
xa: **Certifying Authorities** licensed by the **CCA** issue Digital Signature Certificates.
Digital signature functions: **authentication, integrity, non-repudiation**.

30.s:
Consider the following statements about CERT-In:
1. It functions under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology.
2. It has been operational since January 2008.
3. It is the National Incident Response Centre.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
30.x: Statement 1 is correct: CERT-In is under MeitY. Statement 2 is wrong: it has been operational since January 2004; 2008 is when Sec. 70B gave it statutory backing. Statement 3 is correct: it is the National Incident Response Centre. So 1 and 3 only.
30.tq: 2004 = operational; 2008 = Sec 70B statutory backing.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: CERT-In works under **MeitY**.
Statement 2 is wrong: operational since **January 2004**; **2008** is when **Sec. 70B** was inserted.
Statement 3 is correct: it is the **National Incident Response Centre** — so option **(3) 1 and 3 only** is correct.
xa: CERT-In operates **Cyber Swachhta Kendra**.
It is a **CVE Numbering Authority** for Indian products.

30.s: Which one of the following is NOT a function of CERT-In?
o: Conducting general elections through electronic voting
Dissemination of information relating to cyber incidents
Coordinating emergency response to cyber incidents
30.x: CERT-In collects, analyses and disseminates incident information, issues forecasts and alerts, and coordinates emergency responses; conducting elections is not its function.
30.tq: Find the unrelated function among closely associated cyber-security functions.
xs: **Conducting general elections through electronic voting** is not a CERT-In function — so option **(1)** is correct.
CERT-In collects/analyses/**disseminates incident information**, issues **forecasts and alerts**, and coordinates **emergency response**.
xa: It also issues **guidelines, advisories and vulnerability notes**.
It has empanelled **200 IT security auditing organisations**.

30.s:
Under the CERT-In Directions, 2022, consider the following statements:
1. Cyber incidents must be reported within 6 hours.
2. ICT logs must be kept for 5 years.
3. VPN providers must keep subscriber data for 5 years.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
30.x: Statement 1 is correct: report within 6 hours. Statement 2 is wrong: ICT logs are kept for 180 days. Statement 3 is correct: VPN providers keep subscriber data for 5 years. So 1 and 3 only.
30.tq: 6 hours / 180 days / 5 years.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: report incidents **within 6 hours**.
Statement 2 is wrong: ICT logs are kept for **180 days**.
Statement 3 is correct: VPN providers keep subscriber data for **5 years** — so option **(3) 1 and 3 only** is correct.
xa: ⚠ **6** hours = report; **180** days = logs; **5** years = VPN subscriber data.
Directions dated **28 Apr 2022**, under **Sec 70B**.

30.s:
Which of the following entities are covered by the mandatory incident-reporting requirement under the CERT-In Directions, 2022?
1. Service providers and intermediaries
2. Data centres and body corporates
3. Government bodies
Which of the statements given above are correct?
30.x: The directions cover service providers, intermediaries, data centres, body corporates and government bodies.
30.tq: Check the full composition of the covered entities.
xs: The 2022 Directions cover **service providers, intermediaries, data centres, body corporates and government bodies** — so option **(4) 1, 2 and 3** is correct.
**Virtual asset service providers** are also covered.
xa: Report within **6 hours**; logs for **180 days**.
A **VPN-provider framework** is being drafted.

30.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. CERT-In operates Cyber Swachhta Kendra.
2. CERT-In is a CVE Numbering Authority for Indian products.
3. CERT-In has empanelled 200 IT security auditing organisations.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
30.x: CERT-In operates Cyber Swachhta Kendra, serves as a CVE Numbering Authority for Indian products, and has empanelled 200 IT security auditing organisations.
30.tq: Combine related institutional roles and test the numerical detail in the list.
xs: CERT-In sets up and runs **Cyber Swachhta Kendra**, an automated threat-intelligence exchange platform.
It is a **CVE Numbering Authority** for Indian products and empanelled **200 IT security auditing organisations** — so option **(4) 1, 2 and 3** is correct.
xa: **APTS** = first CERT-In empanelled organisation in AP.
CERT-In ran **115 cybersecurity exercises** with about **1,500 organisations**.

30.s: The State CSIRTs mentioned as operational are located in:
30.x: State CSIRTs are operational in West Bengal and Madhya Pradesh.
30.tq: Use the location pair without confusing it with the location of a national headquarters.
xs: State CSIRTs are operational in **West Bengal and Madhya Pradesh** — so option **(3)** is correct.
AP is not in the list of operational State CSIRTs.
xa: **NCCC** gives **situational awareness** of threats.
AP Police **Cybercrime Coordination Centre** at Krishnalanka PS, **Vijayawada**.

30.s: The National Cyber Coordination Centre (NCCC) primarily provides:
30.x: NCCC is associated with situational awareness of cyber threats.
30.tq: Match the coordination centre with its information-awareness function.
xs: The **NCCC** provides **situational awareness of cyber threats** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Forensic certification is **Sec. 79A** examiners; free malware tools come from **Cyber Swachhta Kendra**.
xa: **CERT-In** = National Incident Response Centre.
Compensation for data failures falls under **Sec. 43A**.

30.s: According to CERT-In data, the number of cyber security incidents it handled in 2025 was approximately:
30.x: CERT-In recorded about 29.44 lakh incidents in 2025, a five-year high, up from 20.41 lakh in 2024. 20.41 lakh is the 2024 figure; 13.91 lakh and 50 lakh are not the reported figures.
30.tq: CERT-In incidents: 2024 = 20.41 lakh -> 2025 = 29.44 lakh.
xs: CERT-In handled about **29.44 lakh** incidents in **2025** — so option **(2)** is correct.
⚠ **20.41 lakh** is the **2024** figure.
xa: 2025 was a **five-year high**.
Incidents must be reported **within 6 hours**.

30.s: Cyber Surakshit Bharat, launched in 2018, primarily provided training for:
o: Armed Forces cyber command personnel only
30.x: Cyber Surakshit Bharat, associated with MeitY and launched in 2018, focused on training Chief Information Security Officers.
30.tq: Link a named programme with its target beneficiaries.
xs: **Cyber Surakshit Bharat** (**2018**) trains **Chief Information Security Officers** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It is a **MeitY** initiative with industry partners, also covering front-line IT officials of government bodies.
xa: CERT-In ran **23** trainings in **2024** (**12,014** participants).
**CyTrain** (I4C) trains police, prosecutors and judges.

30.s:
Consider the following statements regarding cybersecurity awareness observances:
1. Cyber Security Awareness Month is observed in October.
2. Safer Internet Day is observed in February.
3. Cyber Jagrookta Diwas is observed on the first Wednesday of every month.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
30.x: All three statements correctly state the specified periods or frequency of these cybersecurity awareness observances.
30.tq: Check the month and recurring-day details independently before selecting the combined code.
xs: **Cyber Security Awareness Month** = **October**; **Safer Internet Day** = **February**.
**Cyber Jagrookta Diwas** = **1st Wednesday monthly** — all three hold, so option **(4) 1, 2 and 3** is correct.
xa: Telangana Cyber Security Bureau runs **#OnlineButUnafraid** workshops.
**Cyber Surakshit Bharat** (**2018**) trains CISOs.

30.s:
Consider the following statements about the web portal MySecurity.in:
1. It is a platform for innovation in security-related web applications.
2. It was launched by the Ministry of Home Affairs.
3. It is open to any individual or company.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
30.x: All three are correct: MySecurity.in is a platform for innovation in security-related web applications, launched by the Ministry of Home Affairs, and open to any individual or company (APPSC 2018 PYQ). Options leaving out any statement are wrong.
30.tq: MySecurity.in = MHA portal, security web-app innovation, open to all.
xs: **MySecurity.in** is a platform for innovation in **security-related web applications**, launched by the **Ministry of Home Affairs**.
It is open to **any individual/company** — all three correct, so option **(4) 1, 2 and 3** (APPSC **2018** PYQ).
xa: The cyber exercise on '**Scenario Building & Response**' was held in **New Delhi** (APPSC **2019**).
**I4C** is also under **MHA**.

30.s: The cyber exercise on 'Scenario Building & Response' was held in:
30.x: The cyber exercise on 'Scenario Building & Response' was held in New Delhi (APPSC 2019 PYQ). Hyderabad, Bengaluru and Pune are IT hubs used as distractors.
30.tq: Scenario Building & Response exercise = New Delhi.
xs: The '**Scenario Building & Response**' cyber exercise was held in **New Delhi** — so option **(3)** is correct (APPSC **2019** PYQ).
I4C's HQ is also in **New Delhi**.
xa: CERT-In: **115 cybersecurity exercises** (incl. tabletop) with about **1,500 organisations**.
Earlier: **109 drills** with **1,438** organisations up to **Mar 2025**.

30.s: NCIIPC was set up under which provision of the Information Technology Act?
30.x: NCIIPC was established under Section 70A and functions under the National Technical Research Organisation (NTRO).
30.tq: Identify the statutory section by linking it to critical-information infrastructure protection.
xs: **NCIIPC** was set up under **Section 70A** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**69A** = blocking; **79A** = Examiner of Electronic Evidence; **66F** = cyber terrorism.
xa: NCIIPC functions under **NTRO**.
**70B** = CERT-In.

30.s: NCIIPC functions under which organisation?
o: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology
30.x: NCIIPC functions under the National Technical Research Organisation (NTRO).
30.tq: Distinguish the functional parent body from the ministry associated with CERT-In.
