xs: **NCIIPC** functions under the **National Technical Research Organisation** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**MHA** runs **I4C**; **MeitY** runs **CERT-In**; the **NSCS** houses the National Cyber Security Coordinator.
xa: NCIIPC protects **critical information infrastructure** (**Sec. 70A**).
NTRO = **technical intelligence**.

30.s: Which one of the following is NOT listed as a critical sector protected by NCIIPC?
30.x: The listed critical sectors include power and energy, BFSI, telecom, transport, government, strategic enterprises and public enterprises; tourism and hospitality is not included in the specified list.
30.tq: Find the sector outside the defined critical-infrastructure grouping.
xs: **Tourism and hospitality** is not an NCIIPC critical sector — so option **(4)** is correct.
Listed sectors: **power and energy, BFSI, telecom, transport, government, strategic and public enterprises**.
xa: NCIIPC is under **NTRO**, set up under **Sec. 70A**.
⚠ **CERT-In** = MeitY (Sec. 70B).

30.s:
Consider the following statements about Cyber Swachhta Kendra:
1. It is the Botnet Cleaning and Malware Analysis Centre.
2. It is set up and operated by CERT-In.
3. Its free detection and removal tools are available only to government organisations.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
30.x: Statement 1 is correct: that is its full name. Statement 2 is correct: CERT-In set it up and runs it (not NCIIPC). Statement 3 is wrong: the free tools are for citizens and organisations. So 1 and 2 only.
30.tq: CSK = CERT-In; free tools for everyone.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: full name = **Botnet Cleaning and Malware Analysis Centre**.
Statement 2 is correct: set up and run by **CERT-In**.
Statement 3 is wrong: its free tools are for **citizens and organisations** — so option **(1) 1 and 2 only** is correct.
xa: Coverage: about **98%** of Indian internet users + **1,415 organisations** (as of **Jul 2025**).
Free tools: **USB Pratirodh, AppSamvid, M-Kavach**.

30.s:
Which of the following are free tools associated with Cyber Swachhta Kendra?
1. USB Pratirodh
2. AppSamvid
3. M-Kavach
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
30.x: USB Pratirodh, AppSamvid and M-Kavach are listed as free tools associated with Cyber Swachhta Kendra; M-Kavach is associated with C-DAC.
30.tq: Recognise the complete set of named tools rather than one familiar product.
xs: **USB Pratirodh, AppSamvid and M-Kavach** are Cyber Swachhta Kendra's free tools — so option **(4) 1, 2 and 3** is correct.
**M-Kavach** is from **C-DAC**.
xa: Cyber Swachhta Kendra is run by **CERT-In**.
It covers about **98%** of Indian internet users.

30.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C):
1. It was approved under the Ministry of Home Affairs.
2. It became fully operational in 2020.
3. It is a statutory body created by an Act of Parliament.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
30.x: I4C was approved under the Ministry of Home Affairs and became fully operational in 2020. It is an executive framework, not a statutory body.
30.tq: Identify the wrong institutional-status statement before choosing the coded option.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: **I4C** was approved in **2018** under **MHA** and became **fully operational in 2020**.
Statement 3 is wrong: I4C is **not statutory** — an **executive framework** — so option **(1) 1 and 2 only** is correct.
xa: Upgraded to an **Attached Office in 2024**; HQ **New Delhi**.
Components: **cybercrime.gov.in**, **1930** helpline, **CFCFRMS**, **Samanvaya**, **SAHYOG**, **CyTrain**.

30.s: I4C was upgraded to an Attached Office in which year?
30.x: I4C was upgraded to an Attached Office in 2024.
30.tq: Discriminate between the years of operationalisation and institutional upgrading.
xs: **I4C** was upgraded to an **Attached Office in 2024** — so option **(4)** is correct.
⚠ **2020** is when I4C became **fully operational**; it was approved in **2018**.
xa: I4C is **not statutory** — an **executive framework** under **MHA**.
HQ: **New Delhi**.
**Cyber Commandos** (police cyber units under I4C) also date to **2024**.

30.s: The headquarters of I4C is located at:
30.x: The headquarters of I4C is in New Delhi.
30.tq: Use location-based recall for a national institution.
xs: I4C's headquarters is in **New Delhi** — so option **(1)** is correct.
I4C works under the **Ministry of Home Affairs**.
xa: The '**Scenario Building & Response**' cyber exercise was also held in **New Delhi** (APPSC **2019**).
I4C approved **2018**, fully operational **2020**, Attached Office **2024**.

30.s: Which I4C component is intended for reporting all cyber crimes, particularly crimes against women and children?
30.x: The National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, cybercrime.gov.in, is used for reporting cyber crimes, especially those against women and children.
30.tq: Match the component with its distinctive operational role.
xs: The **National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal** (**cybercrime.gov.in**) is for reporting all cyber crimes, esp. against **women and children** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**SAHYOG** = takedown notices; **Samanvaya** = joint investigation and data sharing; **NCAP** = AI/Big Data crime analytics.
xa: **1930** helpline = report financial fraud; "**golden hour**" freezing.
**Meta** will report child-safety matters directly to the I4C portal.

30.s: The helpline number 1930 is primarily associated with:
o: Training police officers in cyber forensics
Reporting cyber crimes against children only
Reporting financial fraud and initiating rapid freezing of funds
30.x: The 1930 helpline is used to report financial fraud, particularly for action during the ‘golden hour’ to freeze funds.
30.tq: Use a number-to-function association.
xs: The **1930** helpline is for **reporting financial fraud** and **"golden hour" freezing** of funds — so option **(4)** is correct.
Training = **CyTrain**; takedown notices = **SAHYOG**; child crimes go to the **Reporting Portal**.
xa: **CFCFRMS** does **real-time freezing** of defrauded funds.
Money Restoration Portal: **57 banks**, **36,290** cases, **₹18.05 crore** (Aug 2026).

30.s:
Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?

a. CFCFRMS — Real-time freezing of defrauded funds
b. NCAP — Takedown notices to intermediaries
c. SAHYOG — AI and Big Data crime analytics
d. Samanvaya — Online training of judges
30.x: CFCFRMS facilitates real-time freezing of defrauded funds. NCAP undertakes AI and Big Data crime analytics, SAHYOG issues takedown notices, and CyTrain provides online training to police, prosecutors and judges.
30.tq: Start from the sure component-role pair and reject swapped functions.
xs: Only pair a is correct: **CFCFRMS** = **real-time freezing of defrauded funds** — so option **(1) a only** is correct.
**NCAP** = AI/Big Data crime analytics, **SAHYOG** = takedown notices — pairs b and c are swapped.
Online training of judges is **CyTrain**, not **Samanvaya** — pair d is wrong.
xa: Samanvaya = **joint investigation and data-sharing** platform.
CFCFRMS SOP (**Jan 2026**): banks may refund frauds **below ₹50,000** without a court order.

30.s: Samanvaya, an I4C platform, is primarily associated with:
o: Freezing bank accounts without any complaint
Issuing digital certificates to government departments
Inter-state cybercrime data sharing and joint investigation support
30.x: Samanvaya supports inter-state cybercrime data sharing and joint investigation.
30.tq: Distinguish the inter-state coordination platform from financial-fraud tools.
xs: **Samanvaya** supports **inter-state cybercrime data sharing and joint investigation** — so option **(4)** is correct.
Fund freezing is **CFCFRMS**; digital certificates come from **Certifying Authorities**.
xa: Only **14** States notified Cyber Crime Coordination Centres; e-Zero FIR in **19 States**.
**NCAP** gives **AI/Big Data** crime analytics.

30.s:
Which one of the following is correctly matched?

a. CyTrain — Online training for police, prosecutors and judges
b. Cybercrime Forensic Lab Consortium — Financial-fraud helpline
c. CFCFRMS — Cybercrime data-sharing platform
 d. National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal — Takedown notices to intermediaries
30.x: Only pair a is correct: CyTrain gives online training to police, prosecutors and judges. The Cybercrime Forensic Lab Consortium is a forensic-lab component of I4C (the financial-fraud helpline is 1930); CFCFRMS freezes defrauded funds in real time (data sharing is Samanvaya); takedown notices are issued through SAHYOG, not the Reporting Portal. So a only.
30.tq: Find the one correctly paired role when several I4C functions are deliberately swapped.
xs: Only pair a is correct: **CyTrain** = **online training for police, prosecutors and judges** — so option **(1) a only** is correct.
The financial-fraud helpline is **1930**, not the Forensic Lab Consortium.
**CFCFRMS** freezes funds (data sharing is **Samanvaya**); takedowns are via **SAHYOG**, not the Reporting Portal.
xa: **Cybercrime Forensic Lab Consortium** is a component of I4C.
**Cyber Commandos** = specially trained police cyber units under I4C.

30.s: Which of the following statements is correct regarding Cyber Commandos?
o: They are private ethical-hacking teams appointed by banks.
They are specially trained police cyber units under I4C.
They are military units under the Ministry of Defence only.
They are judicial officers attached to cyber courts.
30.x: Cyber Commandos are specially trained police cyber units functioning under I4C.
30.tq: Reject the authority-swapping trap in an institutional description.
xs: **Cyber Commandos** are **specially trained police cyber units under I4C** — so option **(2)** is correct.
They were created in **2024**.
xa: **CyTrain** trains police, prosecutors and judges online.
AP plans **20 cyber constables per district** and a **cyber war room**.

30.s: Under the CFCFRMS Standard Operating Procedure of January 2026, banks may refund frauds below which amount without a court order?
30.x: The January 2026 CFCFRMS SOP permits banks to refund frauds below ₹50,000 without a court order.
30.tq: Use exact-figure recall and distinguish the threshold from nearby amounts.
xs: The **CFCFRMS SOP (Jan 2026)** lets banks refund frauds **below ₹50,000** without a court order — so option **(3)** is correct.
Frozen funds are released within **90 days** absent orders.
xa: **RBIH-I4C MoU** signed **11 May 2026**.
Money Restoration Portal: **57 banks**, **36,290** cases, **₹18.05 crore**.

30.s: Frozen funds under the MHA procedure are to be released within 90 days when:
o: The bank changes the SIM card
The victim scans a new QR code
30.x: Frozen funds are released within 90 days if no court order has been issued.
30.tq: Match the procedural time limit with its stated condition.
xs: Frozen funds are released within **90 days** when **a court order is absent** — so option **(1)** is correct.
This is part of the **CFCFRMS SOP (Jan 2026)**.
xa: Banks may refund frauds **below ₹50,000** without a court order.
**CFCFRMS** = real-time freezing of defrauded funds.

30.s: Which institution is associated with implementing the Andhra Pradesh Cyber Security Policy, 2017?
30.x: APTS implements the Andhra Pradesh Cyber Security Policy, 2017.
30.tq: Use the implementing-agency trap by separating State and national institutions.
xs: **APTS** implements the **AP Cyber Security Policy (2017)** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**CERT-In** (MeitY) and **I4C** (MHA) are national bodies.
xa: APTS secures critical government infrastructure via **APCSOC** and does **capacity building**.
APTS = **first CERT-In empanelled organisation in AP**.

30.s: Which one of the following is NOT a stated function or achievement of APTS in Andhra Pradesh cyber security?
o: Auditing Government of Andhra Pradesh applications
Serving as the national headquarters of I4C
30.x: APTS undertakes capacity building, supports critical-infrastructure security through APCSOC and audits government applications. It is not the national headquarters of I4C.
30.tq: Find the institutionally misplaced function.
xs: **Serving as the national headquarters of I4C** is not an APTS function — so option **(3)** is correct.
I4C's HQ is in **New Delhi** under **MHA**.
APTS does **capacity building**, monitors infrastructure via **APCSOC**, and audits **GoAP applications**.
xa: **270 GoAP applications** audited; **125 audit certificates**.
Mandatory audits of all **Secretariat departments, HoDs, PSUs**.

30.s: The Cybercrime Coordination Centre inaugurated at Krishnalanka Police Station is located in:
30.x: The centre was inaugurated at Krishnalanka Police Station in Vijayawada.
30.tq: Test a specific location associated with a State cybercrime initiative.
xs: The **Krishnalanka PS** Cybercrime Coordination Centre is in **Vijayawada** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It was inaugurated by DGP **Harish Kumar Gupta**, with a **cyber radar wing** and **lab**.
xa: AP plans: a **cyber war room**, a **cyber guard policy**, **20 cyber constables per district**.
AP Police-**IIT Tirupati** MoU for a cyber crime training academy.

30.s: In the context of Andhra Pradesh cyber security institutions, which organisation holds the distinction of being the first CERT-In-empanelled organisation in the State?
30.x: APTS is the first CERT-In-empanelled organisation in Andhra Pradesh and is also identified as the first CERT-In-empanelled auditor in the State.
30.tq: Use the FIRST/LAST cue to identify the uniquely designated organisation.
xs: **APTS** is the **first CERT-In empanelled organisation in AP** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**APCSOC** is the monitoring centre APTS runs, not the empanelled body.
xa: CERT-In has empanelled **200 IT security auditing organisations**.
APTS implements the **AP Cyber Security Policy (2017)**.

30.s: The Budapest Convention on cybercrime was adopted under the auspices of the:
30.x: The Budapest Convention is associated with the Council of Europe.
30.tq: Apply the international-organisation substitution trap.
xs: The **Budapest Convention** comes from the **Council of Europe** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**India, Russia, China** are **not signatories**.
xa: India presses for **data sovereignty** and domestic legal channels.
The **ITU** publishes the **Global Cybersecurity Index**, not the convention.

30.s: Which of the following countries were identified as not being signatories to the Budapest Convention?
o: China, Germany and the United Kingdom
30.x: India, Russia and China were identified as non-signatories to the Budapest Convention.
30.tq: Test membership through a confusable country grouping.
xs: **India, Russia and China** are not signatories to the Budapest Convention — so option **(3)** is correct.
The convention is a **Council of Europe** instrument.
xa: India's stance: **data sovereignty** and **domestic legal channels**.
**Global Cybersecurity Index 2024** (ITU): India **Tier-1**, score **98.49**.

30.s: In the ITU Global Cybersecurity Index 2024, India was placed in:
30.x: India was placed in Tier-1 of the ITU GCI 2024 with a score of 98.49. Tier-2 and Tier-3 are wrong tiers, and 89.49 / 79.49 are wrong scores.
30.tq: GCI 2024: India Tier-1, 98.49.
xs: India is **Tier-1, with a score of 98.49** in the ITU **Global Cybersecurity Index 2024** — so option **(1)** is correct.
⚠ **89.49** and **79.49** are reversed-digit distractors.
xa: The GCI is by the **ITU**.
CERT-In incidents hit a five-year high of **29.44 lakh** in **2025**.

30.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: CERT-In — Technical intelligence under the NSA
NCSC — Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology
30.x: I4C is associated with the Ministry of Home Affairs. CERT-In is the national incident response agency, NCIIPC protects critical information infrastructure, and NCSC functions under the National Security Council Secretariat.
30.tq: Start with the sure parent-body pairing and eliminate swapped institutional roles.
xs: **I4C — Ministry of Home Affairs** is correctly matched — so option **(3)** is correct.
**CERT-In** = national incident response (**MeitY**); technical intelligence is **NTRO**.
**NCIIPC** protects critical infrastructure; **NCSC** sits in the **National Security Council Secretariat**.
xa: ⚠ **CERT-In** = MeitY (Sec. 70B); **NCIIPC** = NTRO (Sec. 70A); **I4C** = MHA (not statutory).
NTRO's parent: **NSA / PMO**.

30.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: NCSC — National Cyber Security Coordinator; National Security Council Secretariat
NTRO — National incident response agency; MeitY
NCIIPC — Grievance officer for intermediaries; MHA
30.x: NCSC is the National Cyber Security Coordinator associated with the National Security Council Secretariat. NTRO is associated with technical intelligence, while I4C is under MHA and NCIIPC protects critical information infrastructure.
30.tq: Match each body with its exact role and parent organisation.
xs: **NCSC — National Cyber Security Coordinator; National Security Council Secretariat** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**NTRO** = technical intelligence (not incident response); **I4C** = MHA; **NCIIPC** protects critical infrastructure.
xa: The national incident response agency is **CERT-In** under **MeitY**.
Grievance officers are an **IT Rules 2021** duty of intermediaries.

30.s: CERT-In operates under which Union Ministry?
o: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology
30.x: CERT-In operates under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY).
30.tq: Identify the parent ministry of the specialised cyber-security body.
xs: **CERT-In** operates under the **Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**MHA** runs **I4C**; the **Ministry of Defence** made **Maya OS**.
xa: CERT-In: operational since **Jan 2004**; statutory under **Sec. 70B**.
It is the **National Incident Response Centre**.

30.s: CERT-In became operational in:
30.x: CERT-In has been operational since January 2004.
30.tq: Distinguish the operational year from the year of statutory backing.
xs: CERT-In has been operational since **January 2004** — so option **(3)** is correct.
⚠ **2008** is when **Sec. 70B** (statutory backing) was inserted; **2000** is the IT Act itself.
xa: CERT-In works under **MeitY**.
It is a **CVE Numbering Authority** for Indian products.

30.s: I4C, in the context of India’s cyber-security architecture, is correctly described as:
o: An executive body under the Ministry of Home Affairs, established in 2018 and operational in 2020
A statutory body established in 2004 under MeitY
A constitutional body headquartered in Mumbai
A technical-intelligence body under the Prime Minister’s Office
30.x: I4C is an executive, not statutory, body under the Ministry of Home Affairs; it was established in 2018, became operational in 2020 and is headquartered in New Delhi.
30.tq: Separate I4C’s parent ministry, legal character and timeline from those of CERT-In.
xs: I4C is **an executive body under the Ministry of Home Affairs, established in 2018 and operational in 2020** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It is **not statutory**, its HQ is **New Delhi** (not Mumbai), and **2004 under MeitY** describes **CERT-In**.
xa: Upgraded to an **Attached Office in 2024**.
Technical intelligence under the PMO is **NTRO**.

30.s: Cyber Swachhta Kendra is best described as the:
o: Central database of electronic evidence examiners
Botnet Cleaning and Malware Analysis Centre
30.x: Cyber Swachhta Kendra is the Botnet Cleaning and Malware Analysis Centre, set up and operated by CERT-In.
30.tq: Identify the exact official description of the cyber-cleaning platform.
xs: **Cyber Swachhta Kendra** is the **Botnet Cleaning and Malware Analysis Centre** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It is set up and run by **CERT-In** and offers **free detection and removal tools**.
xa: Free tools: **USB Pratirodh, AppSamvid, M-Kavach**.
Covers about **98%** of Indian internet users + **1,415 organisations**.

30.s: As of July 2025, Cyber Swachhta Kendra was reported to cover approximately what proportion of Indian internet users and how many organisations?
30.x: Cyber Swachhta Kendra was reported to cover about 98% of Indian internet users and 1,415 organisations as of July 2025.
30.tq: Retain both the percentage and the organisation count as a combined quantitative fact.
xs: Cyber Swachhta Kendra covers about **98% and 1,415 organisations** (as of **Jul 2025**) — so option **(1)** is correct.
Its tools are for **citizens and organisations**.
xa: It is run by **CERT-In**.
**M-Kavach** is from **C-DAC**.

30.s: Which Indian agency, besides being the national incident response agency, also functions as a CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) Numbering Authority?
30.x: CERT-In, under MeitY, is the national incident response agency and is also a CVE Numbering Authority. NCIIPC protects critical information infrastructure, I4C handles cyber crime under MHA and NTRO does technical intelligence.
30.tq: CERT-In numbers the bugs: CVE IDs.
xs: **CERT-In** is both the national incident response agency and a **CVE Numbering Authority** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**NCIIPC** protects critical infrastructure; **I4C** handles cyber crime (MHA); **NTRO** does technical intelligence.
xa: CERT-In empanelled **200 IT security auditing organisations**.
It runs **Cyber Swachhta Kendra**.

30.s: Which of the following bodies, functioning under the NTRO, is responsible for protecting India's Critical Information Infrastructure?
30.x: NCIIPC (National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre), under NTRO, protects Critical Information Infrastructure. Cyber Swachhta Kendra cleans botnets, CERT-In handles incident response and I4C deals with cyber crime under MHA.
30.tq: The 'CII' sits inside NC-II-PC.
xs: **NCIIPC**, under **NTRO**, protects India's **Critical Information Infrastructure** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Cyber Swachhta Kendra** cleans botnets; **CERT-In** does incident response; **I4C** deals with cyber crime.
xa: NCIIPC set up under **Sec. 70A**.
Critical sectors: **power and energy, BFSI, telecom, transport, government, strategic and public enterprises**.

30.s: The Supreme Court’s August 2026 direction concerning digital-arrest scams related to:
o: Making the Budapest Convention binding in India
30.x: The Supreme Court directed the formulation of standard operating procedures concerning digital-arrest scams.
30.tq: Match the judicial intervention with its immediate administrative outcome.
xs: The SC (**Aug 2026**) directed **formulating standard operating procedures** on **digital-arrest scams** — so option **(3)** is correct.
66A was **struck down** in 2015, so it cannot replace 69A; India is **not a Budapest signatory**.
xa: Only **14 States** notified State Cyber Crime Coordination Centres; e-Zero FIR in **19 States**.
CERT-In incidents: five-year high of **29.44 lakh** in **2025**.

30.s: Which criticism has been made regarding the Information Technology Act in the context of emerging cyber threats?
o: It contains no provision relating to electronic records.
It abolishes all government takedown powers.
It lacks provisions specifically addressing AI impersonation and virtual-arrest threats.
30.x: A criticism is that the IT Act lacks specific provisions for AI impersonation and virtual-arrest threats.
30.tq: Distinguish a stated legislative gap from exaggerated absolute claims.
xs: The IT Act **lacks provisions specifically addressing AI impersonation and virtual-arrest threats** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It does recognise **electronic records** (**Sec. 4**) and keeps **takedown** powers (69A), so options (1) and (3) are wrong.
xa: Other debates: the **3-hour takedown rule** and **290** MHA notices a day.
VPN regulation is also debated.

30.s: The debate surrounding the three-hour takedown rule and MHA notices primarily concerns the balance between:
o: Surveillance and takedown powers on one side and free speech on the other
30.x: The debate concerns surveillance and takedown powers versus free speech, with the wider discussion also linked to Section 66A, Section 69A and VPN regulation.
30.tq: Identify the competing constitutional and regulatory interests in a policy debate.
xs: The debate is **surveillance and takedown powers on one side and free speech on the other** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It links to **66A** (struck down) and **69A** (blocking upheld), and to **VPN regulation**.
xa: Takedown within **three hours** of a court order or government intimation (MeitY, **27 Mar 2026**).
⚠ **66A** struck down; **69A** upheld; **79** read down (**Shreya Singhal, 2015**).

31.s:
The National Cyber Security Policy, 2013 aimed at which of the following?
1. Securing and developing resilient cyberspace
2. Creating a trained cyber security workforce
3. Promoting research and development and indigenous security technology
4. Establishing an Information Security Assurance Framework
Which of the statements given above are correct?
31.x: The policy aimed at resilient cyberspace, trained manpower, research and development, indigenous security technology and an Information Security Assurance Framework.
31.tq: Use the all-inclusive option after checking each policy objective separately.
xs: All four were aims of the **National Cyber Security Policy 2013** — so option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4** is correct.
Statement 1: its vision is a **secure and resilient cyberspace** for citizens, businesses and government.
Statement 2: it set a workforce target of **5 lakh** cyber security professionals in **5 years**.
Statements 3 and 4: objectives include **R&D**, **indigenous security technology** and an **Information Security Assurance Framework**.
xa: Other objectives: protect **public and private infrastructure**, safeguard **citizens' data**, **public-private partnership**, a **culture of cyber security**.
Nodal agencies: **CERT-In** (incident response), **NCIIPC** (critical infrastructure), **NCCC** (situational awareness).
⚠ Trap: there is no notified "NCSP 2020" — the 2020 document is only a **draft National Cyber Security Strategy**.

31.s: The manpower target under the National Cyber Security Policy, 2013 was to create how many cyber security professionals in five years?
31.x: The target was to develop 5 lakh cyber security professionals within five years.
31.tq: Test the exact policy target rather than the broader objective.
xs: NCSP 2013 aimed to create **5 lakh** cyber security professionals in **5 years** — so option **(3)** is correct.
The policy was released in **2013** by the IT ministry, now **MeitY**.
xa: Its vision: a **secure and resilient cyberspace** for citizens, businesses and government.
Capacity-building also runs through **ISEA** (MeitY) and **CERT-In** trainings — **12,014** IT professionals in **23** trainings (2024).
Every ministry/department must designate a **Chief Information Security Officer (CISO)**.

31.s: The National Cyber Security Policy was released in 2013 by which Union Ministry?
o: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology
31.x: The National Cyber Security Policy 2013 was released by the Information Technology Ministry, now known as MeitY.
31.tq: Use the ministry-ownership trap by distinguishing MeitY from neighbouring ministries.
xs: NCSP **2013** was released by the IT ministry, now the **Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY)** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Its vision is a **secure and resilient cyberspace** for citizens, businesses and government.
xa: The **Cyber Crisis Management Plan (CCMP)** is also a **MeitY** framework against cyber attacks and cyber terrorism.
**CERT-In**, the nodal agency for incident response, held **205 CCMP workshops** till July 2025.
The **Cyber Diplomacy Division** sits in the **MEA**, not MeitY — a confusable pair.

31.s: Which of the following is NOT an objective of the National Cyber Security Policy 2013?
o: Replacing all private cyber security institutions with government agencies
Promoting public-private partnership and research and development
31.x: The policy promotes public-private partnership, research and development, infrastructure protection and data security. It does not seek to replace all private cyber security institutions.
31.tq: Find the option that introduces an extreme and unsupported institutional replacement.
xs: **Replacing all private cyber security institutions with government agencies** is not an objective — so option **(1)** is correct.
The policy instead promotes **public-private partnership** along with **R&D** (option 4).
Protecting **public and private infrastructure** (option 2) and safeguarding **citizens' data** (option 3) are listed objectives.
xa: Other objectives: **capacity building**, **indigenous security technology**, **conformity assessment with incentives**, a **culture of cyber security**.
It also calls for an **Information Security Assurance Framework**.
Workforce target: **5 lakh** professionals in **5 years**.

31.s: Which organisation is the nodal agency for incident response and crisis management in India?
31.x: CERT-In is the nodal agency for cyber incident response and crisis management. NCIIPC is associated with the protection of critical information infrastructure.
31.tq: Discriminate between CERT-In’s incident-response role and NCIIPC’s critical-infrastructure role.
xs: **CERT-In** is the nodal agency for **incident response and crisis management** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**NCIIPC** handles **critical infrastructure**; **NCCC** handles **situational awareness and timely information-sharing**.
**SEBI** is a market regulator with its own **CSCRF** (2024) for regulated entities.
xa: CERT-In held **205 CCMP workshops** till July 2025 and issues guidelines for **sectoral CSIRTs**.
CERT-In trained **12,014** IT professionals in **23** trainings (2024).
India is a member of the **Asia-Pacific CERT (APCERT)** — CSIRTs from **13 economies**.

31.s: With reference to the National Cyber Security Policy 2013 and the proposed national cyber security strategy, which one of the following is correct?
o: The draft strategy was notified as the operative national policy in 2020.
The 2013 policy was withdrawn immediately after the draft strategy was prepared.
The 2013 policy remains operative, while the proposed 2020 strategy document was not released as a notified policy.
Both documents were formally notified together in 2020.
31.x: The 2013 policy remains the operative policy. The document sometimes referred to as the 2020 policy was a draft strategy and was not released as a notified policy.
31.tq: Separate an operative policy from a draft document by focusing on notification status.
xs: The **2013 policy remains operative**; the 2020 document is a **draft strategy, not notified** — so option **(3)** is correct.
The draft **National Cyber Security Strategy** is listed as "**Proposed**" and still pending/not notified, so options 1 and 4 are wrong.
Nothing withdrew the 2013 policy, so option 2 is wrong.
xa: ⚠ Trap: "**National Cyber Security Policy 2020**" or "NCSP updated in 2020" is WRONG.
The draft was prepared under the **National Cyber Security Coordinator (NSCS)**.
Its purpose: address **evolving threats** and expanding digital infrastructure — a next-generation framework for **cyber resilience**.
Criticism: the **2013 policy was never updated**.

31.s: The draft National Cyber Security Strategy was prepared under the coordination of the
31.x: The draft National Cyber Security Strategy was prepared under the National Cyber Security Coordinator.
31.tq: Apply the ‘who prepared or coordinated it?’ method to distinguish the responsible authority.
xs: The draft strategy was prepared under the **National Cyber Security Coordinator (NSCS)** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It is a **draft**, listed as "**Proposed**" and not notified; the **2013 policy** remains operative.
xa: Aim: a next-generation framework for **cyber resilience** and **critical-infrastructure security**.
⚠ Some notes call it an "updated NCSP 2020" — wrong; it is a **strategy**, not a released policy.
The 2013 policy was released by the IT ministry, now **MeitY**.

31.s:
Consider the following statements about the Cyber Crisis Management Plan (CCMP):
1. It is a MeitY framework for countering cyber attacks and cyber terrorism.
2. It is implemented only by Central Government ministries, not by State Governments.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
31.x: Statement 1 is correct: CCMP is MeitY's framework against cyber attacks and cyber terrorism. Statement 2 is wrong: it is implemented by all Central and State Governments. So 1 only.
31.tq: CCMP = MeitY, all Centre and State Governments.
xs: Only statement 1 is correct — so option **(1) 1 only** is correct.
Statement 1 correct: **CCMP** is a **MeitY** framework for countering **cyber attacks and cyber terrorism**.
Statement 2 wrong: CCMP is implemented by all **Central and State Governments**.
xa: **CERT-In** held **205 CCMP workshops** till July 2025.
Every ministry/department/organisation must designate a **Chief Information Security Officer (CISO)**.
CERT-In is the nodal agency for **incident response and crisis management**.

31.s: Every ministry, department and organisation is required to designate a
31.x: Every ministry, department and organisation must designate a Chief Information Security Officer, or CISO.
31.tq: Apply the institutional-designation rule to the authority responsible for information security.
xs: Every ministry, department and organisation must designate a **Chief Information Security Officer (CISO)** — so option **(3)** is correct.
This requirement sits alongside the **Cyber Crisis Management Plan**, the **MeitY** framework against cyber attacks and cyber terrorism.
xa: CCMP is implemented by all **Central and State Governments**; CERT-In held **205 CCMP workshops** till July 2025.
RBI requires **Urban Co-operative Banks** to keep a **dedicated cyber team**, board-approved policy, **MFA** and an incident plan.

31.s: The National Cyber Coordination Centre primarily facilitates
31.x: NCCC supports situational awareness and timely information-sharing in the cyber domain.
31.tq: Match the body with its operational function rather than with a general security label.
xs: The **NCCC** (National Cyber Coordination Centre) handles **situational awareness and timely information-sharing** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Monetary policy, sentencing and defence procurement are not cyber-policy functions in the notes.
xa: **CERT-In** = incident response and crisis management; **NCIIPC** = critical infrastructure.
Criticism: **weak coordination** among CERT-In, the **MHA portal** and state police.
Every ministry must designate a **CISO**.

31.s: Which of the following is correctly matched?
o: RBI Cyber Security Framework for banks — 2016
CERT-In sectoral CSIRT guidelines — only for foreign companies
31.x: The RBI Cyber Security Framework for banks dates to 2016. SEBI’s CSCRF is from 2024, power-sector CERTs operate under the Ministry of Power, and CERT-In guidelines concern sectoral CSIRTs.
31.tq: Start with the sure date–framework pair and eliminate options with swapped years, ministries or scope.
xs: The **RBI Cyber Security Framework for banks** dates to **2016** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**SEBI CSCRF** is from **2024**, not 2016.
Power-sector CERTs come under the **Ministry of Power**, not Finance.
**CERT-In** issues guidelines for **sectoral CSIRTs**, not only for foreign companies.
xa: ⚠ RBI banks framework = **2016**; SEBI CSCRF = **2024**.
Power-sector CERTs: **CERT-Thermal, CERT-Hydro, CERT-Transmission, CERT-Distribution**.
**MeitY Digital Threat Report 2025-26** (2nd ed.) is for **BFSI**, with an **18-month roadmap** to continuous cyber resilience.

31.s: Which of the following is NOT a stated cyber-security requirement for Urban Co-operative Banks under the RBI framework?
o: Reporting cyber attacks only after approval from SEBI
31.x: Urban Co-operative Banks are required to have a dedicated cyber team, a board-approved policy, MFA, an incident plan and to report all cyber attacks to RBI. SEBI approval is not the stated requirement.
31.tq: Find the wrong authority in a regulatory-compliance statement by asking which regulator has jurisdiction.
xs: UCBs must **report all cyber attacks to RBI** — not after **SEBI approval** — so option **(3)** is correct.
A **dedicated cyber team**, a **board-approved policy** and **MFA** are all stated requirements.
xa: UCBs must also have an **incident plan**.
The **RBI Cyber Security Framework for banks** dates to **2016**.
SEBI's own framework, **CSCRF** (2024), covers SEBI-regulated entities.
**RBI Innovation Hub-I4C MoU** on data-sharing: **11 May 2026**.

31.s: The SEBI Cybersecurity and Cyber Resilience Framework (CSCRF) for regulated entities was introduced in
31.x: SEBI’s Cybersecurity and Cyber Resilience Framework for regulated entities dates to 2024.
31.tq: Distinguish the SEBI framework’s year from the RBI banking framework’s earlier year.
xs: **SEBI CSCRF** for regulated entities dates to **2024** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**2016** is the year of the **RBI Cyber Security Framework for banks** — the classic confusion.
xa: **CERT-In** issues guidelines for **sectoral CSIRTs**.
**MeitY Digital Threat Report 2025-26** targets the **BFSI** sector.

31.s: Which of the following is NOT one of the power-sector sectoral CERTs under the Ministry of Power?
31.x: The power sector has CERT-Thermal, CERT-Hydro, CERT-Transmission and CERT-Distribution. CERT-Banking is not one of these power-sector CERTs.
31.tq: Use the common sector label to identify the item belonging to a different sector.
xs: **CERT-Banking** is not a power-sector CERT — so option **(2)** is correct.
The power-sector CERTs under the **Ministry of Power** are **CERT-Thermal, CERT-Hydro, CERT-Transmission and CERT-Distribution**.
xa: Guidelines for **sectoral CSIRTs** are issued by **CERT-In**.
Banking is covered by the **RBI Cyber Security Framework** (**2016**).
Securities market: **SEBI CSCRF** (2024).

31.s: Under the January 2026 CFCFRMS SOP, frozen funds are to be released within
31.x: The SOP provides for release of frozen funds within 90 days.
31.tq: Test the prescribed time limit directly and avoid confusing it with the roadmap period.
xs: Under the **CFCFRMS SOP** (MHA, Jan 2026), frozen funds are released within **90 days** — so option **(3)** is correct.
The same SOP allows refunds below **Rs 50,000** **without a court order**.
xa: **Money Restoration portal**: **57 banks**, all **36** States/UTs, **36,290** cases, **Rs 18.05 crore**.
**RBI Innovation Hub-I4C MoU** for data-sharing: **11 May 2026**.
Current relevance: an **SC order** on **digital-arrest SOPs** and victim restoration.

31.s: Which one of the following correctly states the outlay and laboratory coverage of the CCPWC scheme?
o: Rs 132.93 crore and cyber forensic-cum-training laboratories in 33 States/UTs
Rs 205 crore and laboratories in all 36 States/UTs
Rs 18.05 crore and laboratories in 13 States/UTs
Rs 53 crore and laboratories in 24 States/UTs
31.x: The CCPWC scheme has an outlay of Rs 132.93 crore and provides cyber forensic-cum-training laboratories in 33 States and Union Territories.
31.tq: Pair the financial figure with its geographical coverage; avoid mixing it with figures from other cyber programmes.
xs: **CCPWC** has an outlay of **Rs 132.93 crore** with **cyber forensic-cum-training laboratories** in **33 States/UTs** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Rs 18.05 crore** is the Money Restoration portal's recovery; **205** is the number of CCMP workshops — distractors.
xa: **24,600+** personnel trained in digital forensics and investigation.
Linked to the **National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal** (women/children complaints) and **Nirbhaya Fund** cyber-safety projects.
CCPWC = **Cyber Crime Prevention against Women and Children**.

31.s: The National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, in the context of the CCPWC scheme, is linked particularly with complaints relating to
31.x: The portal is linked with reporting complaints involving women and children. The scheme is also linked with cyber-safety projects under the Nirbhaya Fund.
31.tq: Identify the intended beneficiary group rather than assuming that every cyber portal has a general or sector-specific mandate.
xs: Under **CCPWC**, the portal is linked with complaints relating to **women and children** — so option **(4)** is correct.
The scheme is also linked with **Nirbhaya Fund** cyber-safety projects.
xa: Outlay **Rs 132.93 crore**; labs in **33 States/UTs**.
**24,600+** personnel trained in digital forensics.
**Cyber Shakti** trains **women government officials** — **305** beginner, **53** advanced.

31.s: ISEA, associated with cybersecurity awareness and capacity building in India, stands for:
31.x: ISEA stands for Information Security Education and Awareness.
31.tq: Direct recall of the expansion of a commonly confusable cybersecurity acronym.
xs: ISEA stands for **Information Security Education and Awareness** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It is a **MeitY** capacity-building project.
xa: **CERT-In** training: **12,014** IT professionals in **23** trainings (2024).
**NM-ICPS** supports cyber-security and **AI** research.
NCSP 2013 target: **5 lakh** cyber professionals in **5 years**.

31.s: Which Union Ministry is associated with the ISEA capacity-building project?
o: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology
31.x: ISEA is a capacity-building project of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY).
31.tq: Who-would-do-this-job method for identifying the responsible ministry.
xs: **ISEA** is a capacity-building project of the **Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY)** — so option **(2)** is correct.
ISEA = **Information Security Education and Awareness**.
xa: MeitY also frames the **Cyber Crisis Management Plan** and the **Digital Threat Report 2025-26**.
⚠ **CFCFRMS SOP** is from the **MHA**, not MeitY.
**CERT-In** trained **12,014** IT professionals in **23** trainings (2024).

31.s: The National Mission on Interdisciplinary Cyber-Physical Systems (NM-ICPS) supports research primarily in which area mentioned in the context of cybersecurity capacity building?
o: Universal acceptance of Indian language domains
Digital arrest investigation and victim restoration
31.x: NM-ICPS supports cybersecurity and artificial intelligence research.
31.tq: Application of the mission's stated research focus without confusing it with awareness campaigns or policing.
xs: **NM-ICPS** supports **cybersecurity and artificial intelligence** research — so option **(1)** is correct.
Digital-arrest victim restoration is the subject of the **SC order on digital-arrest SOPs**, not NM-ICPS.
xa: **ISEA** (MeitY) is a capacity-building project.
**CCPWC** trained **24,600+** personnel in digital forensics.
**Cyber Shakti** trains women government officials: **305** beginner (online), **53** advanced (offline).

31.s: The Telangana Cyber Security Bureau's campaign titled “#OnlineButUnafraid” was aimed at which group?
o: Victims seeking restoration after digital arrest fraud
State police officers responsible for critical infrastructure
31.x: The Telangana Cyber Security Bureau launched the #OnlineButUnafraid campaign for women journalists.
31.tq: Direct recall of the campaign-name and target-group pairing.
xs: **#OnlineButUnafraid** by the **Telangana Cyber Security Bureau** targets **women journalists** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It is a **state campaign**, unlike central schemes such as CCPWC or ISEA.
xa: **Cyber Shakti** trains **women government officials**.
**CCPWC** focuses on cyber crime against **women and children**, outlay **Rs 132.93 crore**.
AP angle: **AP Cyber Security Policy 2017**, implemented by **APTS**.

31.s: Cyber Shakti is associated with training for which group?
31.x: Cyber Shakti is a programme for women government officials, with 305 participants at the beginner level and 53 at the advanced level.
31.tq: Identify the beneficiary group and avoid confusing it with other cyber programmes.
xs: **Cyber Shakti** trains **women government officials** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**305** trained at beginner level (online) and **53** at advanced level (offline).
xa: ⚠ Women journalists = Telangana's **#OnlineButUnafraid**; women and children = **CCPWC** scheme.
CCPWC labs in **33 States/UTs**; **24,600+** personnel trained.
**ISEA** is MeitY's capacity-building project.

31.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. India is part of the Asia-Pacific CERT.
2. India and the United States have a Memorandum of Understanding on cybercrime investigation.
3. The Cyber Diplomacy Division is located in the Ministry of Home Affairs.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
31.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because the Cyber Diplomacy Division is a division of the Ministry of External Affairs.
31.tq: Check both membership and agreement facts, then catch the swapped-ministry trap in statement 3.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — so option **(1) 1 and 2 only** is correct.
Statement 1 correct: India is a member of the **Asia-Pacific CERT (APCERT)**.
Statement 2 correct: there is an **India-US MoU** on cybercrime investigation.
Statement 3 wrong: the **Cyber Diplomacy Division** is in the **MEA**, not the MHA.
xa: APCERT: coalition of CSIRTs from **13 economies**; first conference **March 2002, Tokyo**.
The Cyber Diplomacy Division is the nodal point on cyber security, **data protection**, cybercrime and **internet governance**.
India is also in the US-led **Counter Ransomware Initiative** and the **Quad Senior Cyber Group**.

31.s: Which one of the following is NOT a member of the Colombo Security Conclave as listed?
31.x: The listed members are India, Sri Lanka, Mauritius, Maldives, Bangladesh and Seychelles. Nepal is not included in that list.
31.tq: Test membership by comparing every option against the stated group composition.
xs: **Nepal** is not a member of the **Colombo Security Conclave** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Members: **India, Sri Lanka, Mauritius, Maldives, Bangladesh, Seychelles**.
xa: **Cyber security** is one of its **five pillars**.
**Quad** has a **Senior Cyber Group** and cybersecurity partnership.
**APCERT** links CSIRTs from **13 economies**.

31.s: Cyber security is one of how many pillars of the Colombo Security Conclave?
31.x: Cyber security is one of the five pillars of the Colombo Security Conclave.
31.tq: Use the exact pillar count and avoid substituting the number of member countries.
xs: Cyber security is one of the **five** pillars of the **Colombo Security Conclave** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Its members: **India, Sri Lanka, Mauritius, Maldives, Bangladesh, Seychelles**.
xa: ⚠ "Five pillars" also appears in **GCI 2024**, where India was strong in all **five pillars**.
India is a member of the US-led **Counter Ransomware Initiative**.
**MEA's Cyber Diplomacy Division** is the nodal point for cyber diplomacy.

31.s:
Consider the following statements about India’s international cyber cooperation:
1. India is a member of the US-led Counter Ransomware Initiative.
2. India participates in the Quad Senior Cyber Group and cybersecurity partnership.
3. Faster CERT-In agreements with foreign counterparts have been urged to address cross-border threats.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
31.x: All three statements are correct. India participates in the Quad cyber mechanisms, is a member of the US-led Counter Ransomware Initiative and has been urged to conclude faster CERT-In agreements with foreign counterparts.
31.tq: Group the related cooperation mechanisms and verify that each statement describes a distinct international cyber measure.
xs: All three statements are correct — so option **(4) 1, 2 and 3** is correct.
Statement 1: India is a member of the **US-led Counter Ransomware Initiative**.
Statement 2: **Quad** has a **Senior Cyber Group** and cybersecurity partnership.
Statement 3: **faster CERT-In agreements** with foreign counterparts are urged against **cross-border threats**.
xa: India is a member of **APCERT** (first conference **March 2002, Tokyo**).
**Colombo Security Conclave**: cyber security is one of **five pillars**.
**India-US MoU** on cybercrime investigation.

31.s:
Consider the following statements regarding India's performance in the ITU Global Cybersecurity Index 2024:
1. India received a score of 98.49.
2. India was assessed as strong in all five pillars of cybersecurity.
3. India was assigned a numerical rank instead of a tier.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
31.x: India received a score of 98.49 and was strong in all five pillars. Statement 3 is false because the 2024 Index uses tiers instead of numerical ranks.
31.tq: Find the false statement by distinguishing the current tier system from the earlier ranking system.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — so option **(1) 1 and 2 only** is correct.
Statement 1 correct: India scored **98.49** in **GCI 2024**.
Statement 2 correct: India was strong in all **five pillars**.
Statement 3 wrong: GCI 2024 uses **tiers instead of ranks**; India is in **Tier-1 "Role Modelling"**.
xa: ⚠ GCI 2020 = rank **10**; GCI 2024 = **Tier-1**, no ranks.
The GCI is published by the **ITU**.

31.s: India was ranked 10th in which edition of the ITU Global Cybersecurity Index?
31.x: India was ranked 10th in the GCI 2020. The GCI 2024 shifted from numerical ranks to tiers.
31.tq: Numerical-year discrimination between the earlier rank-based edition and the later tier-based edition.
xs: India was ranked **10th** in **GCI 2020** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**GCI 2024** has no ranks; it uses **tiers**, and India is **Tier-1 "Role Modelling"**.
xa: GCI 2024 score: **98.49**, strong in all **five pillars**.
The index is brought out by the **ITU** (International Telecommunication Union).

31.s: In the ITU Global Cybersecurity Index 2024, India was placed in which category, with what score?
o: Tier-1 (Role Modelling), with a score of 98.49
Tier-1 (Role Modelling), with a score of 88.49
31.x: India was placed in Tier-1, described as ‘Role Modelling’, and secured a score of 98.49 in the ITU Global Cybersecurity Index 2024.
31.tq: Separate the category from the score and check both parts of the option.
xs: India was placed in **Tier-1 (Role Modelling)** with a score of **98.49** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Options 1 and 2 give the wrong tier; option 4 gives the wrong score (**88.49**).
xa: India was strong in all **five pillars**.
⚠ In **GCI 2020** India held rank **10**; GCI 2024 replaced ranks with tiers.

31.s: Which one of the following correctly identifies the subject of the Supreme Court order referred to in the context of current cybercrime concerns?
o: Implementation of the Andhra Pradesh Cyber Security Policy
Ranking of countries in the ITU Global Cybersecurity Index
Training of IT professionals through ISEA
Digital-arrest standard operating procedures and restoration of victims' losses
31.x: The Supreme Court order concerned standard operating procedures for digital arrests and restoration of victims' losses.
31.tq: Identify the institutional subject matter rather than matching the issue with a similarly related cyber programme.
xs: The SC order concerned **digital-arrest SOPs** and **restoration of victims'** losses — so option **(4)** is correct.
AP Cyber Security Policy, GCI ranking and ISEA training are separate topics, not the SC order.
xa: **CFCFRMS SOP** (MHA, Jan 2026): refunds below **Rs 50,000** without court order; frozen funds released within **90 days**.
**Money Restoration portal**: **57 banks**, **36,290** cases, **Rs 18.05 crore**.
**RBI Innovation Hub-I4C MoU** on data-sharing: **11 May 2026**.

31.s:
Consider the following statements about the National Cyber Security Policy 2013:
1. It had not been updated even by the time of the criticism referred to in the material.
2. Weak coordination was identified among CERT-In, the MHA portal and State police.
3. The criticism stated that coordination among these bodies was fully effective.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
31.x: The 2013 policy was criticised for never having been updated, and coordination among CERT-In, the MHA portal and State police was described as weak. Statement 3 reverses that criticism.
31.tq: Use the negative statement carefully: the criticism concerned weak, not fully effective, coordination.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — so option **(1) 1 and 2 only** is correct.
Statement 1 correct: the **2013 policy was never updated**.
Statement 2 correct: there is **weak coordination** among **CERT-In**, the **MHA portal** and **state police**.
Statement 3 wrong: it reverses the criticism.
xa: The 2020 document is only a **draft National Cyber Security Strategy**, still not notified.
Current relevance: **SC order** on digital-arrest SOPs and victim restoration.

31.s:
Consider the following statements about the Andhra Pradesh Cyber Security Policy 2017:
1. It is implemented by APTS.
2. It has five verticals.
3. Its verticals include securing critical government infrastructure and capacity building.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
31.x: Statement 1 is correct: APTS implements it. Statement 2 is wrong: it has four verticals. Statement 3 is correct: securing critical government infrastructure and capacity building are among them. So 1 and 3 only.
31.tq: AP policy 2017 = APTS, four verticals.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — so option **(3) 1 and 3 only** is correct.
Statement 1 correct: the **AP Cyber Security Policy 2017** is implemented by **APTS**.
Statement 2 wrong: it has **four verticals**, not five.
Statement 3 correct: verticals include **securing critical government infrastructure** and **capacity building**.
xa: Telangana's state campaign: **#OnlineButUnafraid** for women journalists.
National counterpart: **NCSP 2013**, vision of a **secure and resilient cyberspace**.

32.s: The right to privacy was declared to be intrinsic to life and personal liberty under Article 21 in:
o: Gobind v. State of Madhya Pradesh
Kharak Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh
K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India
32.x: In K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India, decided in 2017, the Supreme Court held that privacy is intrinsic to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and protected under Part III.
32.tq: Identify the authoritative later case rather than the earlier cases that only raised or partially recognised privacy concerns.
xs: **K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017)** declared privacy intrinsic to life and liberty under **Art. 21** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It overruled **M.P. Sharma (1954)** and **Kharak Singh (1962)** to the extent they denied privacy.
**Gobind v State of MP (1975)** only recognised privacy as part of personal liberty.
xa: Bench: **nine judges, unanimous**, **24 August 2017**; privacy also linked to **Art. 19**.
Tests for state intrusion: **legality**, **legitimate aim**, **proportionality**.
⚠ Puttaswamy = **9** judges, unanimous (2017); Aadhaar = **5** judges, **4:1** (2018).

32.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the bench and conclusion in K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India?
o: A nine-judge bench unanimously recognised privacy as intrinsic to life and personal liberty
A seven-judge bench unanimously held that privacy is outside Part III
A five-judge bench by a majority held that privacy is only a statutory right
A nine-judge bench held that privacy is available only to citizens
32.x: A unanimous nine-judge bench recognised privacy as intrinsic to life and personal liberty and protected under Article 21 and Part III.
32.tq: Check the bench strength, unanimity and constitutional status together.
xs: A **nine-judge bench**, **unanimously**, held privacy **intrinsic to life and personal liberty** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It made privacy a **Fundamental Right** under **Art. 21** and **Part III** — not a statutory right, not outside Part III.
xa: Date: **24 August 2017**.
Overruled **M.P. Sharma (1954)** and **Kharak Singh (1962)** to the extent they denied privacy.
Follow-up: the **DPDP Act 2023** with a **Data Protection Board**.

32.s: K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India overruled M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh to the extent that those decisions:
o: Recognised proportionality as the sole test for all restrictions
Denied the existence of privacy as a protected constitutional interest
Declared education to be a Directive Principle
32.x: Puttaswamy overruled M.P. Sharma (1954) and Kharak Singh (1962) insofar as they denied privacy as a constitutional protection.
32.tq: Focus on the limited extent of overruling instead of treating the earlier judgments as wholly erased.
xs: Puttaswamy overruled them to the extent they **denied privacy** as a protected constitutional interest — so option **(2)** is correct.
**M.P. Sharma** was **1954**; **Kharak Singh** was **1962**.
xa: Yet **Kharak Singh v State of UP (1962)** is also cited for early recognition of privacy concerns under **Art. 21**.
**Gobind v State of MP (1975)** recognised privacy as part of personal liberty.
Puttaswamy: **nine-judge**, unanimous, **24 August 2017**.

32.s: A government measure restricts personal data without any supporting law, although it claims to pursue a public objective. Which requirement of the privacy test is most clearly absent?
32.x: The legality requirement demands that an intrusion into privacy be supported by a law. A claimed public objective cannot substitute for the existence of legal authority.
32.tq: Apply the first step of the privacy test by asking whether the restriction has a legal basis.
xs: With no supporting law, the first test — **Legality** (a law) — is missing; option **(2)** is correct.
A public objective would satisfy the **legitimate aim** test, so option 1 is not what is absent.
The three tests are **legality**, **legitimate aim / need** and **proportionality**.
xa: These tests were later applied to **Aadhaar (2018)**.
**NAFRS** (facial recognition) runs **without a statute**, so it is questioned under the Puttaswamy tests.
Any state surveillance must meet the **Puttaswamy tests**.

32.s:
Consider the following statements about the follow-up to the Puttaswamy judgment (2017):
1. The judgment directed the government to enact a data-protection law.
2. The resulting law, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023, provides for a Data Protection Authority in each State.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
32.x: Statement 1 is correct: Puttaswamy directed the government to enact a data-protection law. Statement 2 is wrong: the DPDP Act 2023 provides for a single Data Protection Board (of India), not State-wise authorities; a DPA per member state is the GDPR model. So only 1 is correct; '2 only', 'Both' and 'Neither' are wrong.
32.tq: India = one Data Protection Board; EU = a DPA in each member state.
xs: Only statement 1 is correct — so option **(1) 1 only** is correct.
Statement 1 correct: Puttaswamy **directed the government to enact a data-protection law**.
Statement 2 wrong: the **DPDP Act 2023** creates a single **Data Protection Board of India**; one DPA per member state is the **GDPR** model.
xa: The Board is an **adjudicatory body**, HQ **New Delhi**; appeals lie to **TDSAT**.
DPDP Act: Presidential assent **11 August 2023**.

32.s: The proportionality requirement in privacy jurisprudence was subsequently applied in the context of Aadhaar in:
32.x: The proportionality framework developed in privacy jurisprudence was subsequently applied to Aadhaar in 2018.
32.tq: Separate the year of the Puttaswamy judgment from the year of its later application to Aadhaar.
xs: The Puttaswamy tests, including proportionality, were later applied to **Aadhaar** in **2018** — so option **(3)** is correct.
The Aadhaar judgment: **five-judge** bench, **26 Sep 2018**, **4:1**.
xa: Puttaswamy itself: **2017**, nine judges, unanimous.
The **DPDP Act** followed in **2023**.
Upheld: Aadhaar Act; **PAN/ITR linking**. Struck down: **Sec. 57** use by private entities.

32.s: On which date was the nine-judge Puttaswamy privacy judgment delivered?
32.x: The unanimous nine-judge Puttaswamy judgment was delivered on 24 August 2017.
32.tq: Distinguish the Puttaswamy date from the Aadhaar judgment date.
xs: The nine-judge **Puttaswamy** judgment came on **24 August 2017** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**26 September 2018** is the **Aadhaar** judgment; **25 May 2018** is when **GDPR** took effect.
xa: ⚠ Puttaswamy = **9** judges unanimous; Aadhaar = **5** judges, **4:1**.
Privacy declared a Fundamental Right under **Art. 21** and Part III.

32.s:
Arrange the following cases in chronological order:
A. Puttaswamy v Union of India
B. Gobind v State of Madhya Pradesh
C. Kharak Singh v State of Uttar Pradesh
D. M.P. Sharma v Satish Chandra
32.x: The correct sequence is M.P. Sharma (1954), Kharak Singh (1962), Gobind (1975), and Puttaswamy (2017).
32.tq: Fix the earliest and latest cases first, then place the two intervening cases by year.
xs: Order: **M.P. Sharma (1954)** → **Kharak Singh (1962)** → **Gobind (1975)** → **Puttaswamy (2017)** — so option **(1) D, C, B, A** is correct.
Puttaswamy overruled the first two to the extent they **denied privacy**.
xa: **Gobind v State of MP** recognised privacy as part of **personal liberty**.
Next in the line: **Aadhaar** judgment, **26 Sep 2018**.

32.s:
Match the following cases with the propositions associated with them:

List-I (Case)
 a. Kharak Singh v State of Uttar Pradesh
 b. Gobind v State of Madhya Pradesh
 c. Puttaswamy v Union of India

List-II (Proposition)
 i. Privacy recognised as part of personal liberty
 ii. Privacy recognised as a Fundamental Right and informational privacy affirmed
 iii. Early recognition of privacy concerns under Article 21

Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
32.x: Kharak Singh is associated with early privacy concerns under Article 21; Gobind recognised privacy as part of personal liberty; Puttaswamy affirmed privacy as a Fundamental Right and informational privacy.
32.tq: Start with the distinctive Puttaswamy pair and then distinguish the two earlier recognitions.
xs: Correct match: **a–iii, b–i, c–ii** — option **(2)**.
**Kharak Singh (1962)**: early recognition of privacy concerns under **Art. 21**.
**Gobind (1975)**: privacy part of **personal liberty**.
**Puttaswamy (2017)**: privacy a **Fundamental Right**; **informational privacy**.
xa: **M.P. Sharma (1954)** and Kharak Singh were overruled to the extent they denied privacy.
Puttaswamy bench: **nine judges**, unanimous.

32.s: The constitutional test for State intrusion into the right to privacy consists of:
32.x: The three-part test for State intrusion is legality, legitimate aim and proportionality.
32.tq: Recall the three-part constitutional test as a complete sequence.
xs: The test is **Legality, legitimate aim and proportionality** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Legality** means a law must exist; **legitimate aim** a valid state need; **proportionality** a balanced measure.
xa: These tests were applied to **Aadhaar (2018)**.
Interception safeguards trace to **PUCL v UoI (1997)**.
Any state surveillance, e.g. **facial recognition**, must meet the Puttaswamy tests.

32.s:
Consider the following statements about the Aadhaar judgment of 2018:
1. It was decided by a five-judge Bench.
2. The decision was by a majority of 4:1.
3. Justice D.Y. Chandrachud dissented.
4. The judgment was delivered on 26 September 2018.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: All four statements are correct: the Aadhaar judgment was delivered by a five-judge Bench on 26 September 2018 by 4:1, with Justice D.Y. Chandrachud dissenting.
32.tq: Combine bench strength, majority, dissent and date in one constitutional case cluster.
xs: All four statements are correct — so option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4** is correct.
**Five-judge** bench, majority **4:1**, delivered **26 Sep 2018**.
**Justice D.Y. Chandrachud** dissented, including on passage as a **Money Bill**.
xa: Upheld: Aadhaar Act and passage as **Money Bill**; mandatory for welfare (**Sec. 7**); **PAN/ITR linking**.
Struck down: **Sec. 57** (private entities); bank-account and **SIM** linking.

32.s:
With reference to the Aadhaar judgment (2018), consider the following statements:
1. Mandatory Aadhaar for welfare benefits under Section 7 was upheld.
2. Aadhaar linking with PAN and income-tax returns under Section 139AA of the Income-tax Act was upheld.
3. Mandatory Aadhaar linking with bank accounts and mobile SIMs was upheld.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
32.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: the Court upheld mandatory Aadhaar for welfare benefits (Sec. 7) and PAN/ITR linking (s.139AA). Statement 3 is wrong: mandatory linking with bank accounts and mobile SIMs was struck down. So '1 only' misses 2, while '2 and 3 only' and '1, 2 and 3' wrongly include 3.
32.tq: Upheld = State-linked (welfare, tax); struck down = private/commercial (banks, SIMs, Sec. 57).
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — so option **(2) 1 and 2 only** is correct.
Statement 1 correct: mandatory Aadhaar for welfare under **Sec. 7** was upheld.
Statement 2 correct: **PAN/ITR linking** under IT Act **s.139AA** was upheld.
Statement 3 wrong: mandatory linking with **bank accounts** and **mobile SIMs** was struck down.
xa: ⚠ **PAN** linking upheld; **bank account** and **SIM** linking struck down.
Also struck down: **Sec. 57** (use by private entities) and requirement for CBSE/NEET/UGC and school admissions.

32.s: Which one of the following was struck down or read down in the Aadhaar judgment?
o: The Aadhaar Act itself in its entirety
Section 57 concerning use by private entities
Section 139AA concerning PAN and income-tax returns
32.x: Section 57 of the Aadhaar Act, concerning use by private entities, was struck down. The Aadhaar Act was upheld, as were Section 7 welfare authentication and Section 139AA linkage.
32.tq: Find the provision belonging to the struck-down column rather than the upheld column.
xs: **Section 57**, allowing use by **private entities**, was struck down — so option **(2)** is correct.
The **Aadhaar Act** itself was held valid, including its passage as a **Money Bill**.
**Sec. 7** (welfare) and **s.139AA** (PAN/ITR) were upheld.
xa: Bench: **five judges**, **4:1**, **26 Sep 2018**; **Justice D.Y. Chandrachud** dissented.
Also struck down: mandatory **bank account** and **SIM** linking.

32.s: Which of the following was among the criticisms of the Aadhaar framework at the time of the 2018 judgment?
o: Lack of any provision for welfare authentication
Biometric data risks and absence of a data-protection law
32.x: The criticisms included risks associated with biometric data, the absence of a data-protection law, and mandatory linking requirements.
32.tq: Select the criticism that matches the privacy and data-protection concerns.
xs: Criticisms included **biometric data risks** and the **absence of a data-protection law** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Mandatory **linking** was the third criticism.
xa: The data-protection gap was later filled by the **DPDP Act 2023**.
The judgment was **4:1**; **Justice D.Y. Chandrachud** dissented.

32.s:
Consider the following statements about the Supreme Court-appointed technical committee in the Pegasus matter:
1. It was supervised by Justice R.V. Raveendran.
2. It found malware on 5 of the 29 phones examined.
3. It conclusively linked the malware found to Pegasus.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
32.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: the committee (2021) was supervised by Justice R.V. Raveendran and found malware on 5 of 29 phones. Statement 3 is wrong: it could not conclusively link the malware to Pegasus (2022). So '1 only' misses 2; '2 and 3 only' and '1, 2 and 3' wrongly include 3.
32.tq: Pegasus committee: malware found, Pegasus not proved.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — so option **(2) 1 and 2 only** is correct.
Statement 1 correct: the committee was supervised by **Justice R.V. Raveendran** (2021).
Statement 2 correct: it found malware on **5 of 29** phones.
Statement 3 wrong: it **could not conclusively link** the malware to **Pegasus** (2022).
xa: Interception law: **Sec. 69 IT Act**; Telegraph Act **s.5(2)** now under the **Telecommunications Act 2023**.
Safeguards on interception: **PUCL v UoI (1997)**.

32.s:
Consider the following statements regarding interception of communications in India:
1. Section 69 of the IT Act provides for interception.
2. The interception power under Section 5(2) of the Telegraph Act, 1885 is now under the Telecommunications Act, 2023.
3. Safeguards on interception were laid down in Kharak Singh v State of UP (1962).
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
32.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: interception law rests on Sec. 69 IT Act and Telegraph Act s.5(2), now the Telecommunications Act 2023. Statement 3 is wrong: interception safeguards come from PUCL v Union of India (1997), not Kharak Singh. So '1 only' misses 2; '2 and 3 only' and '1, 2 and 3' wrongly include 3.
32.tq: Phone-tapping safeguards = PUCL (1997); Kharak Singh is an early privacy case on police surveillance.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — so option **(2) 1 and 2 only** is correct.
Statement 1 correct: **Sec. 69 IT Act** provides for interception.
Statement 2 correct: Telegraph Act 1885 **s.5(2)** is now the **Telecommunications Act 2023**.
Statement 3 wrong: interception safeguards came from **PUCL v UoI (1997)**, not Kharak Singh.
xa: **Kharak Singh (1962)** is an early privacy case under **Art. 21**.
**Pegasus** committee: **Justice R.V. Raveendran**; malware on **5 of 29** phones.

32.s:
Consider the following statements regarding facial-recognition surveillance:
1. A Member of Parliament approached the Supreme Court against the Delhi Police’s use of facial-recognition technology during NEET-UG protests.
2. The National Automated Facial Recognition System operates without a specific statute.
3. State surveillance must satisfy the tests laid down in Puttaswamy.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: All three statements are correct. The challenge concerned Delhi Police use during NEET-UG protests, NAFRS operates without a statute, and surveillance must meet the Puttaswamy tests.
32.tq: Check each statement independently, especially the statutory-status statement containing ‘without’.
xs: All three statements are correct — so option **(4) 1, 2 and 3** is correct.
An **MP** moved the SC against **Delhi Police's FRT** use in **NEET-UG protests**.
**NAFRS** runs **without a statute**.
Any state surveillance must meet the **Puttaswamy tests**.
xa: The tests: **legality**, **legitimate aim**, **proportionality**.
AP angle: AP Police **AI4AP** pilot in **Chittoor, Guntur, Annamayya** raises DPDP compliance issues.

32.s:
Arrange the following developments in the history of India’s personal-data protection legislation:
A. PDP Bill introduced in the Lok Sabha and referred to the JPC
B. DPDP Act passed and assent given
C. Justice B.N. Srikrishna Committee drafted the 2018 Bill
D. PDP Bill withdrawn and a narrower DPDP draft released

Select the correct chronological sequence.
32.x: The sequence was 2017–18 Committee and draft, 2019 introduction and JPC reference, 2022 withdrawal and narrower draft, followed by the 2023 Act.
32.tq: Order the four legislative milestones by their stated years.
xs: Order: **Srikrishna draft 2018** → **PDP Bill 2019 to JPC** → **withdrawn 2022** → **DPDP Act 2023** — so option **(1) C, A, D, B** is correct.
The **Srikrishna Committee** report and draft PDP Bill came in **July 2018**.
xa: **2021**: JPC report with **93 amendments**, covering personal and non-personal data.
**2012**: **Justice A.P. Shah** Group of Experts on Privacy.
DPDP Act assent: **11 Aug 2023**.

32.s: The Justice B.N. Srikrishna Committee was constituted by which ministry in relation to the Personal Data Protection Bill?
o: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology
32.x: The Justice B.N. Srikrishna Committee was associated with the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology and drafted the Personal Data Protection Bill, 2018.
32.tq: Use the correct ministry-authority pairing and reject neighbouring ministries.
xs: The **Justice B.N. Srikrishna Committee** was set up by **MeitY** (**Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology**) — so option **(1)** is correct.
It drafted the **Personal Data Protection Bill, 2018**; report in **July 2018**.
xa: ⚠ **Justice A.P. Shah** group was under the **Planning Commission** (report **2012**).
**Kris Gopalakrishnan committee (2020)**: **non-personal data**.
The PDP Bill was introduced in **2019** and sent to a **JPC**.

32.s:
Consider the following statements about the Personal Data Protection (PDP) Bill:
1. It was introduced in the Rajya Sabha in 2019 and sent to a Joint Parliamentary Committee.
2. The JPC report of 2021 proposed 93 amendments and covered both personal and non-personal data.
3. The Bill was withdrawn in 2022 citing compliance burden and ambiguity.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
32.x: Statement 1 is wrong: the PDP Bill was introduced in the Lok Sabha in 2019 (then sent to the JPC). Statement 2 is correct: the 2021 JPC report had 93 amendments and covered personal and non-personal data. Statement 3 is correct: it was withdrawn in 2022 over compliance burden and ambiguity. So '1 and 2 only' and '1, 2 and 3' wrongly include 1; '3 only' misses 2.
32.tq: PDP Bill path: Srikrishna draft 2018 - Lok Sabha + JPC 2019 - 93 amendments 2021 - withdrawn 2022 - DPDP Act 2023.
xs: Statements 2 and 3 are correct — so option **(2) 2 and 3 only** is correct.
Statement 1 wrong: the PDP Bill was introduced in the **Lok Sabha** in **2019**, not the Rajya Sabha.
Statement 2 correct: the **2021** JPC report had **93 amendments**, covering personal and **non-personal data**.
Statement 3 correct: withdrawn in **2022** over **compliance burden** and **ambiguity**.
xa: After withdrawal, a narrower **DPDP draft** was released; the **DPDP Act** passed in **2023**.
The PDP Bill traces to the **Justice B.N. Srikrishna Committee** (MeitY).

32.s:
Match the following committees with their principal association.

List-I (Committee or group)
a. Justice A.P. Shah Group of Experts
b. Justice B.N. Srikrishna Committee
c. Kris Gopalakrishnan Committee
d. A.K. Bhargava Committee

List-II (Association)
i. Non-personal data
 ii. Privacy
 iii. Personal Data Protection Bill
 iv. Net neutrality

Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
32.x: The A.P. Shah Group dealt with privacy, the Srikrishna Committee with the Personal Data Protection Bill, the Kris Gopalakrishnan Committee with non-personal data and the A.K. Bhargava Committee with net neutrality.
32.tq: Start with the distinctive net-neutrality pairing and eliminate the remaining mismatches.
xs: Correct match: **a–ii, b–iii, c–i, d–iv** — option **(1)**.
**Justice A.P. Shah**: Group of Experts on **Privacy** (**2012**).
**Justice B.N. Srikrishna**: **PDP Bill 2018** (MeitY).
**Kris Gopalakrishnan (2020)**: **non-personal data**; **A.K. Bhargava**: DoT's **2015 net-neutrality** panel.
xa: ⚠ Trap: an "A.P. Shah Committee (2015)" on net neutrality is wrong — that was **A.K. Bhargava**.
The A.P. Shah group worked under the **Planning Commission**.

32.s: The Justice A.P. Shah Group of Experts on Privacy submitted its report in:
32.x: The Justice A.P. Shah Group of Experts on Privacy was associated with a 2012 report.
32.tq: Confusable-year discrimination between the privacy group and the later net-neutrality reference.
xs: The **Justice A.P. Shah** Group of Experts on Privacy reported in **2012** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It was set up under the **Planning Commission**.
xa: ⚠ **2015** is the **A.K. Bhargava** net-neutrality committee (DoT), not A.P. Shah.
**2017** = Puttaswamy; **2020** = **Kris Gopalakrishnan** committee on non-personal data.

32.s: The President of India gave assent to the Digital Personal Data Protection Act on:
32.x: Presidential assent to the Act was given on 11 August 2023.
32.tq: Numerical date discrimination among closely related data-protection dates.
xs: The **DPDP Act** got Presidential assent on **11 August 2023** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**3 January 2025** = draft Rules; **14 November 2025** = final Rules notified.
xa: The Act covers **digital personal data** only and uses gender-neutral wording.
It also covers entities abroad offering goods/services to people in India.

32.s:
With reference to the applicability of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, consider the following statements:
1. It applies to personal data processed digitally.
2. It applies to personal data collected in non-digital form and digitised subsequently.
3. It covers non-personal data.
4. It may cover entities outside India offering goods or services to persons in India.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: The Act covers personal data collected in digital form, or collected in non-digital form and digitised subsequently, and certain entities outside India offering goods or services in India. It excludes non-personal data.
32.tq: Find the excluded category while testing territorial and functional scope.
xs: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct — so option **(2) 1, 2 and 4 only** is correct.
Statements 1 and 2: the Act covers data **processed digitally** or **collected digitally**.
Statement 3 wrong: it **excludes non-personal data**.
Statement 4 correct: it covers entities abroad **offering goods/services** to people in India.
xa: ⚠ DPDP covers only **digital** personal data; **GDPR** covers all personal data.
Non-personal data was the subject of the **Kris Gopalakrishnan committee (2020)**.

32.s:
Consider the following statements regarding terms used in the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023:
1. 'Data Principal' is the gender-neutral term for the individual whose personal data is processed.
2. In the case of a child under 18, the Data Fiduciary is treated as the Data Principal.
3. A 'Data Fiduciary' decides the purpose and means of processing personal data.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
32.x: Statement 1 is correct: the Data Principal is the individual whose data is processed (gender-neutral). Statement 2 is wrong: for a child under 18, the parent or guardian is the Data Principal, not the Data Fiduciary. Statement 3 is correct: the Data Fiduciary decides purpose and means. So '1 only' misses 3; '2 and 3 only' and '1, 2 and 3' wrongly include 2.
32.tq: Principal = the person (or parent/guardian for a child); Fiduciary = the entity deciding why and how.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — so option **(2) 1 and 3 only** is correct.
Statement 1 correct: **Data Principal** is the gender-neutral term for the individual whose data is processed.
Statement 2 wrong: for a child (under **18**), the **parent/guardian** is the Data Principal.
Statement 3 correct: the **Data Fiduciary** decides **purpose and means** of processing.
xa: GDPR equivalents: **Data Subject / Data Controller**.
**Consent Manager**: registered entity through which a principal gives, manages and withdraws consent.

32.s: Which one of the following is NOT an additional obligation of a Significant Data Fiduciary?
o: Appointment of a Data Protection Officer in India
Automatic exemption from all consent requirements
