xa: Hydrazine, **MMH** and **UDMH** are also listed as **earth-storable** liquids — throttleable and **restartable**.
**Solid** (HTPB) motors are the ones that **cannot be throttled or stopped**.
⚠ **Hypergolic** = ignite on contact; **Cryogenic** = LH2 + LOX; **Semi-cryogenic** = kerosene + LOX.

36.s:
Which of the following is correctly matched?
1. HTPB — solid propellant example
2. Hydrazine, MMH and UDMH — earth-storable liquid examples
3. Kerosene and LOX — semi-cryogenic combination
4. Solid fuel and liquid oxidiser — hybrid combination
36.x: All four pairings are correct examples of the respective propellant categories.
36.tq: Verify each category–example pair before selecting the complete combination.
xs: All four pairs are correct — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.
**HTPB** is the **solid** example (PSLV/GSLV first stage, **S200**).
**Hydrazine, MMH, UDMH** are **earth-storable liquids**; **kerosene + LOX** is **semi-cryogenic**.
**Solid fuel + liquid oxidiser** is a **hybrid** — it can be stopped/restarted.
xa: **Cryogenic** = **LH2 + LOX** — most efficient but complex.
**Hypergolic** = hydrazine family + **N2O4**, igniting on contact; ideal for spacecraft manoeuvring.
Isp: solid ~**260 s**; earth-storable ~**290-320 s**; cryogenic ~**450 s** (highest).
Hybrids are **rarely built for large thrust**.

36.s:
Consider the following statements about cryogenic propulsion:
1. Liquid hydrogen is the fuel and liquid oxygen the oxidiser.
2. Liquid hydrogen is stored at about -183°C and liquid oxygen at about -253°C.
3. Its exhaust is only water vapour.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
36.x: Statement 1 is correct: LH2 is the fuel, LOX the oxidiser. Statement 2 swaps the temperatures: LH2 is about -253°C and LOX about -183°C. Statement 3 is correct: the exhaust is only water vapour. Hence '1 and 3 only'; options including 2 are wrong and '1 and 2 only' also leaves out 3.
36.tq: Hydrogen is the colder one (-253°C), closer to absolute zero.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option **(3) 1 and 3 only**.
Statement 1 correct: **liquid hydrogen** is the **fuel** and **liquid oxygen** the **oxidiser**.
Statement 2 wrong: the temperatures are swapped — **LH2 is -253°C** and **LOX is -183°C**.
Statement 3 correct: the **exhaust is only water vapour**.
xa: Cryogenic specific impulse ~**450 s** — the **highest** of all propellant categories.
LH2 density is only **0.071 g/ml** → huge tanks; unsuited to **military missiles**.
Used in **rocket upper stages**/space shuttle; **Discovery's** tanks held LH2 + LOX (UPPSC **2006**).
The propellant pair was asked in **UPPSC 2004**.

36.s: Which characteristic of cryogenic propulsion is correctly stated?
o: It uses dense kerosene and is non-toxic.
It has a specific impulse of approximately 260 seconds and cannot be restarted.
It is unsuitable for upper stages because of its low efficiency.
It has a specific impulse of approximately 450 seconds, the highest among the listed categories.
36.x: Cryogenic propulsion has an approximate specific impulse of 450 seconds and is the most efficient category listed.
36.tq: Associate the highest specific impulse with cryogenic propellants, not solid or semi-cryogenic systems.
xs: Cryogenic propulsion has a specific impulse of ~**450 seconds**, the **highest** among the categories — option **(4)**.
**Dense kerosene, non-toxic** describes **semi-cryogenic** (kerosene + LOX), not cryogenic.
Isp ~**260 s** and no throttling/stopping describe **solid** (HTPB) propellants.
Cryogenic is the **most efficient** and is used for **upper stages**, so option (3) is wrong.
xa: Propellants: **LH2 (-253°C)** fuel + **LOX (-183°C)** oxidiser; exhaust only **water vapour**.
ISRO cryogenic engines: **CE-7.5** (GSLV Mk II) and **CE-20** (LVM3 **C25**).
Earth-storable liquids give Isp ~**290-320 s**.

36.s: Why are liquid hydrogen cryogenic systems unsuitable for military missiles?
o: Liquid hydrogen has an exceptionally high density and requires no insulation.
Liquid hydrogen has very low density, about 0.071 g/ml, requires huge tanks and is difficult to store for long periods.
Liquid hydrogen cannot produce water vapour on combustion.
Liquid hydrogen ignites spontaneously on contact with nitrogen tetroxide.
36.x: The very low density of liquid hydrogen, about 0.071 g/ml, necessitates large tanks and makes long-term storage difficult.
36.tq: Link the numerical density with the storage and tank-size consequence.
xs: LH2 has a very **low density (0.071 g/ml)**, needs **huge tanks** and is **hard to store long** — option **(2)**; hence unsuited to **military missiles**.
Option (1) reverses the fact: LH2 density is very low, not high.
LH2 + LOX exhaust is **only water vapour**, so option (3) is wrong.
Igniting on contact with **N2O4** is the property of **hypergolic** hydrazine propellants.
xa: Cryogenic engines are used in **rocket upper stages** and the space shuttle.
LH2 is stored at **-253°C** and LOX at **-183°C**.
Cryogenic Isp ~**450 s** — the highest.

36.s: Cryogenic engines (liquid hydrogen + liquid oxygen) are mainly used in:
o: Military missiles kept ready for long periods
36.x: Cryogenic propulsion is used in rocket upper stages (and was used on the space shuttle) because of its very high specific impulse (~450 s). Its low-density LH2 needs huge tanks and cannot be stored long, so it is unsuited to military missiles; attitude-control thrusters use hypergolic propellants that ignite on contact; sounding rockets use solid motors.

xs: Cryogenic (LH2 + LOX) engines are mainly used in **rocket upper stages** — option **(1)** (UPSC **1995**, UPPSC **1993**).

**Hypergolic** propellants (ignite on contact) are the ones ideal for **spacecraft manoeuvring**.
xa: They were also used on the **space shuttle** — **Discovery's** tanks held LH2 + LOX.
Isp ~**450 s** — highest; exhaust only **water vapour**.
Indian examples: **CE-7.5** (GSLV Mk II upper stage) and **CE-20** (LVM3 **C25** upper stage).

36.s: Which engine is correctly matched with its propellant combination and application?
o: Vikas — UH25 and N2O4 — PSLV second stage
CE-7.5 — kerosene and LOX — GSLV Mk II upper stage

SE2000 — LOX and LH2 — NGLV upper stage

xs: **Vikas** — **UH25 + N2O4** — **PSLV second stage** is correctly matched — option **(1)**.

36.s: The CE-7.5 engine is associated with which combination?
o: 75 kN, LOX–LH2 staged-combustion engine for the GSLV Mk II cryogenic upper stage
UH25–N2O4 engine for the PSLV second stage
200 kN, LOX–LH2 gas-generator engine for the LVM3 C25 stage
Semi-cryogenic kerosene–LOX engine for the NGLV
36.x: CE-7.5 is a 75 kN staged-combustion LOX–LH2 engine used in the GSLV Mk II cryogenic upper stage.
36.tq: Combine thrust rating, engine cycle and stage application to reject mixed attributes.
xs: **CE-7.5** is a **75 kN, LOX + LH2, staged-combustion** engine for the **GSLV Mk II cryogenic upper stage** — option **(1)**.
**UH25 + N2O4** for the PSLV second stage is **Vikas**.
**200 kN gas-generator** engine for **LVM3 C25** is **CE-20**; kerosene-LOX for NGLV is **SE2000**.
xa: CE-7.5 was built by **LPSC**; GSLV Mk II flew with it on **5 Jan 2014**.
⚠ **CE-7.5** = staged combustion; **CE-20** = gas-generator cycle.
CE-20 passed a **bootstrap-mode start** test (Nov **2025**).

36.s: Which statement regarding CE-20 is correct?
o: It is a 75 kN staged-combustion engine used in GSLV Mk II.
It is a solid motor used in the PSLV first stage.
It is a kerosene–LOX engine replacing the L110 core.

xs: **CE-20** is a **200 kN-class gas-generator LOX + LH2** engine for the **LVM3 C25** upper stage — option **(4)**.
The **75 kN staged-combustion** engine of GSLV Mk II is **CE-7.5**.
The **kerosene + LOX** engine replacing the **L110** core is **SE2000**; solid **HTPB** motors power the PSLV first stage.
xa: CE-20 flew on **Chandrayaan-2, 3** and **all LVM3 commercial flights**.
It passed a **bootstrap-mode start** test — starts on its own propellant flow, key for **in-space restart** (Nov **2025**).
⚠ **CE-7.5** = GSLV Mk II; **CE-20** = LVM3 C25.

36.s:
The CE-20 engine has been used for which of the following missions or flight categories?
1. Chandrayaan-2
2. Chandrayaan-3
3. All LVM3 commercial flights
36.x: CE-20 powers the LVM3 C25 upper stage used for Chandrayaan-2, Chandrayaan-3 and all LVM3 commercial flights.

xs: CE-20 powers the **LVM3 C25** stage used for **Chandrayaan-2**, **Chandrayaan-3** and **all LVM3 commercial flights** — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
It is a **200 kN-class**, **LOX + LH2**, **gas-generator-cycle** engine.
xa: CE-20 passed a **bootstrap-mode start** test (Nov **2025**) → key for **in-space restart**.

36.s: What is the significance of the CE-20 bootstrap-mode start test?
o: It eliminates the need for liquid oxygen in the engine.
It proves that CE-20 can operate only with solid propellant.
It demonstrates starting on the engine’s own propellant flow without external gas, supporting in-space restart.
It converts CE-20 into a hypergolic engine.
36.x: Bootstrap mode starts the engine using its own propellant flow without external gas and is important for in-space restart capability.
36.tq: Connect the test method with its operational consequence rather than with a propellant change.
xs: The bootstrap-mode test shows CE-20 **starting on its own propellant flow without external gas**, key for **in-space restart** — option **(3)**.
CE-20 still burns **LOX + LH2**, so options (1), (2) and (4) are wrong — it is neither solid nor **hypergolic**.
xa: The test was passed in **Nov 2025**.
CE-20: **200 kN** class, **gas-generator** cycle, **LVM3 C25** upper stage.

o: Replacing the C25 in GSLV Mk II only

36.s: The SE2000 semi-cryogenic engine uses:

36.s:
Consider the following statements about the 300 mN Stationary Plasma Thruster life-tested by ISRO:
1. It is a Hall-type thruster that uses xenon.
2. Its specific impulse is about six times that of chemical systems.
3. It is meant to replace chemical propulsion in the booster stages of future launch vehicles.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
36.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: it is a Hall-type xenon thruster with ~6x the specific impulse of chemical systems. Statement 3 is wrong: it will replace chemical propulsion on future communication satellites, not launch-vehicle boosters. So '1 and 2 only'; the other options include statement 3 or omit a true one.
36.tq: Electric thrusters have tiny thrust (mN) - good for satellites in orbit, useless for lift-off.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 correct: it is a **Hall-type** thruster using **xenon**.
Statement 2 correct: specific impulse ~**6x** chemical systems.
Statement 3 wrong: it will replace chemical propulsion on future **communication satellites**, not launch-vehicle boosters.
xa: ISRO completed a **1,000-hour life test** of the **300 mN** Stationary Plasma Thruster.
**LOX-methane** is the other green option — cleaner + cheaper, key for **Mars-return**.
**POEM** reuses the spent **PS4** stage as an orbital platform.

36.s: Why is LOX-methane considered important for Mars-return missions and in-situ resource utilisation?
o: It can be stored indefinitely without refrigeration.
Methane can be produced from Martian resources, while the combination is cleaner and cheaper.
LOX-methane is a hypergolic combination that ignites on contact.
Methane has the highest density of all cryogenic fuels and needs no oxidiser.
36.x: LOX-methane is considered cleaner and cheaper, and methane can be produced from Martian resources.
36.tq: Use the cause–application link instead of confusing methane with hypergolic or earth-storable propellants.
xs: LOX-methane is **cleaner and cheaper**, and **methane can be made from Martian resources** — option **(2)**.
This makes it key for **Mars-return** and **In-Situ Resource Utilization** (**2026**).
It is not hypergolic — **hydrazine + N2O4** are the ones that **ignite on contact**.
xa: Astrobase's **EVEREST** is an **800 kN full-flow staged combustion LOX-methane** engine.
**Starship** uses ~**1,200 t** liquid methane + LOX.
ISRO's **300 mN** Hall thruster (**xenon**) gives Isp ~**6x** chemical systems.

xs: POEM = **PSLV Orbital Experimental Module** — option **(4)**.
It reuses the **spent PS4 stage** as an **orbital platform** for start-up/academic payloads.
xa: Other ISRO green/electric efforts: a **1,000-hour life test** of a **300 mN** **Stationary Plasma Thruster**.

36.s:
Match List-I with List-II regarding air-breathing engines:

List-I (Engine)
a. Ramjet
b. Scramjet

List-II (Characteristic)
i. Combustion with subsonic airflow
ii. Combustion with supersonic airflow
iii. Speed generally above Mach 2
iv. Speed generally in the Mach 5–6 and above range

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
o: a–i and iii; b–ii and iv
a–ii and iii; b–i and iv
a–i and iv; b–ii and iii
a–ii and iv; b–i and iii
36.x: A ramjet uses forward speed for compression, has subsonic combustion and operates above Mach 2. A scramjet has supersonic combustion and is designed for speeds of about Mach 5–6 and above.
36.tq: Start from the sure pair linking scramjet with supersonic combustion, then eliminate codes.
xs: **Ramjet**: **subsonic** combustion, above **Mach 2**; **Scramjet**: **supersonic** combustion, **Mach 5-6+** — option **(1) a–i and iii; b–ii and iv**.
Both use **forward speed** for compression — **no compressor**.
xa: Scramjets use **atmospheric oxygen** → cut oxidiser weight.
Challenge: sustaining combustion is like **"a candle in a hurricane"**.
ISRO's **ATV** flight-tested scramjets in **Aug 2016**; **HSTDV** is **DRDO's** scramjet vehicle.

36.s: Which one of the following best explains the principal advantage of a scramjet over a conventional rocket during atmospheric flight?
o: It operates with subsonic airflow at speeds below Mach 2.
It eliminates the need for fuel during hypersonic flight.
It carries atmospheric oxygen, thereby reducing the weight of the onboard oxidiser.
It uses a compressor to compress atmospheric air before combustion.
36.x: A scramjet uses oxygen from the atmosphere, so it need not carry the entire oxidiser required by a rocket. It still requires fuel and works with supersonic airflow.
36.tq: Use the function-based option; distinguish an air-breathing engine from a rocket.
xs: A scramjet uses **atmospheric oxygen**, so it **cuts onboard oxidiser weight** — option **(3)**.
It still needs **fuel**, so option (2) is wrong.
It burns in **supersonic** airflow at **Mach 5-6+** — subsonic combustion above **Mach 2** is a **ramjet**.
Compression comes from **forward speed**, **no compressor**, so option (4) is wrong.
xa: Challenge: **"a candle in a hurricane"**.
India became the **4th** country (after **US, Russia, China**) to demonstrate scramjet flight (ATV, **Aug 2016**).
DRDO's actively cooled scramjet combustor ran **20 minutes** on indigenous **endothermic hydrocarbon** fuel (May **2026**).

36.s: The major operational challenge in sustaining combustion in a scramjet is popularly compared with which of the following situations?
o: Boiling water in a pressure cooker
Lighting a candle in a hurricane
Starting a diesel engine in winter
Flying a glider in still air
36.x: Maintaining stable combustion in the extremely fast supersonic airflow of a scramjet is likened to trying to keep a candle alight in a hurricane.
36.tq: Recognise the distinctive analogy associated with the technical difficulty.
xs: Sustaining scramjet combustion is likened to **"a candle in a hurricane"** — option **(2)**.
The airflow through the combustor is **supersonic**, at speeds of **Mach 5-6+**.
xa: A **ramjet** burns in **subsonic** airflow above **Mach 2**.
Scramjets use **atmospheric oxygen** → lower oxidiser weight.
⚠ **ATV** = ISRO (**2016**); **HSTDV** = DRDO.

Statement 1 correct: **ATV** flight-tested scramjet engines from **Sriharikota** in **Aug 2016**.
Statement 2 wrong: India was the **4th** country, after the **US, Russia and China** — not the third.

36.tq: Check each statement against the vehicle, duration and fuel details before selecting the combined code.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
**HSTDV** (Hypersonic Technology Demonstrator Vehicle) is **DRDO's** scramjet vehicle.
DRDO's **actively cooled full-scale scramjet combustor** ran **20 minutes** on **indigenous endothermic hydrocarbon fuel** (May **2026**).
xa: ⚠ **ATV** = ISRO (**2016**); **HSTDV** = DRDO.
ISRO's ATV made India the **4th** country to demonstrate scramjet flight.
Scramjets burn in **supersonic** airflow at **Mach 5-6+**.

36.s: Which of the following correctly describes ISRO's RLV-TD ‘Pushpak’?
o: A reusable winged vehicle intended to support a Two-Stage-To-Orbit system
A single-use solid-propellant launch vehicle for lunar missions
A cryogenic upper stage used in the GSLV Mk II
A reusable capsule designed exclusively for crewed re-entry
36.x: Pushpak is ISRO’s reusable winged vehicle and is intended to contribute to a Two-Stage-To-Orbit system.
36.tq: Use the exact vehicle-purpose association rather than confusing it with a launcher stage.
xs: **RLV-TD "Pushpak"** is ISRO's **reusable winged vehicle**, aimed at a **Two-Stage-To-Orbit (TSTO)** system — option **(1)**.
It is not single-use, not a cryogenic stage (GSLV Mk II uses **CE-7.5**) and not a crew capsule.
xa: Pushpak completed **LEX-03**, an **autonomous landing experiment**.
Reusability can cut launch cost **up to 80%**, reduce **space debris** and allow **rapid turnaround**.
Challenges: reusable **Thermal Protection System**, autonomous precision landing, high R&D cost.

36.s: The RLV-TD ‘Pushpak’ completed which of the following experiments?
o: Integrated hot test of a semi-cryogenic engine
36.x: Pushpak completed LEX-03, an autonomous landing experiment.
36.tq: Match the named vehicle with its specific test or mission.
xs: Pushpak completed **LEX-03**, the **autonomous landing experiment** — option **(1)**.
The **PHTA** hot test and integrated semi-cryogenic tests belong to **SE2000**; the **bootstrap-mode** test belongs to **CE-20**.
xa: Pushpak aims at a **Two-Stage-To-Orbit (TSTO)** system.
Benefits of reuse: cost cut **up to 80%**, less debris, rapid turnaround.
**Autonomous precision landing** is itself listed as a key challenge.

36.s: Which one of the following is NOT a stated benefit of reusable launch systems?
o: Elimination of the need for thermal protection systems
Reduction in launch cost by up to 80 percent
36.x: Reusable vehicles require a reusable Thermal Protection System; its elimination is not a benefit identified for such systems.
36.tq: Find the option that reverses a stated benefit into an impossibility.
xs: Eliminating **thermal protection systems** is NOT a benefit — option **(2)**; a **reusable Thermal Protection System** is a key **challenge**.
The stated benefits are **launch cost cut up to 80%**, **less space debris** and **rapid turnaround**.
xa: Other challenges: **autonomous precision landing** and **high R&D cost**.
ISRO's **RLV-TD "Pushpak"** completed **LEX-03**, aiming at **TSTO**.
**Falcon 9** first stages have been recovered **520+** times.

36.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
36.x: New Glenn is associated with Blue Origin. Falcon 9 and Starship belong to SpaceX, while Zhuque-3 belongs to LandSpace.
36.tq: Start with the company–vehicle pair that is directly identifiable and eliminate swapped-company options.
xs: **New Glenn — Blue Origin** is correct — option **(3)**; its booster is recovered by **vertical landing**.
**Falcon 9** and **Starship** belong to **SpaceX**; **Zhuque-3** belongs to **LandSpace (China)**.
xa: Falcon 9 first stages recovered **520+** times (Jan **2026**); "Falcon" was an **APPSC 2024 PYQ**.
**Starship** is fully reusable, burning ~**1,200 t** liquid methane + LOX.
Zhuque-3 **attempted recovery** of orbital-class stages.

36.s: Which reusable rocket is associated with first-stage recovery more than 520 times?
36.x: Falcon 9’s first stages had been recovered more than 520 times as stated.
36.tq: Link the distinctive numerical figure with the correct vehicle rather than with another reusable rocket.
xs: **Falcon 9** (SpaceX) first stages have been recovered **520+** times — option **(4)**.
**New Glenn** (Blue Origin) recovers its booster by vertical landing; **Zhuque-3** (LandSpace) only **attempted** recovery.
xa: "Falcon" appeared in the **APPSC 2024 PYQ**.
**Starship** (SpaceX) is **fully reusable** and needs **10+ in-orbit refuellings** for NASA's moon landing.
ISRO's reusable effort: **RLV-TD "Pushpak"** (**LEX-03**).

36.s: Which one of the following statements about Starship is correct?
o: It uses approximately 1,200 tonnes of liquid methane and LOX and is fully reusable.
Its booster is recovered only by parachute.
It is an orbital-class recovery vehicle developed by LandSpace.
It uses refined kerosene and LOX and has no planned in-orbit refuelling.
36.x: Starship is described as fully reusable and using about 1,200 tonnes of liquid methane and LOX.
36.tq: Separate the vehicle’s propellants and reusability from the characteristics of other rockets.
xs: **Starship** is **fully reusable** and uses ~**1,200 t** of **liquid methane + LOX** — option **(1)**.
It is a **SpaceX** vehicle, not **LandSpace** (which makes **Zhuque-3**).
It burns methane, not kerosene, and needs **10+ in-orbit refuellings** for NASA's moon landing.
xa: NASA flagged Starship's **cryogenic propellant transfer in orbit** as a top risk (Mar **2026**).
**Falcon 9** first stages recovered **520+** times.
**New Glenn** (Blue Origin) recovers its booster by **vertical landing**.

36.s:
With reference to the proposed NGLV 'Soorya', consider the following statements:
1. It is planned as a reusable heavy-lift rocket.
2. It is designed to carry about 20,000 kg to low Earth orbit.
3. It is planned to use semi-cryogenic propulsion.
4. Its projected payload to low Earth orbit is about 2.5 times that of LVM3.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
36.x: Soorya is planned as a reusable heavy-lift NGLV using semi-cryogenic propulsion, with a payload of about 20,000 kg to LEO—approximately 2.5 times the LVM3 capacity.
36.tq: Treat the payload, propulsion, reusability and comparison figures as separate statements and verify all four.
xs: All four statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.
**NGLV "Soorya"** is a planned **reusable heavy-lift** rocket using **semi-cryogenic** propulsion.
Payload: **20,000 kg to LEO** — about **2.5x LVM3**.
xa: Size ~**90 m** tall; lift-off mass ~**1,000 t**.
Launch site: **Third Launch Pad**, Sriharikota.
Purpose: **Bharatiya Antariksh Station** (**2035**) and crewed lunar landing (**2040**).
Its semi-cryogenic engine is **SE2000** (refined kerosene + LOX).

36.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched in relation to NGLV 'Soorya'?
o: Launch site — Third Launch Pad, Sriharikota
36.x: Soorya is planned to use semi-cryogenic propulsion, not exclusively solid propulsion. Its projected height is about 90 metres, lift-off mass about 1,000 tonnes, and launch site the Third Launch Pad at Sriharikota.
36.tq: Find the option that reverses the propulsion detail while retaining the correct vehicle specifications.
xs: "Exclusively **solid** propulsion" is wrong — Soorya uses **semi-cryogenic** propulsion — option **(2)**.
The other pairs are right: lift-off mass ~**1,000 t**, height ~**90 m**, **Third Launch Pad**, Sriharikota.
xa: Payload **20,000 kg to LEO** (~**2.5x** LVM3).
It is planned as a **reusable heavy-lift** rocket.
Its goals: **Bharatiya Antariksh Station** (**2035**) and crewed lunar landing (**2040**).

36.s:
The proposed NGLV 'Soorya' is intended to support which of the following future objectives?
1. Bharatiya Antariksh Station by 2035
2. Crewed lunar landing by 2040
3. Scramjet testing from Sriharikota in August 2016

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
36.x: Soorya is intended to support the Bharatiya Antariksh Station planned for 2035 and a crewed lunar landing planned for 2040. Scramjet testing in August 2016 was a separate ATV activity.
36.tq: Separate the NGLV's future mission objectives from the unrelated scramjet demonstration.
xs: Soorya supports the **Bharatiya Antariksh Station (2035)** and a **crewed lunar landing (2040)** — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 3 is wrong: the **Aug 2016** scramjet test was ISRO's **ATV** flight, unrelated to NGLV.
xa: NGLV: **reusable heavy-lift**, **semi-cryogenic**, **20,000 kg to LEO**.
It will fly from the **Third Launch Pad**, Sriharikota.
Size ~**90 m**; lift-off mass ~**1,000 t**.

36.s: Which of the following correctly describes Skyroot's Vikram-1 on Mission Aagaman?
o: A reusable heavy-lift vehicle using semi-cryogenic propulsion for the Bharatiya Antariksh Station
A single-stage suborbital vehicle designed for a crewed lunar landing
A three-stage vehicle using only liquid propulsion, designed to place 20,000 kg into LEO
A four-stage vehicle with three solid stages and one liquid stage, designed to place 290 kg into a 500 km SSO
36.x: Skyroot's Vikram-1 has three solid stages and one liquid stage and is designed for a 290 kg payload to a 500 km sun-synchronous orbit. It reached orbit on Mission Aagaman as India's first private orbital rocket.
36.tq: Match the vehicle with its stage composition and payload class, avoiding the specifications of NGLV.
xs: **Vikram-1** has **3 solid + 1 liquid stage** and carries **290 kg to 500 km SSO** — option **(4)**.
**Reusable heavy-lift semi-cryogenic** for the space station describes **NGLV "Soorya"**, which also carries **20,000 kg to LEO**.
xa: Vikram-1 reached orbit on **Mission Aagaman** (Jul **2026**) → **India's first private orbital rocket**.
Skyroot also static-tested the **KALAM 1200** solid motor at **SDSC-SHAR**.
Agnikul's **Agnilet** flew in **2024** from the private pad **"Dhanush"**.

36.s: Why are reusability and advanced propulsion considered important for India's future space activities?
o: They can help India compete in commercial launch services and enable more cost-effective human spaceflight.
They restrict launch vehicles to suborbital missions only.
They remove the need for all atmospheric flight tests.
They make every launch vehicle independent of fuel and oxidiser.
36.x: Reusability and advanced propulsion can reduce launch costs, improve commercial competitiveness and support cost-effective human spaceflight. They do not eliminate the need for propellants or testing.
36.tq: Select the option that links the technology to both stated economic and human-spaceflight outcomes.
xs: Reusability + advanced propulsion are needed for **commercial launch competition** and **cost-effective human spaceflight** — option **(1)**.
They do not remove the need for **fuel/oxidiser** or **flight tests**, nor restrict rockets to suborbital use.
xa: Reuse can cut launch cost **up to 80%**, reduce **space debris** and allow **rapid turnaround**.
Skyroot's **Vikram-1** became India's **first private orbital rocket** (Jul **2026**).
ISRO's **NGLV "Soorya"** is planned as a **reusable heavy-lift** rocket.

36.s: NASA has flagged which of the following as a top risk to Starship's Moon-landing plan?
o: The use of an endothermic hydrocarbon fuel in an HSTDV combustor
The absence of a solid stage in Vikram-1
36.x: Cryogenic propellant transfer in orbit has been identified as a top risk to Starship's Moon-landing plan.
36.tq: Use the distinctive risk-technology association rather than confusing it with propulsion tests on other vehicles.
xs: NASA flagged **cryogenic propellant transfer in orbit** as a top risk to **Starship's** moon-landing plan — option **(3)** (Mar **2026**).
Starship needs **10+ in-orbit refuellings** for NASA's moon landing.
xa: Starship is **fully reusable**, using ~**1,200 t** of liquid methane + LOX.
**Subsonic combustion** is a **ramjet** feature; the endothermic-fuel combustor is **DRDO's**.
Skyroot's **Vikram-1** has **3 solid + 1 liquid** stage.

37.s: Which one of the following statements about a geostationary satellite is NOT correct?
o: Its orbital plane is the equatorial plane with zero inclination.
Its orbital period is approximately 24 hours.
It orbits at approximately 35,786 km above the equator.
Its fixed orbital height varies according to the mass of the satellite.
37.x: The geostationary orbital height is fixed and does not depend on the satellite’s mass. The other statements correctly describe geostationary orbit.
37.tq: Find the exception by checking the physical condition that does not affect orbital height.
xs: The NOT-correct statement is that GEO **height varies with satellite mass** — option **(4)**; the height is **fixed** and does **not depend on mass** (CGPSC 2018).
Statements (1)–(3) are true: **equatorial plane** (zero inclination), period **24 hours**, altitude ~**35,786 km** above the equator.
xa: GEO satellites move **west to east**, so they look **stationary**.
Period of **24 hours** was asked in **UPPSC 2016**.
Launchers put satellites into an elliptical **GTO**; the satellite's **own motor** raises it to **GEO**.

37.s: A geostationary satellite appears stationary to an observer because it
o: moves from east to west in a polar plane
moves from west to east in the equatorial plane with a period matching Earth’s rotation
remains permanently fixed above the North Pole
moves randomly around the Earth at a very low altitude
37.x: A geostationary satellite moves west to east in the equatorial plane and has a 24-hour period, matching Earth’s rotation.
37.tq: Combine direction, plane and period to explain the apparent stationary position.
xs: It moves **west to east** in the **equatorial plane** with a **24-hour** period matching Earth's rotation — option **(2)**.
It does not move east to west, sit above the North Pole or fly at low altitude — it is ~**35,786 km** (~**36,000 km**) up.
xa: ⚠ GEO height is **fixed** and does **not depend on satellite mass**.
Inclination is **zero** — the orbit lies in the equatorial plane.
Satellites reach GEO via an elliptical **GTO**.

37.s: Which of the following correctly describes the usual process of placing a communication satellite in geostationary orbit?
o: The launcher places it in an elliptical GTO, after which the satellite’s own motor raises it to GEO.
The satellite first descends into the atmosphere and is then lifted by solar radiation.
The launcher directly places it in a circular polar orbit and the satellite remains there.
The launcher places it directly in a sub-GTO and no onboard propulsion is required.
37.x: Launch vehicles generally inject satellites into an elliptical geostationary transfer orbit (GTO); the satellite’s own motor raises it to geostationary orbit (GEO).
37.tq: Distinguish the transfer orbit from the final geostationary orbit.
xs: The launcher places the satellite in an elliptical **GTO**, and its **own motor raises it to GEO** — option **(1)**.
GEO is an **equatorial** orbit, not polar, so option (3) is wrong; onboard propulsion is needed, so option (4) is wrong.
xa: GEO altitude: ~**35,786 km** above the equator; period **24 hours**.
Motion **west to east** → the satellite appears **stationary**.
⚠ GEO height does **not** depend on satellite mass.

37.s: Which one of the following correctly explains APPLE?
o: Asian Public Platform for Long-distance Education, launched in 2004 as EDUSAT
Ariane Passenger PayLoad Experiment, launched in 1981 as India’s first experimental communication satellite
Aerial Payload and Propulsion Laboratory Experiment, launched in 2002 as a navigation satellite
Advanced Polar Payload Launch Experiment, launched in 1992 as India’s first meteorological satellite
37.x: APPLE stands for Ariane Passenger PayLoad Experiment and was India’s first experimental communication satellite, launched in 1981.
37.tq: Expand the acronym and match it with its historical role.
xs: **APPLE** = **Ariane Passenger PayLoad Experiment** (**1981**), India's **first experimental communication satellite** — option **(2)**; it flew on **Ariane**.
**EDUSAT** (**2004**) is GSAT-3; the first exclusive weather satellite is **KALPANA-1** (**2002**).
xa: **INSAT-1A** (**1982**) was the **first INSAT**.
INSAT system **commissioned 1983** → operational since **INSAT-1B**.
**INSAT-2** (**1992-1999**) was the **first fully indigenous** INSAT series.

37.s: Which of the following is a feature of the multipurpose INSAT design?
o: Telecommunication, television broadcasting, meteorology, disaster warning and search-and-rescue are integrated on one geostationary platform.
Only military communication is provided through a network of polar satellites.
Only weather imaging is performed, without broadcasting or disaster services.
Education and telemedicine are excluded from the satellite-based service framework.
37.x: INSAT integrates telecommunications, television broadcasting, meteorology, disaster warning and search-and-rescue on one geostationary platform. It is regarded as one of the largest domestic systems in the Asia-Pacific region.
37.tq: Select the option that captures the full multipurpose design rather than a single service.
xs: INSAT integrates **telecom, TV broadcasting, meteorology, disaster warning and search-and-rescue** on **one geostationary platform** — option **(1)**.
It is not military-only or weather-only; services include **EDUSAT** and **telemedicine**.
xa: INSAT is **one of the largest domestic systems** in the Asia-Pacific.
Its dual role (**meteorological + communication**) was keyed as "Meteorological Satellite" in **JPSC 2021**.
Controlled from **MCF, Hassan (Karnataka)**.

37.s:
Consider the following statements about the INSAT system:
1. It is a joint venture of DoS, DoT, IMD, All India Radio and Doordarshan.
2. It is coordinated by the INSAT Coordination Committee (ICC).
3. It is controlled from the Master Control Facility at Sriharikota.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
37.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: INSAT is a joint venture of DoS, DoT, IMD, AIR and Doordarshan, coordinated by the ICC. Statement 3 is wrong: the MCF is at Hassan, Karnataka. So '1 and 2 only'; the other options include statement 3 or omit a true one.
37.tq: Launches from Sriharikota, but satellites are controlled from MCF Hassan.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 correct: INSAT is a joint venture of **DoS, DoT, IMD, All India Radio and Doordarshan**.
Statement 2 correct: it is coordinated by the **INSAT Coordination Committee (ICC)**.
Statement 3 wrong: it is controlled from **MCF, Hassan (Karnataka)**, not Sriharikota.
xa: System **commissioned 1983**; operational since **INSAT-1B**.
**10** in-orbit communication satellites were transferred to **NSIL** in **2022**.
India has **19** operational communication satellites (**2026**).

37.s: INSAT-4C was lost because
o: GSLV-F01 failed during the EDUSAT mission
Falcon 9 failed during the GSAT-N2 mission
37.x: INSAT-4C was lost in 2006 when GSLV-F02 failed. It was replaced by INSAT-4CR, launched in September 2007 by GSLV-F04.
37.tq: Link the failed satellite with the correct launch vehicle and year.
xs: **INSAT-4C** was lost when **GSLV-F02** failed in **2006** — option **(1)**.
It was replaced by **INSAT-4CR** (Sep **2007**, **GSLV-F04**).
**GSLV-F01** successfully launched **EDUSAT** (**2004**); **GSAT-N2** flew on **Falcon 9**.
xa: **INSAT-4A** (**2005**) and **INSAT-4B** (**2007**) were launched by **Ariane** from **Kourou**.
Operator today: **NSIL** (**10** satellites transferred in **2022**).

37.s: The Indian National Satellite (INSAT) system is best described as a:
o: Combined communication and meteorological satellite system
37.x: INSAT serves both communication and meteorology from geostationary orbit (JPSC 2021 keyed it as a 'meteorological satellite'), and also carries broadcasting, disaster warning and search-and-rescue. It is not purely military, not a sun-synchronous remote-sensing system (that is IRS), and not a navigation system (that is NavIC).
37.tq: INSAT = comms + weather, from GEO.
xs: INSAT is a **combined communication and meteorological** system — option **(2)**; JPSC **2021** keyed it as "**Meteorological Satellite**".
It sits on a **geostationary** platform, so it is not a sun-synchronous remote-sensing system, and it also serves civil broadcasting, so it is not purely military.
xa: It also carries **TV broadcasting, disaster warning and search-and-rescue**.
Joint venture of **DoS, DoT, IMD, AIR and Doordarshan**, coordinated by the **ICC**.
First INSAT: **INSAT-1A** (**1982**); system commissioned **1983**.

37.s: In 2022, India's in-orbit communication satellites (10 of them) were transferred to which entity?
37.x: In 2022, 10 in-orbit communication satellites were transferred to NSIL, ISRO's commercial-arm CPSE, which now operates them. Antrix is the older commercial arm; IN-SPACe is the regulator; DoT was one of the original INSAT partners but is not the operator.
37.tq: Satcom operator today = NSIL (2022).
xs: In **2022**, **10** in-orbit communication satellites were transferred to **NewSpace India Limited (NSIL)** — option **(3)**.
NSIL is today's **operator** of the communication fleet.
xa: India has **19** operational communication satellites (**2026**).
**DoT** was one of the original INSAT joint-venture partners (with **DoS, IMD, AIR, Doordarshan**).
Control centre: **MCF, Hassan (Karnataka)**.

37.s: Which one of the following statements about GSAT-11 is correct?
o: It is a dedicated Navy satellite launched in 2013.
It was the first operational satellite of the INSAT system in 1983.
It is a 2015 satellite with a large deployable antenna for mobile communication.
It is India’s heaviest communication satellite, weighing approximately 5.8 tonnes, and supports high-speed rural broadband.
37.x: D is correct: GSAT-11 (2018), about 5.8 tonnes, is the heaviest ISRO-built communication satellite and serves high-speed internet and rural broadband. A describes GSAT-7 'Rukmini' (Navy, 2013), B describes INSAT-1B (system commissioned 1983) and C describes GSAT-6 (2015).
37.tq: Use the distinctive weight and broadband function to separate GSAT-11 from the other satellites.
xs: **GSAT-11** (**2018**) is the **heaviest ISRO-built** communication satellite (~**5.8 t**), for **high-speed internet and rural broadband** — option **(4)**.
The **2013 Navy** satellite is **GSAT-7 "Rukmini"**; the **2015** deployable-antenna satellite is **GSAT-6**.
The system was **commissioned in 1983**, operational since **INSAT-1B**.
xa: ⚠ **GSAT-11** = heaviest ISRO-built (launched abroad); **CMS-03** = heaviest communication satellite from **Indian soil** (**4,410 kg**).
GSAT-11 supports **Digital India** and is a **Ka-band** high-throughput satellite.
It was launched from **Kourou** by **Ariane**.

37.s:
Consider the following statements regarding INSAT-1 series:
1. The first INSAT satellites were bought abroad.
2. The INSAT system was commissioned in 1983.
3. The series began from 1992 with INSAT-2A.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
37.x: The INSAT-1 satellites were procured from abroad and the INSAT system was commissioned in 1983. Statement 3 is false because the INSAT-2 series began in 1992.
37.tq: Split the options by checking the series start dates before considering the combined code.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 correct: the **INSAT-1** satellites were **bought abroad**.
Statement 2 correct: the INSAT system was **commissioned in 1983**.
Statement 3 wrong: **1992** marks the **INSAT-2** series (**2A-2E**, **1992-1999**), not INSAT-1.
xa: **INSAT-1A** (**1982**) was the first INSAT.
INSAT-2 was the **first fully indigenous** INSAT series.
**APPLE** (**1981**) was India's first experimental communication satellite.

37.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: GSAT-8 — Cyclone-warning satellite without communication payloads
37.x: EDUSAT, also designated GSAT-3, was intended for education and provided two-way classroom links. The other satellites have been matched with incorrect functions.
37.tq: Start with the sure purpose-satellite pair and reject swapped applications.
xs: **EDUSAT (GSAT-3)** — **two-way classroom links** is correct — option **(1)**.
**INSAT-3D** is for **advanced meteorology**; **GSAT-8** is a **communication** satellite carrying **GAGAN**.
The first experimental communication satellite was **APPLE**, not GSAT-11.
xa: EDUSAT: launched **20 Sep 2004** by **GSLV-F01**; **1,950.5 kg**; at **74°E**.
Other social services: **GRAMSAT**, telemedicine, **Village Resource Centres**.
**Swayam Prabha** uses **GSAT-15** for **40 free DTH education channels**.

37.s: Which one of the following combinations regarding INSAT-3D and INSAT-3DR is correct?
o: INSAT-3D—1983; television broadcasting; INSAT-3DR—1992; mobile communication
INSAT-3D—2013; advanced meteorology; INSAT-3DR—2016; advanced meteorology
37.x: INSAT-3D was launched in 2013 and INSAT-3DR in 2016; both serve advanced meteorological purposes.
37.tq: Compare the two closely named satellites by year and common application.
xs: **INSAT-3D** (**2013**) and **INSAT-3DR** (**2016**) both serve **advanced meteorology** — option **(3)**.
They track **cyclones, monsoon and rainfall**; with 3D, 3DR cut cyclone deaths (**Phailin, Fani, Amphan**).
xa: **INSAT-3DS** data now feed **Bhuvan** cyclone and flood warnings (Apr **2026**).
Their warnings sharply cut cyclone deaths on the **east coast, incl. AP**.
**KALPANA-1** (**Sep 2002**, PSLV) was the **first exclusive meteorological** satellite.

37.s: Which one of the following statements about GSAT-8 is correct?
o: It was launched on 21 May 2011 by Ariane-5 and carried a GAGAN payload.
It was launched in 2020 by GSLV-F01 for two-way classroom links.
It was launched in 2018 by Falcon 9 and carried only a military payload.
It was launched in 2004 by PSLV and functioned as an exclusive weather satellite.
37.x: GSAT-8 was launched on 21 May 2011 by Ariane-5 and carried a GAGAN payload; GSAT-10 and GSAT-15 also carried GAGAN payloads.
37.tq: Use the date-launcher-payload combination to distinguish GSAT-8 from nearby GSAT missions.
xs: **GSAT-8** was launched on **21 May 2011** by **Ariane-5** and carries a **GAGAN** payload — option **(1)**.
**GSLV-F01** launched **EDUSAT** (**2004**); the PSLV-launched exclusive weather satellite was **KALPANA-1** (**2002**).
xa: **GAGAN** payloads also fly on **GSAT-10** and **GSAT-15**.
Other Kourou/Ariane launches: **INSAT-3A**, **INSAT-4A**, **INSAT-4B**, **GSAT-11**, **GSAT-31**, **GSAT-30**.
GSAT-15 also serves **Swayam Prabha** (**40** DTH education channels).

37.s:
Arrange the following satellites in chronological order of their stated launch dates:
A. GSAT-30
B. KALPANA-1
C. EDUSAT
D. GSAT-8
37.x: KALPANA-1 was launched in 2002, EDUSAT in 2004, GSAT-8 in 2011 and GSAT-30 in 2020.
37.tq: Fix the earliest and latest items first, then place the middle satellites by year.
xs: The order is **B, C, D, A** — option **(1)**.
xa: KALPANA-1 (METSAT) was the **first exclusive meteorological** satellite, launched by **PSLV**.
EDUSAT flew on **GSLV-F01**; GSAT-30 flew from **Kourou** (APPSC **2018** PYQ: telecommunication).
**GSAT-31** was launched from Kourou on **6 Feb 2019**.

37.s: Which of the following is correctly matched?
o: INSAT-2 — first fully indigenous INSAT series
KALPANA-1 — first South Asia regional communication satellite
INSAT-3DR — first fully indigenous INSAT series
37.x: INSAT-2 was the first fully indigenous INSAT series. KALPANA-1, not GSAT-9 or INSAT-3DR, was the first exclusive weather satellite.
37.tq: Start with the sure satellite-series and first-achievement pair.
xs: **INSAT-2** (**2A-2E**, **1992-1999**) was the **first fully indigenous** INSAT series — option **(1)**.
**KALPANA-1** was the **first exclusive weather satellite**, not a South Asia satellite.
The South Asia Satellite is **GSAT-9**; **INSAT-3DR** (**2016**) is an advanced meteorology satellite.
xa: The earlier **INSAT-1** series was **bought abroad**.
**INSAT-1A** (**1982**) was the first INSAT.
GSAT-9 flew in **May 2017** on **GSLV-F09**; **Pakistan opted out**.

37.s: Which satellite was described as the heaviest communication satellite launched from Indian soil, weighing 4,410 kg and intended for the Navy?
37.x: CMS-03, also designated GSAT-7R, weighed 4,410 kg and was described as the heaviest communication satellite launched from Indian soil for the Navy.
37.tq: Combine payload mass, satellite identity and user organisation.
xs: **CMS-03 (GSAT-7R)**, **4,410 kg**, is the **heaviest communication satellite launched from Indian soil**, for the **Navy** — option **(4)**.
It flew on **LVM3-M5** in **Nov 2025**.
xa: ⚠ **GSAT-11** (~**5.8 t**) is the heaviest **ISRO-built**, but was launched abroad.
CMS-03 gives **encrypted, anti-jam** naval links up to **2,000 km** from the coast.
It replaced **GSAT-7 "Rukmini"**; it carries **UHF, S, C, Ku** bands.

37.s: GSAT-30, launched on 17 January 2020 from Kourou, French Guiana, is primarily a:
37.x: GSAT-30 is a telecommunication satellite launched by Ariane from Kourou on 17 Jan 2020 (APPSC 2018 PYQ theme). Navigation is NavIC/NVS, earth observation is EOS/IRS, and the exclusive weather satellite was KALPANA-1.
37.tq: GSAT = communication; Kourou 2020 = GSAT-30.
xs: **GSAT-30** is a **telecommunication** satellite — option **(1)** (APPSC **2018** PYQ).
It was launched on **17 Jan 2020** from **Kourou** by Ariane.
The **exclusive meteorological** satellite was **KALPANA-1**.
xa: **GSAT-31** was also launched from Kourou on **6 Feb 2019**.
Other Kourou launches: **INSAT-3A** (**2003**), **INSAT-4A** (**2005**), **INSAT-4B** (**2007**), **GSAT-8**, **GSAT-11**.
**GSAT-N2** instead flew on SpaceX **Falcon 9** from **Cape Canaveral**.

37.s: Which one of the following sets contains only Indian communication satellites launched from Kourou by Ariane?
37.x: INSAT-3A, INSAT-4A, INSAT-4B and GSAT-8 are among the Indian communication satellites launched from Kourou by Ariane.
37.tq: Group the satellites by launcher and location, rejecting satellites associated with Indian or US launchers.
xs: **INSAT-3A, INSAT-4A, INSAT-4B and GSAT-8** were all launched from **Kourou** by **Ariane** — option **(1)**.
**EDUSAT** flew on **GSLV-F01**, **CMS-03** on **LVM3-M5**, and **GSAT-N2** on **Falcon 9**; **GSAT-7B** is only proposed.
xa: Kourou is in **French Guiana**.
**INSAT-4C** was lost on **GSLV-F02** (**2006**).

37.s: GSAT-N2 was launched by
o: US Space Shuttle from Kennedy Space Center
37.x: GSAT-N2 was launched by SpaceX’s Falcon 9 from Cape Canaveral.
37.tq: Separate the recent commercial foreign launch from the earlier Ariane launches.
xs: **GSAT-N2** was launched by **SpaceX Falcon 9** from **Cape Canaveral** — option **(2)**.
Ariane-5 from **Kourou** launched other GSATs such as **GSAT-8**; **GSLV-F02** failed with **INSAT-4C**.
xa: GSAT-N2 (**GSAT-20**), **Nov 2024**, is for **broadband and in-flight connectivity**.
It is a **Ka-band** high-throughput satellite, listed with **GSAT-19, GSAT-29, GSAT-11**.
These broadband satellites complement **BharatNet**.

37.s: Which satellite is correctly matched with its principal use?
o: GSAT-6 — Large deployable antenna for mobile and strategic communication
GSAT-11 — First operational satellite of the INSAT system
37.x: GSAT-6, launched in 2015, has a large deployable antenna and supports mobile and strategic communication. GSAT-7 serves the Navy, GSAT-7A serves the Air Force, and INSAT-1B marked operationalisation of INSAT.
37.tq: Start with the satellite-use pair and watch for swapped defence roles and chronology.
xs: **GSAT-6** (**2015**) has a **large deployable antenna for mobile/strategic use** — option **(3)**.
**GSAT-7** is the **Navy** satellite and **GSAT-7A** the **Air Force** satellite — options (1) and (2) swap them.
The INSAT system became operational with **INSAT-1B** (**1983**), not GSAT-11.
xa: ⚠ **Rukmini** = Navy; **Angry Bird** = Air Force; **GSAT-7B** = Army.
GSAT-7 was replaced by **CMS-03** (GSAT-7R).
**GSAT-11** (**2018**) is the heaviest ISRO-built communication satellite.

37.s:
Arrange the following satellites in chronological order of the years stated for them:
A. GSAT-7
B. GSAT-6
C. GSAT-7A
D. GSAT-11
37.x: The sequence is GSAT-7 (2013), GSAT-6 (2015), GSAT-7A (2018) and GSAT-11 (2018).
37.tq: Fix the earliest satellite first and then distinguish the two 2018 entries by their stated sequence.
xs: The order is **A, B, C, D** — option **(1)**.
xa: GSAT-7 **"Rukmini"** = Navy; GSAT-7A **"Angry Bird"** = Air Force.
GSAT-6 has a **large deployable antenna** for mobile/strategic use.
GSAT-11 (~**5.8 t**) is the **heaviest ISRO-built** communication satellite.

37.s:
Match the strategic satellites with their users:

a. GSAT-7 'Rukmini'
b. GSAT-7A 'Angry Bird'
c. GSAT-7B (proposed)

i. Indian Air Force
ii. Indian Army
iii. Indian Navy
37.x: GSAT-7 'Rukmini' (2013) is the Navy satellite (later replaced by CMS-03), GSAT-7A 'Angry Bird' (2018) is the dedicated Air Force satellite, and GSAT-7B is proposed for the Army. The other codes swap the Navy and Air Force or the Army.
37.tq: Rukmini = Navy; Angry Bird = Air Force; 7B = Army.
xs: **Rukmini — Navy**, **Angry Bird — Air Force**, **GSAT-7B — Army** — option **(1) a-iii, b-i, c-ii**.
**GSAT-7 "Rukmini"** (**2013**) is the Navy satellite, later replaced by **CMS-03**.
**GSAT-7A "Angry Bird"** (**2018**) is the dedicated **Air Force** satellite; **GSAT-7B** is **proposed** for the Army.
xa: **CMS-03 (GSAT-7R)**, **4,410 kg**, gives **encrypted, anti-jam** links up to **2,000 km** from the coast.
**GSAT-6** (**2015**) has a large deployable antenna for mobile/strategic use.
**UHF** band is used for **military** communication.

37.s:
Match List-I (Band) with List-II (Typical use):
List-I
a. C / extended C
b. Ku
c. Ka
d. S
List-II
i. High-throughput broadband
ii. DTH and VSAT
iii. Telecom and TV distribution
iv. Mobile satellite services and DWS downlink
Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
37.x: C/extended C is used for telecom and TV distribution (iii), Ku for DTH and VSAT (ii), Ka for high-throughput broadband such as GSAT-11 and GSAT-N2 (i), and S for mobile satellite services and the DWS downlink (iv). Option B swaps C and Ku, option C swaps Ku and Ka, option D swaps C and S.
37.tq: Higher band letter, higher frequency, more bandwidth: Ka is the broadband band.
xs: **C** → telecom/TV distribution; **Ku** → DTH, VSAT; **Ka** → high-throughput broadband; **S** → mobile services and DWS downlink — option **(1) a-iii, b-ii, c-i, d-iv**.
Ka-band broadband satellites include **GSAT-11** and **GSAT-N2**.
xa: C-band covers **4-8 GHz**; Ku-band **12-18 GHz**.
**UHF** is used for **military** links (CMS-03 has **UHF, S, C, Ku**).
**MF is not used** in INSAT/GSAT communication (RPSC **2021**).
⚠ DWS: uplink **C-band**, downlink **S-band**.

37.s: Which of the following satellites is associated with UHF, S and C bands in the stated communication configuration?
37.x: CMS-03 has UHF, S and C bands in the stated configuration; UHF is associated with military applications.
37.tq: Identify the satellite from the unusual combination of three transponder bands.
xs: **CMS-03** carries **UHF, S, C and Ku** bands — option **(4)**.
**UHF** is the **military** band, fitting CMS-03's **Navy** role.
**INSAT-3D** and **KALPANA-1** are meteorological satellites; **EDUSAT** is for education.
xa: CMS-03 (**GSAT-7R**) flew on **LVM3-M5** in **Nov 2025**; **4,410 kg**.
It gives **encrypted, anti-jam** naval links up to **2,000 km** from the coast.
**S-band** serves mobile satellite services and the **DWS downlink**.

37.s: Which of the following sets contains only high-throughput or broadband satellites?
37.x: GSAT-19, GSAT-29, GSAT-11 and GSAT-N2 are identified with high-throughput broadband services for underserved areas, in-flight links and defence, complementing BharatNet.
37.tq: Group satellites by service category and reject meteorological, educational and strategic-only sets.
xs: **GSAT-19, GSAT-29, GSAT-11 and GSAT-N2** are the high-throughput/broadband satellites — option **(1)**.
**KALPANA-1, INSAT-3D/3DR** are meteorological; **GSAT-7** series and **GSAT-6** are strategic; **APPLE/INSAT-1** are early satellites.
xa: Uses: **underserved areas**, **in-flight links**, **defence**.
They **complement BharatNet**.
**Ka-band** is used for high-throughput broadband (GSAT-11, GSAT-N2).

37.s: Which one of the following frequency bands is NOT used for INSAT/GSAT satellite communication?
37.x: MF is not used in INSAT/GSAT communication (RPSC 2021). C/extended C serves telecom and TV distribution, Ku serves DTH and VSAT, and S serves mobile satellite services and the DWS downlink.
37.tq: Satellites use C, Ku, Ka, S, UHF; not MF.
xs: **MF (Medium Frequency)** is **not used** in INSAT/GSAT communication — option **(4)** (RPSC **2021**).
**C-band** serves telecom and TV distribution; **Ku** serves **DTH and VSAT**; **S** serves mobile satellite services and the **DWS downlink**.
xa: **Ka-band** is for high-throughput broadband (**GSAT-11**, **GSAT-N2**).
**UHF** is for **military** use (CMS-03).
C-band: **4-8 GHz**; Ku-band: **12-18 GHz**.

37.s: Which of the following best describes the stated role of Starlink’s proposed Indian satellite internet service in 2025?
o: Registering newspapers through a satellite-based portal
Replacing all terrestrial fibre networks in urban areas
Providing broadband to remote, disaster-hit and mobile areas
37.x: Starlink’s India launch was imminent in 2025 and its stated advantage was broadband access for remote, disaster-hit and mobile areas.
37.tq: Apply the service’s coverage advantage to the locations and situations described.
xs: Starlink's India launch (imminent in **2025**) was to bring **broadband to remote, disaster-hit and mobile areas** — option **(4)**.
It is not a Navy-only service nor a replacement for urban fibre.
xa: Satcom covers the **20-25%** of Indians outside easy terrestrial coverage.
ISRO's own broadband satellites — **GSAT-19, -29, -11, GSAT-N2** — complement **BharatNet**.
**GSAT-N2** also offers **in-flight connectivity**.

37.s: Which of the following is NOT an application served by the INSAT/GSAT system?
o: Extraction of petroleum directly from underground reservoirs
37.x: INSAT/GSAT applications include DSNG, mobile satellite services and satellite-aided search and rescue, but satellites do not directly extract petroleum from underground reservoirs.
37.tq: Find the unrelated activity among the recognised communication and service applications.
xs: **Extracting petroleum from underground reservoirs** is NOT an INSAT/GSAT application — option **(1)**.
INSAT/GSAT services include **DSNG** (satellite news gathering), **mobile satellite services** and **satellite-aided search and rescue**.
xa: Other services: **DTH**, **VSAT** business networks, radio networking.
Social uses: **EDUSAT**, **GRAMSAT**, telemedicine, **Village Resource Centres**.
Search-and-rescue transponders work under **COSPAS-SARSAT**.

37.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Application)
A. DTH
B. VSAT
C. DSNG
D. MSS

List-II (Description)
I. Mobile satellite services
II. Satellite news gathering
III. Direct-to-Home broadcasting
IV. Business networks through very small aperture terminals

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
37.x: DTH means Direct-to-Home broadcasting, VSAT supports business networks, DSNG means satellite news gathering, and MSS means mobile satellite services.
37.tq: Begin with the unambiguous acronym expansions and complete the matching code.
xs: **DTH** – Direct-to-Home; **VSAT** – business networks; **DSNG** – satellite news gathering; **MSS** – mobile satellite services — option **(1) A–III, B–IV, C–II, D–I**.
All four are listed INSAT/GSAT communication services.
xa: **Ku-band** carries **DTH and VSAT**; **S-band** carries mobile satellite services.
**Swayam Prabha** uses **GSAT-15** for **40 free DTH education channels**.
Other services: radio networking, **telemedicine**, **Village Resource Centres**.

37.s: Which one of the following statements regarding Swayam Prabha is correct?
o: It uses INSAT-4CR to provide satellite-aided search-and-rescue services.
It uses KALPANA-1 to transmit cyclone warnings to coastal receivers.
It uses GSAT-11 to provide only military broadband channels.
It uses GSAT-15 to beam 40 free DTH education channels.
37.x: Swayam Prabha uses GSAT-15 to provide 40 free Direct-to-Home education channels.
37.tq: Match the named education initiative with its satellite and channel count.
xs: **Swayam Prabha** uses **GSAT-15** to beam **40 free DTH education channels** — option **(4)**.
Search-and-rescue is via INSAT under **COSPAS-SARSAT**; cyclone warnings go via the **DWS**.
xa: GSAT-15 also carries a **GAGAN** payload (with **GSAT-8**, **GSAT-10**).
**EDUSAT (GSAT-3)** provided **two-way classroom links**.
Other social services: **GRAMSAT**, telemedicine, **Village Resource Centres**.

37.s: In the Disaster Warning System, cyclone warnings from the Cyclone Warning Centre at Chennai are
o: sent upward through S-band and received through C-band by all receivers without selection
sent upward through UHF and received through MF by television households
sent upward through C-band and received through S-band by selectively addressable receivers
sent upward through Ku-band and received through Ka-band only by military stations
37.x: The warning signal goes up on C-band and comes down on S-band to selectively addressable DWS receivers along the coast.
37.tq: Trace the communication path in order: uplink band, downlink band and receiver type.
xs: DWS warnings go **up on C-band** and **down on S-band** to **selectively addressable receivers** — option **(3)**.
The warnings originate at the **Cyclone Warning Centre, Chennai**.
**MF** is not used in INSAT communication; **UHF** is a military band.
xa: DWS receivers are placed **along the coast**.
**INSAT-3D/3DR** warnings sharply cut cyclone deaths on the east coast, incl. **AP**.
INSAT also carries **search-and-rescue** transponders under **COSPAS-SARSAT**.

37.s: Which organisation receives Bay of Bengal cyclone-track data supplied by SDSC-SHAR for disaster-management purposes?
37.x: SDSC-SHAR supplies Bay of Bengal cyclone-track data to the Andhra Pradesh State Disaster Management Authority (APSDMA).
37.tq: Identify the receiving disaster-management authority rather than the supplying centre.
xs: **SDSC-SHAR** supplies **Bay of Bengal cyclone-track data** to **APSDMA** — option **(4)**.
**AIR** is a partner in the INSAT joint venture; the **ICC** coordinates INSAT; **BharatNet** is the terrestrial broadband network.
xa: The **DWS** relays warnings from the **Cyclone Warning Centre, Chennai** (uplink **C-band**, downlink **S-band**).
**INSAT-3D/3DR** early warnings cut cyclone deaths (**Phailin, Fani, Amphan**).
**INSAT-3DS** data feed **Bhuvan** cyclone and flood warnings (Apr **2026**).

37.s: INSAT’s search-and-rescue transponders operate under the international programme known as
37.x: INSAT carries search-and-rescue transponders under the international COSPAS-SARSAT programme.
37.tq: Separate search-and-rescue terminology from navigation and education programmes.
xs: INSAT's search-and-rescue transponders work under the international **COSPAS-SARSAT** programme — option **(3)**.
**Swayam Prabha** is a DTH education service; **GAGAN** is a payload on **GSAT-8, -10, -15**; **BharatNet** is terrestrial broadband.
xa: INSAT's multipurpose platform also covers telecom, **TV broadcasting**, **meteorology** and **disaster warning**.
⚠ DWS: uplink **C-band**, downlink **S-band**.
INSAT is controlled from **MCF, Hassan**.

37.s: The South Asia Satellite is designated as which of the following?
37.x: The South Asia Satellite is designated as GSAT-9.
37.tq: Direct identification of a satellite designation.
xs: The South Asia Satellite is **GSAT-9** — option **(3)**.
**GSAT-8** carries **GAGAN**; **INSAT-3DR** is meteorological; **GSAT-7R** is the Navy's **CMS-03**.
xa: Launched in **May 2017** on **GSLV-F09**.
**Pakistan opted out** of it.
Strategic GSATs: **Rukmini** (Navy), **Angry Bird** (Air Force), **GSAT-7B** (Army, proposed).

37.s: GSAT-9, the South Asia Satellite, was launched in which month and year using GSLV-F09?
37.x: GSAT-9 was launched in May 2017 by the GSLV-F09 launch vehicle.
37.tq: Distinguish the closely placed launch year and vehicle details.
xs: **GSAT-9** was launched in **May 2017** on **GSLV-F09** — option **(2)**.
It is the **South Asia Satellite**.
xa: **Pakistan opted out** of the project.
**GSAT-6** was launched in **2015** with a large deployable antenna.
**GSAT-7A "Angry Bird"** (**2018**) serves the Air Force.

37.s: Which South Asian country opted out of the South Asia Satellite (GSAT-9) launched by India in May 2017?
37.x: Pakistan opted out of the South Asia Satellite (GSAT-9, GSLV-F09, May 2017). Nepal, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka are among the neighbours meant to benefit from it.
37.tq: GSAT-9 = South Asia Satellite; Pakistan out.
xs: **Pakistan opted out** of the South Asia Satellite — option **(3)**.
The satellite is **GSAT-9**, launched in **May 2017** on **GSLV-F09**.
xa: Strategic GSATs: **GSAT-7 "Rukmini"** (Navy, **2013**), **GSAT-7A "Angry Bird"** (Air Force, **2018**).
**GSAT-7B** is proposed for the **Army**.

37.s: Which one of the following correctly describes CMS-03, also designated GSAT-7R?
o: A weather satellite launched by GSLV-F09 for cyclone-warning services
A commercial communication satellite placed in low Earth orbit by LVM3-M6
An encrypted satellite providing anti-jam naval links up to 2,000 km from the coast, launched by LVM3-M5
A navigation satellite providing regional positioning services through PSLV
37.x: CMS-03/GSAT-7R is associated with encrypted, anti-jam naval links extending up to 2,000 km from the coast and was launched using LVM3-M5.
37.tq: Match the satellite with its specific defence application and launch vehicle.
xs: **CMS-03 (GSAT-7R)** gives **encrypted, anti-jam naval links** up to **2,000 km** from the coast and flew on **LVM3-M5** — option **(3)**.
**GSLV-F09** launched **GSAT-9**, the South Asia Satellite.
xa: Launched **Nov 2025**; **4,410 kg** — heaviest communication satellite from **Indian soil** (LENS gives **4,400 kg**).
It replaced **GSAT-7 "Rukmini"** for the **Navy**.
Bands: **UHF, S, C, Ku**.

37.s: The early-warning capability of INSAT-3D and INSAT-3DR has had which of the following effects?
o: It sharply reduced cyclone-related deaths on the east coast, including Andhra Pradesh.
It provided encrypted naval communication up to 2,000 km from the coast.
It made BlueBird Block-2 the largest satellite in low Earth orbit.
It enabled the South Asian countries to opt out of satellite services.
37.x: INSAT-3D and INSAT-3DR early warnings sharply reduced cyclone deaths along the east coast, including Andhra Pradesh.
37.tq: Identify the concrete consequence of a satellite-based warning system.
xs: **INSAT-3D/3DR** early warnings **sharply cut cyclone deaths** on the **east coast, incl. Andhra Pradesh** — option **(1)**.
Encrypted naval links up to **2,000 km** are **CMS-03's** role, not INSAT-3D's.
xa: INSAT-3D (**2013**) and INSAT-3DR (**2016**) serve **advanced meteorology** (cyclone, monsoon, rainfall).
Cyclones cited: **Phailin, Fani, Amphan**.
**INSAT-3DS** data feed **Bhuvan** warnings (Apr **2026**).

37.s: KALPANA-1 holds which distinction in the Indian satellite programme?
o: First fully indigenous communication satellite series
First satellite for encrypted naval links
First commercial communication satellite in low Earth orbit
37.x: KALPANA-1 was India's first exclusive weather satellite.
37.tq: Direct recall of a first-in-category distinction.
xs: **KALPANA-1** is India's **first exclusive weather satellite** — option **(4)**.
The **first fully indigenous** INSAT series is **INSAT-2** (**1992-1999**); encrypted naval links are **CMS-03**.
xa: KALPANA-1 (**METSAT**) was launched in **Sep 2002** by **PSLV**.
Later weather satellites: **INSAT-3D** (**2013**), **INSAT-3DR** (**2016**), **INSAT-3DS**.
INSAT is a dual **meteorological + communication** system (JPSC **2021**).

38.s:
Consider the following statements about GPS:
1. It was started by the US Department of Defense in 1973.
2. Its original design has 24 satellites in 6 orbits at about 20,200 km.
3. Each GPS satellite circles the Earth once a day.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
38.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: GPS began in 1973 under the US DoD, with 24 satellites in 6 orbits at 20,200 km. Statement 3 is wrong: each satellite circles the Earth twice a day (once a day would be geosynchronous). So '1 and 2 only'; the other options include statement 3 or omit a true one.
38.tq: 20,200 km is well below 36,000 km, so the period is shorter than a day - 12 hours.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 correct: **GPS** is a **US Department of Defense** programme started in **1973**.
Statement 2 correct: **24** satellites in **6** orbits at **20,200 km**.
Statement 3 wrong: each GPS satellite circles the Earth **twice a day**, not once.
xa: First GPS satellite: **1978**; now about **30** satellites (Mar **2026**).
⚠ **GPS** = 24 satellites, 6 orbits, global; **NavIC** = **7** satellites, regional.

38.s: An error of approximately one microsecond in an atomic clock used for positioning may produce a position error of about:
38.x: A one-microsecond clock error can produce an approximate position error of 300 metres, illustrating the importance of atomic clocks in navigation.
38.tq: Convert the stated clock-error relationship without changing the unit scale.
xs: A **1 microsecond** clock error gives a position error of ~**300 metres** (300 m) — option **(3)**.
This is why navigation satellites carry **atomic clocks**.
xa: NavIC's first-generation **SpectraTime** (Swiss) rubidium clocks kept failing → ISRO switched to **indigenous SAC clocks** in **2018**.
**NVS-01** was the first with an **indigenous rubidium atomic clock**.
NavIC SPS gives timing better than **40 ns**.

38.s: Which of the following statements about GPS signals is correct?
o: GPS signals are confined to marine navigation.
GPS uses signals on L1 at 1,575.42 MHz and on L2.
GPS operates only on NavIC’s S band.
GPS transmits only a civilian L5 signal and no L1 signal.
38.x: GPS uses the L1 signal at 1,575.42 MHz and the L2 signal. Its applications extend well beyond marine navigation.
38.tq: Match the exact frequency and bands while rejecting scope and system swaps.
xs: GPS uses **L1 (1,575.42 MHz)** and **L2** signals — option **(2)**.
**L5 and S** are **NavIC's** bands, not GPS's, so options (3) and (4) are wrong.
xa: GPS: **US DoD**, started **1973**, first satellite **1978**.
Design: **24** satellites, **6** orbits, **20,200 km**.
NavIC's newer **NVS** satellites add a civilian **L1** signal, compatible with other GNSS.

38.s: Although GPS was designed with 24 satellites, approximately how many GPS satellites are in operation as of March 2026?
38.x: GPS was designed with 24 satellites in 6 orbits, but about 30 satellites are now in operation (March 2026).
38.tq: Designed 24, now ~30.
xs: About **30** GPS satellites operate now (Mar **2026**) — option **(3)**.
The original design was **24** satellites in **6** orbits.
xa: They orbit at **20,200 km**, each circling **twice a day**.
GPS started in **1973**; first satellite **1978**.
NavIC, by contrast, has **7** satellites (**3 GEO + 4** inclined GSO).

38.s:
Consider the following statements about NavIC:
1. It was formerly called IRNSS.
2. It became fully operational in 2013.
3. Its genesis lies in the US denial of GPS data during the 1999 Kargil War.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
38.x: Statement 1 is correct: NavIC was formerly IRNSS. Statement 2 is wrong: NavIC became fully operational in 2018 (navigation satellites have been launched since 2013). Statement 3 is correct: GPS data denial in the 1999 Kargil War prompted it. So '1 and 3 only'; options including 2 are wrong and '1 and 2 only' also drops 3.
38.tq: Kargil 1999 -> idea; 2013 first launches; 2018 fully operational.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option **(3) 1 and 3 only**.
Statement 1 correct: **NavIC** (Navigation with Indian Constellation) was formerly **IRNSS**.
Statement 2 wrong: NavIC became **fully operational in 2018**; **2013** is when navigation satellite launches began.
Statement 3 correct: the US **denied GPS data** in the **1999 Kargil War**.
xa: Full form "Navigation with Indian Constellation" was asked in **CGPSC 2021**.
**11** navigation satellites launched since **2013** (Mar **2026**).
Coverage: India + **1,500 km** beyond its borders.

38.s:
With reference to the NavIC constellation, consider the following statements:
1. It consists of seven satellites.
2. Three satellites are in geostationary orbit.
3. Four satellites are in inclined geosynchronous orbit at about 29° to the equator.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
38.x: NavIC’s planned constellation has seven satellites: three in geostationary orbit and four in inclined geosynchronous orbit at about 29° to the equator.
38.tq: Verify the total and split the constellation into its two orbital groups.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
NavIC has **7 satellites**: **3 GEO** + **4 inclined GSO** at **29°** to the equator.
xa: Coverage: India + **1,500 km** beyond its borders.
Bands: **L5 and S**; **NVS** satellites add civilian **L1**.
⚠ **GPS** = **24** satellites, **6** orbits, **20,200 km**, global.

38.s: The primary service area of NavIC extends over India and approximately:
38.x: NavIC provides coverage over India and approximately 1,500 km beyond India’s borders.
38.tq: Distinguish the regional coverage figure from global-system coverage.
xs: NavIC covers India and about **1,500 km beyond its borders** — option **(1)**.
This **regional** coverage is listed as a limitation versus **global GPS**.
xa: Constellation: **7** satellites (**3 GEO + 4** inclined GSO).
SPS accuracy: better than **20 m** for all civilians.
**Restricted Service (RS)** is **encrypted**, for authorised/military users.

38.s: Which frequency bands are associated with the original NavIC services?
38.x: NavIC traditionally provides signals in the L5 and S bands. The NVS series additionally introduces an L1 civilian signal.
38.tq: Avoid importing the familiar GPS bands into the NavIC question.
xs: Original NavIC signals are in the **L5 and S** bands — option **(4)**.
**L1 and L2** are **GPS** signals; newer **NVS** satellites add a civilian **L1** to NavIC.
xa: The L1 signal is **compatible with other GNSS** → eases **phone adoption**.
Thin receiver ecosystem: **L5/S** were not in common phone chips until L1 on NVS.
**Qualcomm Snapdragon** chipsets support NavIC.

38.s: The major signal-related improvement introduced by the NVS series is the addition of:
38.x: The NVS series adds a civilian L1 signal compatible with other GNSS systems, helping mobile-phone adoption.
38.tq: Identify the exact new band and its civilian-use implication.
xs: The **NVS** series adds a **civilian L1 signal** — option **(4)**.
L1 is **compatible with other GNSS**, easing **phone adoption**.
xa: Original NavIC bands: **L5 and S**.
**NVS-01** (**May 2023**, **GSLV-F12**) is the second-generation satellite with the first **indigenous rubidium clock**.
GPS's L1 runs at **1,575.42 MHz**.

38.s: Which one of the following correctly describes NavIC’s Standard Positioning Service?
o: It is available only to authorised military users and is encrypted.
It is available only outside India and offers accuracy better than 100 metres.
It is a timing-only service without positioning capability.
It is available to all civilians and offers accuracy better than 20 metres.
38.x: The Standard Positioning Service is available to all civilian users and has a design positioning accuracy better than 20 metres.
38.tq: Contrast civilian SPS with the authorised and encrypted Restricted Service.
xs: **Standard Positioning Service (SPS)** is for **all civilians**, accuracy better than **20 m** — option **(4)**.
Encrypted service for authorised/military users is the **Restricted Service (RS)**, so option (1) is wrong.
SPS also gives **timing** better than **40 ns** — it is not timing-only.
xa: Some notes claim better than **10 m** over India and **20 m** in the extended area.
Coverage: India + **1,500 km**.
NavIC bands: **L5 and S**.

38.s:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
A. First GPS satellite launched
B. GPS programme initiated
C. NavIC became fully operational
D. NVS-01 launched
38.x: The GPS programme began in 1973, its first satellite was launched in 1978, NavIC became fully operational in 2018, and NVS-01 was launched in 2023.
38.tq: Place the events by their years, using the first two close milestones carefully.
xs: The order is **B, A, C, D** — option **(1)**.
**GPS programme**: **1973**; **first GPS satellite**: **1978**.
**NavIC fully operational**: **2018**; **NVS-01**: **May 2023** (GSLV-F12).
xa: NavIC's genesis: US denied GPS data in the **1999 Kargil War**.
**NVS-02** flew on **GSLV-F15** in **Jan 2025** — the **100th** Sriharikota launch.
**IRNSS-1F** lost its last clock on **13 Mar 2026**.

38.s: Which statement regarding the IRNSS satellite launches is correct?
o: All IRNSS satellites were launched from a foreign spaceport using only GSLV vehicles.
All IRNSS satellites were launched from Sriharikota, and the IRNSS-1 series used PSLV launch vehicles.
The IRNSS-1 series was launched only by reusable spaceplanes.
The IRNSS satellites were placed in orbit without launch vehicles.
38.x: The IRNSS satellites were launched from Sriharikota, and the IRNSS-1 series was launched using PSLV vehicles.
38.tq: Combine launch-location and launch-vehicle facts while rejecting absolute but unsupported alternatives.
xs: All IRNSS satellites were launched from **Sriharikota**, with the **IRNSS-1 series on PSLV** — option **(2)**.
None flew from a foreign spaceport.
xa: **IRNSS-1A to 1G** formed the 7 + replacements; **11** navigation satellites since **2013**.
NVS series uses **GSLV**: **NVS-01** (**GSLV-F12**) and **NVS-02** (**GSLV-F15**).
**IRNSS-1D** was decommissioned to **600 km above GEO** (**9 Apr 2026**).

38.s: Which one of the following correctly describes NVS-01?
o: It was launched in January 2025 by GSLV-F15 and suffered a valve glitch.
It was launched in March 2016 by PSLV and was decommissioned above GEO.
It was launched in May 2023 by GSLV-F12 and was the first satellite with an indigenous rubidium atomic clock.
It was launched in 2018 by a foreign launch vehicle without an atomic clock.
38.x: NVS-01, the second-generation satellite, was launched in May 2023 on GSLV-F12 and was the first to carry an indigenous rubidium atomic clock.
38.tq: Match the satellite with its launch date, vehicle and distinctive payload.
xs: **NVS-01** was launched in **May 2023** on **GSLV-F12** and was the **first with an indigenous rubidium atomic clock** — option **(3)**.
**Jan 2025, GSLV-F15, valve glitch** describes **NVS-02**; **Mar 2016, PSLV** describes **IRNSS-1F**.
xa: NVS-01 is the **second-generation** NavIC satellite.
First-generation clocks came from Swiss firm **SpectraTime** and kept failing.
NVS-01 is one of only **3** PNT-capable satellites left (with **IRNSS-1B, 1I**).

38.s: NVS-02 was launched by GSLV-F15 in January 2025, but a valve glitch:
o: left it in the wrong orbit, after which it was salvaged for alternate use
prevented it from carrying any navigation payload
caused it to land in the Bay of Bengal
38.x: A valve glitch left NVS-02 in the wrong orbit, but the satellite was salvaged for alternate use. The launch was also the 100th Sriharikota launch.
38.tq: Track the failure consequence without confusing it with total mission destruction.
xs: A **valve glitch** left **NVS-02** in the **wrong orbit**; it was **salvaged for alternate use** — option **(1)**.
It was launched on **GSLV-F15** in **Jan 2025**.
xa: It was the **100th Sriharikota launch**.
The NVS-02 failure plus **atomic-clock failures** left NavIC unable to replace GPS over India (Mar **2026**).
**NVS-01** (**May 2023**) went up on **GSLV-F12**.

38.s: The launch of NVS-02 in January 2025 was significant because it marked the:
38.x: The NVS-02 mission marked the 100th launch from Sriharikota.
38.tq: Retain the milestone number separately from the satellite’s technical failure.
xs: **NVS-02** (**GSLV-F15**, **Jan 2025**) was the **100th launch from Sriharikota** — option **(4)**.
A **valve glitch** put it in the wrong orbit; it was salvaged for alternate use.
xa: All IRNSS/NavIC satellites were launched from **Sriharikota**.
**NVS-01** flew in **May 2023** on **GSLV-F12**.
**11** navigation satellites launched since **2013**.

38.s: Which statement correctly describes the change in atomic clocks used in IRNSS satellites?
o: IRNSS satellites never used rubidium clocks.
ISRO replaced indigenous clocks with Swiss clocks in 2018 because the indigenous clocks failed.
The clock issue concerned only GPS satellites and not IRNSS satellites.
ISRO replaced repeatedly failing Swiss SpectraTime rubidium clocks with indigenous clocks in 2018.
38.x: First-generation IRNSS satellites used rubidium clocks supplied by Swiss firm SpectraTime, which repeatedly failed; ISRO switched to indigenous clocks in 2018.
38.tq: Track the direction of the technology switch and the supplier’s identity.
xs: ISRO replaced the failing **Swiss SpectraTime rubidium clocks** with **indigenous clocks (SAC)** in **2018** — option **(4)**.
Option (2) reverses it: the **Swiss** clocks failed, not the indigenous ones.
xa: **NVS-01** was the **first with an indigenous rubidium atomic clock**.
**IRNSS-1F's** last clock failed on **13 Mar 2026**.
A **1 microsecond** clock error ≈ **300 m** position error.

38.s: On 13 March 2026, the failure of the last clock on IRNSS-1F resulted in which situation?
o: IRNSS-1F immediately became a new GEO satellite.
Only three PNT-capable satellites remained, below the four needed for the required service.
The constellation gained two additional PNT-capable satellites.
All seven satellites became fully operational.
38.x: After the last clock on IRNSS-1F failed, only IRNSS-1B, IRNSS-1I and NVS-01 remained PNT-capable—three satellites, below the four needed.
38.tq: Count the surviving satellites and compare the number with the service threshold.
xs: Only **3** PNT-capable satellites (**IRNSS-1B, 1I, NVS-01**) remained, **below the 4 needed** — option **(2)**.
**IRNSS-1F** was launched in **Mar 2016**; its **10-year** life ended **10 Mar 2026**.
xa: 1F still continues **one-way messaging** (**15 and 20 Mar 2026**).
**IRNSS-1D** was decommissioned to **600 km above GEO** (**9 Apr 2026**).
ISRO was urged to fix issues before the next **NVS** launches.

38.s: Which company developed India’s first NavIC-based device intended to provide precise directions for infrastructure projects?
38.x: Elena Geo Systems developed India’s first NavIC-based device for precise directions on infrastructure projects.
38.tq: Match the specialised company with its specific technological product.
xs: India's first NavIC-based device was made by **Elena Geo Systems** — option **(3)** (APPSC **2023**).
It gives **precise directions on infrastructure projects**.
**SpectraTime** was the Swiss clock supplier; **AAI** co-developed **GAGAN**; **Qualcomm** makes NavIC-supporting chipsets.
xa: **Qualcomm Snapdragon** chipsets support NavIC.
**MoRTH's AIS-140** rule made NavIC trackers compulsory in **public transport vehicles**.
