65.x: The capacities are Bhadla 2,245 MW, Pavagada 2,050 MW, Kurnool 1,000 MW and Rewa 750 MW. Therefore, the descending order is A, B, D, C.
65.tq: Arrange numerical values from largest to smallest before checking the options.
xs: **Bhadla 2,245 MW > Pavagada 2,050 MW > Kurnool 1,000 MW > Rewa 750 MW** — **A, B, D, C**, option **(1)**.
Bhadla (Jodhpur, **Rajasthan**) is the **largest commissioned** park.
xa: **Khavda** (Kutch, Gujarat): ~**30 GW** solar-wind, world's largest RE park when complete.
**Ananthapuramu-I (NP Kunta)**: **1,500 MW**.
Pavagada is in **Karnataka**; Rewa in **MP**.

65.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
65.x: Kurnool Solar Park has a stated capacity of 1,000 MW. Pavagada, not Kurnool, has a capacity of 2,050 MW.
65.tq: Find the swapped capacity among closely related solar parks.
xs: **Kurnool — 2,050 MW** is wrong: Kurnool is **1,000 MW**; **2,050 MW** is **Pavagada** — option **(1)**.
**NP Kunta 1,500 MW**, **Kadapa 1,000 MW** and **Rewa 750 MW** are correct.
xa: Kurnool and **YSR Kadapa** anchor **Rayalaseema's RE cluster** (Jul 2026).
**Ramagiri** (Ananthapuramu): hybrid solar-wind park.
AP solar: **5,614.52 MW**; nodal agency **NEDCAP**.

65.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Khavda Renewable Energy Park — Kutch, Gujarat
Omkareshwar Floating Solar Park — Jodhpur, Rajasthan
Bhadla Solar Park — Khandwa, Madhya Pradesh
Kurnool Ultra Mega Solar Park — Kutch, Gujarat
65.x: Khavda Renewable Energy Park is located in Kutch, Gujarat. Omkareshwar is in Khandwa, Madhya Pradesh, Bhadla is in Jodhpur, Rajasthan, and Kurnool is in Andhra Pradesh.
65.tq: Use location swaps as the principal elimination trap.
xs: **Khavda RE Park** is in **Kutch, Gujarat** — option **(1)**.
**Omkareshwar** is in **Khandwa, MP**; **Bhadla** in **Jodhpur, Rajasthan**; **Kurnool** in **Andhra Pradesh**.
xa: ⚠ **Bhadla** = largest commissioned park; **Khavda** = largest RE park when complete; **Omkareshwar** = largest floating.
Khavda: ~**30 GW** solar-wind.
Omkareshwar: **278 MW**, to reach **600 MW**.

65.s: Which one of the following statements about the Khavda Renewable Energy Park is correct?
o: It is expected to have approximately 30 GW of solar-wind capacity when complete.
It is a 750 MW park in Madhya Pradesh.
It is a 1,000 MW park located in Andhra Pradesh.
It is India's largest floating solar park with 278 MW capacity.
65.x: Khavda Renewable Energy Park in Gujarat's Kutch region is projected to have approximately 30 GW of solar-wind capacity when complete and is described as the world's largest renewable-energy park.
65.tq: Match the distinctive large figure with the correct project rather than a similar park.
xs: **Khavda** will have ~**30 GW** solar-wind capacity when complete — option **(1)**.
**750 MW in MP** = **Rewa**; **1,000 MW in AP** = **Kurnool**/**Kadapa**; **278 MW floating** = **Omkareshwar**.
xa: It will be the **world's largest RE park** when complete.
Located in **Kutch, Gujarat**.
Gujarat leads India's installed RE.

65.s: Ramagiri in Ananthapuramu district of Andhra Pradesh is known for which type of renewable-energy park?
o: Ultra mega solar park of 2,245 MW
65.x: Ramagiri hosts a hybrid solar-wind park. AP's floating plant is NTPC Simhadri; AP has no geothermal park of this kind; the 2,245 MW park is Bhadla in Rajasthan.
65.tq: Ramagiri = hybrid; NP Kunta = 1,500 MW solar; Simhadri = floating.
xs: **Ramagiri** (Ananthapuramu) is a **hybrid solar-wind park** (APPSC-G2 2023 match) — option **(2)**.
AP's **floating** plant is **NTPC Simhadri**; the **2,245 MW** park is **Bhadla** (Rajasthan).
xa: AP ultra mega parks: **Kurnool**, **NP Kunta**, **Kadapa**.
**Ananthapuramu-I (NP Kunta)**: **1,500 MW**.
AP offered **50,000 acres** of barren land for solar lease.

65.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched with the PM Surya Sarovar Yojana?
o: CFA up to ₹1 crore per MW — SECI implements the scheme
CFA up to ₹1 lakh per MW — IEX implements the scheme
CFA up to ₹5 crore per MW — CERC implements the scheme
CFA up to ₹30 lakh per MW — MNRE implements the scheme
65.x: The PM Surya Sarovar Yojana provides Central Financial Assistance up to ₹1 crore per MW and is implemented by SECI.
65.tq: Start with the sure assistance figure and verify the implementing agency.
xs: **PM Surya Sarovar Yojana** gives **CFA up to Rs 1 crore/MW** and is implemented via **SECI** — option **(1)**.
The other options give wrong CFA figures and wrong agencies (**IEX**, **CERC**, **MNRE**).
xa: Outlay: **Rs 5,070 crore**; target **5,000 MW** floating by **2030-31**.
Mandatory **2-hour storage (10,000 MWh)**.
Cabinet approval: **31 Jul 2026**.
⚠ **PM Surya Ghar** = rooftop (Feb 2024); **PM Surya Sarovar** = floating (Jul 2026).

65.s:
With reference to floating solar potential in India, consider the following statements:
1. The national assessment estimates approximately 102.18 GW on reservoirs.
2. Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh are the leading States with approximately 16 GW and 14 GW respectively.
3. Installed floating solar capacity is approximately 0.7 GW.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
65.x: The stated national floating-solar potential is 102.18 GW, with Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh leading at about 16 GW and 14 GW, while installed capacity is only about 0.7 GW.
65.tq: Check potential, regional leadership and installed capacity as separate quantities.
xs: Statement 1 is **correct**: floating potential is **102.18 GW** on reservoirs.
Statement 2 is **correct**: leaders are **Maharashtra ~16 GW** and **MP ~14 GW**.
Statement 3 is **correct**: installed floating is only ~**0.7 GW** — so **all three**, option **(4)**.
xa: The assessment was the **first national** one, by **NISE** (Jun 2026).
**Omkareshwar** (**278 MW**) is India's largest floating plant.
World floating capacity: ~**9.6 GW** (2024), **90%** in Asia.

65.s: The first national assessment titled “Solar PV Potential of India (Floating Solar)” was associated with which institution?
65.x: The first national assessment of floating solar PV potential was undertaken by the National Institute of Solar Energy (NISE).
65.tq: Identify the correct technical institution rather than a project implementing agency.
xs: The first national assessment, **"Solar PV Potential of India (Floating Solar)"**, was by **NISE** (National Institute of Solar Energy) — option **(1)**.
NISE is an **autonomous body of MNRE** at **Gurugram**.
xa: It estimated **102.18 GW** floating potential on reservoirs.
NISE also estimated **748 GW** ground potential.
**SECI** implements the floating **PM Surya Sarovar Yojana**.

65.s: What storage requirement is associated with the PM Surya Sarovar Yojana?
65.x: The scheme includes a mandatory two-hour storage requirement amounting to 10,000 MWh.
65.tq: Keep duration and storage quantity together when identifying the correct provision.
xs: PM Surya Sarovar mandates **2-hour storage (10,000 MWh)** (Aug 2026) — option **(1)** (Two-hour storage).
**10,000 MWh** = **2 hours** of the **5,000 MW** target.
xa: CFA up to **Rs 1 crore/MW**, via **SECI**.
Outlay **Rs 5,070 crore**.
**Modhera** (Gujarat) pairs a **6 MW** plant with **15 MWh BESS**.

65.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched with the Omkareshwar floating solar project?
o: Narmada, Khandwa, Madhya Pradesh — 278 MW, with a proposed expansion to 600 MW
Kutch, Gujarat — 30 GW, with a proposed expansion to 60 GW
Visakhapatnam, Andhra Pradesh — 1,000 MW, with a proposed expansion to 5,000 MW
Jodhpur, Rajasthan — 2,245 MW, with a proposed expansion to 10,000 MW
65.x: Omkareshwar floating solar project is on the Narmada in Khandwa district of Madhya Pradesh. Its capacity is 278 MW and it is planned to reach 600 MW.
65.tq: Match the project with its river, location and two-stage capacity figures.
xs: **Omkareshwar** is on the **Narmada**, **Khandwa, MP** — **278 MW**, to reach **600 MW** — option **(1)**.
**Kutch, 30 GW** = **Khavda**; **Jodhpur, 2,245 MW** = **Bhadla**; **Visakhapatnam** = **NTPC Simhadri**.
xa: Omkareshwar is **India's largest floating** plant.
⚠ **Bhadla** = largest park; **Khavda** = largest RE park when complete; **Omkareshwar** = largest floating.
Installed floating solar in India: ~**0.7 GW**.

65.s:
Consider the following statements about floating solar projects:
1. They save land compared with land-based solar installations.
2. They can reduce evaporation from water bodies.
3. Water cooling can improve efficiency.
4. Their upfront cost is approximately 25% higher.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
65.x: All four statements are correct. Floating solar saves land, reduces evaporation, benefits from water cooling and has an upfront cost approximately 25% higher than comparable land-based installations.
65.tq: Balance environmental advantages against the cost disadvantage in a comparison question.
xs: Floating solar **saves land**, **cuts evaporation**, gains efficiency from **water cooling**, but **costs ~25% more upfront** — all four, option **(4)**.
The **25%** higher upfront cost is the main minus.
xa: Floating potential: **102.18 GW**; installed ~**0.7 GW**.
**PM Surya Sarovar** targets **5,000 MW** floating by **2030-31**.

65.s: Which one of the following statements regarding global floating solar deployment is correct?
o: World floating solar capacity was approximately 9.6 GW in 2024, with about 90% located in Asia.
World floating solar capacity was approximately 0.7 GW in 2024, with about 10% located in Asia.
World floating solar capacity was approximately 30 GW in 2024, with no concentration in Asia.
World floating solar capacity was approximately 102.18 GW in 2024, entirely outside Asia.
65.x: Global floating solar capacity was approximately 9.6 GW in 2024, and around 90% of it was located in Asia.
65.tq: Separate the global figure from India's national potential and installed-capacity figures.
xs: World floating solar was ~**9.6 GW** in **2024**, about **90%** in **Asia** — option **(1)**.
**0.7 GW** is **India's** installed floating capacity; **102.18 GW** is India's **potential**; **30 GW** is Khavda.
xa: India's floating leaders by potential: **Maharashtra ~16 GW**, **MP ~14 GW**.
**Omkareshwar**: **278 MW**.
Pluses: **saves land**, **cuts evaporation**.

65.s: Which of the following correctly describes the PM Surya Sarovar Yojana?
o: It involves ₹5,070 crore and targets 500 MW by 2025–26.
It involves ₹50,700 crore and targets 50,000 MW by 2030–31.
It involves ₹5,070 crore and targets 5,000 MW by 2030–31.
It involves ₹507 crore and targets 500 MW by 2026–27.
65.x: The scheme involves ₹5,070 crore and targets 5,000 MW of floating solar capacity by 2030–31.
65.tq: Pair the scheme’s financial outlay with its capacity and deadline.
xs: **PM Surya Sarovar**: **Rs 5,070 crore**, target **5,000 MW** floating by **2030-31** — option **(3)**.
The other options distort the outlay, target or year.
xa: CFA up to **Rs 1 crore/MW**; implemented via **SECI**.
**2-hour storage (10,000 MWh)** mandatory.
Cabinet cleared it on **31 Jul 2026**.

65.s: Under the PM Surya Sarovar Yojana, Central Financial Assistance of up to how much is provided, and through which agency is the scheme implemented?
o: Rs 1 crore per MW, through SECI
Rs 10 lakh per MW, through NISE
Rs 1 crore per MW, through IREDA
Rs 5 crore per MW, through NTPC
65.x: The scheme gives CFA of up to Rs 1 crore/MW and the 5,000 MW target is to be delivered via SECI. NISE did the floating-potential assessment, IREDA and NTPC are not the stated agency, and Rs 10 lakh or Rs 5 crore per MW are wrong amounts.
65.tq: Surya Sarovar: Rs 5,070 cr, Rs 1 cr/MW, 5,000 MW by 2030-31, SECI.
xs: CFA is up to **Rs 1 crore per MW**, through **SECI** — option **(1)**.
**IREDA** is an RE financier and **NISE** a research body — neither implements this scheme.
xa: Outlay: **Rs 5,070 crore**.
**2-hour storage** (**10,000 MWh**) is mandatory.

65.s:
With reference to the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM), consider the following statements:
1. ALMM registration has been compulsory for the relevant manufacturers since 2019.
2. Only ALMM-listed modules may be used in government-funded, open-access and net-metering projects.
3. ALMM applies only to projects implemented by private developers.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
65.x: ALMM registration has been compulsory since 2019, and only listed modules can be used in government-funded, open-access and net-metering projects. Statement 3 is false because the requirement also covers government-linked projects such as PM Surya Ghar, PM-KUSUM and SECI tenders.
65.tq: Find the false scope statement by checking the word only and the project categories.
xs: Statement 1 is **correct**: **ALMM** registration with **MNRE** has been compulsory since **2019**.
Statement 2 is **correct**: only ALMM modules in **Govt-funded, open-access and net-metering** projects.
Statement 3 is **wrong**: ALMM covers Govt schemes like **PM Surya Ghar**, **PM-KUSUM** and **SECI tenders** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: ⚠ **List-I = modules**; **List-II = cells (Jun 2026)**; **List-III = ingots and wafers (Jun 2028)**.
Capacity gap: modules ~**190 GW** vs cells ~**25 GW**.
**DCR**: domestic cells/modules in CPSU, PM-KUSUM, rooftop subsidy projects.

65.s: The Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM) is administered by which Union Ministry for solar project eligibility?
o: Ministry of New and Renewable Energy
65.x: ALMM is the approved list maintained under the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE).
65.tq: Use the institutional-ownership approach: identify the ministry directly associated with renewable-energy regulation.
xs: **ALMM** is a compulsory **MNRE** (Ministry of New and Renewable Energy) registration since **2019** — option **(1)**.
The **Ministry of Power** issued the **Green Energy Open Access Rules, 2022**, not ALMM.
xa: **List-II (ALCM)** for cells from **1 June 2026**.
**List-III** for ingots and wafers mandatory from **June 2028**.
ALMM applies to **PM Surya Ghar**, **PM-KUSUM** and **SECI** tenders.

65.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the coverage of the three ALMM lists?
o: List-I: cells; List-II: modules; List-III: solar parks
List-I: modules; List-II: cells; List-III: ingots and wafers
List-I: ingots; List-II: wafers; List-III: modules
List-I: manufacturers; List-II: importers; List-III: developers
65.x: ALMM List-I covers modules, List-II covers cells and List-III covers ingots and wafers.
65.tq: Start from the sure pair and distinguish the manufacturing stages.
xs: ALMM **List-I = modules**, **List-II = cells**, **List-III = ingots and wafers** — option **(2)**.
The order follows the supply chain backward: module → cell → ingot/wafer.
xa: **List-II (ALCM)** from **1 June 2026**.
**List-III** mandatory from **June 2028**.
Module capacity **~190 GW** vs cells **~25 GW**.

65.s:
Consider the following statements about the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM):
1. ALMM List-II for cells (ALCM) applies from 1 June 2026.
2. ALMM List-III for ingots and wafers became mandatory from 1 June 2026 as well.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
65.x: Statement 1 is correct: List-II for cells (ALCM) applies from 1 June 2026. Statement 2 is wrong: List-III for ingots and wafers becomes mandatory only from June 2028. So '1 only'; '2 only' and 'Both' accept the wrong date, and 'Neither' rejects the correct ALCM date.
65.tq: ALMM moves up the chain: modules (List-I, 2019) -> cells (2026) -> ingots/wafers (2028).
xs: Statement 1 is **correct**: **ALMM List-II (ALCM)** for cells applies from **1 June 2026**.
Statement 2 is **wrong**: **List-III** (ingots and wafers) is mandatory only from **June 2028** — so **1 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: **List-I** covers **modules**.
ALMM registration compulsory since **2019**.
The **ALCM** cell mandate is in force (Jun 2026).

65.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the relative scale of ALMM-listed manufacturing capacity:
1. The module list covers approximately 190 GW of capacity.
2. The cell list covers approximately 25 GW of capacity.
3. Cell capacity is substantially higher than module capacity.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
65.x: The module list covers about 190 GW, whereas the cell list covers only about 25 GW. Therefore, statement 3 reverses the comparison.
65.tq: Check the direction of the comparison before evaluating the numerical statements.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are **correct**: modules ~**190 GW**, cells only ~**25 GW** (Jun 2026).
Statement 3 is **wrong**: **cell capacity lags module capacity** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: PLI added **11 GW** module + **5 GW** cell capacity in 2025.
Module capacity: **172 GW** (2026).
⚠ "Cell capacity lags module capacity" is a listed criticism.

65.s:
Domestic Content Requirement (DCR) mandates the use of domestic cells and modules in which of the following?
1. CPSU projects
2. PM-KUSUM
3. Rooftop subsidy projects
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
65.x: DCR requires domestic cells and modules in CPSU projects, PM-KUSUM and rooftop subsidy projects.
65.tq: Test the complete list by checking whether all three applications fall within the domestic-content rule.
xs: **DCR** makes domestic cells/modules mandatory in **CPSU**, **PM-KUSUM** and **rooftop subsidy** projects — all three, option **(4)**.
**CPSU Scheme Phase-II** uses **VGF** with domestic cells/modules.
xa: **ALMM** applies to Govt-funded, open-access and net-metering projects.
CPSU Phase-II commissioned **2.87 GW** in 2025.
PLI Tranche-II targets **39,600 MW** integrated capacity.

65.s: Which one of the following best describes the growth of India’s annual solar module manufacturing capacity?
o: 2.3 GW in 2014 to about 144 GW in November 2025 and 172 GW in 2026
5 GW in 2014 to 39.6 GW in November 2025 and 144 GW in 2026
11 GW in 2014 to 172 GW in November 2025 and 2.3 GW in 2026
144 GW in 2014 to 172 GW in November 2025 and 2.3 GW in 2026
65.x: Module capacity increased from 2.3 GW in 2014 to about 144 GW per year by November 2025 and 172 GW in 2026.
65.tq: Check the first, middle and final values in the capacity sequence.
xs: Module capacity: **2.3 GW (2014)** → ~**144 GW/yr (November 2025)** → **172 GW (2026)** — option **(1)**.
The other options shuffle these figures or use PLI numbers (**39.6 GW**, **11 GW**, **5 GW**).
xa: Module imports fell **65%** (**$2,152 M** in FY25 → **$758 M**).
PLI (**2021**) Tranche-II targets **39,600 MW**.
Cells only ~**25 GW** vs modules ~**190 GW**.

65.s: The Goods and Services Tax on solar devices was reduced from 12 per cent to 5 per cent with effect from:
65.x: GST on solar devices was reduced from 12 per cent to 5 per cent from 22 September 2025.
65.tq: Distinguish a tax-rate change from the dates of import monitoring and customs duties.
xs: **GST** on solar devices was cut **12% → 5%** from **22 September 2025** — option **(2)**.
**1 Nov 2025** = **REEIMS** portal; **1 June 2026** = **ALCM**; **April 2022** = **BCD**.
xa: **BCD**: **40%** on modules, **25%** on cells from April 2022.
**REEIMS** is the import-monitoring portal.
Module imports fell **65%**.

65.s: Which of the following pairs of Basic Customs Duty rates is correctly matched with solar imports from April 2022?
65.x: From April 2022, the Basic Customs Duty was 40 per cent on modules and 25 per cent on cells.
65.tq: Check the module-cell order carefully because the two rates are deliberately reversible distractors.
xs: From **April 2022**, **BCD** is **40% on modules** and **25% on cells** — option **(4)**.
Option (3) swaps the rates; **5%** and **12%** are **GST** figures.
xa: **REEIMS** import-monitoring portal from **1 Nov 2025**.
Module imports fell from **$2,152 M** to **$758 M**.

65.s:
The following policy developments are associated with solar manufacturing. Arrange them in chronological order:
A. Introduction of PLI for High-Efficiency Solar PV Modules
B. Imposition of 40 per cent BCD on modules and 25 per cent on cells
C. Reduction of GST on solar devices from 12 per cent to 5 per cent
D. Operationalisation of the REEIMS portal
65.x: The sequence is PLI in 2021, BCD from April 2022, GST reduction on 22 September 2025 and REEIMS from 1 November 2025.
65.tq: Fix the earliest and latest events first, then place the two 2025 measures by date.
xs: The GST cut came a few weeks before **REEIMS**.
xa: BCD: **40%** modules, **25%** cells.
PLI Tranche-II targets **39,600 MW**.
**ALMM List-II** for cells came later, **1 June 2026**.

65.s: The International Solar Alliance (ISA) was launched at which place and event?
o: Gwal Pahari during the laying of the headquarters foundation stone
New Delhi during the founding conference of ISA
65.x: The ISA was launched jointly by India and France on 30 November 2015 at COP21 in Paris.
65.tq: Use the event-location pair to distinguish the launch from later ISA milestones.
xs: The **ISA** was launched by **India and France** on **30 November 2015** at **COP21, Paris** — option **(1)**.
**Gwal Pahari** = HQ foundation stone (**2016**); **New Delhi** = founding conference (**2018**) and the **8th Assembly**.
xa: ISA is a **treaty-based intergovernmental organisation**; HQ **Gurugram (Haryana)**.
**Framework Agreement** in force **6 Dec 2017**.

65.s: The foundation stone of the International Solar Alliance headquarters was laid at which location?
65.x: The foundation stone was laid at the National Institute of Solar Energy campus at Gwal Pahari, Gurugram, on 25 January 2016.
65.tq: Test the precise location rather than the broader city or country.
xs: The HQ foundation stone was laid at the **NISE campus, Gwal Pahari, Gurugram** on **25 Jan 2016** — option **(2)**.
It was laid by **PM Modi** and French President **Hollande**.
xa: ISA launched **30 Nov 2015** at **COP21, Paris**.
**NISE** is an **autonomous body of MNRE**.
Founding conference: **11 March 2018, New Delhi**.

65.s: The Framework Agreement of the International Solar Alliance entered into force on:
65.x: The ISA Framework Agreement entered into force on 6 December 2017, giving the organisation its treaty-based character.
65.tq: Distinguish the agreement’s effective date from the launch and foundation-stone dates.
xs: The ISA **Framework Agreement** entered into force on **6 December 2017**, making ISA a **treaty-based** body — option **(1)**.
**11 Mar 2018** = founding conference; **25 Jan 2016** = HQ foundation stone; **30 Nov 2015** = launch.
xa: **2020 amendment** opened membership to **all UN members**.
**Romania** ratified the Framework Agreement (2026).
⚠ Order: launch **2015** → HQ stone **2016** → in force **2017** → founding conference **2018**.

65.s: The founding conference of the International Solar Alliance was held on:
65.x: The founding conference of the ISA was held on 11 March 2018 in New Delhi.
65.tq: Use date-place pairing to separate the founding conference from other milestones.
xs: The ISA founding conference was held on **11 March 2018** in **New Delhi** — option **(3)**.
The other dates are the **in-force** date (**6 Dec 2017**), **launch** (**30 Nov 2015**, Paris) and **HQ stone** (**25 Jan 2016**).
xa: The **8th ISA Assembly** was also held in **New Delhi** (**137** nations).
HQ: **Gurugram (Haryana)**.
Aim: **$1 trillion** solar investment by **2030**.

65.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: OSOWOG — Pooling demand for bulk procurement of solar equipment
Common procurement platform — Pooling demand to reduce costs through scale
ISA Academy — Treaty-making body of the ISA
65.x: The common procurement platform pools demand so that costs can be reduced through economies of scale. OSOWOG concerns an interconnected solar grid, while STAR-C concerns training and best practices.
65.tq: Start from the sure functional pair and eliminate swapped purposes.
xs: The **common procurement platform** **pools demand to cut costs by scale** (UPSC) — option **(3)**.
**OSOWOG** is the **interconnected global grid**; **STAR-C** is a **knowledge/training** network — options (1) and (2) swap them.
**ISA Academy** was launched at the **8th Assembly**; it is not a treaty-making body.
xa: **Global Solar Facility**: fund to **de-risk solar investment** in underserved regions.
The **OSOWOG** roadmap was operationalised at the **8th Assembly**.
Projects worth **$50 billion+** approved.

65.s: Which of the following initiatives was launched at the 8th Assembly of the International Solar Alliance held in New Delhi?
65.x: The Global SIDS Initiative, ISA Academy, Global Capability Centre and SUNRISE were launched at the 8th ISA Assembly in New Delhi.
65.tq: Find the initiative belonging to the ISA rather than a domestic solar programme.
xs: The **Global SIDS Initiative Declaration** was launched at the **8th ISA Assembly, New Delhi** — option **(3)**.
**NSM** (2010) and **PM-KUSUM** (2019) are **domestic** Indian schemes, not ISA launches.
xa: Also launched there: **ISA Academy**, **ISA Global Capability Center**, **SUNRISE** Community of Practice.
The Assembly drew **137** nations.
**OSOWOG** roadmap operationalised at the **8th Assembly**.

65.s: Which initiative of the International Solar Alliance is intended to share solar power across time zones through a transnational grid?
65.x: OSOWOG, or One Sun One World One Grid, is the transnational grid concept for sharing solar power across time zones.
65.tq: Separate similarly grouped ISA initiatives by their stated function.
xs: **OSOWOG** (One Sun One World One Grid) is a **transnational, interconnected global grid** to share solar power **across borders and time zones** — option **(4)**.
**STAR-C** = knowledge/training; **Global Solar Facility** = de-risking fund; **SUNRISE** = Community of Practice.
xa: Its roadmap was operationalised at the **8th Assembly**.
ISA aims to mobilise **$1 trillion** by **2030**.
ISA HQ: **Gurugram**.

65.s: The roadmap for One Sun One World One Grid was operationalised at which event?
65.x: The OSOWOG roadmap was operationalised at the eighth Assembly of the International Solar Alliance.
65.tq: Match an initiative with the specific institutional milestone at which it advanced.
xs: The **OSOWOG** roadmap was operationalised at the **8th Assembly** of ISA — option **(2)** (eighth Assembly).
The **8th Assembly** in **New Delhi** (**137** nations) also launched the **ISA Academy** and **SUNRISE**.
xa: OSOWOG shares solar power **across borders and time zones**.
ISA has **116+** members (2024).
**Global SIDS Initiative Declaration** launched there too.

65.s: The Global Solar Facility of the ISA primarily seeks to:
o: Produce green hydrogen from solar power
Train solar engineers in member countries
De-risk solar investment in underserved regions
65.x: The Global Solar Facility is an ISA fund designed to de-risk solar investment in underserved regions through instruments such as payment guarantees and insurance.
65.tq: Identify an institutional instrument by the problem it is designed to solve.
xs: The **Global Solar Facility** is an ISA fund to **de-risk solar investment in underserved regions** (payment guarantees, insurance) — option **(4)**.
**Transnational grid** = **OSOWOG**; **training** = **STAR-C** / ISA Academy.
xa: ISA target: **$1 trillion** by **2030**.
Projects worth **$50 billion+** approved; **100+ GW** targeted.
The **common procurement platform** pools demand.

65.s: What is the principal function of STAR-C under the International Solar Alliance?
o: Providing payment guarantees for solar projects
Operating a knowledge, training and best-practice network
65.x: STAR-C, or Solar Technology Application Resource Centre, is a knowledge, training and best-practice network among ISA members.
65.tq: Discriminate between financing, grid and capacity-building functions.
xs: **STAR-C** (Solar Technology Application Resource Centre) is a **knowledge, training and best-practice** platform — option **(4)**.
**Transnational grid** = **OSOWOG**; **payment guarantees** = **Global Solar Facility**.
xa: It is also called **ISTAR-C**.
**ISA Academy** was launched at the **8th Assembly**.
ISA Framework Agreement in force **6 Dec 2017**.

65.s: The International Solar Alliance aims to mobilise solar investment of approximately:
65.x: The ISA's stated goal is to mobilise $1 trillion of solar investment by 2030.
65.tq: Match the target figure with its corresponding deadline.
xs: ISA aims to mobilise **$1 trillion** in solar investment by **2030** — option **(3)**.
Progress: projects worth **$50 billion+** approved; **100+ GW** targeted.
xa: Launched **30 Nov 2015** at **COP21, Paris**.
**OSOWOG** roadmap at the **8th Assembly**.

65.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the change in membership eligibility of the International Solar Alliance?
o: Membership was initially for Sunshine Countries and was later opened to all UN members through a 2020 amendment.
Membership is available only to countries that have installed more than 1 GW of solar capacity.
Membership continues to be restricted exclusively to countries between the tropics.
Membership was initially restricted to European countries and later opened to Asian countries.
65.x: The ISA initially focused on Sunshine Countries located between the tropics. A 2020 amendment opened membership to all United Nations members.
65.tq: Track the change from the original restricted membership to the amended broader rule.
xs: A **2020 amendment** opened ISA membership to **all UN members** — option **(1)**.
Membership is not tied to installed capacity, the tropics alone, or Europe.
xa: **Romania** ratified the Framework Agreement (2026).
ISA is a **treaty-based intergovernmental organisation**.

65.s: Which one of the following is NOT an initiative of the International Solar Alliance?
o: One Sun One World One Grid (OSOWOG)
65.x: PM-KUSUM is a domestic MNRE scheme for solarising farm power, not an ISA project. OSOWOG (transnational solar grid), STAR-C (knowledge and training centres) and the Global Solar Facility (de-risking fund) are ISA initiatives.
65.tq: PM-KUSUM = India's MNRE scheme, not ISA (APPSC-G2 2025 trap).
xs: **PM-KUSUM** is a **domestic MNRE scheme**, **not an ISA project** (APPSC-G2 2025) — option **(4)**.
**OSOWOG**, **STAR-C** and the **Global Solar Facility** are ISA initiatives.
xa: PM-KUSUM (**2019**): Comp A plants, **Comp B** standalone pumps, **Comp C** pump solarisation.
ISA 8th Assembly launched the **ISA Academy** and **SUNRISE**.
ISA aims at **$1 trillion** by **2030**.

65.s: Which of the following is NOT identified as one of the three ultra mega solar parks in Andhra Pradesh?
65.x: Kurnool, NP Kunta and Kadapa are the three Andhra Pradesh ultra mega solar park locations. Omkareshwar is associated with the largest floating solar plant.
65.tq: Find the location belonging to a different category rather than an Andhra Pradesh park.
xs: **Omkareshwar** is a **floating** plant in **Khandwa, MP**, not an AP park — option **(4)**.
AP's three ultra mega parks: **Kurnool**, **NP Kunta**, **Kadapa** (+ **Ramagiri** hybrid park).
xa: **NP Kunta (Ananthapuramu-I)**: **1,500 MW**; **Kurnool**, **Kadapa**: **1,000 MW** each.
Omkareshwar: **278 MW**, India's **largest floating** plant.

65.s: Which one of the following statements about the PM Surya Sarovar Yojana is correct?
o: It was approved for promoting floating solar projects.
It was introduced for mandatory solar modules in SECI tenders only.
It was approved to replace the PLI scheme for solar modules.
It was approved for regulating solar-cell imports.
65.x: The Cabinet approved PM Surya Sarovar Yojana for floating solar projects.
65.tq: Match the scheme with its stated purpose while rejecting neighbouring policy functions.
xs: The Cabinet cleared **PM Surya Sarovar Yojana** for **floating solar** (Aug 2026) — option **(1)**.
Module rules come from **ALMM**, manufacturing support from **PLI**, and import monitoring from **REEIMS** — not this scheme.
xa: Target: **5,000 MW** floating by **2030-31**, via **SECI**.
CFA up to **Rs 1 crore/MW**; outlay **Rs 5,070 crore**.
**2-hour storage** mandatory.

65.s:
Consider the following statements regarding solar-sector challenges:
1. Solar-cell capacity is lagging behind module capacity.
2. Grid curtailment is a reported concern.
3. India has already established comprehensive solar-panel recycling norms.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
65.x: Cell capacity lag and grid curtailment are identified concerns. Statement 3 is false because solar-waste recycling norms are still absent.
65.tq: Identify the negative policy-status statement and check whether it reverses the stated criticism.
xs: Statement 1 is **correct**: **cell capacity lags module capacity**.
Statement 2 is **correct**: **curtailment** and **transmission lag** are concerns.
Statement 3 is **wrong**: there are **no solar-waste/panel recycling norms** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: Modules ~**190 GW** vs cells ~**25 GW**.
Rooftop costs **₹2.2-3.5 lakh** — another debate point.
The **ALCM** cell mandate (Jun 2026) aims to close the gap.

65.s: Which of the following correctly matches the Andhra Pradesh solar-sector institution with its role?
o: NEDCAP—state nodal agency for solar development
MNRE—operator of the Ramagiri hybrid park only
65.x: NEDCAP is the nodal agency associated with Andhra Pradesh’s solar programme. SECI, MNRE and REEIMS have different national-level roles.
65.tq: Ask who would perform the state-level nodal function and reject bodies with different mandates.
xs: **NEDCAP** is AP's **nodal agency** for solar — option **(1)**.
**SECI** implements central tenders; **REEIMS** is an import-monitoring portal; **MNRE** is the Union ministry.
xa: AP parks: **Kurnool**, **NP Kunta**, **Kadapa** + **Ramagiri** hybrid.
AP offered **50,000 acres** of barren land for solar lease (Apr 2026).

65.s:
Assertion (A): India’s solar sector faces a risk of unused generation even when installed solar capacity is increasing.
Reason (R): Grid curtailment and transmission lag can restrict the evacuation of generated solar electricity.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
65.x: Both statements are true, and curtailment and transmission constraints directly explain why increasing installed capacity may not translate into fully utilised generation.
65.tq: Test whether the reason directly explains the practical effect stated in the assertion.
xs: **Both A and R are true** and **R is the correct explanation** — option **(1)**.
**Curtailment and transmission lag** (Sep 2025; Jul 2026) leave solar generation unused even as capacity grows.
xa: Solar PV CUF is only ~**21%**.
Installed solar hit **164.59 GW** (Aug 2026).
Other debates: **cell capacity lags**, **no panel recycling norms**.

65.s:
Which one of the following correctly describes the Andhra Pradesh solar-energy cluster?
1. Kurnool and YSR Kadapa parks anchor the Rayalaseema renewable-energy cluster.
2. About 50,000 acres of barren land have been offered for solar lease.
3. NEDCAP is the nodal agency.
4. NTPC Simhadri has a floating solar plant in Visakhapatnam.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
65.x: All four statements are correct descriptions of the Andhra Pradesh solar-energy cluster and related initiatives.
65.tq: Combine location, land, agency and project clues to identify the complete State profile.
xs: **Kurnool** and **YSR Kadapa** anchor **Rayalaseema's RE cluster**; **50,000 acres** offered; **NEDCAP** is nodal agency; **NTPC Simhadri** floating plant is at **Visakhapatnam** — all four, option **(4)**.
All four facts are in the AP angle of the notes.
xa: **Ramagiri** (Ananthapuramu): hybrid solar-wind park.
AP: **4,11,915** rooftop systems (**4 Aug 2026**).
AP has **9.10%** of India's RE potential.

65.s: Under PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana, Andhra Pradesh had about 4.12 lakh rooftop systems by August 2026. Where does this place the State?
o: It has no installations under the scheme
65.x: AP had 4,11,915 rooftop systems (4 Aug 2026), placing it among the top four States. It is not last, it does have installations, and it is a State, not a Union Territory.
65.tq: AP in PM Surya Ghar: 4,11,915 systems, top four States.
xs: AP had **4,11,915** rooftop systems (**4 Aug 2026**), **among the top four states** — option **(1)**.
That is about **4.12 lakh** systems under **PM Surya Ghar**.
xa: PM Surya Ghar: >**75 lakh** applications, >**39.7 lakh** RTS systems nationally (**22 Jul 2026**).
Scheme goal: **1 crore** households, **300 units** free/month.
AP nodal agency: **NEDCAP**.

66.s:
Consider the following statements about wind turbines:
1. In a horizontal-axis wind turbine (HAWT) the rotor axis is parallel to the wind and yaw control is needed.
2. A vertical-axis wind turbine (VAWT) can take wind from any direction and has higher efficiency than a HAWT.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
66.x: Statement 1 is correct: a HAWT has its rotor axis parallel to the wind, usually 3 blades, and needs yaw control. Statement 2 is wrong: a VAWT (Darrieus, Savonius) does take wind from any direction but has lower efficiency. So '1 only'; '2 only' and 'Both' accept the wrong efficiency claim, and 'Neither' rejects the correct HAWT description.
66.tq: VAWT: any wind direction but lower efficiency - the 'higher efficiency' clause is the trap.
xs: Statement 1 is **correct**: a **HAWT** has its rotor axis **parallel to the wind**, usually **3 blades**, and needs **yaw control**.
Statement 2 is **wrong**: a **VAWT** takes wind from any direction but has **lower efficiency** — so **1 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: ⚠ **Darrieus** and **Savonius** are **VAWT** designs.
The **HAWT** is the standard utility turbine.
**Betz limit**: at most **16/27 = 59.3%** of wind's kinetic energy can be captured.

66.s:
Consider the following statements about wind power:
1. By the Betz limit, at most 16/27 (about 59.3%) of the wind's kinetic energy can be captured.
2. The power available to a turbine varies with the square of wind speed.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
66.x: Statement 1 is correct: the Betz limit is 16/27, about 59.3%. Statement 2 is wrong: power varies with the cube of wind speed (and with swept area), not the square. So '1 only'; '2 only' and 'Both' accept the wrong power law, and 'Neither' rejects the correct Betz limit.
66.tq: Betz = 16/27 = 59.3%; wind power ~ cube of speed.
xs: Statement 1 is **correct**: the **Betz limit** is **16/27**, about **59.3%**.
Statement 2 is **wrong**: power varies with the **cube** of wind speed (and swept area), not the square — so **1 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: Hence higher **hub heights** matter: potential is **695.5 GW** at **120 m** but **1,163.9 GW** at **150 m**.
**IEC Class I** turbines suit **high-wind** sites; **Class III** suit **low-wind** sites.
Offshore winds are **stronger and steadier** → higher capacity factor.

66.s: Capacity Utilisation Factor of a power plant is best expressed as:
o: Installed capacity divided by annual fuel consumption
Maximum possible output divided by actual output
Annual generation divided by transmission loss
Actual output divided by output at full rated power over the relevant time
66.x: Capacity Utilisation Factor is the ratio of actual output to the output possible at full rated power over the relevant period.
66.tq: Apply the numerator–denominator relationship rather than relying on the term alone.
xs: **CUF** = **actual output / output at full rated power** over the relevant time — option **(4)**.
Option (2) inverts the ratio (maximum possible ÷ actual).
xa: Wind CUF **36-40%** vs solar ~**21%** vs coal ~**85%** (Aug 2026).
Offshore sites give a **higher capacity factor** thanks to steadier winds.
Power rises with the **cube** of wind speed.

66.s: Which one of the following statements about onshore and offshore wind power is NOT correct?
o: Offshore projects eliminate all environmental and navigational risks.
Floating turbines can be used in deep water.
Offshore sites generally have stronger and steadier winds.
Onshore projects are generally cheaper and easier to maintain.
66.x: Offshore projects do not eliminate risks; they may involve corrosion, undersea cables, navigation issues and marine-ecology concerns.
66.tq: Identify the absolute claim contradicted by the stated disadvantages of offshore projects.
xs: **Offshore projects eliminate all environmental and navigational risks** is NOT correct — option **(1)** is the answer.
Offshore cons: **costly**, harder upkeep, **corrosion**, **undersea cables**, **navigation and marine-ecology** risks.
**Floating turbines** for deep water, **stronger, steadier** offshore winds, and **cheaper** onshore upkeep are all true.
xa: Offshore advantage: **no land conflict**.
Offshore target: **30 GW by 2030**.
Onshore is the **cheapest new electricity** globally; costs fell **4%** in 2025 (IRENA).

66.s: Which statement correctly describes IEC wind-turbine classes?
o: The classes are based exclusively on turbine colour and blade number.
Class I is intended for high-wind sites and Class III for low-wind sites.
Class III is designed for the highest wind speeds.
Class I is intended only for offshore sites and Class III only for deserts.
66.x: IEC turbine classes are determined by site wind speed: Class I is for high-wind sites and Class III for low-wind sites.
66.tq: Compare the end classes and watch for reversal of high-wind and low-wind applications.
xs: IEC classes are set by **site wind speed**: **Class I for high-wind**, **Class III for low-wind** sites — option **(2)**.
They are not about colour, blade count, or offshore/desert location; Class III is for the **lowest** winds.
xa: Power varies with the **cube of wind speed** and swept area.
**HAWT** = standard utility turbine; **VAWT** has **lower efficiency**.

66.s: Which of the following correctly describes the energy-conversion sequence in a wind turbine?
o: Mechanical energy in the generator → wind energy → electricity
Electrical energy → chemical energy → kinetic energy
Wind’s kinetic energy → blade/rotor rotation → generator → electricity
66.x: Wind’s kinetic energy rotates the blades and rotor; the generator then converts the mechanical energy into electricity.
66.tq: Follow the conversion chain from the natural source to the final output.
xs: Wind's **kinetic energy → blade/rotor rotation → generator → electricity** — option **(4)**.
I.e. kinetic → **rotational (mechanical)** energy of the rotor → **electrical** energy in the generator (UPSC S&T).
xa: Only up to **59.3%** (Betz limit) of wind's kinetic energy can be captured.
**HAWT** rotor axis is **parallel** to the wind.
**VAWT** types: **Darrieus**, **Savonius**.

66.s:
Assertion (A): Offshore wind projects generally achieve a higher capacity factor than comparable onshore projects.
Reason (R): Offshore locations generally experience stronger and steadier winds.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
66.x: Both statements are true, and stronger and steadier offshore winds explain the generally higher capacity factor of offshore projects.
66.tq: Test whether the reason directly explains the comparison in the assertion.
xs: **Both A and R are true** and **R is the correct explanation** — option **(1)**.
Offshore sites have **stronger, steadier winds** → **higher capacity factor** (UPSC).
xa: Offshore also avoids **land conflict**.
Cons: costly, **corrosion**, **undersea cables**, marine-ecology risks.
India's offshore zones: **Gujarat coast** and **Tamil Nadu coast / Gulf of Mannar**.

66.s:
Assertion (A): Onshore wind is considered the cheapest new electricity source globally.
Reason (R): Onshore wind projects have no maintenance or land-related costs.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
66.x: The assertion is true as stated. The reason is false because onshore projects still involve land use and maintenance, even though they are generally cheaper than offshore projects.
66.tq: Reject an absolute reason while retaining the supported assertion.
xs: **A is true but R is false** — option **(3)**: onshore wind is the **cheapest new electricity** globally (costs fell **4%** in 2025, IRENA).
R is false: onshore is **cheaper and easier to maintain** than offshore, but still has **maintenance** and **land** needs.
xa: Offshore needs **no land** but is costlier and harder to maintain.
Wind CUF in India: **36-40%**.
**Repowering** replaces ageing turbines on the same sites.

66.s: The Capacity Utilisation Factor (CUF) of wind power in India is typically in which range, compared with about 21% for solar and about 85% for coal?
66.x: Wind CUF is about 36-40%, higher than solar (~21%) but well below coal (~85%). 10-15% is too low even for solar, 60-65% overstates wind, and 85-90% is the coal range.
66.tq: CUF order: coal ~85% > wind 36-40% > solar ~21%.
xs: Wind CUF is **36-40%** (Aug 2026) — option **(2)**.
That is above solar (~**21%**) but below coal (~**85%**).
xa: CUF = **actual output / maximum possible output**.
Offshore wind gives a **higher capacity factor**.
Wind is the **2nd-largest RE source** after solar.

66.s: Which of the following correctly represents the approximate share of India’s wind-energy potential located in the eight principal windy states?
66.x: Nearly two-thirds of India’s wind-energy potential lies in the eight identified windy states.
66.tq: Use the approximate-share clue and reject extreme alternatives.
xs: Nearly **two-thirds** (**2/3**) of wind potential lies in the **8 windy states** — option **(2)**.
The 8: **Rajasthan, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Madhya Pradesh, Telangana**.
xa: **NIWE, Chennai** prepares the **Indian Wind Atlas**.
**Gujarat** has the largest installed wind (**12,314 MW**).

66.s: Which one of the following is NOT included among the eight states accounting for nearly two-thirds of India’s wind-energy potential?
66.x: The eight states are Rajasthan, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Madhya Pradesh and Telangana. Kerala is not included in this group.
66.tq: Find the one state outside the stated regional group.
xs: **Kerala** is not among the **8 windy states** — option **(2)**.
The 8 include **Telangana**, **Andhra Pradesh** and **Madhya Pradesh**, plus Rajasthan, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.
xa: These hold nearly **2/3** of India's wind potential.
AP's wind zones: **Rayalaseema** — Anantapur and Kurnool.
Offshore zones: **Gujarat** and **Tamil Nadu** coasts.

66.s: Which of the following correctly matches the hub height with the assessed wind potential?
66.x: The assessed potential is 695.5 GW at a 120-metre hub height and 1,163.9 GW at a 150-metre hub height.
66.tq: Start with the lower hub-height value and check the increase at the higher height.
xs: Wind potential: **695.5 GW at 120 m** and **1,163.9 GW at 150 m** — option **(1)**.
Option (2) swaps them; **56.09 GW** is installed capacity and **100 GW** the 2030 target.
xa: ⚠ Higher hub = more potential: power ∝ **cube** of wind speed.
Installed: **58.14 GW** (Aug 2026).
**NIWE** does **wind resource assessment**.

66.s: The National Institute of Wind Energy (NIWE) is headquartered at:
66.x: NIWE is located in Chennai and functions as an autonomous body under the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy.
66.tq: Use the organisation–headquarters association rather than the locations of major windy states.
xs: **NIWE** (National Institute of Wind Energy) is in **Chennai** — option **(3)**.
It is an **autonomous body under MNRE**.
xa: Focal point for **wind R&D**, **resource assessment**, site identification, testing and certification.
It prepares the **Indian Wind Atlas**.
NIWE is the **nodal agency** under the **Offshore Wind Policy 2015**.

66.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the National Institute of Wind Energy:
1. It is an autonomous body under the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy.
2. It undertakes wind-resource assessment and identification of potential sites.
3. It prepares the Indian Wind Atlas.
4. It provides support for testing and certification of wind technologies.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
66.x: All four statements correctly describe NIWE’s institutional status and functions, including resource assessment, site identification, atlas preparation, testing and certification support.
66.tq: Check the organisation’s status and each listed function before choosing the complete code.
xs: **NIWE** is an **autonomous body under MNRE**; does **wind resource assessment** and **site identification**; prepares the **Indian Wind Atlas**; supports **testing and certification** — all four, option **(4)**.
It is the focal point for **wind R&D**.
xa: Located in **Chennai**.
Nodal agency for the **National Offshore Wind Energy Policy 2015** (MNRE = nodal ministry).
Potential: **1,163.9 GW** at **150 m** hub height.

66.s:
Consider the following statements regarding India’s wind-power capacity:
1. India’s installed wind capacity was 21.04 GW in March 2014.
2. Installed wind capacity crossed 50 GW in March 2025.
3. Installed wind capacity was 56.09 GW on 31 March 2026.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
66.x: All three statements are correct: capacity rose from 21.04 GW in March 2014, crossed 50 GW in March 2025 and reached 56.09 GW on 31 March 2026.
66.tq: Check each dated milestone independently before selecting the combined code.
xs: Wind was **21.04 GW (Mar 2014)**, crossed **50 GW (Mar 2025)**, and reached **56.09 GW (31 Mar 2026)** — all three, option **(4)**.
Growth Mar 2014 → Mar 2026 = **2.66x**.
xa: **6.34 GW** added in calendar 2025, up **85.4%** on 2024's **3.42 GW**.
Target: **100 GW by 2030**.

66.s: According to the latest capacity comparison given, wind accounted for what percentage of India’s total power capacity?
66.x: The latest stated wind capacity of 56.81 GW represented 10.47% of the total 542 GW capacity.
66.tq: Separate capacity share from renewable share and capacity-utilisation figures.
xs: Wind (**56.81 GW**) was **10.47%** of **542 GW** total capacity — option **(4)**.
**52.27%** = non-fossil share; **16.5%** = Gujarat's RE share; **36-40%** = wind CUF.
xa: Wind is the **2nd-largest RE source** after solar (**157.05 GW**).
Large hydro: **51.96 GW**.

66.s: Which renewable energy source had the largest installed capacity in the stated comparison?
66.x: Solar power, at 157.05 GW, was the largest renewable source in the comparison, followed by wind at 56.81 GW and large hydro at 51.96 GW.
66.tq: Rank the comparable values before selecting the largest source.
xs: **Solar power** (**157.05 GW**) was the largest RE source — option **(1)**.
Then **wind 56.81 GW**, just ahead of **large hydro 51.96 GW**; nuclear is **not RE**.
xa: Wind = **10.47%** of total capacity.
Wind CUF **36-40%** vs solar ~**21%**.
Wind target: **100 GW by 2030**.

66.s: What was the record addition to India’s wind capacity during financial year 2025–26?
66.x: The record addition during FY 2025–26 was 6.05 GW. The 6.34 GW figure refers to calendar year 2025.
66.tq: Distinguish the financial-year figure from the calendar-year figure.

Statement 1 correct: **bio-power** = **biomass**, **bagasse cogeneration**, **waste-to-energy**.
Statement 2 correct: **geothermal, tidal, OTEC** are **under development**.
Statements 3 and 4 correct: **nuclear** is non-fossil but **not renewable**, its **8.78 GW** counted separately.
xa: **Large hydro** was added to MNRE's RE list in **2019**.
**Bio-power capacity**: **11.75 GW** (**Aug 2026**); national **WtE** capacity **0.88 GW**.
**OTEC** needs a ~**20 deg C** temperature difference; viable in the tropics (**30N-30S**).

67.s: Which of the following correctly describes biogas?
o: A mixture mainly containing methane and carbon dioxide, produced by anaerobic digestion
A petroleum product obtained from crude oil
A mixture of hydrogen and oxygen produced by electrolysis
A pure methane gas produced in the presence of oxygen
67.x: Biogas is produced through anaerobic digestion of organic matter and mainly contains methane and carbon dioxide, along with small quantities of other gases.
67.tq: Discriminate between composition and production conditions.
xs: **Biogas** is a mixture of **methane + CO2** (with traces of other gases) produced by **anaerobic digestion** of organic matter — option **(1)**.
It forms in the **absence of oxygen**, so "pure methane produced in the presence of oxygen" is wrong.
xa: **Methane** is the major share, ~**50-75%**.
**Methanogenic archaea** (methanogens) perform the final methane-forming step.
The leftover **slurry** is a good **organic manure**.
**Gobar gas** = biogas from **cattle dung**.

67.s: Methane generally constitutes approximately what share of biogas?
67.x: Methane is the major component of biogas and generally accounts for about 50–75 percent.
67.tq: Select the stated composition range rather than the extreme percentage.
xs: **Methane** forms the major share of biogas, about **50-75 percent** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The rest is mainly **CO2**, with traces of other gases.
xa: Biogas comes from **anaerobic digestion** of organic matter.
**Methanogenic archaea / methanogens** carry out the final methane-forming step without oxygen.
**Compressed Biogas (CBG)** = purified, compressed biogas, **chemically identical to CNG**.

67.s: Gobar gas is best described as:
o: Gas produced only from municipal plastic waste
Compressed natural gas extracted from coal seams
67.x: Gobar gas is biogas generated from cattle dung.
67.tq: Distinguish the feedstock-specific term from the broader term biogas.
xs: **Gobar gas** is **biogas produced from cattle dung** — option **(3)**.
It is **biomass energy** (**APPSC 2019**).
xa: The floating-drum **"Gramalakshmi"** plant of **Jashbhai Patel** (**1950s**) was popularised by **KVIC**.
**GOBARdhan** (**2018**) converts cattle dung and farm waste into compost, biogas and **CBG/bio-CNG**.
Biogas slurry is a good **organic manure**.

67.s: The final methane-forming step in biogas production is carried out by:
67.x: Methanogenic archaea, also called methanogens, carry out the final methane-forming step during anaerobic digestion.
67.tq: Identify the specific microbial group associated with the final process step.
xs: **Methanogenic archaea** (methanogenic bacteria / methanogens) carry out the final methane-forming step — option **(2)**.
They work in the **absence of oxygen**, so aerobic organisms are ruled out.
xa: Biogas = **methane** (~**50-75%**) + **CO2**, by **anaerobic digestion**.
⚠ **Bioethanol** uses yeast **Saccharomyces cerevisiae**; **biobutanol** uses **Clostridium acetobutylicum**.
**Biomethanation**: microbes convert wet organic waste → biogas.

67.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the residue left after biogas production is correct?
o: It is a good organic manure
It is suitable only for making petroleum
It is unusable because all nutrients are destroyed
67.x: The slurry remaining after anaerobic digestion is a useful organic manure.
67.tq: Apply the production-process knowledge to the by-product.
xs: The **slurry** left after biogas production is a **good organic manure** — option **(1)**.
It is a by-product of **anaerobic digestion**, not petroleum or radioactive waste.
xa: **Gobar gas** = biogas from **cattle dung**; **GOBARdhan** turns dung into **compost** and biogas.
Biogas methane share: ~**50-75%**.
**Source segregation** is essential for both **gasification** and **anaerobic digestion**.

67.s: Biomass energy is best understood as:
o: Solar energy stored by plants through photosynthesis
Energy obtained from tidal currents alone
Heat stored only in the Earth's mantle
67.x: Biomass energy represents solar energy captured and stored by plants through photosynthesis. It may be burned directly or converted into biogas and biofuels.
67.tq: Trace the energy source through the biological conversion chain.
xs: **Biomass energy** is **solar energy stored by plants** through **photosynthesis** — option **(1)**.
It is burned directly or converted to **biogas/biofuels**.
Earth's internal heat is **geothermal**; tidal currents are **ocean energy** — not biomass.
xa: **Gobar gas** is biomass energy (**APPSC 2019**).
Agricultural waste: **crop residue** (stubble, paddy-husk), **manure**, **cattle dung**, **dairy waste** — all biodegradable.
**Biomass gasification**: biomass heated with **controlled oxygen** → **syngas** (CO + H2 + CO2).

67.s: Which one of the following is an example of biomass energy?
67.x: Gobar gas is a form of biomass energy because it is produced from organic biological material, especially cattle dung.
67.tq: Classify the example according to its biological feedstock.
xs: **Gobar gas** is an example of **biomass energy** (**APPSC 2019**) — option **(3)**.
Biomass energy = solar energy stored by plants in **photosynthesis**; geothermal steam comes from **Earth's internal heat**.
xa: **Nuclear** is non-fossil but **not renewable**.
Biogas is produced by **anaerobic digestion**; methane ~**50-75%**.
The **"Gramalakshmi"** floating-drum gobar gas plant was by **Jashbhai Patel** (**1950s**).

67.s:
Consider the following statements about the 'Gramalakshmi' gobar gas plant:
1. It is a floating-drum plant developed by Jashbhai Patel in the 1950s.
2. It was popularised by MNRE.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
67.x: Statement 1 is correct: Jashbhai Patel's floating-drum Gramalakshmi plant dates to the 1950s. Statement 2 is wrong: it was popularised by KVIC, not MNRE. So '1 only'.
67.tq: Gramalakshmi = Jashbhai Patel + KVIC.
xs: Only statement 1 is correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: **"Gramalakshmi"** is a **floating-drum** plant of **Jashbhai Patel** (**1950s**).
Statement 2 wrong: it was popularised by **KVIC**, not MNRE.
xa: **Gobar gas** = biogas from cattle dung; it is **biomass energy**.
MNRE runs the **Biogas Programme** under the **National Bioenergy Programme 2021-26** for small/medium rural plants.
**GOBARdhan** (**2018**) is the umbrella for cattle dung → biogas/bio-CNG.

67.s: Which of the following groups consists entirely of biodegradable agricultural and livestock wastes?
o: Cattle dung, fluorescent lamps, manure and tyres
Stubble, mercury, pesticides and dairy waste
Paddy husk, lead, manure and solvents
Crop residue, cattle dung, dairy waste and manure
67.x: Crop residue, manure, cattle dung and dairy waste are biodegradable agricultural or livestock wastes. Lead, mercury, solvents, pesticides and fluorescent lamps are hazardous materials.
67.tq: Identify the option containing only members of the same waste category.
xs: **Crop residue, cattle dung, dairy waste and manure** are all biodegradable farm wastes — option **(4)**.
The other options mix in non-biodegradable or hazardous items (**mercury**, **lead**, **tyres**, solvents).
xa: Agricultural waste includes **stubble** and **paddy-husk** as crop residue.
**Biomass gasification** uses farm residue and helps cut **stubble burning**.
**2G biofuels** use non-food **lignocellulosic residue** — straw, husk, wood chips, bamboo.

67.s: Compressed Biogas (CBG) is:
o: Unpurified biogas stored at atmospheric pressure
Compressed carbon dioxide used as a fuel
Purified and compressed biogas chemically identical to CNG
67.x: CBG is purified and compressed biogas. Chemically, it is identical to compressed natural gas and is considered renewable and carbon-neutral.
67.tq: Separate CBG from raw biogas and from similarly named fossil-fuel gases.
xs: **CBG** is **purified, compressed biogas**, **chemically identical to CNG** — option **(3)**.
It is renewable and carbon-neutral, promoted under **SATAT**.
xa: **SATAT** was launched in **2018** by **MoPNG**.
CBG progress remains "limited" despite SATAT, even as **90%** of LPG imports pass **Hormuz**.
Draft **CAFE III** norms (from **Apr 2027**) let makers claim credit for **ethanol, CBG**.

67.s: SATAT, launched in 2018 by the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, aims primarily to promote:
o: CBG production from agricultural residue and municipal waste
Ethanol production only from imported crude oil
67.x: SATAT, or Sustainable Alternative Towards Affordable Transportation, was launched in 2018 by MoPNG to promote CBG from agricultural residue and municipal waste.
67.tq: Expand the acronym and match the initiative with its ministry and objective.
xs: **SATAT** (**2018**, **MoPNG**) promotes **Compressed Biogas (CBG)** from **agri-residue** and **municipal waste** — option **(1)**.
SATAT = **Sustainable Alternative Towards Affordable Transportation**.
xa: ⚠ **SATAT** = MoPNG; **National Bioenergy Programme** = MNRE; **co-firing** = Ministry of Power (**SAMARTH**).
CBG is **chemically identical to CNG**.

67.s:
GOBARdhan is an umbrella initiative for converting cattle dung and farm solid waste into:

1. Compost
2. Biogas or CBG/bio-CNG
3. Petroleum crude

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
67.x: GOBARdhan promotes conversion of cattle dung and farm solid waste into compost, biogas and CBG/bio-CNG. Petroleum crude is not an output of the initiative.
67.tq: Find the false output by distinguishing biological conversion from petroleum production.
xs: GOBARdhan converts cattle dung and farm waste into **compost** and **biogas / CBG / bio-CNG** — statements 1 and 2, option **(2)**.
**Petroleum crude** is not an output, so statement 3 is wrong.
xa: GOBARdhan = **Galvanizing Organic Bio-Agro Resources Dhan** (**2018**).
Replicable models: **Zakariyapura** (household units), **Varanasi** (centralised dairy plant), **Banas** (centralised large-scale).
**SATAT** (**2018**, MoPNG) promotes CBG from agri-residue and MSW.

67.s:
Consider the following statements about GOBARdhan:
1. GOBARdhan stands for Galvanizing Organic Bio-Agro Resources Dhan.
2. It was launched in 2020.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
67.x: Statement 1 is correct: that is the expansion. Statement 2 is wrong: GOBARdhan was launched in 2018 (same year as SATAT). So '1 only'; the other options include the wrong year or reject the correct expansion.
67.tq: GOBARdhan and SATAT are both 2018.
xs: Only statement 1 is correct — option **(1)**: GOBARdhan = **Galvanizing Organic Bio-Agro Resources Dhan**.
Statement 2 wrong: GOBARdhan dates from **2018**, not 2020.
xa: It is an umbrella for converting **cattle dung** and farm solid waste to **compost, biogas, CBG/bio-CNG**.
**SATAT** was also launched in **2018** (MoPNG).
Models: **Zakariyapura**, **Varanasi**, **Banas**.

67.s:
Which of the following set of models is correctly associated with the stated biogas application?

1. Zakariyapura — household units
2. Varanasi — centralised plant for a dairy
3. Banas — centralised large-scale model

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
67.x: Zakariyapura represents household units, Varanasi a centralised dairy plant and Banas a centralised large-scale model.
67.tq: Match each place with its scale and application before selecting the code.
xs: All three pairs are correct — option **(4)**.
**Zakariyapura** = **household units**; **Varanasi** = **centralised plant for a dairy**; **Banas** = **centralised large-scale**.
xa: These are **GOBARdhan** replicable models (GOBARdhan, **2018**).
**Gobar gas** = biogas from cattle dung; slurry is good **organic manure**.
**Biogas Programme** (MNRE) supports **small/medium rural plants** under the National Bioenergy Programme **2021-26**.

67.s: The Compressed Biogas Obligation under SATAT is scheduled as:
o: 5 percent in FY 2026–28, followed by 1 percent from 2028–29
3 percent, 4 percent and 5 percent in FY 2026–28, followed by 1 percent from 2028–29
1 percent, 3 percent and 4 percent in FY 2026–28, followed by 5 percent from 2028–29
1 percent, 2 percent and 3 percent in FY 2026–28, followed by 4 percent from 2028–29
67.x: The CBG obligation is 1 percent, 3 percent and 4 percent during FY 2026–28, rising to 5 percent from FY 2028–29.
67.tq: Read the obligation as a rising sequence and retain the transition year.
xs: The SATAT **CBG Obligation** is **1 percent, 3 percent, 4 percent** in **FY26-28**, then **5 percent from 2028-29** — option **(3)**.
The obligation rises step by step to push **Compressed Biogas** into the gas mix.
xa: **SATAT**: launched **2018** by **MoPNG** to promote CBG from **agri-residue** and **MSW**.
**CBG** is purified, compressed biogas **chemically identical to CNG**.
⚠ Do not confuse with **biomass co-firing**: **5%** rising to **7%** (Ministry of Power, **2021**).

67.s: Which of the following correctly matches a programme with its principal activity?
o: Biomass Power and Bagasse Co-generation Programme — power from agro-residue and sugar-mill bagasse
67.x: The Biomass Power and Bagasse Co-generation Programme supports power generation from agro-residue and sugar-mill bagasse.
67.tq: Match each programme with its stated sector rather than its broad energy category.
xs: The **Biomass Power and Bagasse Co-generation Programme** (MNRE) produces power from **agro-residue** and **sugar-mill bagasse** — option **(1)**.
**SATAT** promotes **CBG**; **GOBARdhan** converts **cattle dung**; the **Biogas Programme** funds small rural biogas plants — none deals with geothermal, nuclear or tidal power.
xa: **Biomass Programme** funds **pellet and briquette** manufacturing.
**Bagasse cogeneration**: sugar mills burn bagasse → **steam + power** together.
AP: bagasse cogeneration **206.95 MW**, biomass **171.25 MW** (APSES **2025-26**).

67.s: In bagasse cogeneration, sugar mills primarily:
o: Use municipal plastic to produce uranium
Store tidal water for drinking purposes
Burn sugarcane residue to produce steam and power together
67.x: Bagasse, the residue of sugarcane processing, is burned in sugar mills to generate steam and electricity together.
67.tq: Connect the industrial residue with its practical energy use.
xs: In **bagasse cogeneration**, sugar mills **burn bagasse** (cane residue) to produce **steam and power together** — option **(3)**.
Bagasse is the **cane residue** left after crushing, so the mill uses its own waste as fuel.
xa: MNRE runs the **Biomass Power and Bagasse Co-generation Programme**.
Sugar mills may now make **ethanol** directly from **cane juice**.
**Power alcohol** in India comes mainly from **molasses**, a sugar-industry by-product.
AP bagasse cogeneration: **206.95 MW** (APSES **2025-26**).

67.s:
Consider the following statements about the National Bioenergy Programme:

1. Its Phase-I period is from 1 April 2021 to 31 March 2026.
2. Its Phase-I outlay is ₹858 crore.
3. It is administered by MNRE through State Nodal Agencies.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
67.x: All three statements are correct: Phase I covers 1 April 2021 to 31 March 2026, has an outlay of ₹858 crore and is implemented by MNRE through State Nodal Agencies.
67.tq: Verify the period, financial figure and implementing structure separately.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4)**.
Phase-I runs **1 Apr 2021 - 31 Mar 2026**, with outlay **₹858 cr**.
It is run by **MNRE** via **State Nodal Agencies**.
xa: Components: **Waste to Energy**, **Biomass** (briquettes, pellets, cogeneration), **Biogas** (small/medium rural plants).
Inspection: **Sardar Swaran Singh National Institute of Bio-Energy, Kapurthala (Punjab)**.
⚠ **SATAT** belongs to **MoPNG**, not MNRE.

67.s:
Under the National Bioenergy Programme, the Waste to Energy component includes:

1. Biogas and BioCNG
2. Power from urban, industrial and farm waste
3. Small and medium rural biogas plants for cooking and lighting

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
67.x: Waste to Energy covers biogas, BioCNG and power from urban, industrial and farm waste. Small and medium rural plants for cooking and lighting belong to the Biogas component.
67.tq: Separate closely related subcomponents instead of treating all activities as one category.
xs: The **Waste to Energy** component covers **biogas/BioCNG** and **power from urban, industrial and farm waste** — option **(2)**.
Small/medium **rural biogas plants** for cooking and lighting fall under the separate **Biogas** component.
xa: The **Biomass** component covers **briquettes, pellets, cogeneration**.
National **WtE** capacity: **0.88 GW**.
WtE routes: **incineration**, **pyrolysis**, **gasification**, **biomethanation**, **landfill gas recovery**, **RDF**.

67.s: The Biomass Programme primarily provides financial support for which of the following purposes?
o: Construction of tidal power plants in coastal areas
Production of hydrogen exclusively from seawater
Import of uranium for nuclear power generation
Manufacture of pellets and briquettes for power generation
67.x: The Biomass Programme funds the manufacture of biomass pellets and briquettes intended for power generation.
67.tq: Identify the precise purpose of the programme rather than choosing a neighbouring renewable-energy activity.
xs: MNRE's **Biomass Programme** funds **pellet and briquette** manufacturing for power generation — option **(4)**.
It is distinct from tidal, hydrogen or uranium schemes — it works on **biomass** fuel supply.
xa: **Biomass co-firing** (as of **31 Jul 2025**): ~**29.78 LMT** pellets co-fired in **71** coal plants → ~**3.57 MT CO2** cut.
**Co-firing policy** (Ministry of Power, **2021**): **5%** biomass, rising to **7%**, run by **SAMARTH**.
The National Bioenergy Programme's **Biomass** component covers briquettes, pellets and **cogeneration**.

67.s:
Consider the following statements regarding biomass co-firing in coal-based power plants:
1. The Ministry of Power policy issued in 2021 mandated 5% biomass co-firing.
2. The mandated level was to rise to 7%.
3. The policy applied only to hydroelectric power plants.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
67.x: The 2021 Ministry of Power policy mandated 5% biomass co-firing in coal plants, with a planned increase to 7%. It did not apply only to hydroelectric plants.
67.tq: Find the false statement by checking the technology and plant type against the policy.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1)**.
Statements 1 and 2: the **Ministry of Power** policy (**2021**) mandates **5% biomass co-firing** in **coal plants**, rising to **7%**.
Statement 3 wrong: it applies to **coal** plants, not hydro.
xa: It is run by National Mission **SAMARTH**.
As of **31 Jul 2025**: ~**29.78 LMT** pellets co-fired in **71** coal plants, cutting ~**3.57 MT CO2**.
MNRE's **Biomass Programme** funds the pellets and briquettes.

67.s: Which institutional mechanism is associated with implementation of biomass co-firing in thermal power plants?
67.x: National Mission SAMARTH is associated with the biomass co-firing initiative in thermal power plants.
67.tq: Distinguish the implementing mission from other energy policies and schemes.
xs: Biomass co-firing in coal plants is run by **National Mission SAMARTH** — option **(4)**.
The **NBCC** relates to biofuel policy; **CAFE III** is a vehicle-efficiency norm; the **Small Hydro Power Development Scheme** concerns small hydro.
xa: Co-firing policy: **Ministry of Power**, **2021** — **5%** rising to **7%**.
⚠ **SATAT** = MoPNG; **National Bioenergy Programme** = MNRE; co-firing = Ministry of Power.
~**29.78 LMT** pellets co-fired in **71** coal plants (as of **31 Jul 2025**).

67.s: Inspection under MNRE's National Bioenergy Programme is entrusted to the Sardar Swaran Singh National Institute of Bio-Energy located at:
67.x: SSS-NIBE is at Kapurthala, Punjab. Chennai hosts NIWE and NIOT, Gurugram hosts NISE, and Dehradun hosts CSIR-IIP - none is the bioenergy inspection body.
67.tq: Bio-energy institute = Kapurthala (SSS-NIBE).
xs: The **Sardar Swaran Singh National Institute of Bio-Energy** is at **Kapurthala, Punjab** — option **(1)**.
It handles **inspection** under MNRE's **National Bioenergy Programme**.
xa: **NIOT, Chennai** (MoES) is India's lead **ocean-energy** research body.
**IIT Roorkee**'s Dept. of Hydro and Renewable Energy gives **small hydro** technical support.
**CSIR-NIIST** and the **DBT-ICT Centre** do **algal biofuel** research.

67.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched with the generation of biofuel?
o: 2G — food crops such as sugarcane and corn
67.x: Third-generation biofuels use algae or algal biomass. First-generation fuels use food crops, second-generation fuels use non-food lignocellulosic material, and fourth-generation fuels use genetically engineered organisms.
67.tq: Start with the sure generation–feedstock pair and eliminate the reversed classifications.
xs: **3G** biofuels use **algal biomass** — option **(3)** (PYQ **2023**; APPSC-GS **2023** key).
**1G** uses **food crops** (sugarcane, corn); **2G** uses **non-food lignocellulosic residue** — options (1) and (2) are swapped.
**4G** uses **genetically modified algae/microbes**, not untreated residues.
xa: ⚠ **3G** = algae; **4G** = genetically modified algae/microbes that capture more CO2 (RPSC **2024** key).
3G examples: **algal biodiesel**, **biobutanol**.
**NPB 2018**: 3G biofuels are classed as **advanced biofuels**.

67.s: Which of the following feedstocks is characteristic of second-generation biofuels?
67.x: Second-generation biofuels use non-food lignocellulosic residues such as rice straw, straw, husk, wood chips and bamboo.
67.tq: Classify the feedstock according to whether it is food-based, residual or genetically modified.
xs: **Rice straw** is a **2G** (non-food lignocellulosic) feedstock — option **(4)**.
**Corn grain** and **sugarcane juice** are **1G** food-crop feedstocks; **GM algae** is **4G**.
xa: 2G feedstocks: crop residue, **straw**, **husk**, **wood chips**, **bamboo**, forest waste, non-edible oils.
**IOCL Panipat (2022)** used **rice straw** and **bagasse** — first commercial 2G plant.
2G avoids the **food-fuel conflict** but needs complex thermochemical/biochemical conversion.

67.s: The first commercial 2G ethanol plant at Panipat used which of the following as its principal feedstock?
67.x: The IOCL Panipat plant, described as the first commercial 2G plant in 2022, used rice straw as feedstock.
67.tq: Link the plant with its distinctive residue feedstock rather than with first-generation materials.
xs: **IOCL Panipat (2022)**, Haryana — India's first commercial 2G plant — uses **rice straw** (and bagasse) — option **(2)**.
**Molasses** is a 1G feedstock; **palm stearin** is for **biodiesel**.
xa: **Numaligarh Refinery** (**Golaghat, Assam**) uses **bamboo** — dedicated **14 Sep 2025**.
IOCL Panipat became India's first ISCC **CORSIA**-certified **SAF** producer (**Aug 2025**).
Other 2G plants: **HPCL Bathinda** (Punjab), **BPCL Bargarh** (Odisha).

67.s: Which one of the following is a major advantage of second-generation biofuels over first-generation biofuels?
o: They avoid the food-versus-fuel conflict by using non-food residues.
They require no biochemical or thermochemical conversion.
They are produced exclusively from edible vegetable oils.
They use only genetically modified algae.
67.x: Second-generation biofuels use non-food lignocellulosic residues and therefore avoid the food-fuel conflict, although their conversion is technically complex.
67.tq: Apply the food-versus-fuel distinction to identify the advantage of the technology.
xs: **2G biofuels** avoid the **food-versus-fuel conflict** by using **non-food residues** — option **(1)**.
They still need complex **thermochemical/biochemical conversion**, so option (2) is wrong.
Edible oils are **1G**; GM algae are **4G**.
xa: **1G** = food-fuel conflict — e.g. sugar prices rising (**Sep 2026**).
**PM JI-VAN Yojana (2019)** supports 2G ethanol; extended to **2028-29**.
**NPB 2018**: **2G ethanol** is an **advanced biofuel**.

67.s:
Consider the following statements about the Numaligarh bamboo bioethanol plant:
1. It was dedicated on 14 September 2025.
2. It is described as India's first commercial-scale bamboo bioethanol plant.
3. It is a first-generation plant based mainly on corn.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
67.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because bamboo is a non-food lignocellulosic feedstock associated with second-generation bioethanol.
67.tq: Reject the generation mismatch by checking the plant's non-food feedstock.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1)**.
**Numaligarh Refinery** (**Golaghat, Assam**) was dedicated on **14 Sep 2025** as India's first commercial-scale **bamboo** bioethanol plant.
Statement 3 wrong: it is a **2G** plant using **bamboo**, not a 1G corn plant.
xa: **IOCL Panipat (2022)** = first commercial **2G** plant (rice straw, bagasse).
⚠ First 2G **bamboo** plant = **Numaligarh**; first commercial 2G = **Panipat**.
**Corn** and **sugarcane** are **1G** food-crop feedstocks.

67.s:
Assertion (A): Fourth-generation biofuels have the potential to be carbon-negative.
Reason (R): They use genetically engineered algae or microbes designed to capture more carbon dioxide.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
67.x: Both statements are true, and the enhanced carbon-dioxide capture by genetically engineered algae or microbes explains the potential carbon-negative character of fourth-generation fuels.
67.tq: Test whether the biological feature in the Reason directly explains the environmental outcome in the Assertion.
xs: Both A and R are **true**, and R is the **correct explanation** of A — option **(1)**.
**4G** biofuels use **genetically modified algae/microbes** that capture more **CO2**, giving **carbon-negative fuels** (RPSC **2024** key).
xa: ⚠ **3G** = (natural) **algae**; **4G** = **genetically modified** algae/microbes.
**1G** = food crops; **2G** = non-food lignocellulosic residue.
**BioE3 Policy 2024** backs **bio-jet fuel**.

67.s:
Consider the following statements about algal biofuel:
1. Algae give a high yield per unit area.
2. Algal cultivation can use wastewater and CO2.
3. Lipid extraction from algae requires little energy.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
67.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: these are the stated advantages. Statement 3 is wrong: energy-intensive lipid extraction is a stated limitation (with high cultivation/harvesting cost, contamination, scale-up and heavy water/nutrient needs). So '1 and 2 only'.
67.tq: Algae: high yield + wastewater/CO2 use; but costly, energy-intensive extraction.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1)**.
Statements 1 and 2: algae give **high yield per unit area** and can use **wastewater and CO2**.
Statement 3 wrong: **lipid extraction** is **energy-intensive**.
xa: Other limitations: high **cultivation and harvesting cost**, **contamination** and scale-up problems, heavy **water and nutrient** needs.
**CSIR-NIIST** and **DBT-ICT Centre** research algal biofuel.
**3G** biofuels = **algae** (PYQ **2023**).

67.s:
Match the following 2G ethanol plants with their locations or feedstocks:

List-I (Plant)
a. IOCL Panipat
b. Numaligarh Refinery
c. HPCL Bathinda
d. BPCL Bargarh

List-II (Location or feedstock)
i. Odisha
ii. Haryana; rice straw and bagasse
iii. Golaghat, Assam; bamboo
iv. Punjab

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
