Scientists alone must replace all administrative members.
All Category B projects must automatically be transferred to the central EAC.
State committees may retain proposals indefinitely without escalation.
77.x: The amendment permits the Centre to remove members of EAC, SEAC or SEIAA mid-term for persistent delays. It also introduced an escalation mechanism rather than automatic transfer of all Category B projects to the central EAC.
77.tq: Identify the precise institutional power among reversed alternatives.
xs: The Centre **may remove EAC, SEAC or SEIAA members mid-term for persistent delays** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Category B **no longer defaults to the central EAC** — escalation goes to **SCEIA** after **120 days**, so options (3) and (4) are wrong.
xa: Member tenure: **3 to 4 years**; max **two terms**; age limit **70**.
Concern: **bureaucrats replace scientists**; speed over science.
MoEFCC had proposed **SCEIA and SAEIA** earlier (Mar 2026).

77.s: The principal criticism of the July 2026 amendment to the EIA framework is that it may:
o: Replace scientists with bureaucrats and prioritise speed over science
Give excessive control to local communities over scientific appraisal
Make every project subject to a full EIA
77.x: The amendment has been criticised on the ground that bureaucratic control may replace scientific expertise and that speed may be prioritised over scientific appraisal.
77.tq: Identify the stated criticism rather than the procedural detail.
xs: The main criticism: **bureaucrats replace scientists** and **speed over science** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The amendment speeds appraisal (**120-day** escalation, removal of members for delays), it does not abolish clearances.
xa: Wider criticism: EIAs by **proponent-paid consultants**; **no central baseline data bank**; weak emergency plans.
Fix suggested: **independent EIA authority**.
Post-facto clearances risk becoming "**the design**" (31 Jul 2026).

77.s: PARIVESH is best described as:
o: A single-window portal for online environment, forest, wildlife and CRZ clearances
A programme for preparing baseline biodiversity data
A committee for appraisal of Category A projects
77.x: PARIVESH is an online single-window platform for environment, forest, wildlife and Coastal Regulation Zone clearances.
77.tq: Distinguish a digital clearance platform from statutory bodies.
xs: PARIVESH is a **single-window portal for online environment, forest, wildlife and CRZ clearances** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It is not a tribunal (the **NGT**) or an appraisal committee (the **EAC**).
xa: Launched **2018**; now **PARIVESH 3.0** using **AI** (Economic Survey 2025-26).
Platform for the **120-day** escalation to **SCEIA**.
Expansion: **Pro-Active and Responsive facilitation by Interactive, Virtuous and Environmental Single-window Hub**.

77.s: PARIVESH was launched in:
77.x: The PARIVESH portal was launched in 2018.
77.tq: Recall the launch year against years of major EIA notifications.
xs: **PARIVESH** was launched in **2018** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**1994** and **2006** are EIA notification years; **2020** is the draft notification.
xa: It covers **environment, forest, wildlife and CRZ** clearances.
**PARIVESH 3.0** uses **AI**.
It now routes **120-day** escalations to **SCEIA** (23 Jul 2026).

77.s: What is the correct expansion of the acronym PARIVESH?
o: Public Assessment and Regulation of Industrial Ventures for Ecological Safety Hub
Provisional Assessment and Review Interface for Vigilance in Environmental Statutory Hearings
Participatory Authority for Regional Impact Verification and Environmental Safety Headquarters
Pro-Active and Responsive facilitation by Interactive, Virtuous and Environmental Single-window Hub
77.x: PARIVESH expands to Pro-Active and Responsive facilitation by Interactive, Virtuous and Environmental Single-window Hub.
77.tq: Test the exact official expansion rather than a look-alike phrase.
xs: PARIVESH = **Pro-Active and Responsive facilitation by Interactive, Virtuous and Environmental Single-window Hub** — so option **(4)** is correct.
The words "**Single-window Hub**" reflect its role as one online window for clearances.
xa: Launched **2018** as a single window for environment, forest, wildlife and **CRZ** clearances.
**PARIVESH 3.0** uses **AI** (Economic Survey 2025-26).
⚠ PARIVESH is a portal; **SCEIA** and **SAEIA** are backup appraisal bodies.

77.s: PARIVESH 3.0 is associated with the use of:
o: Artificial intelligence in the clearance portal
Satellite launch technology for biodiversity mapping
77.x: PARIVESH 3.0 uses artificial intelligence as part of the upgraded single-window clearance system.
77.tq: Match the technology with the correct environmental-governance platform.
xs: **PARIVESH 3.0** uses **artificial intelligence** in the clearance portal — so option **(3)** is correct (Economic Survey 2025-26).
It upgrades the single-window clearance portal; blockchain, biometric voting or satellite launches are not mentioned.
xa: PARIVESH was launched in **2018**.
It is a **single window** for environment, forest, wildlife and **CRZ** clearances.
It auto-transfers delayed SEAC proposals to **SCEIA** after **120 days**.

77.s: Which of the following correctly represents the backup arrangement referred to for environmental appraisal bodies in 2026?
o: NGT for SEIAA and NEAA for SEAC
SCEIA for SEIAA and SAEIA for SEAC
EAC for SEIAA and CPCB for SEAC
SAEIA for SEIAA and SCEIA for SEAC
77.x: The stated backup bodies are SAEIA in place of SEIAA and SCEIA in place of SEAC.
77.tq: Discriminate between the similar abbreviations by matching each backup body to its parent body.
xs: **SAEIA** stands in for **SEIAA** and **SCEIA** for **SEAC** — so option **(4)** is correct.
Option (2) swaps the pair.
xa: Tenure of backup bodies: **6 + 6 months** (max 1 year).
They step in when a State's **SEIAA or SEAC lapses**.
MoEFCC had proposed **SCEIA and SAEIA** earlier (**Mar 2026**).

77.s: Under the stated revised arrangements, the tenure of SEIAA, EAC and SEAC members is:
o: Four years, with a maximum of two terms and an age limit of 70
Five years, with unlimited terms and no age limit
Three years, with one renewal and a maximum age of 65
77.x: The tenure was raised to four years, with a maximum of two terms and an age limit of 70 years for members of SEIAA, EAC and SEAC.
77.tq: Combine tenure, term limit and age limit to avoid selecting a partly correct option.
xs: Members' tenure is **four years**, **max two terms**, **age limit 70** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The notes record tenure going from **3 to 4 years** for **SEIAA, EAC and SEAC** members (23 Jul 2026).
xa: The Centre may **remove members mid-term** for persistent delays.
Concern: **bureaucrats replace scientists**.
Backup bodies **SAEIA/SCEIA**: tenure **6 + 6 months**.

77.s: The Draft EIA Notification, 2020 proposed which of the following?
o: Post-facto clearance through appraisal, penalties, compensation and remediation plans
A complete ban on environmental clearance after project commencement
Clearance based only on investment size
Abolition of public consultation for all projects
77.x: The draft proposed post-facto environmental clearance through appraisal, penalties, compensation and remediation plans. It was not finalised.
77.tq: Recognise the controversial proposal associated with the draft notification.
xs: The Draft 2020 proposed **post-facto clearance through appraisal, penalties, compensation and remediation plans** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It did not ban post-commencement clearance — it proposed **retrospective EC on payment of penalties**.
xa: Draft 2020 also cut public-hearing notice **30 to 20 days**.
Wide protest; **not been finalised** (Aug 2026).
⚠ Clearance based on investment size was the **1994** approach; **2006** moved to impact potential.

77.s:
Consider the following provisions associated with the Draft EIA Notification, 2020:
1. The public-hearing notice period was proposed to be reduced from 30 days to 20 days.
2. More projects were proposed to be moved to Category B2 or exempted.
3. Compliance reports were proposed to be submitted yearly instead of half-yearly.
4. Violations could be reported by any member of the public without restriction.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
77.x: The draft proposed a 20-day notice period, more B2 or exempt projects and yearly compliance reports. It restricted reporting of violations to the violator or government, so statement 4 is false.
77.tq: Locate the false statement by testing the reporting restriction.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 3** are correct — so option **(1)** is correct.
Draft 2020: notice cut **30 to 20 days**; more projects moved to **B2/exempt**; compliance reports **yearly instead of half-yearly**.
Statement 4 is wrong: violations were reportable **only by the violator or government**.
xa: It also proposed **post-facto clearance** on payment of penalties.
The draft has **not been finalised**.
EIA 2006: notice at least **30 days**; hearing within **45 days**.

77.s: Which statement regarding the Draft EIA Notification, 2020 is correct?
o: It was not finalised and was criticised for provisions including post-facto clearance.
It proposed longer public consultation periods than the 2006 notification.
It was finally enacted without modification.
It abolished penalties and remediation plans for violations.
77.x: The 2020 draft was not finalised and was contested, particularly for proposing post-facto clearance and shorter consultation periods.
77.tq: Reject absolute claims about a draft becoming final law.
xs: The Draft 2020 **was not finalised** and was criticised for **post-facto clearance** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It proposed **shorter** consultation (**30 to 20 days**), not longer.
It relied on **penalties, compensation, remediation plans** for violations — it did not abolish them.
xa: Other contested items: more **B2/exempt** projects; **yearly** compliance reports.
**Vanashakti** final verdict (**29 July 2026**) quashed the **2021 Office Memorandum** on retrospective EC.
Prior EC is **mandatory** under EIA 2006.

77.s:
Consider the following statements about Supreme Court cases on environmental clearance:
1. Common Cause v. Union of India (2017) concerned mining in Odisha without or beyond environmental clearance and directed compensation equal to 100% of the value of illegally extracted minerals.
2. Noble M. Paikada v. Union of India (2024) examined the 2020 exemption from environmental clearance for extraction of ordinary earth for linear projects.
3. In Noble M. Paikada, the Supreme Court upheld the blanket exemption as valid.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
77.x: Statement 1 is correct: Common Cause (2017) dealt with Odisha mining without or beyond EC and ordered compensation of 100% of the value of illegally extracted minerals. Statement 2 is correct: Noble M. Paikada (2024) examined the 2020 exemption from EC for extraction of ordinary earth for linear projects. Statement 3 is wrong: the Court held the blanket exemption arbitrary, not valid. Hence 1 and 2 only.
77.tq: Common Cause = Odisha mining, 100% value; Paikada = ordinary earth exemption, held arbitrary.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1: **Common Cause v UoI (2017)** — Odisha mining without or beyond EC; compensation of **100%** of the mineral's value.
Statement 2: **Noble M. Paikada v UoI (2024)** — the **2020 exemption from EC** for ordinary earth for linear projects (**APPSC 2024**).
Statement 3 is wrong: the SC held the **blanket exemption arbitrary**.
xa: **Alembic Pharmaceuticals (2020)**: ex post facto EC contrary to EIA; **2002** MoEF circular quashed.
⚠ Vanashakti: **May 2025** struck down → **Nov 2025** recalled (**2:1**) → **29 July 2026** final, prospective.
**S.P. Muthuraman (2025)** also held retrospective ECs illegal.

77.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Alembic Pharmaceuticals v. Rohit Prajapati:
1. It was decided in 2020.
2. The Supreme Court held that ex post facto environmental clearance was contrary to the EIA regime.
3. The 2002 Ministry of Environment and Forests circular permitting such clearance was quashed.
4. The Court necessarily directed closure of every project concerned.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
77.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 4 is false because compensation was imposed instead of ordering closure in every case.
77.tq: Find the wrong consequence in an otherwise case-specific statement set.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 3** are correct — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Alembic Pharmaceuticals v Rohit Prajapati (2020)** held ex post facto EC **contrary to the EIA regime**.
It **quashed the 2002 MoEF circular** allowing such clearance.
Statement 4 is wrong: **compensation was imposed instead of closure**.
xa: **Common Cause v UoI (2017)**: Odisha mining; compensation of **100%** of the mineral's value.
**S.P. Muthuraman (2025)** also held retrospective ECs illegal.
Exam angle: prior EC is **mandatory** under EIA 2006; post-facto only as a narrow exception.

77.s: In its May 2025 ruling in Vanashakti v. Union of India, the Supreme Court described retrospective environmental clearances as:
o: a gross illegality and an anathema to environmental law
a mandatory feature of the EIA Notification, 2006
77.x: The May 2025 Vanashakti ruling characterised retrospective environmental clearances as a gross illegality and an anathema to environmental law.
77.tq: Recall the exact judicial characterisation used in a landmark ruling.
xs: The May 2025 **Vanashakti** ruling called retrospective ECs a **gross illegality** and an **anathema** to environmental law — so option **(1)** is correct.
It **struck down** the **2017 Notification / 2021 OM**.
xa: ⚠ Vanashakti: **May 2025** struck down → **Nov 2025** recalled (**2:1**) → **29 July 2026** final, prospective.
The recall relied on **D Swamy (2021)** and **Pahwa Plastics (2022)**.
Prior EC is **mandatory** under EIA 2006.

77.s:
With reference to the Vanashakti litigation, consider the following statements:
1. The May 2025 ruling struck down the 2017 Notification and the 2021 Office Memorandum.
2. In November 2025, the ruling was recalled by a 2:1 majority.
3. The recall relied, among other decisions, on D. Swamy (2021) and Pahwa Plastics (2022).
4. Approximately ₹20,000 crore worth of projects was reported to be at stake.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
77.x: All four statements are correct. The May 2025 ruling struck down the specified instruments, was recalled in November 2025 by a 2:1 majority, relied on the cited earlier cases, and affected projects valued at approximately ₹20,000 crore.
77.tq: Track multiple stages of a case without confusing the original ruling with its recall.
xs: All four statements — **1, 2, 3 and 4** — are correct, so option **(4)** is correct.
**May 2025** ruling struck down the **2017 Notification / 2021 OM**; **Nov 2025** recall by **2:1** majority.
The recall relied on **D Swamy (2021)** and **Pahwa Plastics (2022)**, which allowed post-facto EC in exceptional cases.
About **₹20,000 crore** of projects faced demolition (LENS, Nov 2025).
xa: Final verdict: **29 July 2026**, led by **CJI Surya Kant**; ruling **prospective**.
May 2025 language: "**gross illegality**" and "anathema".
**S.P. Muthuraman (2025)** also held retrospective ECs illegal.

77.s: The final Vanashakti verdict dated 29 July 2026 was delivered by a Bench led by:
77.x: The final Vanashakti verdict of 29 July 2026 was delivered by a Bench led by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant.
77.tq: Use the date-and-presiding-authority pair to separate successive rulings.
xs: The final Vanashakti verdict of **29 July 2026** was by a Bench led by **CJI Surya Kant** — so option **(4)** is correct.
Sources: **LENSD 31 Jul 2026**; **TH 21 Aug 2026**.
xa: It nullified the **2021 Office Memorandum** (retrospective EC on paying penalties).
Ex post facto EC must meet **Arts 14 and 21** (proportionality); SC keeps power under **Article 142**.
Critics call the OM-vs-notification distinction a "**fig-leaf**".

77.s: Which one of the following correctly states the effect of the final Vanashakti verdict of 29 July 2026?
o: It retrospectively validated all clearances obtained under the 2021 Office Memorandum.
It prospectively nullified the 2021 Office Memorandum, while earlier clearances under the 2017 Notification and 2021 Office Memorandum survived.
It made the 2017 Notification available to all fresh violators seeking regularisation.
It permanently prohibited the Centre from issuing any time-limited notification under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.
77.x: The final verdict prospectively nullified the 2021 Office Memorandum, but earlier environmental clearances under the 2017 Notification and 2021 Office Memorandum survived. It did not open those instruments to fresh violators or permanently bar time-limited notifications under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.
77.tq: Distinguish prospective effect, retrospective validation and future eligibility.
xs: The verdict **prospectively nullified the 2021 Office Memorandum**, while **earlier ECs under the 2017 Notification and 2021 OM survive** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Fresh violators** cannot seek regularisation under the 2017 Notification or 2021 SOP, so option (3) is wrong.
The Centre **may issue time-limited notifications under EPA 1986**, so option (4) is wrong.
xa: Bench led by **CJI Surya Kant** (**29 July 2026**).
Ex post facto EC must pass **Arts 14 and 21** (proportionality).
SC keeps its power under **Article 142**.

77.s: In the context of environmental clearance, which of the following is the correct general rule?
o: Prior clearance is required only for products assessed through LCA.
Environmental clearance is needed only after an environmental audit identifies non-compliance.
Prior environmental clearance is mandatory under the EIA framework, while post-facto approval is only a narrow exception.
Post-facto approval is the normal rule and prior clearance is optional.
77.x: The general rule under the EIA framework is that prior environmental clearance is mandatory. Post-facto approval, where recognised at all, is treated only as a narrow exception.
77.tq: Distinguish the governing rule from exceptional regularisation mechanisms.
xs: **Prior EC is mandatory under EIA; post-facto approval is only a narrow exception** — so option **(3)** is correct.
This is the exam angle in the notes: prior EC mandatory under **EIA 2006**.
An **environmental audit** is an after-the-fact compliance check, and **LCA** is a product tool — neither is the clearance trigger.
xa: **Vanashakti (29 July 2026)**: ex post facto EC only via **Arts 14 and 21** test and **Article 142**.
**Alembic (2020)**: ex post facto EC contrary to the EIA regime.
**Draft 2020** proposed post-facto clearance but was **not finalised**.

77.s: According to the final Vanashakti verdict of 29 July 2026, any ex post facto environmental clearance must satisfy the test of:
o: Article 252 read with the Water Act, 1974
Article 323B read with the NGT Act, 2010
77.x: The Court held that ex post facto EC must meet Articles 14 and 21 (a proportionality test), while the Supreme Court keeps its power under Article 142. Articles 48A and 51A(g) are a Directive Principle and a Fundamental Duty, not the test laid down. Article 252 is the Water Act's basis; Article 323B concerns tribunals generally.
77.tq: Vanashakti 2026: Arts 14 + 21 test; Art 142 reserved for the SC.
xs: Ex post facto EC must satisfy **Articles 14 and 21 (proportionality)** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The SC also **keeps its power under Article 142**.
⚠ **Article 252** is the **Water Act's** basis — not this test.
xa: The ruling was **prospective** — earlier ECs under the **2017 Notification and 2021 OM** survive.
The Centre may issue **time-limited notifications under EPA 1986**.
Verdict date **29 July 2026**; Bench led by **CJI Surya Kant**.

77.s: The time limit prescribed in the August 2023 direction for the Border Roads Organisation to plant the trees was:
77.x: The NGT directed the plantation of the trees within one month.
77.tq: Separate the quantity of the direction from its compliance period.
xs: The NGT gave the **Border Roads Organisation** **one month** to plant trees — so option **(3)** is correct.
The **Aug 2023** order (Uttarakhand) required at least **10,000 trees** within **one month** (PYQ).
xa: **Rat-hole mining** in **Meghalaya (2014)** was declared illegal/banned by NGT.
NGT fined **Maharashtra and West Bengal (2022)** for waste mismanagement.
**LG Polymers** (May 2020): **Rs 50 crore** interim deposit.

77.s: In 2022, the National Green Tribunal imposed fines on states in connection with waste mismanagement. Which pair was specifically associated with such fines?
77.x: Maharashtra and West Bengal were cited as examples of states fined by the NGT for waste mismanagement in 2022.
77.tq: Match the environmental violation with the correctly associated states.
xs: NGT fined **Maharashtra and West Bengal** in **2022** for waste mismanagement — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Rajasthan and MP** (with UP) got the **Jan 2026** suo motu notice on sewage in drinking water; **Odisha and Chhattisgarh** feature in the **Polavaram** submergence dispute.
xa: Other NGT directions: **Ganga pollution control**, waste management, industrial monitoring.
Docket includes **Dhanauri wetland** and **Saparnika river** (2026).
**BRO** (Uttarakhand, Aug 2023): **10,000 trees** in one month.

77.s: Which of the following correctly describes the NGT action concerning the LG Polymers incident at Visakhapatnam?
o: It transferred the matter to the National Environment Appellate Authority without any financial direction.
It took suo motu cognisance and ordered an interim deposit of Rs 50 crore.
It ordered a permanent ban on all chemical industries in Andhra Pradesh.
It directed the Border Roads Organisation to undertake plantation in Uttarakhand.
77.x: Following the Visakhapatnam styrene leak in May 2020, the NGT took suo motu cognisance and ordered an interim deposit of Rs 50 crore.
77.tq: Match the authority’s action to the correct incident instead of confusing separate NGT orders.
xs: The NGT **took suo motu cognisance and ordered an interim deposit of Rs 50 crore** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The incident was the **Visakhapatnam styrene leak, May 2020** (LG Polymers).
BRO plantation in **Uttarakhand** is a separate NGT order (**Aug 2023**).
xa: The **LG Polymers** leak is part of the AP angle, handled by NGT.
NGT **Jan 2026** suo motu: Rajasthan, MP, UP over sewage in drinking water.
Rat-hole mining: **Meghalaya (2014)**.

77.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Great Nicobar project—High-Powered Committee on NGT directions
Sewage in drinking water—suo motu notice to Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh
Styrene leak—Maharashtra and West Bengal waste-management fines
77.x: The styrene leak concerned LG Polymers at Visakhapatnam and led to an interim deposit of Rs 50 crore. Maharashtra and West Bengal were associated with fines for waste mismanagement.
77.tq: Find the swapped incident-and-state pairing.
xs: **Styrene leak — Maharashtra and West Bengal fines** is wrongly matched — so option **(4)** is correct.
The styrene leak was **LG Polymers, Visakhapatnam** (May 2020) → **Rs 50 crore** interim deposit.
**Maharashtra and West Bengal (2022)** were fined for **waste mismanagement**.
xa: **Rat-hole mining — Meghalaya (2014)**; **Great Nicobar — High-Powered Committee** on NGT directions.
Sewage in drinking water: suo motu notice to **Rajasthan, MP, UP** (15 Jan 2026).
BRO: **10,000 trees** within one month (Aug 2023).

77.s: The High-Powered Committee relating to the Great Nicobar project was set up pursuant to directions of the:
77.x: A High-Powered Committee was set up on the directions of the National Green Tribunal in relation to the Great Nicobar project.
77.tq: Use the ‘who directed the committee’ approach to distinguish environmental institutions.
xs: The Great Nicobar **High-Powered Committee** was set up on directions of the **National Green Tribunal** — so option **(3)** is correct.
The opposition demanded the report be made public (**11 May 2026**).
xa: Criticism: **thin baseline data** in the Great Nicobar EIA.
Other NGT orders: **rat-hole mining** ban (Meghalaya, 2014); **LG Polymers** Rs 50 crore deposit.
⚠ CPCB is a statutory board, not the body that set up this committee.

77.s: The inter-state dispute concerning the Polavaram project primarily relates to submergence in:
77.x: The Polavaram inter-state dispute concerns submergence in neighbouring Odisha and Chhattisgarh and was raised before the Supreme Court.
77.tq: Identify the neighbouring states directly affected by the project’s submergence issue.
xs: The Polavaram dispute is over **submergence in Odisha and Chhattisgarh** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It was raised before the **Supreme Court**.
xa: **Telangana** moved the SC seeking an EIA review of **Indira Sagar Polavaram** (**APPSC 2018**).
EIA in India began with **river-valley projects**.
AP angle also: APPCB hearing on the **Water Aerodrome at Prakasam Barrage**.

77.s:
Consider the following statements regarding criticisms of the Environmental Impact Assessment process:
1. EIA reports are often prepared by consultants paid by the project proponents.
2. There is no central baseline data bank for EIA purposes.
3. Emergency plans associated with projects may be weak.
4. Certain projects or situations may be exempted from public hearings.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
77.x: All four statements describe identified criticisms of the EIA process: proponent-paid consultants, absence of a central baseline data bank, weak emergency plans and exemptions from hearings.
77.tq: Test the complete set of criticisms by checking each statement independently.
xs: All four — **1, 2, 3 and 4** — are criticisms of EIA, so option **(4)** is correct.
EIA is prepared by **proponent-paid consultants**; there is **no central baseline data bank**.
**Weak emergency plans** and **hearings exempted** complete the list.
xa: Fix: **independent EIA authority**.
Exempted from hearings: **defence and strategic** projects, **B2** projects.
Post-facto clearances risk becoming "**the design**".

77.s: Which one of the following has been suggested as a measure to address the criticism that EIA consultants may lack independence?
o: Transfer of EIA preparation entirely to project proponents
Permitting post-facto clearances as a routine measure
Creation of an independent EIA authority
77.x: An independent EIA authority has been suggested to improve the credibility and independence of environmental assessments.
77.tq: Match the identified institutional defect with the appropriate reform.
xs: The suggested fix is an **independent EIA authority** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It answers the criticism that EIAs are prepared by **proponent-paid consultants**.
Routine post-facto clearance and abolishing hearings would worsen, not fix, the problem.
xa: Other criticisms: **no central baseline data bank**; **weak emergency plans**.
UPSC way-forward: **sector-wide EIAs** (strategic/cumulative).
Jul 2026 concern: **bureaucrats replace scientists**.

77.s:
With reference to environmental clearance issues in Andhra Pradesh, consider the following statements:
1. Telangana approached the Supreme Court seeking a review of the EIA for the Indira Sagar Polavaram project.
2. The Andhra Pradesh Pollution Control Board conducted a public hearing concerning a water aerodrome at Prakasam Barrage.
3. The Human Rights Forum described the draft EIA for the water aerodrome as error-ridden.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
77.x: All three statements are correct. Telangana sought Supreme Court review of the Polavaram EIA, while the APPCB hearing on the Prakasam Barrage water aerodrome drew criticism from the Human Rights Forum for an error-ridden draft EIA.
77.tq: Link the institution, project and criticism without confusing the two Andhra Pradesh examples.
xs: All three statements — **1, 2 and 3** — are correct, so option **(4)** is correct.
Statement 1: **Telangana** moved the SC for EIA review of **Indira Sagar Polavaram** (**APPSC 2018**).
Statements 2 and 3: **APPCB** held a public hearing on the **Water Aerodrome at Prakasam Barrage**; **HRF** called the draft EIA **error-ridden** (22 May 2026).
xa: Public hearings are conducted by the **SPCB**, **District Collector** presiding.
Polavaram dispute: submergence in **Odisha, Chhattisgarh**.
**LG Polymers** (Visakhapatnam, 2020) was handled by NGT.

77.s:
Arrange the following developments relating to EIA in chronological order:
A. Enactment of NEPA in the United States
B. First use of EIA in India
C. First formal EIA notification in India
D. EIA amendment creating SCEIA and prescribing a 120-day timeline
77.x: The sequence is NEPA in 1969, first use of EIA in India in 1978, the first formal notification in 1994, and the later amendment creating SCEIA with a 120-day timeline.
77.tq: Anchor the sequence using the earliest and latest dates first.
xs: The order is **A, B, C, D** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**NEPA 1969** (US) → EIA first used in India **1978** → first formal notification **1994** → **SCEIA** + **120-day** amendment (**23 Jul 2026**).
xa: ⚠ Sources differ on India's start: **1976-77** (DST, river-valley) vs **1978**.
EIA Notification **2006** replaced the 1994 notification.
Public hearing added by the **1997 amendment**.

77.s: Post-facto environmental clearances have been criticised because they may become:
o: a substitute for baseline data collection before a project begins
the first stage of appraisal for river-valley projects
the design of the clearance system when violations are detected only after construction
a compulsory form of public hearing conducted before every project
77.x: The criticism is that post-facto clearances can become “the design” when state appraisal bodies identify violations only after construction has already occurred.
77.tq: Apply the criticism to the sequence of violation detection and construction.
xs: Post-facto clearances may become **the design** when violations are **detected only after construction** — so option **(3)** is correct (31 Jul 2026).
The concern is that **state appraisal bodies** detect violations only after construction.
xa: **Vanashakti** final verdict (**29 July 2026**) nullified the **2021 Office Memorandum** prospectively.
Critics call the OM-vs-notification distinction a "**fig-leaf**".
**Draft 2020** also proposed post-facto clearance.

77.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: River-valley projects — first sector appraised in India
LG Polymers gas leak — Visakhapatnam, 2020 — National Green Tribunal
Great Nicobar EIA — absence of any baseline data collection
NEPA — first EIA law — United States, 1969
77.x: The Great Nicobar EIA was criticised for thin baseline data, not for the complete absence of baseline data collection. The other pairs are correctly matched.
77.tq: Find the overstatement by distinguishing thin or inadequate data from total absence of data.
xs: **Great Nicobar EIA — absence of any baseline data** is wrongly matched — so option **(3)** is correct.
The criticism was **thin baseline data** in the Great Nicobar EIA (11 May 2026), not its total absence.
**River-valley projects** = first sector appraised; **LG Polymers** (Visakhapatnam, 2020) handled by **NGT**; **NEPA 1969** = first EIA law.
xa: A **High-Powered Committee** on the Great Nicobar project was set up on NGT directions.
Wider criticism: **no central baseline data bank**.
EIA first used in India in **1978**; first notification **1994**.

78.s:
Arrange the following developments in chronological order:
A. Ministry of Environment and Forests formed
B. Department of Environment created
C. Ministry renamed MoEFCC
D. Air-pollution functions added to CPCB by the Air Act
Select the correct sequence.
78.x: The correct sequence is Department of Environment in 1980, Air Act in 1981, Ministry of Environment and Forests in 1985, and MoEFCC renaming in 2014.
78.tq: Place the dated institutional milestones from earliest to latest.
xs: The correct order is **B, D, A, C** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**B:** **Department of Environment** created in **1980**; **D:** air functions added to CPCB by the **Air Act 1981**.
**A:** **Ministry of Environment and Forests** formed in **1985**; **C:** renamed **MoEFCC** in **2014** when Climate Change was added.
xa: CPCB itself is older: constituted in **1974** under the **Water Act**, renamed **CPCB** by the **1988** amendment.
⚠ Trap order: **1974** CPCB → **1985** MoEF → **1988** CPCB renamed → **2014** MoEFCC.
**EPA 1986** widened CPCB's scope — it did not add the air functions.
The **1985** formation of the Ministry was an **APPSC 2024** statement marked correct.

78.s:
Consider the following statements about the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change:
1. It receives 0.07% of the Union Budget according to the stated current information.
2. It is the nodal agency for India’s NR7 biodiversity report.
3. It runs Swachh Vayu Sarvekshan.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
78.x: All three statements are correct according to the stated current information: the allocation is 0.07%, MoEFCC is nodal for India’s NR7 biodiversity report, and it runs Swachh Vayu Sarvekshan.
78.tq: Combine current institutional facts while checking each statement independently.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
**Statement 1:** correct — MoEFCC gets only **0.07%** of the Union Budget.
**Statement 2:** correct — it is the **nodal agency** for India's **NR7** biodiversity report.
**Statement 3:** correct — it runs **Swachh Vayu Sarvekshan**.
xa: A stated criticism: MoEFCC is **underfunded and siloed**.
**Guntur** stood **2nd** in the towns category of **Swachh Vayu Sarvekshan 2026** (**130** cities).
**WII** (Dehradun) monitored the **NR7** targets.
Evolution: **Department of Environment** (**1980**) → **MoEF** (**1985**) → **MoEFCC** (**2014**).

78.s:
Consider the following statements about the Central Pollution Control Board:
1. It was constituted in 1974 under the Water Act as the Central Board for the Prevention and Control of Water Pollution.
2. It was renamed CPCB by a 1988 amendment.
3. Its air-pollution functions were added by the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.
4. It is a statutory body under MoEFCC.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
78.x: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: air functions were added by the Air Act, 1981; EPA 1986 only widened its scope. So options including 3, and 1 and 2 only (missing 4), are wrong.
78.tq: CPCB: Water Act 1974 -> Air Act 1981 adds air -> renamed 1988 -> EPA 1986 widens scope.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 4** are correct — option **(2)**.
**Statement 1:** correct — constituted in **1974** under the **Water Act** as the Central Board for the Prevention and Control of Water Pollution.
**Statement 2:** correct — renamed **CPCB** by the **1988** amendment.
**Statement 3:** wrong — air functions came from the **Air Act 1981**; **EPA 1986** only widened its scope.
**Statement 4:** correct — CPCB is a **statutory body under MoEFCC**.
xa: CPCB has a **full-time chairman nominated by the Central Government**.
CPCB (**1974**) is the **oldest national pollution body**.
CPCB runs **NAMP** and the **National AQI** (launched **2015**, daily bulletins).
Air network: **516 cities**, **1,400+** stations with real-time CAAQMS.

78.s: The Chairman of the Central Pollution Control Board is:
o: The Secretary-General of the National Green Tribunal
A full-time chairman nominated by the Central Government
The Chairperson of the National Biodiversity Authority
A part-time member elected by the State Boards
78.x: The CPCB has a full-time Chairman nominated by the Central Government.
78.tq: Identify the appointing authority and full-time status precisely.
xs: CPCB has a **full-time chairman nominated by the Central Government** — option **(2)**.
It is not an elected or part-time post of the State Boards, nor held ex officio by the NGT or NBA heads.
xa: CPCB is a **statutory body under MoEFCC**, constituted in **1974** under the **Water Act**.
CPCB **coordinates SPCBs** and gives them technical help, research and training.
⚠ **NGT vs CPCB:** NGT **adjudicates** and awards compensation; CPCB is the **regulator** that sets standards and monitors.
The NGT Chairperson is currently **Justice Prakash Shrivastava**.

78.s: Which body is primarily responsible for enforcing environmental standards under the Environment (Protection) Act framework?
78.x: The CPCB is the body responsible for enforcing environmental standards under the Environment (Protection) Act framework.
78.tq: Assign the enforcement function to the regulatory rather than adjudicatory body.
xs: The **Central Pollution Control Board** enforces environmental standards under the EPA framework — option **(3)**.
This was the **APPSC-G2 2025** answer.
The **NGT** only **adjudicates** disputes and awards compensation; the **NBA** deals with **biodiversity** access and biopiracy.
xa: CPCB is a **regulator**: sets standards, monitors pollution, advises the Centre.
Its scope was widened by **EPA 1986**; air functions came by the **Air Act 1981**.
CPCB coordinates the **NCAP** with SPCBs, tracked on the **PRANA** portal.
**Environmental (Protection) Fund Rules 2026** finance CPCB and SPCBs.

78.s:
Consider the following pairs relating to CPCB monitoring:
1. NAMP — National Air Monitoring Programme
2. RTWQMS — Real-time water-quality monitoring on the Ganga and Yamuna
3. PRANA — Daily National AQI bulletins
Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched?
78.x: Pairs 1 and 2 are correct. Pair 3 is wrong: PRANA is the portal tracking NCAP; daily bulletins come from the National AQI launched in 2015. So 1 only is incomplete and options with 3 are wrong.
78.tq: NAMP = air, RTWQMS = Ganga/Yamuna water, PRANA = NCAP tracker.
xs: Pairs **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
**Pair 1:** correct — **NAMP** is the **National Air Monitoring Programme**.
**Pair 2:** correct — **RTWQMS** is real-time water-quality monitoring on the **Ganga and Yamuna**.
**Pair 3:** wrong — **PRANA** is the portal tracking **NCAP**; daily bulletins come from the **National AQI** (launched **2015**).
xa: CPCB air network: **516 cities**, **1,400+** stations; **CAAQMS** gives real-time data.
CPCB also runs **National Water Quality Monitoring**.
NGT told southern States and Puducherry to execute **NCAP** plans — **86%** of spend went on **road dust**.
CPCB coordinates **SPCBs** with technical help, research and training.

78.s: Which one of the following is NOT a stated coordinating or supporting function of the CPCB?
o: Adjudicating appeals against orders of the Supreme Court
78.x: The CPCB coordinates SPCBs, provides technical help, supports research and training, and performs monitoring and regulatory functions. It does not adjudicate appeals against Supreme Court orders.
78.tq: Reject the judicial power wrongly attributed to a regulatory board.
xs: **Adjudicating appeals against Supreme Court orders** is not a CPCB function — option **(2)**.
CPCB **coordinates SPCBs**, gives **technical help**, conducts **research** and **training** — options (1), (3), (4) are its functions.
No body hears appeals against the SC; in fact appeals from the **NGT** go **to** the **Supreme Court** within **90 days**.
xa: CPCB is a **regulator**: sets standards, monitors and **advises the Centre**.
Its monitoring: **NAMP**, **National AQI** (**2015**), **RTWQMS** on **Ganga and Yamuna**.
**NCAP** is coordinated with SPCBs and tracked on the **PRANA** portal.
⚠ Adjudication of environmental disputes belongs to the **NGT**, not CPCB.

78.s:
Consider the following statements about consents and powers of State Pollution Control Boards:
1. Consent to Establish is needed before setting up the unit.
2. Consent to Operate is needed before the unit is set up, while Consent to Establish is needed before discharge.
3. SPCBs can levy compensation under Section 33A of the Water Act and Section 31A of the Air Act where harm is clear or imminent.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
78.x: Statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 is wrong: it reverses the two; Consent to Operate is needed before production or discharge. Statement 3 is correct: compensation can be levied under S.33A Water / S.31A Air where harm is clear or imminent. So 1 only is incomplete and options with 2 are wrong.
78.tq: Establish = before building; Operate = before production/discharge.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
**Statement 1:** correct — **Consent to Establish** is taken **before setting up** the unit.
**Statement 2:** wrong — it reverses them; **Consent to Operate** is needed **before production/discharge**.
**Statement 3:** correct — SPCBs can levy compensation under **S.33A Water / S.31A Air Act** where harm is clear or imminent.
xa: Both consents are granted under the **Water and Air Acts**.
SPCBs also **inspect treatment plants**, **analyse samples** and **enforce standards**.
**APPCB** was set up in **1976** by the AP Government under the **Water Act 1974**.
CPCB **coordinates the SPCBs** with technical help, research and training.

78.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Andhra Pradesh Pollution Control Board:
1. It enforces the Water Act, Air Act and Environment Protection Act.
2. It enforces rules relating to hazardous, biomedical, plastic and solid waste.
3. It issues siting guidelines and develops SOPs for marine outfalls and hazardous waste.
4. It promotes cleaner production.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
78.x: All four statements describe stated APPCB responsibilities, including enforcement, waste-management rules, siting guidance, SOPs and cleaner production.
78.tq: Test the full range of State Board responsibilities rather than only its core Acts.
xs: All four statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.
**Statements 1 and 2:** correct — APPCB enforces the **Water, Air, EP Acts** plus **Hazardous, Bio-medical, Plastic, Solid waste** rules.
**Statement 3:** correct — it issues **siting guidelines** and SOPs on **marine outfalls** and hazardous waste.
**Statement 4:** correct — it **promotes cleaner production**.
xa: APPCB was set up in **1976** by the **AP Government** under the **Water Act 1974**.
It is the body **entrusted to implement environmental laws and rules in AP** (**APPSC 2025** answer).
It runs **computerised inspection under EoDB**.
Like other SPCBs it grants **Consent to Establish** and **Consent to Operate**.

78.s: The Andhra Pradesh Pollution Control Board was established in 1976 under the authority of the:
o: Government of India under the Air Act, 1981
Government of Andhra Pradesh under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986
National Green Tribunal under the Water Act, 1974
Government of Andhra Pradesh under the Water Act, 1974
78.x: The APPCB was established in 1976 by the Government of Andhra Pradesh under the Water Act, 1974.
78.tq: Combine the correct State authority, year and parent legislation.
xs: APPCB was set up in **1976** by the **Government of Andhra Pradesh** under the **Water Act, 1974** — option **(4)**.
It is a State body, so not set up by the **Government of India** or the **NGT** (which came only in **2010**).
The **Air Act 1981** and **EPA 1986** came after **1976**, so they could not be its basis.
xa: APPCB is **entrusted to implement environmental laws and rules in AP** (**APPSC 2025** answer).
It enforces **Water, Air, EP Acts** and the **Hazardous, Bio-medical, Plastic, Solid waste** rules.
It issues **siting guidelines** and SOPs on **marine outfalls** and hazardous waste.
CPCB too began under the **Water Act** in **1974**.

78.s: The National Environment Tribunal Act, 1995 was distinctive because it provided for:
o: Strict liability for accidents involving hazardous substances
Establishment of the Central Pollution Control Board
78.x: The National Environment Tribunal Act, 1995 provided for strict liability in cases of accidents involving hazardous substances.
78.tq: Associate the predecessor law with its distinctive liability principle.
xs: The **National Environment Tribunal Act, 1995** provided **strict liability** for damage from **hazardous-substance accidents** — option **(1)**.
**Appeals against environmental clearances** were the job of the **NEAA Act, 1997**.
CPCB was set up in **1974** under the **Water Act**, not by this Act.
xa: The **1995** Act was **never brought into force** and was **repealed by the NGT Act 2010**.
The **1995** Act was an **APPSC 2023** answer.
The **NGT** combines **original jurisdiction** with the **appellate role** of the NEAA.

78.s: The National Environment Appellate Authority Act, 1997 primarily provided for hearing appeals against:
78.x: The National Environment Appellate Authority heard appeals against environmental clearances.
78.tq: Distinguish the appellate authority’s subject matter from the NGT’s wider jurisdiction.
xs: The **NEAA Act, 1997** provided for **appeals against environmental clearances** — option **(2)**.
**Strict liability** for hazardous-substance accidents was the **National Environment Tribunal Act, 1995**.
Appeals go **to** the Supreme Court (from the NGT, within **90 days**), not against its orders.
xa: The **NEAA** was **replaced by the NGT**; its Act was **repealed in 2010**.
The NGT took over the NEAA's **appellate role** and added **original jurisdiction**.
The **1995** Tribunal Act was never brought into force and was also repealed by the **NGT Act 2010**.

78.s: Which statement correctly describes the fate of the National Environment Tribunal Act, 1995?
o: It was brought into force and remains the principal environmental tribunal law.
It was converted into the National Biodiversity Authority Act.
It was replaced by the Water Act, 1974 without repeal.
It was never brought into force and was repealed by the NGT Act, 2010.
78.x: The National Environment Tribunal Act, 1995 was never brought into force and was repealed by the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010.
78.tq: Use the fate-of-legislation trap: enacted does not necessarily mean brought into force.
xs: The **National Environment Tribunal Act, 1995** was **never brought into force** and was **repealed by the NGT Act, 2010** — option **(4)**.
It never became the principal tribunal law; the **NGT** (**2010**) is.
The **NBA** came under the **Biological Diversity Act 2002**, and the **Water Act** dates from **1974** — neither relates to this Act.
xa: The **1995** Act provided **strict liability** for **hazardous-substance accidents**.
The **NEAA Act 1997** (appeals on clearances) was also repealed in **2010**.
The NGT Act was passed on **2 June 2010**; Tribunal set up **18 October 2010**.

78.s: Which of the following statements about the NEAA is correct?
o: It was replaced by the NGT and its Act was repealed in 2010.
It was never concerned with environmental clearances.
It was converted into the CPCB in 1988.
78.x: The National Environment Appellate Authority was replaced by the NGT, and the National Environment Appellate Authority Act was repealed in 2010.
78.tq: Track institutional succession and the repeal year.
xs: The **NEAA** was **replaced by the NGT** and its Act was **repealed in 2010** — option **(2)**.
Option (1) reverses it: the NGT replaced the NEAA, not vice versa.
The NEAA heard **appeals against environmental clearances**, so option (3) is wrong; CPCB was **renamed** in **1988**, not created from the NEAA.
xa: The NEAA came under the **National Environment Appellate Authority Act, 1997**.
NGT = **original jurisdiction** + the NEAA's **appellate role**.
FIRST/LAST: **NGT (2010)** replaced the NEAA.

78.s: The NGT combines which two roles associated earlier with separate environmental institutions?
o: Original jurisdiction over environmental disputes and the appellate role of the NEAA
78.x: The NGT combines original jurisdiction over environmental disputes with the appellate role earlier performed by the NEAA.
78.tq: Link the predecessor authority’s appellate role with the NGT’s original jurisdiction.
xs: The NGT combines **original jurisdiction over environmental disputes** with the **appellate role of the NEAA** — option **(2)**.
The **NEAA** (Act of **1997**) heard appeals against **environmental clearances**; the NGT absorbed that role when the NEAA Act was repealed in **2010**.
Research, education and budget work are not NGT roles — it is an **adjudicatory** body.
xa: The **National Environment Tribunal Act 1995** (strict liability) was never brought into force; repealed by the NGT Act **2010**.
The NGT disposes of cases within **6 months**; appeal to the **Supreme Court** within **90 days**.
⚠ NGT covers **7** Acts but **not** the **Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972** and **Forest Rights Act 2006**.

78.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the constitutional status and powers of the National Green Tribunal?
o: It is a statutory body with powers similar to those of a civil court.
It is a constitutional body with powers exclusively of an administrative authority.
It is an executive body exercising only advisory jurisdiction.
It is a constitutional body established under Article 323B without civil-court powers.
78.x: The NGT is a statutory, not constitutional, body and possesses civil-court powers in matters within its jurisdiction.
78.tq: Discriminate between constitutional, statutory and executive bodies before considering their powers.
xs: The NGT is a **statutory** body with **powers of a civil court** — option **(1)**.
It was set up under the **NGT Act, 2010**, so it is **not a constitutional body** — options (2) and (4) are wrong.
It **adjudicates** disputes and awards compensation, so it is not merely advisory.
xa: It is **not bound by CPC 1908**; it is guided by the **principles of natural justice**.
Cases are to be disposed of within **6 months**.
Appeal lies to the **Supreme Court** within **90 days**.
It gives effect to the right to a healthy environment under **Art. 21**.

78.s: The establishment of the National Green Tribunal gives effect, in the environmental context, to which Fundamental Right?
o: Right to constitutional remedies under Article 32
78.x: The NGT gives effect to the right to a healthy environment, which is treated as part of the right to life under Article 21.
78.tq: Match the environmental entitlement with the relevant Fundamental Right.
xs: The NGT gives effect to the right to a healthy environment under **Article 21** (**right to life**) — option **(1)**.
The notes link the NGT only to **Art. 21**, not to Articles 14, 23 or 32.
xa: NGT purpose: **effective and expeditious disposal** of cases on environmental protection and conservation of forests.
It also enforces **environmental legal rights** and gives **relief and compensation** for damage.
It was set up on **18 October 2010** — asked in **APPSC 2018**.
**APPSC-G2 2025**: purpose = to handle **environmental protection and pollution-control cases**.

78.s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below.

List-I (Type of Bench)
 a. Principal Bench
 b. Zonal Bench
 c. Circuit Bench

List-II (Place)
 i. Jodhpur
 ii. New Delhi
 iii. Pune
 iv. Shillong
78.x: The Principal Bench is at New Delhi; Pune is a zonal bench location; and Jodhpur and Shillong are circuit bench locations.
78.tq: Start with the sure Principal Bench pair and then distinguish zonal from circuit locations.
xs: Correct match: **a–ii, b–iii, c–i and iv** — option **(1)**.
**Principal Bench** → **New Delhi**.
**Zonal Bench** → **Pune** (others: **Kolkata, Bhopal, Chennai**).
**Circuit Benches** → **Jodhpur** and **Shillong** (also **Shimla**).
xa: ⚠ Shillong is a **circuit** bench, not zonal.
Bench locations are as per **IYB 2026**.
Composition: **Chairperson** + **Judicial and Expert Members** (**10 to 20** each).
Exam angle: **bench-to-city matching**.

78.s: Which one of the following is NOT a location of a zonal bench of the National Green Tribunal?
78.x: Pune, Bhopal and Chennai are zonal bench locations. Shillong is a circuit bench location.
78.tq: Find the bench-type mismatch rather than merely identifying a place associated with the NGT.
xs: **Shillong** is a **circuit bench**, not a zonal bench — option **(1)**.
Zonal benches are at **Pune, Kolkata, Bhopal, Chennai** — so Chennai, Bhopal and Pune are zonal.
xa: Circuit benches: **Shimla, Shillong, Jodhpur**.
The **Principal Bench** is at **New Delhi**.
NGT cases in **2026**: Dhanauri wetland, Ganga pollution, Saparnika river.
Current Chairperson: **Justice Prakash Shrivastava**.

78.s: An appeal against an order of the National Green Tribunal lies to the Supreme Court within:
78.x: An appeal against an NGT order may be filed before the Supreme Court within 90 days.
78.tq: Use the exact statutory time limit and compare the middle numerical options carefully.
xs: An appeal against an NGT order lies to the **Supreme Court** within **90 days** — option **(3)**.
The other periods (30, 60, 120 days) are not the NGT Act limit.
xa: The NGT must dispose of cases within **6 months**.
⚠ Sequence: Act **2 June 2010** → set up **18 Oct 2010** → functioning **July 2011**.
It is not bound by **CPC 1908**; follows **natural justice**.
It has **powers of a civil court**.

78.s:
With reference to the National Green Tribunal, consider the following statements:
1. Its Chairperson is a retired judge of the Supreme Court.
2. It is bound by all the procedures of the Code of Civil Procedure.
3. It follows the principles of natural justice.
4. It is required to decide cases within six months.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
78.x: Statements 1, 3 and 4 are correct. Statement 2 is false because the Tribunal is not bound by the Code of Civil Procedure, though it follows natural justice.
78.tq: Split the options by checking the procedural exception concerning the CPC.
xs: Statements **1, 3 and 4** are correct — option **(3)**.
**Statement 1:** correct — the Chairperson is a **retired SC judge**.
**Statement 2:** wrong — the NGT is **not bound by CPC 1908**.
**Statement 3:** correct — it is guided by **principles of natural justice**; **Statement 4:** correct — disposal within **6 months**.
xa: The Act also allows a judge of the SC or **Chief Justice of a High Court** as Chairperson.
It has **powers of a civil court**.
Appeal: to the **Supreme Court** within **90 days**.
Members: **Judicial and Expert Members**, **10 to 20** each.

78.s:
With reference to the composition of the National Green Tribunal, consider the following statements:
1. It has a Chairperson who is a retired Judge of the Supreme Court.
2. It includes Judicial Members and Expert Members.
3. There are 10 to 20 Judicial Members and 10 to 20 Expert Members.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
78.x: The NGT consists of a Chairperson who is a retired Supreme Court judge, along with Judicial and Expert Members, with 10 to 20 members in each category.
78.tq: Verify the composition by separating the chairperson, member categories and numerical range.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
**Statement 1:** correct — **Chairperson** is a **retired SC judge**.
**Statement 2:** correct — it has **Judicial and Expert Members**.
**Statement 3:** correct — **10 to 20** of each.
xa: The Act allows a judge of the SC or **Chief Justice of a High Court** to be Chairperson.
Current Chairperson: **Justice Prakash Shrivastava** (**8 Sep 2026**).
Principal Bench **New Delhi**; zonal benches **Pune, Kolkata, Bhopal, Chennai**.

78.s:
Consider the following statements about the National Green Tribunal:
1. The NGT Act was passed on 2 June 2010.
2. The Tribunal was set up on 18 October 2010.
3. The Tribunal started functioning in July 2010.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
78.x: Statement 1 is correct: the Act was passed on 2 June 2010. Statement 2 is correct: the Tribunal was set up on 18 October 2010 (asked in APPSC 2018). Statement 3 is wrong: it started functioning in July 2011. So 1 only is incomplete and options with 3 are wrong.
78.tq: Act 2 June 2010 -> set up 18 Oct 2010 -> working July 2011.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
**Statement 1:** correct — the NGT Act was passed on **2 June 2010**.
**Statement 2:** correct — the Tribunal was set up on **18 October 2010**.
**Statement 3:** wrong — it started functioning in **July 2011**, not July 2010.
xa: **APPSC 2018** asked the date it was set up: **18 October 2010**.
It is a **statutory** body under the **NGT Act, 2010**, not constitutional.
Disposal within **6 months**; appeal to the SC within **90 days**.

78.s: Which one of the following is NOT a stated purpose of the National Green Tribunal?
o: Relief and compensation for environmental damage
Conservation of forests and natural resources
Conducting elections to local bodies in environmentally sensitive areas
78.x: The NGT deals with environmental protection, conservation of forests and natural resources, enforcement of environmental legal rights, and relief and compensation for damage. Conducting local-body elections is not its function.
78.tq: Find the option outside the tribunal’s stated environmental jurisdiction.
xs: **Conducting local-body elections** is not an NGT purpose — option **(4)**.

Its stated purposes: **effective and expeditious disposal** of environmental and forest-conservation cases, **enforcing environmental legal rights**, and **relief and compensation** — options (1), (2), (3).
xa: **APPSC-G2 2025**: purpose = handle **environmental protection and pollution-control cases**.
It gives effect to the right to healthy environment under **Art. 21**.
NGT **adjudicates**; CPCB is the **regulator**.
Disposal time: **6 months**.

78.s: According to the stated current information, the Chairperson of the National Green Tribunal is:
78.x: Justice Prakash Shrivastava is identified as the Chairperson of the National Green Tribunal as of 8 September 2026.
78.tq: Use the current office-holder without confusing the office with a former Supreme Court office-holder.
xs: The current NGT Chairperson is **Justice Prakash Shrivastava** (**8 Sep 2026**) — option **(2)**.
The notes name no other judge as NGT Chairperson.
xa: The Chairperson is a **retired SC judge**; the Act also allows a **Chief Justice of a High Court**.
Members: **Judicial and Expert Members**, **10 to 20** each.
Principal Bench: **New Delhi**.
NGT cases in **2026**: **Dhanauri wetland**, **Ganga pollution**, **Saparnika river**.

78.s:
Which of the following Acts is outside the scope of the National Green Tribunal as specified in its jurisdictional list?
1. Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972
2. Forest Rights Act
3. Biological Diversity Act, 2002
4. Environment (Protection) Act, 1986
78.x: The Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 and the Forest Rights Act are outside the stated scope. The Biological Diversity Act, 2002 and the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 are covered Acts.
78.tq: Use exclusion testing to distinguish covered Acts from Acts outside the specified scope.
xs: The **Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972** and the **Forest Rights Act** are outside the NGT — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
The **Biological Diversity Act 2002** and **Environment (Protection) Act 1986** are among its **7** Acts.
xa: Other Acts under NGT: **Water Act 1974**, **Water Cess 1977**, **Forest (Conservation) Act 1980**, **Air Act 1981**, **PLI 1991**.
⚠ Exam favourite: "which Act is NOT under NGT" → **Wildlife Act**.
The Forest Rights Act is of **2006**.
**PLI 1991** and **Water Cess 1977** were in the original **Schedule I**.

78.s:
Consider the following Acts:
1. Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974
2. Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980
3. Environment (Protection) Act, 1986
4. Forest Rights Act, 2006
Which of the above are included among the Acts under which the NGT hears cases?
78.x: The Water Act, Forest (Conservation) Act and Environment (Protection) Act are included. The Forest Rights Act, 2006 is outside the NGT’s Schedule I list.
78.tq: Separate the included environmental statutes from the specifically excluded Forest Rights Act.
xs: The **Water Act 1974**, **Forest (Conservation) Act 1980** and **EPA 1986** are under the NGT — option **(1) 1, 2 and 3 only**.
The **Forest Rights Act 2006** is **outside** the NGT's scope, so options with 4 are wrong.
xa: Full list (**7**): Water Act **1974**, Water Cess **1977**, Forest (Conservation) **1980**, Air Act **1981**, EPA **1986**, **PLI 1991**, **Biological Diversity Act 2002**.
⚠ Also outside: **Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972**.
The NGT replaced the **NEAA** (Act of **1997**).

78.s: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the National Green Tribunal from the Central Pollution Control Board?
o: The NGT sets emission standards, whereas the CPCB awards compensation.
The CPCB hears appeals against NGT orders in environmental disputes.
The NGT adjudicates disputes and awards compensation, whereas the CPCB regulates, sets standards and monitors pollution.
Both bodies perform exactly the same adjudicatory and regulatory functions.
78.x: The NGT is an adjudicatory body that decides environmental disputes and awards compensation. The CPCB is a regulatory body that sets standards, monitors pollution and advises the Centre.
78.tq: Separate adjudication from regulation by asking who performs the job.
xs: The **NGT adjudicates disputes and awards compensation**, while the **CPCB regulates, sets standards and monitors** — option **(3)**.
Option (1) swaps the two roles; option (4) wrongly makes them identical.
Appeals from NGT go to the **Supreme Court** within **90 days**, not to the CPCB.
xa: CPCB also **advises the Centre**.
CPCB is a **statutory body under MoEFCC** (**1974**); NGT is a **statutory** tribunal (**2010**).
CPCB runs **NAMP**, **National AQI** and **RTWQMS**.
NGT is guided by **natural justice**, not bound by **CPC 1908**.

78.s:
Consider the following statements about the National Biodiversity Authority:
1. It was established in 2003 under the Biological Diversity Act, 2002.
2. It is headquartered at Bengaluru.
3. The Biological Diversity Rules were issued in 2024, after the Act was amended in 2023.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
78.x: Statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 is wrong: the NBA is headquartered at Chennai. Statement 3 is correct: the Act was amended in 2023 and BD Rules came in 2024. So options with 2 are wrong and 3 only leaves out statement 1.
78.tq: NBA: 2003, Chennai, Act 2002 amended 2023, Rules 2024.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
**Statement 1:** correct — NBA est. **2003** under the **Biological Diversity Act 2002**.
**Statement 2:** wrong — NBA's HQ is **Chennai**.
**Statement 3:** correct — Act amended **2023**, then **BD Rules 2024**.
xa: NBA is an **autonomous statutory body**; there is also an **NBA Fund**.
Three tiers: **NBA** → **SBBs** → **BMCs**.
⚠ NBA = **Chennai**, est. **2003** under BD Act **2002**.
Foreigners need **NBA approval** to access bio-resources.

78.s: Which of the following correctly represents the three-tier institutional structure under biodiversity governance?
o: SBBs at the national level, NBA at the State level and BMCs at the district level
NBA at the national level, SBBs at the State level and BMCs at the local level
NBA at the local level, BMCs at the State level and SBBs at the national level
BMCs at the national level, SBBs at the local level and NBA at the State level
78.x: The three tiers are the National Biodiversity Authority at the national level, State Biodiversity Boards at the State level and Biodiversity Management Committees at the local level.
78.tq: Arrange the bodies by jurisdiction from national to local.
xs: **NBA** (national) → **SBBs** (state) → **BMCs** (local) — option **(2)**.
The other options jumble the levels.
xa: NBA: est. **2003** under **Biological Diversity Act 2002**, HQ **Chennai**.
In AP the state tier is the **APSBB** (State Biodiversity Board).
The **Biological Diversity Act 2002** is one of the Acts under the **NGT**.
Act amended **2023**; **BD Rules 2024**.

78.s: With reference to biopiracy, which one of the following statements is correct?
o: Foreigners may access Indian bio-resources without approval if no patent is sought.
Foreigners require approval of the NBA to access bio-resources or traditional knowledge, and NBA approval precedes intellectual property rights on them.
Only local bodies can grant approval for foreign access to traditional knowledge.
NBA approval is required only after intellectual property rights have been granted.
78.x: Foreigners require NBA approval to access bio-resources or associated traditional knowledge, and such approval precedes the grant of intellectual property rights. Access and benefit-sharing with local communities is also an important safeguard.
78.tq: Apply the approval-sequence rule and reject options that reverse the order or shift authority.
xs: Foreigners need **NBA approval** to access **bio-resources/traditional knowledge**, and **NBA approval precedes IPR** — option **(2)**.
Approval is needed regardless of patents, comes **before** IPR (not after), and is given by the **NBA**, not local bodies.
xa: **Access and benefit-sharing** with local communities is part of the anti-biopiracy safeguards.
NBA: autonomous statutory body, est. **2003**, HQ **Chennai**.
Local tier: **BMCs**; state tier: **SBBs**.

78.s: Which of the following is NOT an initiative associated with the Andhra Pradesh State Biodiversity Board?
o: Implementation of the Namami Gange programme throughout Andhra Pradesh
Biodiversity parks on the flood plains of five polluted rivers
City Biodiversity Index in Visakhapatnam, Vijayawada, Kadapa and Tirupati
78.x: The City Biodiversity Index, biodiversity parks on the flood plains of five polluted rivers and the Gloriosa superba cultivation pilot are APSBB initiatives. Namami Gange is implemented by the NMCG.
78.tq: Find the option belonging to another environmental body rather than the APSBB.
xs: **Namami Gange** is not an APSBB initiative — option **(1)**; it is implemented by the **NMCG**.
APSBB initiatives: **City Biodiversity Index** (**Visakhapatnam, Vijayawada, Kadapa, Tirupati**), **biodiversity parks** on flood plains of **5 polluted rivers**, and **Gloriosa superba** pilot.
xa: The biodiversity parks follow an **NGT/MoEFCC direction**.
NMCG is the successor to **NGRBA** (**2009**, under EPA).
**NRCP** covers **38 rivers** in **16 states** outside the Ganga basin.

78.s: Which one of the following bodies replaced the Environment Pollution (Prevention and Control) Authority (EPCA) in the National Capital Region and adjoining areas?
78.x: The Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM), established under the CAQM Act, 2021, replaced EPCA in the NCR and adjoining areas.
78.tq: Use the replacement relationship and distinguish air-quality authority from water and biodiversity bodies.
xs: The **Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM)** replaced **EPCA** — option **(2)**.
CAQM is based on the **CAQM Act 2021** and covers **NCR and adjoining areas**.
**NMCG** implements Namami Gange; **CGWA** regulates groundwater; **NBA** handles biodiversity.
xa: **CGWA**: constituted **1997** under **S.3(3) EPA**.
NGT fined **12 stadiums ₹5,000 each** for not giving CGWA water-use data.
**NMCG** is the successor to **NGRBA** (**2009**).

78.s: The National Mission for Clean Ganga is the successor set-up to which body?
78.x: NMCG is the successor set-up to the National Ganga River Basin Authority (NGRBA), which was established in 2009 under the Environment (Protection) Act.
78.tq: Use the predecessor–successor relationship and distinguish river-basin institutions from pollution authorities.
xs: **NMCG** is the successor set-up to the **NGRBA** — option **(1)**.
NGRBA was set up in **2009** under the **EPA**; NMCG implements **Namami Gange**.
**CGWA** is a groundwater authority (**1997**), **EPCA** was replaced by **CAQM**, and **NBA** handles biodiversity.
xa: **NRCP** covers **38 rivers** in **16 states** outside the Ganga basin.
CPCB runs **RTWQMS** on the **Ganga and Yamuna**.
**Ganga pollution** was among NGT cases in **2026**.

78.s: The National River Conservation Plan covers pollution abatement in:
o: 16 rivers in 38 districts of the National Capital Region
38 rivers in 16 States outside the Ganga basin
16 rivers in 38 States outside the Ganga basin
38 rivers in all States within the Ganga basin
78.x: The National River Conservation Plan covers pollution abatement in 38 rivers in 16 States outside the Ganga basin.
78.tq: Keep the two figures attached to the correct units—rivers and States—and note the basin exclusion.
xs: **NRCP** covers **38 rivers** in **16 States** **outside the Ganga basin** — option **(2)**.
The other options swap the numbers or wrongly place it inside the Ganga basin or NCR.
xa: The Ganga is handled by **NMCG** (**Namami Gange**), successor to **NGRBA** (**2009**).
APSBB set up **biodiversity parks** on flood plains of **5 polluted rivers**.
CPCB's **RTWQMS** monitors the **Ganga and Yamuna**.

78.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: CGWA — Section 3(3) of the Environment (Protection) Act
78.x: NBA is associated with biodiversity governance, not the National Clean Air Programme. CAQM, CGWA and NMCG are correctly matched with their respective legal basis or programme.
78.tq: Find the body–function mismatch by separating biodiversity, air-quality, groundwater and river missions.
xs: **NBA — National Clean Air Programme** is wrongly matched — option **(4)**.
**NBA** deals with **biodiversity** (BD Act **2002**); **NCAP** is coordinated by **CPCB** with SPCBs, tracked on **PRANA**.
Other pairs are right: **NMCG** — Namami Gange; **CAQM** — CAQM Act **2021**; **CGWA** — **S.3(3) EPA** (**1997**).
xa: CAQM **replaced EPCA** in NCR.
NMCG is the successor to **NGRBA** (**2009**, under EPA).
NBA HQ: **Chennai**, est. **2003**.

78.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Wildlife Institute of India — Dehradun
2. Botanical Survey of India — Kolkata
3. Forest Survey of India — Lucknow
4. G.B. Pant National Institute of Himalayan Environment — Kosi-Katarmal, Almora
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
78.x: The Wildlife Institute of India is at Dehradun, the Botanical Survey of India is at Kolkata and GBPNIHE is at Kosi-Katarmal, Almora. The Forest Survey of India is also at Dehradun, not Lucknow.
78.tq: Find the wrong location by comparing institutes that are commonly associated with Dehradun and Kolkata.
xs: Pairs **1, 2 and 4** are correct — option **(1)**.
**WII** → **Dehradun**; **BSI** → **Kolkata**; **GBPNIHE** → **Kosi-Katarmal, Almora**.

79.s:
With reference to CITES, consider the following statements:
1. Appendix II includes species that are not yet threatened with extinction but whose trade is controlled through permits.
2. Appendix III includes species listed by one Party seeking the assistance of other Parties to control trade.
3. Appendix I consists of species for which commercial trade is permitted without restrictions.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
79.x: Appendix II covers species whose trade requires control and permits, while Appendix III covers species listed by one Party for international assistance. Appendix I generally prohibits commercial trade.
79.tq: Find the false statement by checking the reversed trade rule.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
**Statement 1:** correct — **Appendix II** = not yet threatened, trade **controlled by permits** (export permit).
**Statement 2:** correct — **Appendix III** = listed by **one Party** seeking others' help to control trade.
**Statement 3:** wrong — **Appendix I** commercial trade is **prohibited**.
xa: Appendix I examples: **tiger, snow leopard, rhino**.
Appendix II examples: **corals, many sharks and rays**.
Appendix III example: **walrus** (**Canada**).
Species move between Appendices only by **COP vote**.

79.s: Which of the following statements regarding CITES is NOT correct?
o: It regulates international trade in wild fauna and flora.
Commercial trade is prohibited for approximately 97 per cent of the species covered by it.
Parties designate Management Authorities and Scientific Authorities.
79.x: CITES prohibits commercial trade for approximately 3 per cent of the species covered and regulates the remaining 97 per cent; the statement reverses these proportions.
79.tq: Check the reversed percentage trap in a NOT question.
xs: The wrong statement is that trade is prohibited for **97%** — option **(2)**; CITES **bans commercial trade for ~3%** and **regulates the other 97%**.
Options (1), (3), (4) are correct: it regulates trade in **wild fauna and flora**, covers about **35,000 species**, and Parties have **Management** and **Scientific Authorities**.
xa: CITES has **184 Parties**; Secretariat in **Geneva** (UNEP).
It is **legally binding** but does **not replace national laws**.
In India the **Management Authority** handles permits; the **Scientific Authority** advises.

79.s: Which one of the following is the correct combination regarding CITES Appendix I?
o: Species threatened with extinction; commercial trade is banned except for exceptional non-commercial purposes with permits
Species protected in one country seeking help from others; certificates of origin required
All species listed by a national wildlife authority; trade is unrestricted
Species not necessarily threatened; trade allowed with an export permit
79.x: Appendix I covers species threatened with extinction. Commercial trade is banned, while exceptional non-commercial trade, such as for research, requires import and export permits.
79.tq: Contrast the listing criterion and trade rule instead of relying on the appendix number alone.
xs: **Appendix I** = species **threatened with extinction**; commercial trade **prohibited**, only exceptional **non-commercial** trade (e.g., research) with **import and export permits** — option **(1)**.
Option (2) describes **Appendix III**; option (4) describes **Appendix II**.
xa: Appendix I examples: **tiger, snow leopard, rhino**.
Appendix II: allowed with an **export permit** (corals, many sharks and rays).
Appendix III: allowed with permits/**certificates of origin** (walrus - Canada).
Species move between Appendices only by **COP vote**.

79.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Appendix I — Corals and many sharks and rays
Appendix III — Walrus protected by Canada
Appendix I — Trade allowed merely with a certificate of origin
79.x: The walrus is an example associated with Appendix III, where Canada’s protection and request for cooperation are relevant. Tigers and rhinoceroses are Appendix I species, while corals and many sharks and rays are generally in Appendix II.
79.tq: Start from the sure species-example pair and reject the reversed appendix descriptions.
xs: **Appendix III — Walrus (Canada)** is correctly matched — option **(3)**.
**Corals and many sharks and rays** are **Appendix II**, not I.
**Tiger and rhino** are **Appendix I**, not II.
A **certificate of origin** belongs to **Appendix III** trade, not Appendix I.
xa: Appendix III = protected in **at least one country** that asks others for help.
Appendix I = **threatened with extinction**; commercial trade prohibited.
**54 shark and ray species** were moved to App II at **CoP19** (Panama, **2022**).

79.s: Which one of the following statements about the movement of species between CITES Appendices is correct?
o: It is automatically made every five years by UNEP.
It occurs only through a vote of the Conference of the Parties.
It is decided exclusively by IUCN’s Red List Committee.
It may be done by any national wildlife authority without international approval.
79.x: Species move between CITES Appendices only through a vote of the Conference of the Parties.

xs: Species move between CITES Appendices **only by COP vote** — option **(2)**.
The notes give this power to the **COP** alone — not UNEP, IUCN or national authorities.
xa: The COP meets **every 2-3 years**.
Example: **whale shark, oceanic whitetip, manta rays → I** at **CoP20** (2025).
**Indian star tortoise** uplisted to I on India's proposal at **CoP18, 2019**.

79.s: Which one of the following international agreements is also known as the 'Washington Convention', and whose signing date is observed as World Wildlife Day (3 March)?
79.x: CITES was signed at Washington D.C. on 3 March 1973, hence 'Washington Convention', and 3 March is World Wildlife Day. CMS is the Bonn Convention, Ramsar is tied to World Wetlands Day (2 February), and CBD to the International Day for Biological Diversity (22 May).

xs: **CITES** is the **Washington Convention**, signed **3 March 1973** — now **World Wildlife Day** — option **(3)**.

⚠ **Bonn** = CMS (migratory species); **Washington** = CITES (trade).

79.s: In which year did India become a Party to CITES?

xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.

79.s: Which one of the following species is correctly matched with CITES Appendix I?
79.x: The Indian star tortoise is listed in Appendix I; it was uplisted on India’s proposal at CoP18 in 2019. Red sanders, golden gecko and rosewood are listed in Appendix II.

xs: The **Indian star tortoise** is in **Appendix I** — option **(4)**; uplisted on India's proposal at **CoP18, 2019**.
**Golden gecko**, **red sanders** and **rosewood** are all **Appendix II**.

79.x: The Indian star tortoise was uplisted to Appendix I on India’s proposal at CoP18 in 2019.

79.s:

79.s: Which one of the following statements regarding sharks and rays under CITES is correct?
o: Most are in Appendix II; 54 were added at CoP19, while whale shark, oceanic whitetip and manta rays moved to Appendix I at CoP20.

xs: Sharks and rays: **mostly Appendix II**; **54** added at **CoP19**; **whale shark, oceanic whitetip, manta rays → I** at **CoP20** — option **(1)**.

xa: CoP19: **Panama, 2022**; rosewood and **sea cucumbers** also protected.
CoP20: **Samarkand, Uzbekistan**, **2025** — **77 species** added.
**Wedgefish** is among India's CITES proposals.

79.s: Which of the following groups was among the subjects for which India proposed changes in CITES listings?
o: Tigers, rhinoceroses, walruses, corals and elephants only

79.x: Agenda 21 came from UNCED, the 1992 Rio Earth Summit, the first international Earth Summit. Stockholm 1972 produced the Stockholm Declaration and UNEP, WSSD 2002 the Johannesburg Plan of Implementation, and Rio+20 'The Future We Want'.
79.tq: Agenda 21 / Rio Declaration = Earth Summit 1992.
xs: **Agenda 21** came from **UNCED** — the **UN Conference on Environment and Development** (**1992**), the Rio Earth Summit — option **(2)**.
**Stockholm 1972** gave the **Stockholm Declaration** and **UNEP**; **Rio+20** (**2012**) gave "**The Future We Want**".
xa: Rio **1992** = the **first international Earth Summit** (**APPSC 2025**).
Agenda 21 was an **APPSC-G2 2025** answer.
**Rio+5** (**1997**) reviewed Agenda 21.

79.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Forest Principles adopted at Rio in 1992 are a legally binding convention on forests.
2. The UNCCD, adopted in 1994 as a follow-up to Rio, forms the three 'Rio Conventions' along with the UNFCCC and CBD.
