80.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. The precautionary principle states that lack of full scientific certainty is no reason to postpone cost-effective preventive measures, making statement 2 false.
80.tq: Spot the statement that reverses the precautionary principle.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
**Statement 1:** correct — **intergenerational equity**: the present must not deplete resources at the cost of future generations.
**Statement 2:** wrong — the **precautionary principle** says lack of **full scientific certainty** is **no reason to postpone** preventive measures.
**Statement 3:** correct — **polluter pays**: the polluter bears the cost of preventing and controlling pollution.
xa: These principles were endorsed at **Rio 1992**.
**Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum (1996)** made precaution and polluter pays part of Indian law.
**CBDR**: shared but differentiated duties; developed nations carry more.

80.s: The principle of Common but Differentiated Responsibilities (CBDR) implies that:
o: Responsibilities are shared, but developed nations carry greater duties
Only developing countries bear responsibility for environmental protection
All countries have identical environmental duties and identical capacities
Environmental duties are restricted to countries that caused no historical pollution
80.x: CBDR recognises shared responsibility while assigning greater duties to developed nations in view of their capacities and historical contribution.
80.tq: Discriminate between shared responsibility and identical responsibility.
xs: **CBDR**: duties are **shared but differentiated**; **developed nations carry more** — option **(1)**.
So duties are neither identical for all nor placed only on developing countries.
xa: Other principles: **intergenerational equity**, **precautionary**, **polluter pays**, **carrying capacity**.
All were endorsed at **Rio 1992** and underpin international environmental law.
The **Rio Declaration** has **27 principles**.

80.s: Human use of natural systems remains within carrying capacity when it:
o: Eliminates all human use of ecosystems
Exceeds the regenerative ability of ecosystems
Stays within what ecosystems can support
Maximises resource extraction in the present
80.x: Carrying capacity refers to the level of human use that ecosystems can support without losing their ability to function and regenerate.
80.tq: Apply the definition to distinguish sustainable use from overuse and non-use.
xs: **Carrying capacity**: human use must **stay within what ecosystems can support** — option **(3)**.
Exceeding regeneration or maximising extraction breaches it; eliminating all use is not required.
xa: It refers to the **finite carrying capacity of Earth**.
**Earth Overshoot Day** marks when demand exceeds what Earth can regenerate that year.
**Ecological footprint** is measured in **global hectares**.

80.s: Which of the following is NOT a goal or principle of sustainable development as generally recognised in environmental policy?
o: Maximising economic growth at any cost
80.x: Maximising economic growth at any cost conflicts with sustainable development, which requires balance among economic, social and environmental concerns.
80.tq: Use the absolute phrase at any cost to identify the incompatible objective.
xs: **Maximising economic growth at any cost** is not a principle — option **(4)**; it is the classic odd-one-out trap.
**Precautionary action**, **intergenerational equity** and **polluter pays** are recognised principles.
xa: Others: **CBDR** and **carrying capacity**.
The pillars must be **balanced**, not maximised one at a time.
Principles endorsed at **Rio 1992**.

80.s: Which of the following was NOT an outcome associated with the 1992 United Nations Conference on Environment and Development?
80.x: The Future We Want was adopted at the 2012 Rio+20 Conference. Agenda 21, the Rio Declaration, the UNFCCC and the CBD were associated with the 1992 Earth Summit.
80.tq: Use the summit-outcome association to eliminate the later document.
xs: "**The Future We Want**" came from **Rio+20** (**2012**), not **UNCED 1992** — option **(3)**.
Rio **1992** gave **Agenda 21**, the **Rio Declaration** (**27 principles**), **UNFCCC**, **CBD** and **Forest Principles**.
xa: UNCED: **3-14 June 1992**, **Rio de Janeiro** — the **first Earth Summit**.
Rio+20 (**UNCSD**) also decided to frame the **SDGs** and stressed the **green economy**.
**WSSD 2002** (Johannesburg) gave the **Johannesburg Plan of Implementation**.

80.s: The Rio Declaration adopted at the 1992 Earth Summit contained how many principles?
80.x: The Rio Declaration contains 27 principles relating to environment and development.
80.tq: Separate the numerical details of the Rio Declaration from SDG figures.
xs: The **Rio Declaration** has **27 principles** — option **(3)**.
**17** is the number of **SDGs**; **169** the number of SDG **targets**.
xa: It was adopted at **UNCED**, **3-14 June 1992**, Rio de Janeiro.
Other Rio outputs: **Agenda 21**, **UNFCCC**, **CBD**, **Forest Principles**.
⚠ **17 - 169 - 232** = SDGs - targets - indicators.

80.s: The Johannesburg Plan of Implementation was the principal outcome document of:
o: The 2002 World Summit on Sustainable Development
80.x: The Johannesburg Plan of Implementation was adopted at the 2002 World Summit on Sustainable Development.
80.tq: Match the named document with the summit that produced it.
xs: The **Johannesburg Plan of Implementation** came from the **2002 WSSD** — the **World Summit on Sustainable Development** (Rio+10) — option **(3)**.
**1992** gave **Agenda 21**; **2015** gave the **2030 Agenda**.
xa: **Rio+20** (**2012**) gave "**The Future We Want**".
**MDGs** (**2000-2015**) preceded the SDGs.
WSSD was held at **Johannesburg**.

80.s:
With reference to the 2012 United Nations Conference on Sustainable Development, consider the following statements:
1. It is popularly known as Rio+20.
2. It produced the document titled 'The Future We Want'.
3. It initiated the decision to frame the Sustainable Development Goals.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
80.x: All three statements are correct. The 2012 UNCSD at Rio de Janeiro was known as Rio+20, adopted The Future We Want and decided to frame the SDGs.
80.tq: Use the all-correct combination when the summit, document and institutional decision align.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4)**.
**1:** **UNCSD 2012** is **Rio+20**; **2:** it produced "**The Future We Want**".
**3:** it decided to frame the **SDGs**.
xa: It was held in **June 2012** at **Rio de Janeiro**.
It also stressed the **green economy**.
The SDGs were adopted in **2015** at **New York**.

80.s: The 2015 United Nations Sustainable Development Summit was held in:
80.x: The 2015 UN Sustainable Development Summit was held in New York during the 70th session of the UN General Assembly.
80.tq: Distinguish the venue of the final SDG adoption summit from the Rio conferences.
xs: The **2015** UN Sustainable Development Summit was in **New York** — option **(1)** (UNGA **70th** session, **25 Sept**).
**Rio de Janeiro** hosted **1992** and **2012**; **Johannesburg** hosted **2002**.
xa: Output: "**Transforming our World: the 2030 Agenda**".
**17 SDGs**, **169 targets**, **232** indicators.
In force from **2016**.

80.s: The document titled 'Transforming our World: the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development' contains:
80.x: The 2030 Agenda contains 17 Sustainable Development Goals and 169 targets. It is also associated with 232 indicators.
80.tq: Separate goals, targets and indicators rather than interchanging their figures.
xs: The **2030 Agenda** has **17 goals** and **169 targets** — option **(1)**.
**232** is the number of **indicators**, not targets; **27** is the Rio Declaration's principle count.
xa: ⚠ **17 - 169 - 232** = SDGs - targets - indicators.
Adopted **25 Sept 2015**, New York; in force **2016**.
**MDGs** (**2000-2015**) came before.

80.s: The Sustainable Development Goals formally came into force from:

xa: **17 SDGs**, **169 targets**, **232** indicators.

80.s: Agenda 21 is best described as:
o: A comprehensive action plan for sustainable development at local, national and global levels
A statistical index ranking countries by sustainability
A legally binding treaty limited to climate change mitigation
A declaration containing only principles on biodiversity conservation

xs: **Agenda 21** is a **comprehensive action plan** for sustainable development at **local, national and global** levels — option **(1)**.
It is not an index or a binding climate treaty; the principles document is the **Rio Declaration** (**27** principles).
xa: Agenda 21 came from **UNCED 1992**, Rio de Janeiro.
UNFCCC and CBD also opened at Rio.

80.s:
Arrange the following milestones in chronological order:

80.x: The MDGs began in 2000, WSSD was held in 2002, Rio+20 in 2012 and Agenda 2030 was adopted in 2015.

80.s: Green GDP is obtained by:
o: Adding only gross industrial output to conventional GDP
Subtracting unpaid household work from GDP
Adjusting GDP for natural-resource depletion and environmental damage
Measuring only the value of protected forests
80.x: Green GDP adjusts conventional GDP to account for natural-resource depletion and environmental damage.

xs: **Green GDP** = GDP adjusted for **natural-resource depletion and environmental damage** — option **(3)**.

xa: **Ecological footprint**: productive land and sea needed, in **global hectares**.
**Earth Overshoot Day**: when demand exceeds what Earth regenerates that year.
India: **99th of 167** in **SDR 2025**.

80.s: Which one of the following best describes the Genuine Progress Indicator (GPI)?
o: It measures the date on which annual resource demand exceeds regeneration.
It is GDP without any adjustment for environmental factors.
It measures only the physical area of productive land used by a population.
It adds unpaid work and similar benefits while subtracting pollution, crime and resource loss.
80.x: GPI incorporates benefits such as unpaid work and deducts social and environmental costs including pollution, crime and resource loss.
80.tq: Match the indicator with both its additions and deductions.
xs: The **GPI** **adds unpaid work** and similar benefits and **subtracts pollution, crime and resource loss** — option **(4)**.
Option (1) is **Earth Overshoot Day**; option (3) is the **ecological footprint**.
xa: **Green GDP** adjusts GDP for resource depletion and environmental damage.
NITI Aayog's **SDG India Index** ranks States.
UN SDSN publishes the **Sustainable Development Report**.

80.s: The ecological footprint of a population refers to the:
o: Annual date on which its natural resources are exhausted
Amount of carbon dioxide emitted by its industries alone
Productive land and sea needed to meet its consumption and absorb its wastes
Total number of endangered species in its territory
80.x: An ecological footprint estimates the productive land and sea area required to supply consumption and absorb generated wastes, expressed in global hectares.
80.tq: Use the function of the measure to distinguish it from emissions and biodiversity counts.
xs: **Ecological footprint** = **productive land and sea** needed to meet consumption and **absorb wastes** — option **(3)**.
It is measured in **global hectares**; the annual date is **Earth Overshoot Day**.
xa: **Carrying capacity**: use must stay within what ecosystems can support.
**GPI** subtracts pollution, crime and resource loss.
**Green GDP** adjusts for natural-resource depletion.

80.s: Earth Overshoot Day is the date on which:
o: The global population reaches its carrying capacity permanently
All countries achieve their annual emissions targets
The annual production of renewable resources becomes zero
Humanity's demand exceeds what Earth can regenerate during that year
80.x: Earth Overshoot Day marks the point in a year when humanity's demand on ecological resources exceeds Earth's regenerative capacity for that year.
80.tq: Identify the event described by the date rather than confusing it with a target or permanent limit.
xs: **Earth Overshoot Day** = the date when **humanity's demand exceeds what Earth can regenerate** that year — option **(4)**.
It is a yearly marker, not a permanent population limit.
xa: **Ecological footprint** is in **global hectares**.
**Carrying capacity** principle: human use within what ecosystems can support.
**Green GDP** and **GPI** are alternative progress measures.

80.s: According to the Sustainable Development Report 2025, India was ranked among how many countries in the SDG Index?

**17 SDGs**, **169 targets**, **232** indicators.

80.s: Which landmark judgment recognised sustainable development, the precautionary principle and the polluter-pays principle as part of Indian environmental law?
o: Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India
Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum v. Union of India
Narmada Bachao Andolan v. Union of India
80.x: Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996) recognised sustainable development, the precautionary principle and the polluter-pays principle in Indian environmental law.

xs: **Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996)** made **sustainable development**, the **precautionary principle** and **polluter pays** part of Indian law — option **(3)**.
The notes link **M.C. Mehta v. UoI (1996)** only to **polluter pays**.
xa: Precautionary principle: lack of full scientific certainty is **no reason to postpone** preventive measures.
Polluter pays: the polluter bears the **cost of preventing and controlling** pollution.
The Tribunal must apply all three principles.

80.s: Which one of the following is NOT a bench location of the National Green Tribunal mentioned in the institutional arrangement?

xa: The Tribunal must apply **sustainable development**, **precautionary** and **polluter-pays** principles.

o: Sustainable development, precautionary principle and polluter-pays principle
Public trust doctrine, absolute liability and eminent domain
Common but differentiated responsibilities, prior appropriation and res judicata
Inter-generational equity, federal supremacy and parliamentary privilege
80.x: The NGT must apply the principles of sustainable development, precautionary action and polluter pays.

xs: The NGT must apply **sustainable development**, **precautionary** and **polluter-pays** principles — option **(1)**.
The other combinations are not in its mandate.
xa: HQ **New Delhi**; benches **Bhopal, Pune, Kolkata, Chennai**.
Disposal within **6 months**.
**Vellore (1996)** brought these principles into Indian environmental law.

80.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the National Green Tribunal:
1. Its headquarters is at New Delhi.

3. It has a bench at Hyderabad.

80.tq: NGT: HQ Delhi + Bhopal, Pune, Kolkata, Chennai; 6-month disposal.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.

80.s:

**Statement 2:** wrong — it is aligned with **Viksit Bharat @2047**, not Atmanirbhar Bharat @2035.

80.s: Which set of measures is associated with the Sustainability and Climate Resilience pillar of Swarna Andhra @2047?
o: Renewable energy, green mobility and sustainable urban planning
Coal expansion, private transport and dispersed urbanisation
Nuclear energy, rural depopulation and industrial zoning
River diversion, road widening and conventional urban planning

xa: Aim: "**Wealthy, Healthy and Happy**" AP by **2047**.

80.s:

Only countries that adopted the Paris Agreement

xa: Agenda 2030 is **universal** — applies to all nations.

81.s:

3. Green jobs are limited to work directly related to renewable-energy generation.

82.x: Statement 1 is correct: a green economy decouples growth from resource use and pollution and fosters green industries and jobs. Statement 2 is correct: it was a central theme of Rio+20 (2012). Statement 3 is wrong: green jobs are any work in farming, industry, services or administration that preserves or restores environmental quality. So '1 only' misses Rio+20, and options with 3 are wrong.
82.tq: Green jobs are broad (farming to administration) - 'only renewables' is the trap.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
**Statement 1:** correct — a green economy **decouples** growth from resource use and pollution and fosters **green industries and green jobs**.
**Statement 2:** correct — it was the central theme of **Rio+20, 2012**.
**Statement 3:** wrong — **green jobs** are any work in **farming, industry, services or administration** that preserves or restores environmental quality.
xa: A green economy also **reduces environmental risks and ecological scarcity**.
**UNEP Green Economy Initiative**: **2008**; **PAGE**: **2013**.
**Green Skill Development Programme** (**2017**) trains youth for green jobs.

82.s:

1. The linear model follows the sequence ‘take, make, dispose’.
2. In the circular model, materials are kept in use through reduction, reuse, repair and recycling.
3. In the linear model, waste becomes a resource and decouples growth from resource use.

xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
**Statement 1:** correct — the **linear model** is **take, make, dispose**.
**Statement 2:** correct — the **circular model** keeps materials in use via **reduce, reuse, repair, recycle**.
**Statement 3:** wrong — **waste becoming a resource** is a **circular** feature; in the linear model waste is the **end point**.
xa: Circular economy does not focus exclusively on **carbon or fossil fuels**.

83.s:
Ozone is concentrated predominantly in which layer of the atmosphere?

The approximate altitude range associated with this concentration is:
83.x: Ozone is concentrated mainly in the stratosphere, approximately between 10 and 50 km above Earth. This layer absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation.
83.tq: Use the location-and-range combination to distinguish the ozone layer from adjacent atmospheric layers.
xs: Ozone is concentrated in the **Stratosphere, about 10-50 km** above Earth — so option **(1)** is correct.
This ozone layer shields Earth from harmful **UV-B** radiation.
Some notes give the range as **10-40 km**; either way it is the stratosphere, not the troposphere, mesosphere or thermosphere.
xa: Ozone is measured in **Dobson Units (DU)**; an "ozone hole" means total ozone below **220 DU**.
The ozone hole was first detected over **Antarctica** in the mid-1980s, reported in **1985** by the **British Antarctic Survey**.
PIB reported a dense ozone pocket at **21-23 km** over the **North Bay of Bengal** (16 Aug 2026).

83.s:
Which of the following effects is specifically associated with exposure to UV-B radiation due to ozone depletion?

1. DNA damage in plants and animals
2. Increased incidence of skin cancer
3. Suppression of the human immune system
4. Formation of nitrogen gas in the atmosphere

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
83.x: UV-B exposure can cause DNA damage, skin cancer, eye cataracts and suppression of the human immune system. Formation of nitrogen gas is not an identified effect.
83.tq: Find the unrelated scientific effect among several consequences of the same environmental problem.
xs: UV-B effects are **DNA damage**, **skin cancer** and **immune suppression** — so **1, 2 and 3 only**, option **(1)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: UV-B causes **DNA damage in plants and animals**.
Statements 2 and 3 are correct: in humans it causes **skin cancer**, **eye cataracts**, blindness and **suppression of the immune system**.
Statement 4 is wrong: **formation of nitrogen gas** is not a UV-B effect.
xa: A **1% ozone loss** raises harmful UV by about **2%**.
Crops: reduced growth and photosynthesis in **rice, wheat, corn, soybean**; a 1% UV-B rise may cut food output ~1%.
Marine: damage to **phytoplankton** and fish, shrimp, crab larvae → **food-chain disruption**.
Materials: UV degrades **wood, plastic, rubber, fabrics**.

83.s: An ozone hole is conventionally identified when the total column ozone falls below:
83.x: The term ozone hole is used when total ozone falls below 220 Dobson Units.
83.tq: Separate the threshold value from other familiar ozone-layer measurements.
xs: An ozone hole is identified when total ozone falls below **220 Dobson Units** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Ozone is measured in the **Dobson Unit (DU)**.
xa: The ozone hole was first detected over **Antarctica** in the mid-1980s.
First reported in **1985** by **British Antarctic Survey** scientists (some notes say discovered **1983**).
Thinning is seasonal, in **Southern Hemisphere spring, Aug-Nov**.

83.s: The seasonal thinning of the ozone layer over Antarctica is most pronounced during:
o: Southern Hemisphere autumn, March to May
Southern Hemisphere summer, December to February
Southern Hemisphere spring, approximately August to November
Northern Hemisphere spring, March to May
83.x: The Antarctic ozone hole is a seasonal phenomenon, with maximum thinning during Southern Hemisphere spring, approximately August to November.
83.tq: Link the phenomenon with the correct hemisphere and season.
xs: Antarctic ozone thinning peaks in **Southern Hemisphere spring, approximately August to November** — so option **(3)** is correct.
In the extreme cold of the **polar vortex**, polar stratospheric clouds activate chlorine, which destroys ozone **when sunlight returns** in spring.
xa: Ozone hole = total ozone below **220 DU**.
First detected over **Antarctica** in the mid-1980s; reported **1985** by the British Antarctic Survey.
Antarctic ozone is projected to recover to 1980 levels only by **2066** — the latest of all regions.

83.s: Polar stratospheric clouds contribute to ozone destruction because they:
o: Absorb all incoming solar radiation before it reaches the stratosphere
Convert oxygen directly into carbon dioxide
Prevent the return of sunlight to the polar vortex
Convert stable chlorine compounds into active forms on their surfaces in extreme cold
83.x: In the extremely cold polar vortex, polar stratospheric clouds provide surfaces that convert stable chlorine into active forms. When sunlight returns, these forms catalytically destroy ozone.
83.tq: Identify the causal mechanism rather than merely the associated location.
xs: Polar stratospheric clouds **convert stable chlorine compounds into active forms on their surfaces in extreme cold** — so option **(4)** is correct.
They form in the extreme cold of the **polar vortex**; the active chlorine **destroys ozone when sunlight returns**.
So they do not block sunlight or make CO2 — the ozone loss in fact needs the return of sunlight.
xa: Chlorine and bromine atoms destroy ozone **catalytically**.
The ozone hole is seasonal: **Southern Hemisphere spring, Aug-Nov**.
**Halons** (bromine) are about **100 times more potent** than CFCs.

83.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Antarctic ozone hole:
1. It was first detected over Antarctica in the mid-1980s.
2. A British survey reported it in 1985.
3. Its seasonal thinning is unrelated to the return of sunlight after the polar winter.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
83.x: The ozone hole was detected over Antarctica in the mid-1980s, and a British survey reported it in 1985. The return of sunlight is important in activating chlorine-driven ozone destruction, so statement 3 is false.
83.tq: Reject the statement that reverses the known seasonal mechanism.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: the ozone hole was first detected over **Antarctica** in the **mid-1980s**.
Statement 2 is correct: first reported in **1985** by **British Antarctic Survey** scientists.
Statement 3 is wrong: activated chlorine **destroys ozone when sunlight returns**, so the thinning depends on sunlight.
xa: ⚠ Some notes say the hole was **discovered 1983**; **1985** is the report year.
Season of thinning: **Southern Hemisphere spring, Aug-Nov**.
Ozone hole = total ozone below **220 DU**.
The **Vienna Convention** was also adopted in **1985**.

83.s: A 1% loss of stratospheric ozone is associated with approximately what change in harmful ultraviolet radiation?
83.x: A 1% loss of ozone is associated with an approximately 2% increase in harmful UV radiation.
83.tq: Distinguish the percentage change in ozone from the resulting percentage change in UV exposure.
xs: A **1% ozone loss** raises harmful UV by about **2%** — a **2% increase**, so option **(4)** is correct.
Less ozone means more **UV-B** reaches the surface, so UV rises — never decreases.
xa: Human effects: **skin cancer**, **eye cataracts**, blindness, **immune suppression**.
Crops: a **1% UV-B rise** may cut food output by about **1%**.
UV-B causes **DNA damage** in plants and animals.

Consider the following statements about the effects of increased UV-B radiation on crops:
1. It can reduce growth and photosynthesis in rice, wheat, corn and soybean.
2. A 1% rise in UV-B may reduce food output by approximately 1%.
3. It invariably increases crop productivity by stimulating photosynthesis.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
83.x: Increased UV-B can reduce growth and photosynthesis in the listed crops, and a 1% rise may reduce food output by about 1%. It does not invariably increase productivity.
83.tq: Identify the extreme and reversed claim in the crop-impact statements.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: UV-B **reduces growth and photosynthesis** in **rice, wheat, corn, soybean**.
Statement 2 is correct: a **1% UV-B rise** may cut food output by about **1%**.
Statement 3 is wrong: UV-B harms crops; it does not raise productivity.
xa: A **1% ozone loss** raises harmful UV by about **2%**.
Marine effect: damage to **phytoplankton** and larvae → **food-chain disruption**.
Materials: UV degrades **wood, plastic, rubber, fabrics**.

83.s: Damage to phytoplankton and larvae of fish, shrimp and crabs due to increased UV radiation can primarily lead to:
o: Increased ozone formation in the troposphere
Expansion of the stratospheric ozone layer
Immediate formation of polar stratospheric clouds
83.x: Damage to plankton and aquatic larvae affects the base and links of marine food chains, causing food-chain disruption.
83.tq: Trace the ecological effect from the affected organism to the ecosystem-level consequence.
xs: Damage to plankton and fish, shrimp and crab larvae leads to **food-chain disruption in marine ecosystems** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Phytoplankton** and larvae sit at the base of marine food chains.
UV damage does not create ozone or polar stratospheric clouds.
xa: Crops: reduced growth and photosynthesis in **rice, wheat, corn, soybean**.
Humans: **skin cancer**, **eye cataracts**, **immune suppression**.
Materials: degradation of **wood, plastic, rubber, fabrics**.

83.s:
Consider the following statements about ozone-depleting substances:
1. Halons contain bromine and are used in portable fire extinguishers.
2. Methyl bromide is used as an agricultural fumigant and in quarantine treatment.
3. Carbon tetrachloride and methyl chloroform are associated with solvent use.
4. HFCs are ozone-depleting substances and are the main cause of the ozone hole.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
83.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct: halons (bromine) are used in fire extinguishers, methyl bromide is a fumigant/quarantine agent, and CTC and methyl chloroform are solvents. Statement 4 is wrong: HFCs are non-ODS substitutes (with high global warming potential); CFCs are the main cause of ozone depletion. So '1, 2 and 3 only'.
83.tq: Reject the swapped-category statement that treats a non-ODS substitute as an ozone-depleting substance.
xs: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct — so **1, 2 and 3 only**, option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: **halons** contain **bromine** and are used in **portable fire extinguishers**.
Statement 2 is correct: **methyl bromide** is an **agricultural fumigant** and quarantine treatment.
Statement 3 is correct: **carbon tetrachloride** and **methyl chloroform** are **solvents** and chemical feedstock.
Statement 4 is wrong: **HFCs** are **non-ODS** (but high GWP); **CFCs** are the main cause of ozone depletion.
xa: **HCFCs** are weaker ODS, an **interim/transitional CFC substitute**.
Halons are about **100 times more potent** than CFCs.
⚠ HFCs are controlled by the **Kigali Amendment** because of their warming potential, not ozone.

83.s:
With reference to the destruction of stratospheric ozone, consider the following statements:
1. Ultraviolet radiation releases chlorine and bromine atoms from suitable compounds.

xa: **CFCs** release chlorine in the stratosphere and are the **main cause** of ozone depletion.

83.s: The Prior Informed Consent (PIC) procedure under the Rotterdam Convention implies that:

83.s: Persistent Organic Pollutants are characterised by which combination of properties?

Short persistence, rapid breakdown and local movement only

84.tq: Test the exact level-to-definition relationship.
xs: Genetic diversity is **variation within a species** — option **(4)** is correct.
It is the **basic source of biodiversity**: all rice varieties are **Oryza sativa** but differ in size, aroma and nutrients.
Number of species in an area is **species** diversity; variety of ecosystems is **ecosystem** diversity.
xa: Wild rice **Oryza rufipogon** is the progenitor of cultivated rice.
**Borjuli wetland** (Assam) protects Oryza rufipogon — a **Biodiversity Heritage Site**.
Species diversity includes **richness + abundance**.

84.s: Which one of the following correctly describes species diversity?
o: The variety of climatic zones on Earth
Variation in genes within a single species only
Only the number of species in an area, irrespective of their abundance
The variety of species in an area, involving richness as well as abundance
84.x: Species diversity concerns the variety of species in an area and includes both species richness and abundance.
84.tq: Distinguish species diversity from the narrower concept of richness.
xs: Species diversity is **the variety of species in an area, involving richness as well as abundance** — option **(4)** is correct.
Option (3) is wrong because it ignores **abundance**; option (2) describes **genetic** diversity.
xa: **Species richness** = number of species; **evenness** = relative abundance.
Species diversity is measured by the **Shannon-Wiener** and **Simpson** indices.
**Alpha** diversity = species richness within one community.

84.s:
Consider the following statements about ecosystem diversity:
1. It refers to the variety of ecosystems such as rainforests, deciduous forests and boreal ecosystems.
2. One ecosystem can always replace the functions of another ecosystem.
3. Boreal conifers cannot perform the same ecological role as tropical deciduous trees in every context.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
84.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is false because one ecosystem cannot simply replace another; boreal conifers cannot do the job of tropical deciduous trees in every context.
84.tq: Use the absolute word in the replacement claim as the false-statement trap.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — so **1 and 3 only**, option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: ecosystem diversity is the variety of ecosystems — **rainforest, deciduous, boreal**.
Statement 2 is wrong: **one ecosystem cannot replace another**.
Statement 3 is correct: **boreal conifers ≠ tropical deciduous trees** in function.
xa: Richest ecosystem on land: **tropical rainforests**; in the sea: **coral reefs**.
⚠ **Taiga, deserts and temperate forests** are the usual wrong options for richest ecosystem.
**Gamma** diversity = total diversity across the ecosystems of a whole region.

84.s:
Consider the following statements regarding measures of diversity:
1. Alpha diversity is the diversity within one area or community.
2. Beta diversity is the total diversity across the ecosystems of a whole region.
3. Gamma diversity is the overall diversity across the ecosystems of a whole region or landscape.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
84.x: Statement 1 is correct (alpha = within one community). Statement 2 is wrong: beta diversity is the change or turnover of species between ecosystems along a habitat gradient; regional total is gamma. Statement 3 is correct. So '1 and 3 only'.
84.tq: Alpha = within, beta = between (turnover), gamma = whole region.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — so **1 and 3 only**, option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: **alpha** = diversity within one area or community.
Statement 2 is wrong: **beta** is the **change (turnover)** in species between ecosystems along a habitat gradient.
Statement 3 is correct: **gamma** = total diversity across a whole region or landscape.
xa: ⚠ Alpha = **within**; Beta = **between (turnover)**; Gamma = **whole region**.
These terms originated with **R.H. Whittaker**.
**Point richness** = species count at a single point.

84.s: Species richness and species evenness refer, respectively, to:
o: Relative abundance and total number of species
Total number of species and their relative abundance
Change between ecosystems and total regional diversity
84.x: Species richness is the number of species, while species evenness indicates their relative abundance. Low evenness means that a few species dominate.
84.tq: Discriminate between number and proportional distribution.
xs: Richness and evenness are the **total number of species and their relative abundance** — option **(2)** is correct.
**Low evenness** means a few species dominate.
Option (1) reverses them; option (3) describes beta and gamma diversity.
xa: Example: Forest A (2 tigers, 6 deer, 7 rabbits) is **more even** than Forest B (1, 6, 8).
Indices: **Shannon-Wiener** and **Simpson**.
Functional diversity has its own **richness**, **evenness** and **divergence**.

84.s: Which pair of indices is used for measuring species diversity?
o: Simpson index and Human Development Index
84.x: The Shannon-Wiener and Simpson indices are measures of species diversity.
84.tq: Start from the sure pair of recognised biodiversity indices.
xs: **Shannon-Wiener index and Simpson index** measure species diversity — option **(1)** is correct.
They combine **richness** (number of species) and **evenness** (relative abundance).
xa: **Alpha, beta, gamma** diversity terms come from **R.H. Whittaker**.
**Species-area relationship**: log S = log C + Z log A.
**Functional diversity** = range of ecological roles.

84.s: Forest A contains 2 tigers, 6 deer and 7 rabbits, while Forest B contains 1 tiger, 6 deer and 8 rabbits. Which conclusion is correct?
o: Forest B is more even because it has more rabbits.
Forest A has greater species richness and Forest B has greater ecosystem diversity.
Forest A and Forest B differ in species richness but not in evenness.
Both forests have three species and 15 individuals, but Forest A is more even.
84.x: Both forests contain three species and 15 individuals. Forest A has a more equal distribution of individuals and is therefore more even.
84.tq: Separate richness from the distribution of individuals.
xs: **Both forests have three species and 15 individuals, but Forest A is more even** — option **(4)** is correct.
Richness is equal (**3** species each); Forest A (**2, 6, 7**) spreads individuals more equally than B (**1, 6, 8**).
More rabbits in B means one species dominates more — lower evenness, so option (1) is wrong.
xa: **Species evenness** = relative abundance; low evenness = a few species dominate.
**Species richness** = number of species.
Indices: **Shannon-Wiener** and **Simpson**.

84.s: Functional diversity is primarily concerned with—
o: the number of crop species cultivated by humans
the range of ecological roles performed by organisms
only the number of fossil species in a region
the geographical extent of a biosphere reserve
84.x: Functional diversity measures the range of ecological roles. Its components include functional richness, functional evenness and functional divergence.
84.tq: Link a term with its defining ecological function.
xs: Functional diversity is **the range of ecological roles performed by organisms** — option **(2)** is correct.
Its components: functional **richness**, **evenness** and **divergence**.
xa: Functional **richness** = niches occupied.
Functional **evenness** = abundance spread across niches.
Functional **divergence** = dominance of extreme traits.

84.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Component of functional diversity)
a. Functional richness
b. Functional evenness
c. Functional divergence

List-II (Meaning)
i. Dominance of extreme traits
 ii. Range of niches occupied
 iii. Spread of abundance across niches

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
84.x: Functional richness refers to the niches occupied, functional evenness to the spread of abundance across niches, and functional divergence to the dominance of extreme traits.
84.tq: Start with the direct definition of richness and eliminate the remaining codes.
xs: **a–ii, b–iii, c–i** is the correct match — option **(1)** is correct.
**Richness** → niches occupied; **evenness** → spread of abundance across niches; **divergence** → dominance of extreme traits.
xa: Functional diversity = **range of ecological roles**.
Species-level parallels: **species richness** (number) and **species evenness** (relative abundance).
Diversity indices: **Shannon-Wiener** and **Simpson**.

84.s:
Which of the following combinations correctly represents the estimates of described species and total living species?
1. About 1.5 million living species have been described.
2. About 300,000 fossil species have been described.
3. E. O. Wilson estimated the total number of living species at 10–50 million.
4. Robert May’s estimate was about 7 million living species.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
84.x: All four estimates are stated figures: about 1.5 million described living species, 300,000 described fossil species, Wilson’s 10–50 million estimate and May’s estimate of about 7 million.
84.tq: Separate multiple numerical estimates and retain the complete combination.
xs: All four figures are correct — so **1, 2, 3 and 4**, option **(2)** is correct.
Described species: about **1.5 million** living + **300,000** fossil.
Total estimates: **Wilson (1992)** **10-50 million**; **Robert May** about **7 million**.
xa: Over **70%** of recorded species are **animals**; plants about **22%**.
Among animals, **insects** are richest (over **70%**).
⚠ **Wilson** = 10-50 million; **May** = about 7 million.

84.s: Which one of the following statements about the taxonomic composition of recorded species is correct?
o: Animals constitute over 70% of recorded species, plants account for about 22%, and insects are the richest animal group.
Plants constitute over 70% of all recorded species.
Insects constitute less than 1% of recorded animal species.
Animals and plants each constitute approximately 50% of recorded species.
84.x: Over 70% of recorded species are animals, plants account for about 22%, and insects are the richest group among animals.
84.tq: Use relative shares and the within-group comparison together.
xs: **Animals are over 70%, plants about 22%, and insects are the richest animal group** — option **(1)** is correct.
Insects make up over **70%** of animals, so option (3) is wrong; plants are not over 70%.
xa: Described species: about **1.5 million** living + **300,000** fossil.
**Wilson (1992)**: **10-50 million** species in all.
India: **Hymenoptera** (**106**) topped the new animal species of 2025.

84.s:
Consider the following statements regarding estimates of global biodiversity:
1. About 1.5 million living species have been described.
2. E.O. Wilson estimated that the total number of species could be 10–50 million.
3. The estimate of 10–50 million refers only to described species.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
84.x: About 1.5 million species have been described, while Wilson estimated 10–50 million species in all. Statement 3 is false because the larger estimate includes undescribed species as well.
84.tq: Reject the statement that improperly narrows the scope of a broad estimate.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: about **1.5 million** living species are described.
Statement 2 is correct: **E.O. Wilson (1992)** estimated **10-50 million** species in all.
Statement 3 is wrong: 10-50 million is the **total** estimate, far above the **1.5 million** described.
xa: **Robert May** estimated about **7 million** species.
About **300,000** fossil species are described.
India has identified about **1,50,000** living species.

84.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the latitudinal pattern of biodiversity:
1. Biodiversity generally decreases from the tropics towards the poles.
2. Biodiversity generally decreases from lower to higher altitudes on mountains.
3. An ant survey recorded about 2,000 species near the North Pole and about 10 species at the equator.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
84.x: Biodiversity decreases towards the poles and with increasing altitude. The ant survey recorded about 10 species near the North Pole and up to 2,000 at the equator, making statement 3 false.
84.tq: Check the direction of the gradient and detect the reversed numerical comparison.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: biodiversity falls from the **tropics toward the poles**.
Statement 2 is correct: it falls from **lower to higher altitudes**.
Statement 3 is wrong: it is reversed — about **10** ant species near the North Pole vs up to **2,000** at the equator.
xa: Tropics are richest due to long **undisturbed evolutionary time**, stable climate and more solar energy.
The **Himalayas** are rich as a **meeting point of biogeographical zones**.
Moderate disturbance and habitat heterogeneity also raise diversity.

84.s: Which of the following correctly identifies the ecosystems with the greatest species richness on land and in the sea, respectively?
84.x: Tropical rainforests or tropical moist forests are the richest terrestrial ecosystems, while coral reefs are the richest marine ecosystems.
84.tq: Use the land–sea comparison to distinguish the two richest ecosystems.
xs: **Tropical rainforests and coral reefs** are the richest on land and in the sea — option **(1)** is correct.
Tropical rainforests (**tropical moist forests**) were the answer in PYQs **2017** and **2023**.
⚠ **Taiga, deserts and temperate forests** are the usual wrong options.
xa: Biodiversity is **highest in the tropics** and falls toward the poles.
India has **4 of the 36** hotspots.
India records **20,444** marine species.

84.s: Which one of the following is NOT a recognised explanation for the greater biodiversity of tropical regions?
o: Long, undisturbed evolutionary history without glaciation
Greater solar energy and higher productivity
A less seasonal and more predictable climate
Frequent continental-scale glaciation and severe seasonal fluctuations
84.x: Tropical richness is associated with long evolutionary time without glaciation, stable climate, solar energy and productivity. Frequent severe glaciation is not an explanation for tropical richness.
84.tq: Find the option that reverses the standard explanation for a biodiversity pattern.
xs: **Frequent continental-scale glaciation and severe seasonal fluctuations** is not a reason — option **(4)** is correct.
The tropics had **long, undisturbed evolutionary time** with **no glaciation**.
They have a **less seasonal, more stable** climate → niche specialisation, and **more solar energy** → higher **productivity**.
xa: **Moderate disturbance** and **habitat heterogeneity** also raise diversity.
Ant example: about **10 species** near the North Pole vs up to **2,000** at the equator.
UPPSC 2019 A/R: butterflies peak in the tropics because they **cannot tolerate low temperature**.

84.s: The high species richness of the Himalayas is most appropriately explained by the fact that the Himalayas
o: are a meeting point of different biogeographical zones
have no seasonal variation in climate
are entirely covered by tropical rainforests
are located close to the equator
84.x: The Himalayas bring together different biogeographical zones, creating varied habitats and high species richness.
84.tq: Apply the ecological cause to a geographical case rather than selecting a location-based distractor.
xs: The Himalayas are rich because they **are a meeting point of different biogeographical zones** — option **(1)** is correct.
There the **Palearctic** and **Indo-Malayan** realms meet, bringing species from both.
xa: The **Himalaya** zone has the most faunal species in India: **30,377**.
⚠ Largest zone = **Deccan Peninsula**; most faunal species = **Himalaya**.
The Himalaya zone covers **7.2%** of India's land.

84.s:
With reference to the species-area relationship, consider the following statements:
1. Species richness increases with an increase in area.
2. The increase in species richness continues without any limit.
3. The relationship is expressed as log S = log C + Z log A.
4. The value of Z is generally 0.1–0.2 for most areas.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
84.x: Statements 1, 3 and 4 are correct: species richness rises with area, the relation is log S = log C + Z log A, and Z is 0.1-0.2 for most areas. Statement 2 is wrong: richness rises with area only up to a limit. So '1, 3 and 4 only'.
84.tq: Separate the qualified true statement from the absolute statement containing ‘without any limit’.
xs: Statements 1, 3 and 4 are correct — so **1, 3 and 4 only**, option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: species richness **rises with area**.
Statement 2 is wrong: it rises **only up to a limit**.
Statements 3 and 4 are correct: **log S = log C + Z log A**, with **Z 0.1-0.2** for most areas.
xa: For very large areas (whole continents) **Z is 0.6-1.2**.
The relationship was proposed by **Alexander von Humboldt**.
**Point richness** = species count at a single point.

84.s:
The assertion that butterflies have their maximum diversity in the tropics is best explained by which of the following reasons?
Assertion (A): The maximum number of butterfly species is found in tropical regions.
Reason (R): Butterflies generally cannot tolerate low temperatures.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
84.x: Both statements are true, and intolerance to low temperatures helps explain why butterfly diversity is highest in the warmer tropics.
84.tq: Test whether the ecological reason directly explains the geographical diversity pattern.
xs: **Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)** is correct.
Butterflies peak in the **tropics**, and their inability to **tolerate low temperature** explains it (UPPSC 2019).
xa: Biodiversity falls from the **tropics toward the poles**.
Tropics: more **solar energy** → higher **productivity**.
Tropics: less seasonal, more **stable/predictable** climate → **niche specialisation**.

84.s:
With reference to the species-area relationship, consider the following statements:
1. It was proposed by Alexander von Humboldt.
2. The value of Z for very large areas such as whole continents is about 0.6-1.2.
3. Species richness keeps rising with area without any limit.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
84.x: Statement 1 is correct: Alexander von Humboldt proposed the species-area relationship. Statement 2 is correct: Z is 0.1-0.2 for most areas but 0.6-1.2 for very large areas such as whole continents. Statement 3 is wrong: richness rises with area only up to a limit. So '1 and 2 only'; '1 only' misses statement 2, and the options with 3 include a false statement.
84.tq: Species-area = Humboldt; Z 0.1-0.2 normally, 0.6-1.2 for continents.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: **Alexander von Humboldt** proposed the species-area relationship.
Statement 2 is correct: **Z is 0.6-1.2** for very large areas (whole continents), vs **0.1-0.2** for most areas.
Statement 3 is wrong: richness rises with area **only up to a limit**.
xa: Equation: **log S = log C + Z log A**.
**Paul Ehrlich** proposed the **rivet popper hypothesis**.
**R.H. Whittaker** gave the alpha, beta, gamma terms.

84.s: Fuelwood, fodder and wild food collected directly by local people for their own use represent which value of biodiversity?
84.x: Consumptive use value refers to direct use by local people without commercial sale, including fuelwood, fodder and wild food.
84.tq: Distinguish direct household use from commercial use and future potential use.
xs: Fuelwood, fodder and wild food used by local people show **consumptive use value** — option **(2)** is correct.
Consumptive use = used directly, **not sold**.
⚠ **Productive use** = **sold commercially** (timber, fibre, drugs).
xa: **Option value** = unknown future uses (undiscovered medicines, crop genes).
**Aesthetic value** = natural beauty, recreation, ecotourism.
Consumptive use also includes **medicine** gathered locally.

84.s: Which of the following is an example of the productive use value of biodiversity?
o: A sacred grove protected for religious reasons
Timber, fibre, medicines and genetic material sold commercially
Enjoyment of a landscape by visitors
Wild food collected for household consumption
84.x: Productive use value concerns biodiversity products that are commercially marketed, such as timber, fibre, medicines and genetic material for crops.
84.tq: Use the commercial-versus-direct-use distinction to identify the correct value.
xs: **Timber, fibre, medicines and genetic material sold commercially** show productive use value — option **(2)** is correct.
Sacred groves are **social/cultural** value; landscape enjoyment is **aesthetic**; household wild food is **consumptive**.
xa: ⚠ Consumptive = used, **not sold**; productive = **sold commercially**.
**Ethical / existence** value: every species has a **right to exist**.
Productive use also covers **gums** and drugs.

84.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the values of biodiversity:
1. Ecosystem services include clean air and water, crop pollination and climate regulation.
2. Social or cultural value includes sacred species, sacred groves and indigenous knowledge.
3. Ethical or existence value is based on the idea that every species has a right to exist.
4. Aesthetic value includes natural beauty, recreation and ecotourism.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
84.x: All four statements correctly describe ecosystem-service, social or cultural, ethical or existence, and aesthetic values of biodiversity.
84.tq: Identify the value category associated with each example before choosing the complete combination.
xs: All four statements are correct — so **1, 2, 3 and 4**, option **(4)** is correct.
Statement 1: **ecosystem services** = clean air and water, **crop pollination**, **climate regulation**, resilience.
Statement 2: **social / cultural** = **sacred species and groves**, indigenous knowledge.
Statements 3 and 4: **ethical / existence** = right to exist; **aesthetic** = beauty, recreation, **ecotourism**.
xa: **Option value**: undiscovered medicines and crop genes.
Most significant aspect (UPPSC 2015): **maintenance of the ecosystem**.
Role in sustainable development (APPSC 2025): **supports ecosystem services** like food, water and air quality.

84.s: The possible future use of an undiscovered medicinal compound or a new crop gene is referred to as
84.x: Option value refers to possible future benefits, including undiscovered medicines and useful crop genes.
84.tq: Recognise the future-possibility meaning of the term ‘option value’.
xs: Possible future uses like undiscovered medicines and crop genes are **option value** — option **(2)** is correct.
**Consumptive** use is current direct local use; **aesthetic** is beauty; **social** is cultural or sacred value.
xa: **Productive** use = sold commercially (timber, fibre, medicines).
**TKDL** documents traditional formulations to stop wrong patents.
**Bioprospecting** = search in nature for commercially valuable compounds + genes.

84.s: Who proposed the Rivet Popper Hypothesis in ecology?
84.x: The Rivet Popper Hypothesis was proposed by Paul Ehrlich.
84.tq: Use direct person–concept association.
xs: The rivet popper hypothesis was proposed by **Paul Ehrlich** — option **(1)** is correct.
**E.O. Wilson** popularised "biodiversity"; **Partha Dasgupta** wrote the **Dasgupta Review (2021)**.
xa: Analogy: ecosystem = **aeroplane**; species = **rivets**.
Losing a **key rivet** (keystone species) can bring the plane down.
**Humboldt** proposed the **species-area relationship**.

84.s: The Rivet Popper Hypothesis compares an ecosystem to an aeroplane and its species to:
84.x: The hypothesis compares an ecosystem to an aeroplane and species to its rivets; the loss of a key rivet may cause system failure.
84.tq: Identify the central analogy rather than a related ecological term.
xs: Species are compared to **rivets** of an aeroplane — option **(3)** is correct.
The ecosystem is the **aeroplane**; losing a few rivets seems harmless but **each loss weakens** it.
xa: Losing a **key rivet** (**keystone species**) can bring it down.
Proposed by **Paul Ehrlich**.
Most significant aspect of biodiversity (UPPSC 2015): **maintenance of the ecosystem**.

84.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Rivet Popper Hypothesis:
1. The loss of a few species may initially appear harmless.
2. Every species has exactly the same ecological importance.
3. The loss of a keystone species may destabilise or collapse an ecosystem.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
84.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is false because the hypothesis highlights the special importance of key or keystone species.
84.tq: Find the statement that reverses the key-species distinction.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — so **1 and 3 only**, option **(3)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: losing a few rivets (species) **seems harmless**.
Statement 2 is wrong: species are not equal — a **key rivet** (keystone species) matters more.
Statement 3 is correct: losing a **keystone species** can bring the ecosystem down.
xa: Proposed by **Paul Ehrlich**: ecosystem = **aeroplane**, species = **rivets**.
Each loss **weakens** the ecosystem.
Ecosystem services: **pollination**, **climate regulation**, resilience.

84.s: The principal objective of TEEB is to:
o: Make nature’s values visible and incorporate them into decisions
Replace biodiversity legislation with market mechanisms
Calculate only the monetary value of forests
Measure the depreciation of manufactured capital
84.x: TEEB, or The Economics of Ecosystems and Biodiversity, seeks to make nature’s values visible and bring them into decision-making at every level.
84.tq: Choose the option expressing the stated institutional objective precisely.
xs: TEEB aims to **make nature's values visible** and bring them **into decisions** at every level — option **(1)** is correct.
It does not replace laws or value only forests.
xa: TEEB = **The Economics of Ecosystems and Biodiversity**.
It began from a **G8+5** initiative in **2007**; hosted by **UNEP**.
⚠ The **Dasgupta Review (2021)** says **GDP ignores nature's depreciation**.

84.s:
Consider the following statements about TEEB:
1. TEEB is hosted by UNEP.
2. It began from a G8+5 initiative in 2007.
3. It is hosted by the World Economic Forum.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
84.x: TEEB is hosted by UNEP and originated from a G8+5 initiative in 2007. Statement 3 is false because it is not hosted by the World Economic Forum.
84.tq: Apply the wrong-host organisation trap.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(3)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: TEEB is hosted by **UNEP**.
Statement 2 is correct: it began from a **G8+5 initiative, 2007**.
Statement 3 is wrong: ⚠ TEEB is hosted by **UNEP**, not IMF or **WEF**.
xa: Aim: **"make nature's values visible"**.
**Dasgupta Review (2021)** was for the **UK Treasury**.
**Conservation International (1998)** identified the megadiverse countries.

84.s:
Consider the following statements about the Dasgupta Review (2021):
1. It was prepared by Partha Dasgupta for the UK Treasury.
2. It treats nature as an asset.
3. It holds that GDP fully accounts for the depreciation of nature.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
84.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: the Review argues that GDP ignores nature's depreciation. So '1 and 2 only'.
84.tq: Dasgupta: nature is an asset GDP fails to depreciate.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: it was by **Partha Dasgupta** for the **UK Treasury**.
Statement 2 is correct: it treats **nature as an asset**.
Statement 3 is wrong: it says **GDP ignores nature's depreciation**.
xa: **TEEB** (**2007**, UNEP) aims to make nature's values visible.
**LMMC** formed by the **Cancun Declaration, 2002**.
**Biological Diversity Act 2002** was **amended in 2023**.

84.s: What is the role of biodiversity in sustainable development?
o: It mainly increases the area available for urban expansion
It supports ecosystem services such as food, water and air quality
It replaces the need for conservation laws
It matters only for its aesthetic and recreational value
84.x: Biodiversity underpins sustainable development by supporting ecosystem services such as food, water and air quality. It does not provide land for urban expansion, does not replace conservation laws, and its value is not limited to aesthetics and recreation.
84.tq: Biodiversity in sustainable development = ecosystem services (APPSC 2025).
xs: Biodiversity **supports ecosystem services such as food, water and air quality** — option **(2)** is correct (APPSC 2025).
It does not create land for cities, replace conservation laws, or matter only for **aesthetic** value.
xa: Ecosystem services: clean air and water, **crop pollination**, **climate regulation**, resilience.
Most significant aspect (UPPSC 2015): **maintenance of the ecosystem**.
**Rivet popper hypothesis**: losing species weakens the ecosystem.

84.s: The most significant aspect of biodiversity is:
84.x: The most significant aspect of biodiversity is the maintenance of the ecosystem. Timber, ornamental plants and ecotourism are uses of biodiversity (productive or aesthetic values), but they are not its most significant aspect.
84.tq: Most significant aspect = maintenance of the ecosystem (UPPSC 2015).
xs: The most significant aspect is **maintenance of the ecosystem** — option **(2)** is correct (UPPSC 2015).
Timber is **productive** value; ornamentals and **ecotourism** are uses (aesthetic), not the main aspect.
xa: Role in sustainable development (APPSC 2025): **supports ecosystem services**.
Losing a **keystone species** can bring an ecosystem down (rivet popper).
**Ethical / existence** value: every species has a **right to exist**.

84.s: How many countries are recognised as the world's megadiverse countries?
84.x: There are 17 megadiverse countries. The figure 36 refers to the global number of biodiversity hotspots, not megadiverse countries.
84.tq: Distinguish the country count from the separate hotspot count.
xs: There are **17** megadiverse countries — option **(2)** is correct.
⚠ **36** is the number of global **biodiversity hotspots**, not megadiverse countries.
xa: Identified by **Conservation International (1998)**.
Criteria: at least **5,000 endemic plants** + border marine ecosystems.
India is a member of the **LMMC** (Cancun Declaration, **2002**).

84.s: Which one of the following lists contains only megadiverse countries?
o: India, Brazil, China, Colombia, DR Congo, Ecuador, Indonesia, Madagascar
India, Brazil, Japan, China, Canada, Indonesia, Madagascar, Mexico

84.s: India's share of the world's land area, recorded species and population is approximately:

84.s: The two biogeographical realms represented in India are

84.s:

84.s:

Statement 2 is correct: it protects **Oryza rufipogon**, wild ancestor of **Oryza sativa**.
Statement 3 is wrong: the wild rice **tolerates floods + salinity** and resists pests.

**Basmati** (RiceTec): most claims withdrawn after India's challenge.
**TKDL** makes traditional knowledge **prior art** for patent offices.

84.s: The Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL) was established by:
o: NBA and State Biodiversity Boards in 2010
84.x: The TKDL was set up by CSIR and AYUSH in 2001.
84.tq: Use the institution–year association directly.
xs: The TKDL was set up by **CSIR and AYUSH in 2001** — option **(1)** is correct.
It documents traditional formulations in several **international languages** to stop wrong patents.
xa: TKDL makes traditional knowledge **prior art** for patent offices.
**Turmeric** patent revoked **1997** after a **CSIR** challenge.
**ABS** became operational via the **Nagoya Protocol in 2010**.

84.s: Access and Benefit Sharing (ABS) was introduced through the Convention on Biological Diversity in 1992 and made operational by the:
84.x: ABS began with the CBD in 1992 and was made operational through the Nagoya Protocol in 2010.
84.tq: Link the framework to the later protocol that operationalised it.
xs: ABS was made operational by the **Nagoya Protocol, 2010** — option **(2)** is correct.
It began with the **CBD in 1992**.
xa: **Human genetic material** is excluded from ABS.
India leads the world in issuing **IRCCs** under Nagoya.
India's NBA mobilised over **₹266 crore since 2008**; **Red Sanders** = **45% (₹120 crore)**.

84.s: Which one of the following is excluded from the scope of Access and Benefit Sharing as specified?
84.x: Human genetic material is excluded from the stated ABS framework.
84.tq: Look for the explicit exception rather than the general rule.
xs: **Human genetic material** is excluded from ABS — option **(1)** is correct.
Plant compounds, traditional formulations and bio-resources for research fall within ABS.
xa: ABS began with the **CBD (1992)**; operational via **Nagoya (2010)**.
The **Biological Diversity Act 2002** regulates access to bio-resources + traditional knowledge.
APSBB is preparing a first-of-its-kind **Marine ABS framework** for fishers.

84.s: Under the Nagoya framework, the country reported as leading the world in issuing Internationally Recognized Certificates of Compliance is:
84.x: India is reported as the world leader in issuing Internationally Recognized Certificates of Compliance under the Nagoya framework.
84.tq: Identify the country associated with the international compliance record.
xs: **India** leads the world in issuing **IRCCs** under Nagoya — option **(3)** is correct.
IRCC = **Internationally Recognized Certificate of Compliance**.
xa: India's NBA mobilised over **₹266 crore since 2008**.
**Red Sanders** alone = **45% (₹120 crore)** of that.
Nagoya made **ABS** operational in **2010**.

84.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Basmati — US patent to RiceTec, with main claims withdrawn
Neem — EPO patent involving W. R. Grace and USDA, later revoked
Turmeric — US patent on wound healing, revoked after CSIR challenge
Hoodia — patent granted to Mahyco without any benefit-sharing arrangement
84.x: Hoodia involved knowledge of the San people and resulted in a benefit-sharing deal. The other three pairs correctly describe the stated biopiracy cases.
84.tq: Find the altered outcome in a case-based matching question.
xs: **Hoodia — patent granted to Mahyco without any benefit-sharing arrangement** is wrong — option **(4)** is correct.
Hoodia used the **San** people's knowledge (southern Africa) and ended in a **benefit-sharing deal**.
The others are correct: **Basmati** (RiceTec) claims withdrawn; **Neem** (W.R. Grace, USDA) revoked; **Turmeric** revoked after CSIR challenge.
xa: ⚠ **Turmeric** revoked **1997**; **Neem** revoked **2000**.
Basmati patent was a **US** patent of **1997**.
**Biopiracy** = patenting without consent or compensation.

84.s: The Hoodia case is associated with traditional knowledge of which community?
o: The Maori people of New Zealand
The San people of southern Africa
The Toda people of southern India
The Inuit people of the Arctic
84.x: The appetite-suppressant use of Hoodia was based on knowledge of the San people of southern Africa, and a benefit-sharing deal followed.
84.tq: Identify the community associated with the traditional knowledge claim.
xs: Hoodia used knowledge of **the San people of southern Africa** — option **(2)** is correct.
Hoodia is an **appetite suppressant**; the case ended in a **benefit-sharing deal**.
xa: **Turmeric** (wound healing) US patent revoked **1997**.
**Neem** (fungicide) European patent revoked **2000**.
**Biopiracy** = patenting resources or traditional knowledge without consent or compensation.

84.s: The Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL) prevents biopiracy primarily by:
o: Approving commercial release of GM crops
Making traditional knowledge available as prior art to patent offices
84.x: TKDL documents traditional knowledge so that patent offices can treat it as prior art, helping prevent wrongful patents.
84.tq: Connect the database’s function with the patent examination process.
xs: TKDL works by **making traditional knowledge available as prior art to patent offices** — option **(2)** is correct.
It documents traditional formulations in several **international languages** → stops wrong patents.
xa: Set up in **2001** by **CSIR** + **Department of AYUSH**.
**Turmeric** patent was revoked in **1997** after a CSIR challenge.
**Bioprospecting** = search for valuable compounds + genes.

84.s: The Biological Diversity Act, 2002 regulates access to bio-resources and traditional knowledge and implements the:
84.x: The Biological Diversity Act, 2002 regulates access to bio-resources and traditional knowledge and implements the Nagoya Protocol.
84.tq: Distinguish access-and-benefit-sharing law from biosafety and weapons agreements.
xs: The Biological Diversity Act, 2002 implements the **Nagoya Protocol** — option **(1)** is correct.
It regulates access to **bio-resources + traditional knowledge**.
xa: The Act was **amended in 2023**; **Biological Diversity Rules, 2024** apply.
Governance via **NBA, SBBs and BMCs**.
⚠ The **Cartagena Protocol** deals with **biosafety** (LMOs), not access and benefit-sharing.

84.s:
Consider the following statements about the Eastern Ghats:
1. They run from the Godavari delta to Kanyakumari.
2. Their highest peak is Arma Konda (about 1,680 m) in Alluri Sitharama Raju district.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
84.x: Statement 1 is wrong: the Eastern Ghats run from the Mahanadi valley to the Nilgiris. Statement 2 is correct. So '2 only'; '1 only', 'both' and 'neither' are wrong.
84.tq: Eastern Ghats start at the Mahanadi, not the Godavari.
xs: Only statement 2 is correct — so **2 only**, option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 is wrong: the Eastern Ghats run from the **Mahanadi valley to the Nilgiris**.
Statement 2 is correct: the highest peak is **Arma Konda (1,680 m)** in **Alluri Sitharama Raju** district.
xa: Local name in **Srikakulam**: **Mahendra Girulu**.
⚠ Eastern Ghats are **not** among the **36** global hotspots.
Vegetation: deciduous, semi-evergreen, evergreen + savanna, scrub, estuarine.

84.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the vegetation of the Eastern Ghats?
o: Deciduous, semi-evergreen and evergreen forests, together with savanna, scrub and estuarine vegetation
Only mangrove forests and coral reefs
Only alpine grasslands and coniferous forests
84.x: The Eastern Ghats contain deciduous, semi-evergreen and evergreen forests, along with savanna, scrub and estuarine vegetation.
84.tq: Choose the most complete ecological description.
xs: The Eastern Ghats have **deciduous, semi-evergreen and evergreen forests, together with savanna, scrub and estuarine vegetation** — option **(2)** is correct.
So they are neither exclusively evergreen nor only mangroves or alpine.
xa: They run from the **Mahanadi valley to the Nilgiris**.
Highest peak: **Arma Konda (1,680 m)**.
AP has India's **second-largest mangrove ecosystem**.

84.s:
Which of the following statements about the Seshachalam hills is correct?
1. Red Sanders occurs naturally only in the Seshachalam region.
2. Cycas beddomei is a rare endemic cycad of the hills.
3. The Golden Gecko is a micro-endemic fauna of the region.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
84.x: Red Sanders, Cycas beddomei and the Golden Gecko are all characteristic biodiversity elements of the Seshachalam hills. The Golden Gecko is described as micro-endemic.
84.tq: When all three statements are independently supported, select the complete combination.
xs: All three statements are correct — so **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)** is correct.
Statement 1: **Red Sanders** (**Pterocarpus santalinus**) is found naturally only here.
Statement 2: **Cycas beddomei** is a **rare endemic cycad**.
Statement 3: the **Golden Gecko** is **micro-endemic**; the hills also have a distinct wild elephant population.
xa: Golden Gecko + Cycas beddomei are threatened by **mining and fires**.
**Seshachalam Biosphere Reserve** notified **2010**.
APSBB shares **5% of Red Sanders sale profits** with farmers.

84.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Seshachalam — Natural habitat of Red Sanders
Arma Konda — Highest peak of the Eastern Ghats
Coringa — Second-largest mangrove ecosystem in India
Mahendra Girulu — Hills of the Anantapur region
84.x: Mahendra Girulu is the name used for the Eastern Ghats hills in Srikakulam. The other three pairs are correctly matched.
84.tq: Find the location mismatch among closely related regional facts.
xs: **Mahendra Girulu — Hills of the Anantapur region** is wrong — option **(4)** is correct.
Mahendra Girulu is the local name in **Srikakulam**.
The others hold: **Seshachalam** — Red Sanders; **Arma Konda** — highest peak; AP has India's **second-largest mangrove ecosystem**.
xa: Arma Konda (**1,680 m**) is in **Alluri Sitharama Raju** district.
**Seshachalam + Nallamala** corridors: tigers, leopards, elephants; home to **Chenchus (PVTG)**.
**Cycas beddomei** is a rare endemic cycad of Seshachalam.

84.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the Eastern Ghats is correct?
o: They have no recognised biodiversity significance in India.
They are not among the 36 global biodiversity hotspots, although some descriptions call them a biodiversity hotspot.
They are included among all 36 global biodiversity hotspots.
They are a continuous range without any scrub or savanna vegetation.
84.x: Some descriptions call the Eastern Ghats a biodiversity hotspot, but they are not included among the 36 global biodiversity hotspots.
84.tq: Distinguish a descriptive label from formal global classification.
xs: The Eastern Ghats **are not among the 36 global biodiversity hotspots, although some descriptions call them a biodiversity hotspot** — option **(2)** is correct.
They are still rich: AP is one of the **richest biodiversity repositories in south and south-east Asia** (APSES 2024-25).
They do have **savanna** and **scrub** vegetation, so option (4) is wrong.
xa: India has **4 of the 36** hotspots.
Highest peak: **Arma Konda (1,680 m)**.
AP has India's **second-largest mangrove ecosystem**.

84.s:
Which of the following is associated with the Andhra Pradesh State Biodiversity Board?
1. Sharing 5% of Red Sanders sale profits with farmers.
2. Preparing a Marine Access and Benefit Sharing framework for fishers.
3. Working through People’s Biodiversity Registers.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
84.x: The Board shares 5% of Red Sanders sale profits with farmers, works through People's Biodiversity Registers and is preparing a Marine ABS framework for fishers.
84.tq: Test an institutional body through its functions and mechanisms.
xs: All three are APSBB activities — so **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)** is correct.
Statement 1: it shares **5% of Red Sanders sale profits** with farmers (about **₹7 crore** in three months).
Statement 2: it is preparing a first-of-its-kind **Marine ABS framework** for fishers.
Statement 3: it works through **People's Biodiversity Registers** + about **13,000 BMCs**.
xa: APSBB chairman: **N. Vijay Kumar**.
Plans: **OECMs** for the Kunming-Montreal **30x30** target; **City Biodiversity Indices**.
City indices for **Vijayawada, Visakhapatnam, Tirupati, Kadapa**.

84.s:
Consider the following statements regarding biodiversity conservation in Andhra Pradesh:
1. The Seshachalam Biosphere Reserve was notified in 2010.
2. The Seshachalam and Nallamala corridors support tigers, leopards and elephants.
3. Chenchus are associated with these Eastern Ghats landscapes as a Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
84.x: All three statements are correct. The Seshachalam Biosphere Reserve was notified in 2010, the corridors support major mammals, and the Chenchus are a PVTG living in the landscape.
84.tq: Combine date, habitat and community facts in a coded statement question.
xs: All three statements are correct — so **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)** is correct.
Statement 1: **Seshachalam Biosphere Reserve** was notified in **2010**.
Statement 2: **Seshachalam + Nallamala** corridors support **tigers, leopards, elephants**.
Statement 3: they are home to the **Chenchus (PVTG)**.
xa: NSTR-Seshachalam landscape: **68 tigers and 11 cubs**.
**Gaurs** are being reintroduced to improve **genetic diversity**.
**Golden Gecko** + **Cycas beddomei** are Seshachalam micro-endemics.

84.s: India’s fauna count crossed which threshold after 709 additions in 2025?
84.x: India’s fauna count passed 1.05 lakh species after 709 additions in 2025.
84.tq: Use the magnitude and addition figure together to identify the correct threshold.
xs: India's fauna passed **more than 1.05 lakh species** after **709** additions — option **(4)** is correct.
The ZSI count is **1,05,953** species.
⚠ **1.50 lakh** (**1,50,000**) is India's total of living species identified, not the fauna count.
xa: **709** = **483** new to science + **226** new records.
India adds about **500-600** species and records a year.
ZSI-only counts vs ZSI+BSI totals differ.

84.s:
Which of the following are identified as threatened micro-endemics in Andhra Pradesh?
1. Golden Gecko
2. Cycas beddomei
3. Red Sanders
4. Hoolock gibbon
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
84.x: The Golden Gecko and Cycas beddomei of the Seshachalam hills are the threatened micro-endemics (by mining and fires). Red Sanders is noted instead as AP's top ABS earner, and the hoolock gibbon lives in North-East India, not AP. So '1 and 2 only'.
84.tq: Separate the specifically identified micro-endemics from other regional fauna and flora.
xs: The threatened micro-endemics are the **Golden Gecko** and **Cycas beddomei** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)** is correct.
Both are threatened by **mining and fires**, so **Seshachalam Biosphere Reserve** core zones matter.
**Red Sanders** is noted as AP's ABS earner; the **hoolock gibbon** lives in **North-East India**.
xa: **Red Sanders** alone = **45% (₹120 crore)** of NBA's ABS earnings.
Seshachalam fauna also has a distinct wild **elephant** population.
Seshachalam Biosphere Reserve notified **2010**.

84.s: Why should the source of a biodiversity count be specified when citing figures for India?
o: ZSI counts and combined ZSI–BSI totals may differ.
Botanical surveys exclude all animal species by definition.
Fauna counts are legally fixed and cannot be revised.
Only international organisations are authorised to count Indian fauna.
84.x: ZSI-only counts and combined ZSI–BSI totals differ; therefore, the institution or combination of institutions behind a figure should be stated.
84.tq: Apply the source-attribution distinction in statistical questions.
xs: The source matters because **ZSI counts and combined ZSI–BSI totals may differ** — option **(1)** is correct.
Always say which count you quote.
xa: ZSI: India's fauna is **1,05,953 species**.
BSI + ZSI jointly released 2025 additions at **Kolkata**.
Counts change each year — about **500-600** new species and records.

84.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the present legal framework mentioned for India’s biodiversity governance?
o: The Biological Diversity Act, 2002 was amended in 2023 and the Biological Diversity Rules, 2024 apply.
The Biological Diversity Act was enacted in 2023 and rules were framed in 2002.
Only the National Biodiversity Authority has a role in governance.
The Act was repealed in 2024 and replaced by the Nagoya Protocol.
84.x: The Biological Diversity Act, 2002 was amended in 2023, and the Biological Diversity Rules, 2024 apply. Governance involves the NBA, State Biodiversity Boards and Biodiversity Management Committees.
84.tq: Use the year-order trap and check the institutional structure.
xs: **The Biological Diversity Act, 2002 was amended in 2023 and the Biological Diversity Rules, 2024 apply** — option **(1)** is correct.
Governance involves **NBA, SBBs and BMCs**, not only the NBA.
xa: The Act regulates access to **bio-resources + traditional knowledge** and implements **Nagoya**.
India had **54 Biodiversity Heritage Sites** as of Mar 2026.
AP works through about **13,000 BMCs**.

84.s:
Consider the following statements regarding marsupials and India:
1. Marsupials do not occur naturally in India.
2. Marsupials thrive only in montane grasslands with no predators.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
84.x: Marsupials do not occur naturally in India. The second statement is false because the claim that they thrive only in montane grasslands with no predators is incorrect.
84.tq: Reject an absolute ecological claim while retaining the valid distribution statement.
xs: Only statement 1 is correct — so **1 only**, option **(2)** is correct (UPSC 2023).
Statement 1 is correct: **marsupials do not occur naturally in India**.
Statement 2 is wrong: the claim that they "**thrive only in montane grasslands**" is false.
xa: India has **no native kangaroos, giraffes or lemurs**.
India's realms: **Palearctic** + **Indo-Malayan**.
Only the **Asiatic lion** is found naturally in India alone.

84.s: The OECM initiative of the Andhra Pradesh State Biodiversity Board is associated with which international conservation target?
84.x: The OECM initiative is linked with the Kunming–Montreal target of conserving 30 percent by 2030.
84.tq: Associate the conservation measure with the correct global target.
xs: APSBB's **OECM** plan links to the **Kunming–Montreal 30x30 target** — option **(1)** is correct.
**OECMs** = Other Effective Area-based Conservation Measures **outside protected areas**.
xa: APSBB also plans **City Biodiversity Indices** for Vijayawada, Visakhapatnam, Tirupati, Kadapa.
At the State's Biological Diversity Day event (**Guntur**, May 2026), APSBB gave its **Best Individual Biodiversity Conservator Award-2026**.
APSBB chairman: **N. Vijay Kumar**.

85.s: The concept of biodiversity hotspots was introduced in 1988 by whom?
