103.s: The ban on identified single-use plastic items came into effect from:
103.x: The ban on identified single-use plastic items came into effect on 1 July 2022.
103.tq: Distinguish the ban date from the separate thickness-transition dates.
xs: The ban on identified **single-use plastic (SUP)** items came into force on **1 July 2022** — option **(2)** is correct.
**30 Sep 2021** is the **75-micron** carry-bag date; **31 Dec 2022** the **120-micron** date.
xa: Scope: manufacture, import, stocking, distribution, sale and use of identified items banned.
Count: most notes say **19 items**; some say **12** heads.
The ban covers only **11%** of total plastic waste (CSE 2023).

103.s: The EPR Guidelines for plastic packaging became effective in:
103.x: The EPR Guidelines, 2022 for plastic packaging became effective in July 2022.
103.tq: Separate the guideline year from its effective month.
xs: The **EPR Guidelines 2022** for plastic packaging became effective in **July 2022** — option **(2)** is correct (APPSC-GS 2021).
**August 2021** is when the PWM Amendment Rules 2021 came; **March 2026** the 2026 Amendment.
xa: EPR covers **PIBOs** — Producers, Importers and Brand Owners — for packaging not covered by the SUP ban.
Categories: **I Rigid**, **II Flexible**, **III Multi-layered**.
CPCB EPR portal: **69,470 producers, 4,402 recyclers** registered (29 Oct 2025).

103.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Plastic Waste Management (Amendment) Rules, 2026:
1. Plastics are classed as rigid, flexible and multi-layered.
2. Unmet targets may be carried forward for up to three years.
3. Plastic certificates become tradable.
4. Waste-to-energy, co-processing and waste-to-oil are permitted as end-of-life options.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
103.x: The 2026 amendment includes all four measures: classification into three categories, three-year carry-forward, tradable certificates and specified end-of-life options.
103.tq: Check whether every provision in a regulatory amendment is correctly included.
xs: All four statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.
Statement 1: plastics classed as **rigid, flexible and multi-layered** — correct.
Statements 2-3: **carry-forward** of unmet targets up to **3 years**; **tradable plastic certificates** — correct.
Statement 4: **WtE, co-processing, waste-to-oil** allowed at end-of-life — correct.
xa: Recycled content in rigid plastics: **30% to 60% by 2028-29**.
Reuse targets (2025-26): **10%** small containers; **70%** large water packaging.
Critics say compliance was **eased** (4 Apr 2026).

103.s: Which standard must compostable plastics meet?
103.x: Compostable plastics must meet the IS/ISO 17088 standard.
103.tq: Recall the exact technical standard rather than a general environmental certification.
xs: Compostable plastics must meet **IS/ISO 17088** — option **(3)** is correct.
The notes name no other standard for compostable plastics.
xa: **PWM Amendment Rules 2024** defined **biodegradable plastics** and required **CPCB certification** for makers.
**PWM Amendment Rules 2026**: **QR-code traceability**; classes rigid, flexible, multi-layered.

103.s: Under the Plastic Waste Management Amendment Rules, 2024, which of the following is required for makers of biodegradable plastics?
o: Approval only from local village panchayats
Certification by the Central Pollution Control Board
Certification only by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India
Registration with the National Disaster Management Authority
103.x: The 2024 amendment defined biodegradable plastics and required CPCB certification for their makers.
103.tq: Identify the competent certifying authority in a regulatory provision.
xs: The **PWM Amendment Rules 2024** required **CPCB certification** for makers of **biodegradable plastics** — option **(2)** is correct.
They also **defined** biodegradable plastics.
xa: Compostable plastics must meet **IS/ISO 17088**.
**FSSAI** found microplastics in all tested sugar and salt samples — a different context.
Timeline: 2016 Rules → 2021 Amendment → 2022 EPR Guidelines → **2024** Amendment → 2026 Amendment.

103.s:
Consider the following statements about plastic-waste management:
1. Plastic roads are promoted under the Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016.
2. Energy recovery from plastic waste is promoted under the same framework.
3. Plastic waste can serve as a feedstock for advanced biofuel.
4. Waste-to-oil is an allowed end-of-life route.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
103.x: All four are correct: the PWM Rules, 2016 promoted plastic roads and energy recovery, and the PWM (Amendment) Rules, 2026 allow waste-to-oil as an end-of-life route and treat plastic waste as an advanced-biofuel feedstock.
103.tq: Check whether each listed recovery route belongs to the same regulatory framework.
xs: All four statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.
Statements 1-2: **PWM Rules 2016** promoted **plastic roads** and **energy recovery** — correct.
Statements 3-4: **PWM Amendment Rules 2026** treat plastic waste as **advanced-biofuel feedstock** and allow **waste-to-oil** — correct.
xa: 2026 Amendment also allows **WtE** and **co-processing** end-of-life routes.
**RDF** from high-calorific plastic is used in **cement kilns**.

103.s: The Plastic Waste Management (Amendment) Rules, 2021 aimed at phasing out identified single-use plastic items by:
103.x: The 2021 Amendment Rules (12 Aug 2021) aimed to phase out identified SUP by 2022 (APPSC-GS 2021); the ban took effect on 1 July 2022. 2020 precedes the Rules, and 2025 and 2030 are not the stated targets.
103.tq: PWM 2021 → SUP out by 2022; EPR Guidelines July 2022.
xs: The **PWM Amendment Rules 2021** aimed to phase out identified SUP by **2022** — option **(2)** is correct (APPSC-GS 2021).
The ban duly took effect on **1 July 2022**.
xa: The 2021 Rules (**12 Aug 2021**) set carry bags at **75 microns** from 30 Sep 2021 and **120 microns** from 31 Dec 2022.
**EPR Guidelines** effective **July 2022**.

103.s: Which one of the following is NOT included among the identified single-use plastic items listed for prohibition?
o: Plastic sticks used in ear buds
103.x: Plastic ear-bud sticks, plastic flags and thermocol for decoration are included in the listed SUP items. HDPE milk bottles are not included in that list.
103.tq: Find the item outside the specified SUP list rather than choosing a prohibited item.
xs: **HDPE milk bottles** are not in the SUP ban list — option **(3)** is the answer.
Banned items include **ear buds with plastic sticks**, **thermocol for decoration** and **plastic flags**.
xa: Also banned: balloon sticks, candy and ice-cream sticks, plates, cups, cutlery, straws, stirrers, **PVC banners under 100 microns**.
**HDPE** milk/shampoo bottles are **rigid** packaging under **EPR Category I**.
In force from **1 July 2022**.

103.s: Which of the following is NOT among the identified items covered by India's single-use plastic ban?
103.x: Plastic-stemmed earbuds, straws, stirrers and PVC banners below 100 microns are among the identified banned items. Polycarbonate water storage tanks are not listed in this group.
103.tq: Find the item outside the specified banned-item list.
xs: **Polycarbonate water storage tanks** are not among the banned SUP items — option **(3)** is the answer.
Banned: **PVC banners under 100 microns**, **straws and stirrers**, **ear buds with plastic sticks**.
xa: Also banned: wrapping film on sweet boxes and cigarette packets, **thermocol for decoration**.
Polycarbonate releases **BPA** (resin code **7**).
Ban covers only **11%** of total plastic waste.

103.s: Which authorities are primarily responsible for enforcing the identified single-use plastic ban?
o: Only the Ministry of Jal Shakti
SPCBs/PCCs and local bodies, supported by national and state task forces
Only the National Disaster Management Authority
Only municipal corporations in metropolitan cities
103.x: Enforcement involves State Pollution Control Boards or Pollution Control Committees and local bodies, along with a National Level Taskforce and State Special Task Forces.
103.tq: Identify the correct combination of implementing authorities.
xs: Enforcement lies with **SPCBs/PCCs and local bodies**, backed by a **National Level Taskforce** and **State Special Task Forces** — option **(2)** is correct.
No single ministry or only metro corporations enforce it.
xa: AP enforces its SUP and **120-micron** carry-bag ban with **Revenue, Police, PCB**.
AP seizures: **5,505.06 kg** carry bags + **3,571.40 kg** SUP (SES 2025-26).
**Guntur**: complete ban from **15 Aug 2026**; fines up to **₹5,000** via **'Swachh App'**.

103.s: The identified single-use plastic ban covers approximately what proportion of total plastic waste?
103.x: The ban covers only about 11% of total plastic waste.
103.tq: Recall the precise proportion rather than assuming that the ban covers all plastic waste.
xs: The SUP ban covers only **11%** of total plastic waste — option **(2)** is correct (CSE 2023).
**5%**, **25%** and **50%** are not the stated share — the ban's reach is limited.
xa: SUP ban in force **1 July 2022**; **19 items** per most notes.
**70%+** of recycled plastic is handled by informal workers; **NAMASTE** aims to formalise them.
Packaging outside the ban is covered by **EPR Guidelines 2022**.

103.s: Which one of the following correctly describes Extended Producer Responsibility under the plastic-packaging framework?
o: Producers, Importers and Brand Owners handle covered plastic packaging not included in the SUP ban.
It transfers all plastic-waste responsibility to municipal bodies.
It applies only to consumers who purchase plastic goods.
It applies only to manufacturers of rigid plastics.
103.x: EPR applies to Producers, Importers and Brand Owners, or PIBOs, for plastic packaging not covered by the SUP ban.
103.tq: Ask who bears the responsibility and identify the correct institutional actors.
xs: Under EPR, **Producers, Importers and Brand Owners (PIBOs)** handle plastic packaging **not covered by the SUP ban** — option **(1)** is correct.
It does not shift responsibility to municipalities or consumers, and covers rigid, flexible and multi-layered plastics.
xa: Framework: **EPR Guidelines 2022**, effective **July 2022**.
Recyclers generate **EPR certificates** on the **CPCB portal** and sell them to producers.
Fewer than **50%** of producers comply with EPR.

103.s: EPR was first introduced into Indian waste law through the:
103.x: EPR first entered Indian waste law through the E-waste (Management and Handling) Rules, 2011.
103.tq: Use the exact first-introduction instrument rather than a later plastic-specific rule.
xs: EPR first entered Indian law via the **E-waste (Management and Handling) Rules 2011** — option **(1)** is correct.
⚠ Some notes say the **Hazardous Wastes Rules 2016** introduced it first — not correct.
xa: SWM Rules 2016 also put **EPR** on producers/brand owners.
E-waste Rules lineage: **2011 → 2016 → 2022**.
**Battery Waste Management Rules 2022** cover batteries under EPR.

103.s:
Match the plastic category with its recycled-content target progression:
List-I (Category)
 a. Rigid
 b. Flexible, single-layer
 c. Multi-layered
List-II (2025-26 to later)
 i. 5% to 10%
 ii. 10% to 20%
 iii. 30% to 60%
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
103.x: Rigid plastics have a 30% to 60% progression, flexible single-layer plastics 10% to 20%, and multi-layered plastics 5% to 10%.
103.tq: Start with the distinctive rigid-plastic percentage and complete the remaining pairs.
xs: Correct matching is **a–iii, b–ii, c–i** — option **(1)**.
xa: Rigid examples: **PET bottles**, HDPE milk/shampoo bottles; flexible: **carry bags, chips packets**.
Unmet targets can be carried forward up to **3 years** (2026 Amendment).

103.s: Which one of the following statements about the centralised CPCB EPR portal is correct?
o: It is maintained exclusively by the State Pollution Control Boards.
Recyclers generate EPR certificates and sell them to producers.
Only municipal bodies can generate EPR certificates on it.
Producers sell certificates directly to consumers without recycler participation.
103.x: On the centralised CPCB EPR portal, recyclers generate EPR certificates and sell them to producers.
103.tq: Identify the correct role of each participant in the EPR mechanism.
xs: On the centralised **CPCB EPR portal**, **recyclers generate EPR certificates and sell them to producers** — option **(2)** is correct.
It is run by **CPCB**, not SPCBs; municipal bodies and consumers do not trade certificates.
xa: Registered (29 Oct 2025): **69,470 producers**, **4,402 recyclers**.
~**354 LMT** waste recycled across EPR streams.
E-waste EPR: **EPR floor price** protects formal recyclers.

103.s: Nurdles are best described as:
o: Secondary microplastics formed only by tyre wear
Primary microplastic pellets generally measuring 1–5 mm
Biodegradable plastic fibres used in clothing
103.x: Nurdles are primary microplastic pellets, generally 1–5 mm in size.
103.tq: Distinguish a specific microplastic form from its sources and effects.
xs: **Nurdles** are **primary microplastic pellets** of **1-5 mm** — option **(2)** is correct.
**Tyre-wear** microplastics come from **synthetic rubber** — a different source.
xa: India's **first major nurdle landing**: **Kerala**, from the **MSC Elsa 3** shipwreck (LDPE, HDPE).
Microplastics = particles **up to 5 mm** (APPSC-GS 2023).

103.s: India's first major nurdle landing was reported in:
o: Kerala, from the MSC Elsa 3 shipwreck
West Bengal, from a fishing vessel
103.x: The first major nurdle landing in India occurred in Kerala following the MSC Elsa 3 shipwreck. The nurdles included LDPE and HDPE.
103.tq: Combine location, event and source-vessel clues.
xs: India's first major nurdle landing was in **Kerala**, from the **MSC Elsa 3** shipwreck — option **(1)** is correct.
The nurdles were **LDPE and HDPE**.
xa: Nurdles = primary microplastic pellets (**1-5 mm**).
**National Action Plan for Marine Litter** (Dec 2025).

103.s:
Consider the following statements about microplastics:
1. FSSAI detected microplastics in all tested sugar and salt samples.
2. Microbeads in cosmetics are prohibited under the Plastic Waste Management Rules.
3. Microplastics in the Sundarbans can drive plastic-degrading enzymes in microbes carrying antimicrobial-resistance genes.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
103.x: All three statements are correct: an FSSAI study found microplastics in all tested sugar and salt samples; the PWM Rules ban microbeads in cosmetics; and microplastics in the Sundarbans drive plastic-degrading enzymes in microbes carrying AMR genes. Hence '1, 2 and 3'.
103.tq: Test findings, regulatory action and ecological consequence together.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: **FSSAI** found microplastics in **all tested sugar and salt samples** — correct.
Statement 2: PWM Rules ban **microbeads** in cosmetics — correct.
Statement 3: **Sundarbans** microplastics drive plastic-degrading enzymes in microbes carrying **AMR genes** — correct.
xa: Microplastics = particles **up to 5 mm**.
**National Action Plan for Marine Litter** (Dec 2025).

103.s: Microplastics are generally defined as plastic particles of size:
103.x: Microplastics are particles up to 5 mm (APPSC-GS 2023). 'Up to 5 micrometres only' is far too narrow, while 5-50 cm and above 5 mm describe larger debris.
103.tq: Micro = up to 5 mm; nurdles 1-5 mm.
xs: Microplastics are particles **up to 5 mm** — option **(1)** is correct (APPSC-GS 2023).
"**Above 5 mm**" and **5-50 cm** describe larger debris; "5 micrometres only" is far too narrow.
xa: **Nurdles** = primary microplastic pellets, **1-5 mm**.
Hidden sources: **tea bags, chewing gum, wet wipes, glitter, cigarette filters, polyester clothing**.

103.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Bangladesh — first country to ban thin plastic bags in 2002
China — first country to ban thin plastic bags in 2002
New Zealand — first ban on thin plastic bags in 2002
103.x: Bangladesh was the first country to ban thin plastic bags in 2002. China's National Sword Policy began in 2018, while New Zealand's supermarket produce-bag ban was in July 2023.
103.tq: Detect swapped countries and years in closely related international measures.
xs: **Bangladesh** was the **first country** to ban thin plastic bags, in **2002** — option **(2)** is correct.
**National Sword Policy (2018)** is **China's**; **Thailand's** is a **2025** import ban.
**New Zealand** banned thin **produce bags in supermarkets** in **July 2023**, not 2002.
xa: ⚠ Bangladesh = first country (2002, thin bags); New Zealand = first, supermarket produce bags (2023).
India: SUP ban from **1 July 2022**; carry bags **120 microns** from 31 Dec 2022.

103.s: China's National Sword Policy of 2018 and Thailand's 2025 measure primarily restrict:
o: Domestic manufacture of all plastic products
103.x: China's National Sword Policy and Thailand's 2025 measure restrict imports of plastic waste.
103.tq: Identify the regulated activity rather than the broad environmental theme.
xs: China's **National Sword Policy (2018)** and **Thailand's 2025 ban** restrict **plastic waste imports** — option **(1)** is correct.
They do not target hospital use, domestic manufacture or microplastics in food.
xa: **Basel** amendment on **plastic waste** is now operative.
**Global Plastics Treaty** process began at **UNEA-5.2 (Nairobi, March 2022)**.
Transboundary issue = physical transfer of hazardous waste, often to **developing countries**.

103.s: UNEA-5.2, held in Nairobi in March 2022, adopted which resolution that led to the establishment of the Intergovernmental Negotiating Committee (INC)?
103.x: The UNEA-5.2 resolution titled “End Plastic Pollution” established the Intergovernmental Negotiating Committee.
103.tq: Use the exact title of the resolution rather than a broad subject description.
xs: **UNEA-5.2** (Nairobi, March 2022) adopted the resolution "**End Plastic Pollution**" — option **(3)** is correct.
It set up the **Intergovernmental Negotiating Committee (INC)**.
xa: INC venues: **Punta del Este, Paris, Nairobi, Ottawa, Busan (INC-5, 2024), Geneva (INC-5.2, Aug 2025)**.
No agreement — sticking points: **production caps**, chemicals of concern, finance.

103.s: Which one of the following is the correct chronological order of the venues of the Intergovernmental Negotiating Committee on the global plastics treaty, beginning with the earliest?
o: Punta del Este – Paris – Nairobi – Ottawa – Busan – Geneva
Paris – Punta del Este – Nairobi – Busan – Ottawa – Geneva
Nairobi – Punta del Este – Paris – Ottawa – Geneva – Busan
Punta del Este – Nairobi – Paris – Busan – Ottawa – Geneva
103.x: The INC venues were Punta del Este, Paris, Nairobi, Ottawa, Busan and Geneva in that order. Busan hosted INC-5 in 2024 and Geneva hosted INC-5.2 in August 2025.
103.tq: Fix the first and last venues, then arrange the middle venues chronologically.
xs: The INC order is **Punta del Este – Paris – Nairobi – Ottawa – Busan – Geneva** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Busan** hosted **INC-5 (2024)**; **Geneva** hosted **INC-5.2 (Aug 2025)**.
xa: The INC was set up by the **UNEA-5.2** "End Plastic Pollution" resolution (**March 2022**).
Geneva ended with **no agreement**.

103.s:
The INC-5.2 meeting held in Geneva in August 2025 ended with no agreement. Which of the following were identified as major sticking points?
1. Production caps
2. Chemicals of concern
3. Finance
4. Establishment of informal e-waste hubs
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
103.x: Production caps, chemicals of concern and finance were the major sticking points. Informal e-waste hubs were not an issue in the INC negotiations.
103.tq: Eliminate the statement imported from a neighbouring environmental topic.
xs: **Production caps, chemicals of concern and finance** were the sticking points — option **(2) 1, 2 and 3 only**.
Informal e-waste hubs (**Seelampur**, **Moradabad**) are an Indian e-waste issue, not an INC sticking point.
xa: **Busan (INC-5, 2024)** also ended without agreement before Geneva.
Treaty origin: **UNEA-5.2**, Nairobi, March 2022.

103.s: Which country became the first to ban thin plastic produce bags in supermarkets, from July 2023?
103.x: New Zealand banned thin plastic produce bags in supermarkets from July 2023 (APPSC-GS 2022 key). Bangladesh was first to ban thin plastic bags generally (2002), Thailand's 2025 ban concerns plastic-waste imports, and Denmark is linked to a livestock carbon tax.
103.tq: NZ = supermarket produce bags 2023; Bangladesh = thin bags 2002.
xs: **New Zealand** was first to ban thin plastic **produce bags in supermarkets**, from **July 2023** — option **(2)** is correct (APPSC-GS 2022 key).
**Bangladesh** was the first to ban thin plastic bags generally (**2002**); **Thailand's 2025** ban is on plastic waste imports.
xa: ⚠ Do not confuse "first country" (**Bangladesh**) with "first supermarket produce-bag ban" (**New Zealand**).
India's carry-bag minimum is now **120 microns** (31 Dec 2022).

103.s: Which of the following best defines e-waste in the context of the ITU definition?
o: Only hazardous electronic equipment exported across borders
Only discarded computers sent for recycling
All household waste containing any metal component
Discarded electrical and electronic equipment and parts not meant for reuse
103.x: E-waste consists of discarded electrical and electronic equipment and parts that are not intended for reuse.
103.tq: Prefer the definition covering both equipment and parts, and excluding items meant for reuse.
xs: **ITU** defines e-waste as **discarded electrical and electronic equipment and parts not meant for reuse** — option **(4)** is correct.
It is not limited to computers, exports or metal-containing household waste.
xa: **E-waste Rules 2022** cover **106 EEE** items incl. **solar PV** waste.
**Global E-waste Monitor** — **ITU and UNITAR**; **six** categories.
India = **3rd largest** e-waste generator (after China, USA).

103.s: Which one of the following is NOT a hazardous constituent released by old computers?
103.x: Old computers can release beryllium, cadmium, chromium, mercury and lead, besides PCBs and PBBs. Plutonium is not included in this list.
103.tq: Find the outsider among the listed hazardous constituents.
xs: **Plutonium** is not released by old computers — option **(2)** is the answer (UPSC 2013 key).
Old computers release **beryllium, cadmium, chromium, mercury, lead**, plus **PCBs, PBBs**.
⚠ Trap: NOT heptachlor, NOT plutonium.
xa: **Mercury** — brain and kidney damage; **cadmium** — kidney and bone damage.
**RoHS** limits lead, mercury, cadmium in new EEE.

103.s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below.

List-I (Constituent)
a. Lead
b. Mercury
c. Cadmium
d. Brominated flame retardants (PBBs)

List-II (Main harm or characteristic)
i. Kidney and bone damage
ii. Persistent nature and endocrine effects
iii. Nervous-system and kidney effects
iv. Brain and kidney damage; bioaccumulation in fish

Codes:
103.x: Lead affects the nervous system and kidneys; mercury damages the brain and kidneys and bioaccumulates in fish; cadmium damages kidneys and bones; PBBs are persistent and have endocrine effects.
103.tq: Start from the sure pair, especially cadmium with kidney and bone damage.
xs: Correct matching is **a–iii, b–iv, c–i, d–ii** — option **(1)**.
**Lead** — nervous system, kidneys; **mercury** — brain and kidney damage, **bioaccumulates in fish**.
**Cadmium** — kidney and bone damage; **PBBs** — **persistent**, **endocrine effects**.
xa: Old computers also release **beryllium** and **chromium**.
**Fluorescent lamps/CFLs** contain mercury; mercury products phased out under **Minamata**.

103.s: Improper disposal of biomedical waste and e-waste can contribute to biodiversity loss primarily because it:
o: increases the natural regeneration rate of forests
converts all pollutants into harmless nutrients
prevents the release of toxic substances into groundwater
increases soil and water toxicity and damages ecosystems
103.x: Improper disposal releases toxic substances into soil and water, thereby damaging ecosystems and biodiversity.
103.tq: Trace the cause-and-effect chain from waste disposal to ecosystem damage.
xs: Improper disposal **releases toxic substances into soil and water**, damaging **ecosystems and biodiversity** — option **(4)** is correct (APPSC-GS 2025).
It does not neutralise pollutants or help regeneration — options (1)-(3) are wrong.
xa: BMW must be treated to **prevent infection spread** and **protect human health**.
**78%** of e-waste is processed informally, often by **open burning and acid baths**.

103.s: India is presently described as the world’s ______ largest generator of e-waste, after China and the United States.
103.x: India is the third-largest e-waste generator, after China and the United States.
103.tq: Read the ranking together with the named countries to avoid reversing the order.
xs: India is the **third** (3rd) largest e-waste generator, after **China** and **USA** — option **(4)** is correct.
So **second**, **fourth** and **fifth** are wrong.
xa: India's e-waste: **2.2 million tonnes (2025)**.
**First e-waste clinic**: **Bhopal**.
India also ranks third among dry MSW generators for **textile waste**.

103.s: The e-waste generation attributed to India for 2025 was approximately:
103.x: India’s e-waste generation was reported as approximately 2.2 million tonnes in 2025. The 3.54 lakh tonnes figure refers to e-waste collected and processed in FY 2021.
103.tq: Separate generation figures from collection-and-processing figures and compare their units.
xs: India generated about **2.2 million tonnes** of e-waste in **2025** — option **(2)** is correct.
**1.75 MT** is an earlier figure (Oct 2025); **1.6 MT** is recycler capacity; **3.54** lakh tonnes was processed in FY 2021.
xa: **468 authorised recyclers**, **1.6 MT** capacity (CPCB 2024).
**78%** processed informally; only **10-20%** of materials recovered.

103.s: Which organisations jointly publish the Global E-waste Monitor?
103.x: The Global E-waste Monitor is published by the International Telecommunication Union and the United Nations Institute for Training and Research.
103.tq: Identify the correct institutional pair instead of substituting neighbouring UN bodies.
xs: The **Global E-waste Monitor** is published by **ITU and UNITAR** — option **(2)** is correct.
UNFCCC, IUCN, UNEP and WHO are not its publishers.
xa: It uses **six categories**: cooling equipment, screens, lamps, large equipment, small equipment, IT.
The e-waste definition used is also the **ITU** one.
India: **2.2 million tonnes** (2025).

103.s: The Global E-waste Monitor groups e-waste into how many categories?
103.x: The Global E-waste Monitor uses six categories, including cooling equipment, screens, lamps, large equipment, small equipment and IT equipment.
103.tq: Count the classification categories rather than the examples within them.
xs: The Global E-waste Monitor uses **six** (6) categories — option **(3)** is correct.
They are **cooling equipment, screens, lamps, large equipment, small equipment, IT**.
xa: Published by **ITU and UNITAR**.
E-waste Rules 2022 cover **106 EEE** items.

103.s: According to MeitY, approximately how much e-waste was collected and processed in India in FY 2021?
103.x: MeitY put e-waste collected and processed in FY 2021 at about 3.54 lakh tonnes (APPSC-GS 2021 key). 2.2 MT (2025) and 1.75 MT are generation figures, and 35.4 lakh tonnes is ten times the stated value.
103.tq: Processed FY21 = 3.54 lakh t; generated 2025 = 2.2 MT.
xs: **MeitY**: about **3.54 lakh tonnes** of e-waste collected and processed in **FY 2021** — option **(1)** is correct (APPSC-GS 2021 key).
**2.2 MT** (2025) and **1.75 MT** are **generation** figures; **35.4 lakh tonnes** is ten times the stated value.
xa: Only **10-20%** of materials are recovered in informal processing.
**468 authorised recyclers** (CPCB 2024).

103.s:
Consider the following statements about the E-waste (Management) Rules, 2022:
1. They were notified in November 2022 and came into force on 1 April 2023.
2. They replaced the 2016 E-waste Rules, which had in turn replaced the 2011 Rules.
3. They cover 106 EEE items but exclude solar PV modules, panels and cells.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
103.x: Statement 1 is correct: notified Nov 2022, in force 1 April 2023. Statement 2 is correct: they replaced the 2016 Rules, which replaced the 2011 M&H Rules. Statement 3 is wrong: the 106 EEE items include solar PV waste (modules/panels/cells). So '1 only' is incomplete and the options containing 3 are wrong.
103.tq: Remember 2011 -> 2016 -> 2022 lineage; 106 items INCLUDING solar PV.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: notified **November 2022**, in force **1 April 2023** — correct.
Statement 2: replaced the **2016** Rules, which replaced the **2011** M&H Rules — correct.
Statement 3: wrong — the **106 EEE** items **include solar PV** modules/panels/cells.
xa: Only **registered** producers, manufacturers, refurbishers, recyclers may deal in e-waste.
E-waste must **not be mixed** with other waste; enforcement by environmental compensation and audits.

103.s: Which of the following persons or entities may legally deal in e-waste under the E-waste (Management) Rules, 2022?
o: Only registered producers, manufacturers, refurbishers and recyclers
103.x: The Rules permit only registered producers, manufacturers, refurbishers and recyclers to deal in e-waste.
103.tq: Apply the registration requirement to a practical e-waste transaction.
xs: Only **registered producers, manufacturers, refurbishers and recyclers** may deal in e-waste — option **(4)** is correct.
**Unregistered scrap dealers** and informal dismantlers are excluded.
xa: E-waste must **not be mixed** with other waste.
Producers register on the **CPCB portal** and buy **digital EPR certificates**.
Rules in force **1 April 2023**.

103.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Extended Producer Responsibility under the E-waste Rules, 2022:
1. Producers receive annual recycling targets based on earlier sales.
2. Producers register on the CPCB portal.
3. Producers may buy digital EPR certificates from registered recyclers.
4. An EPR floor price is intended to protect formal recyclers.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
103.x: All four statements correctly describe the EPR framework under the 2022 E-waste Rules.
103.tq: Test the complete regulatory chain from target-setting to certificate trading and price protection.
xs: All four statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.
Statement 1: annual **EPR recycling targets** based on earlier sales — correct.
Statements 2-3: register on the **CPCB portal**; buy **digital EPR certificates** from registered recyclers — correct.
Statement 4: **EPR floor price** protects formal recyclers — correct.
xa: The EPR system is built around the **circular economy**.
EPR first entered Indian law via the **E-waste (M&H) Rules 2011**.

103.s: Which one of the following substances is NOT among the hazardous substances for which the E-waste Rules prescribe RoHS limits in new electrical and electronic equipment?
103.x: The Rules prescribe RoHS limits for lead, mercury and cadmium. Nitrogen is not listed among these substances in the stated provision.
103.tq: Identify the non-member of the specific restricted-substance group.
xs: **Nitrogen** is not an RoHS-limited substance — option **(4)** is the answer.
**RoHS** limits **lead, mercury, cadmium** in new EEE.
xa: Old computers release **beryllium, cadmium, chromium, mercury, lead**.
**Lead** harms the nervous system and kidneys; **cadmium** kidneys and bones.

103.s: Which of the following is correctly matched with the Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022?
o: They replaced the 2001 rules and cover EV, portable, automotive and industrial batteries.
They replaced the 2016 E-waste Rules and cover only mobile-phone batteries.
They apply only to lead-acid batteries used in automobiles.
They exclude batteries from the EPR framework.
103.x: The Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022 replaced the 2001 rules and cover electric-vehicle, portable, automotive and industrial batteries under EPR.
103.tq: Distinguish battery rules from e-waste rules using scope and replacement year.
xs: The **Battery Waste Management Rules 2022** replaced the **2001** rules and cover **EV, portable, automotive and industrial** batteries — option **(1)** is correct.
They bring batteries **under EPR**, so option (4) is wrong; they are not limited to lead-acid or mobile batteries.
xa: **E-waste Rules 2022** replaced the **2016** Rules (which replaced 2011).
**Household examples** of hazardous waste include **batteries**; under SWM 2026 they go to the **special care** bin.

103.s: Which pair of places is correctly associated with informal e-waste recycling hubs?
103.x: Seelampur in Delhi and Moradabad are identified as informal e-waste recycling hubs.
103.tq: Match the locations with the distinctive informal e-waste activity.
xs: **Seelampur** (Delhi) and **Moradabad** (UP) are informal e-waste hubs — option **(1)** is correct.
**Indore**, **Tirupati** and **Visakhapatnam** feature in cleanliness rankings, not as e-waste hubs.
xa: **78%** of e-waste is processed informally (Jun 2026).
Informal workers use **open burning and acid baths**.

103.s:
Which practices are commonly associated with informal e-waste dismantling?
1. Open burning
2. Acid baths
3. Processing only through certified facilities
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
103.x: Informal workers often dismantle e-waste through open burning and acid baths. Processing only through certified facilities is a formal, not informal, practice.
103.tq: Identify the two hazardous informal practices and reject the formal-system statement.
xs: Informal dismantling commonly uses **open burning** and **acid baths** — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
Processing only through **certified facilities** is a formal-sector practice — statement 3 is wrong.
xa: **78%** of e-waste processed informally; only **10-20%** of materials recovered.
**R2 (Responsible Recycling)** — global certification for e-waste recyclers (UPSC 2021).

103.s: Which of the following is correctly arranged as the authorised e-waste recycling chain?
o: Producer → consumer → landfill → dismantler → recovered materials
Consumer → collection centre or producer take-back → authorised dismantler → authorised recycler → recovered materials
Consumer → informal hub → landfill → authorised recycler → producer take-back
Consumer → authorised recycler → collection centre → informal hub → recovered materials
103.x: The authorised chain begins with the consumer and collection or producer take-back, followed by dismantling, recycling and recovery of materials.
103.tq: Follow the material flow from generation to recovery and reject informal or disposal stages.
xs: The formal chain is **consumer → collection centre / producer take-back → authorised dismantler → authorised recycler → recovered materials** — option **(2)** is correct.
Chains via **landfill** or **informal hubs** are not the authorised route.
xa: **468 authorised recyclers**, **1.6 MT** capacity (CPCB 2024).
**Urban mining** recovers iron, steel, copper, aluminium, plastics from e-waste.
AP: **Re Sustainability** MoU for e-waste collection in all **123 ULBs**.

103.s: Which one of the following is the most appropriate action for a citizen disposing of an old electronic device?
o: Burn it to recover copper and aluminium
Mix it with municipal solid waste after removing the battery
Sell or deposit it with an authorised recycler or collection centre after wiping data
Hand it over to any informal dismantler without data removal
103.x: Citizens should use authorised recyclers or collection centres and wipe personal data before handing over old electronics.
103.tq: Apply the recommended citizen action while avoiding unsafe informal handling.
xs: Citizens should **sell or deposit old electronics with authorised recyclers or collection centres** after **wiping data** — option **(3)** is correct (APPSC-GS 2025).
**Burning** and **informal** dismantling are harmful; e-waste must **not be mixed** with MSW.
xa: "Invisible e-waste": **vapes, USB cables, LED accessories** thrown in regular trash (Jun 2026).
AP collected **60,392 kg** of e-waste (SES 2025-26).

103.s:
Consider the following statements about India’s e-waste recycling system:
1. E-waste should not be mixed with other waste.
2. Seelampur and Moradabad are identified as informal e-waste hubs.
3. India has 468 authorised recyclers with a combined capacity of 1.6 million tonnes.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
103.x: All three statements are correct. Separate handling is required; Seelampur and Moradabad are informal hubs; and CPCB data mention 468 authorised recyclers with 1.6 million tonnes of capacity.
103.tq: Check the operational rule, locations and capacity figure independently.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: e-waste must **not be mixed** with other waste — correct.
Statement 2: **Seelampur** and **Moradabad** are informal hubs — correct.
Statement 3: **468 authorised recyclers**, **1.6 MT** capacity (CPCB 2024) — correct.
xa: India imports **90%** of its lithium and cobalt — making **urban mining** valuable.
**First e-waste clinic**: **Bhopal**.

103.s: What does the R2 Code of Practices primarily promote?
o: Environmentally responsible practices in electronics recycling
103.x: R2, or Responsible Recycling, is a code of practices promoting environmentally responsible electronics recycling.
103.tq: Expand the abbreviation and link it to its specific sector.
xs: The **R2 Code of Practices** promotes **environmentally responsible practices in electronics recycling** — option **(1)** is correct (UPSC 2021).
**R2 = Responsible Recycling**, a global certification for **e-waste recyclers**.
xa: Formal chain: consumer → collection centre / producer take-back → **authorised dismantler** → **authorised recycler** → recovered materials.
**78%** of e-waste is processed informally, by **open burning and acid baths**.
**468 authorised recyclers**, **1.6 MT** capacity (CPCB 2024).

103.s: India’s first e-waste clinic was established at:
103.x: Bhopal was the location of India’s first e-waste clinic.
103.tq: Use the specific institutional-location association rather than an informal hub location.
xs: India's **first e-waste clinic** was set up at **Bhopal** — option **(4)** is correct.
**Delhi** (Seelampur) and **Moradabad** are **informal e-waste hubs**, not clinic sites.
xa: Delhi's **Burari** = first **C&D recycling plant**.
India = **3rd largest** e-waste generator (after China, USA).
**Bhopal** is also the site of the **1984** gas tragedy (methyl isocyanate).

103.s: The Biomedical Waste Management Rules, 2016 replaced which earlier rules?
o: Municipal Solid Waste (Management and Handling) Rules, 2000
103.x: The Biomedical Waste Management Rules, 2016 replaced the Biomedical Waste (Management and Handling) Rules, 1998, which had ten categories.
103.tq: Use the predecessor-successor relationship to distinguish rules with similar environmental subject matter.
xs: The **BMW Management Rules 2016** replaced the **BMW (M&H) Rules 1998** — option **(3)** is correct.
The 1998 Rules had **10 categories**; the 2016 Rules use **4 colour categories**.
xa: Amended in **2018** and **2019**.
Cover **100%** of healthcare facilities; **barcoding and GPS tracking**.
⚠ "**10** colour-coded categories" mixes up the 1998 Rules.

103.s: Which of the following correctly describes the scope and compliance features of the Biomedical Waste Management Rules, 2016?
o: They cover all healthcare facilities, use four colour categories and require bar coding.
They cover only laboratories and require no tracking mechanism.
They cover municipal waste generators and require three waste streams.
They cover only government hospitals and require ten colour categories.
103.x: The BMW Management Rules, 2016 cover 100% of healthcare facilities, use four colour categories and provide for barcoding and GPS tracking. Ten categories belonged to the 1998 Rules, and the Rules are not limited to laboratories or government hospitals.
103.tq: Reject the options that import the ten-category system of the earlier rules or the municipal three-stream system.
xs: The **BMW Rules 2016** cover **100% of healthcare facilities**, use **4 colour categories** and require **barcoding** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Ten categories** belonged to the **1998** Rules; the Rules are not limited to labs or government hospitals.
**Three streams** belong to the **SWM Rules 2016**, not the BMW Rules.
xa: Tracking: **barcoding and GPS tracking**.
Scale (2024): **1.89 lakh** health-care facilities generate **800+ tonnes/day**.

103.s: The Biomedical Waste Management Rules, 2016 were amended in which of the following years?
103.x: The Biomedical Waste Management Rules, 2016 were amended in 2018 and 2019.
103.tq: Test the paired years directly; both years must match the amendment history.
xs: The **BMW Rules 2016** were amended in **2018 and 2019** — option **(2)** is correct.
**2020** is when CPCB issued **COVID-19 waste guidelines** — not an amendment year.
xa: The 2016 Rules replaced the **1998** Rules (10 categories).
**COVID19BWM** tracking app was issued by **CPCB**.
**HOWM Rules 2016** were amended in **2019, 2020** — ⚠ do not confuse.

103.s: Which of the following is the correct colour-treatment combination for anatomical waste, soiled waste, expired medicines and chemical waste under biomedical waste rules?
o: Yellow — incineration, plasma pyrolysis or deep burial
103.x: Yellow-category waste includes anatomical, soiled, expired medicine and chemical waste and is treated through incineration, plasma pyrolysis or deep burial.
103.tq: Start from the distinctive waste category and match it with its prescribed treatment.
xs: **Yellow** = anatomical, soiled, expired medicines, chemical waste → **incineration / plasma pyrolysis / deep burial** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Red** = contaminated recyclable plastics; **White** = sharps; **Blue** = glassware, metallic implants.
xa: **Red** → autoclave/microwave + shredding, then recycling.
**White (translucent)** → autoclave/dry heat, shredding, encapsulation.
**Blue** → disinfection, then recycling.

103.s:
Match List-I (Biomedical waste) with List-II (Colour category) under the Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, 2016:
List-I
a. Sharps such as needles and blades
b. Glassware and metallic implants
c. Contaminated recyclable plastics such as IV sets and catheters
d. Anatomical waste and expired medicines
List-II
i. Yellow
ii. Red
iii. White (translucent)
iv. Blue
Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
103.x: Sharps go to White (translucent), glassware and metallic implants to Blue, contaminated recyclable plastics to Red, and anatomical waste/expired medicines to Yellow, so a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i. Option 2 swaps sharps and glass; option 3 swaps plastics and anatomical waste; option 4 swaps sharps and plastics.
103.tq: Yellow = burn (anatomical), Red = recyclable plastics, White = sharps, Blue = glass/metal.
xs: Correct matching is **a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i** — option **(1)**.
**Sharps** → **White (translucent)**; **glassware, metallic implants** → **Blue**.
**Recyclable plastics** (IV sets, catheters) → **Red**; **anatomical waste, expired medicines** → **Yellow**.
xa: ⚠ **White** = sharps; **Red** = recyclable plastics; **Blue** = glass; **Yellow** = anatomical.
BMW Rules 2016 use **4 colour categories**.
AP sends BMW to **CBMWTFs** for incineration.

103.s:
Biomedical waste may arise from the diagnosis, treatment or immunisation of humans or animals. Which of the following is included in this waste stream?
1. Blood
2. Sharps
3. Cultures
4. Discarded or expired medicines
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
103.x: Blood, sharps, cultures and discarded or expired medicines are all examples of biomedical waste; anatomical and chemical waste are also included.
103.tq: Check each listed source against the broad definition of waste from healthcare activity.
xs: **Blood, sharps, cultures and discarded/expired medicines** are all biomedical waste — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.
BMW = waste from **diagnosis, treatment or immunisation** of humans/animals; also **anatomical** and **chemical** waste.
xa: About **85%** of healthcare waste is general non-hazardous; **~15%** hazardous (WHO).
Biomedical category examples: **syringes, gloves**.

103.s: According to the stated healthcare-waste composition, approximately what proportion of healthcare waste is general non-hazardous waste?
103.x: Approximately 85% of healthcare waste is general non-hazardous waste, while about 15% is hazardous, including infectious, chemical and radioactive waste.
103.tq: Use the complementary proportions to distinguish the large general fraction from the smaller hazardous fraction.
xs: About **85%** of healthcare waste is **general non-hazardous** — option **(4)** is correct (WHO).
The remaining **~15%** is **hazardous** (infectious, chemical, radioactive) — option (1) is that share.
xa: India (2024): **1.89 lakh** facilities generate **800+ tonnes/day**.
BMW treatment aims to **prevent infection spread** and **protect human health**.

103.s: Which of the following was issued by the CPCB in response to biomedical waste generated during the COVID-19 period?
o: Global E-waste Monitor and Basel Protocol
R2 electronics recycling code and plastic treaty guidelines
COVID19BWM tracking app and COVID-19 waste guidelines
103.x: The CPCB issued COVID-19 biomedical-waste guidelines in 2020 and introduced the COVID19BWM tracking app.
103.tq: Match the emergency, authority and digital tracking instrument.
xs: **CPCB** issued **COVID-19 waste guidelines** in **2020** and the **COVID19BWM** tracking app — option **(3)** is correct.
**Global E-waste Monitor** is by ITU/UNITAR; **R2** is an e-waste certification; **Swachh App** is Guntur's plastic-fine tool.
xa: BMW Rules 2016 use **barcoding and GPS tracking**.

103.s: The main purpose of treating biomedical waste before disposal is to:
o: Increase the calorific value of hospital waste
Prevent the spread of infection and protect human health
Convert all biomedical waste into compost
Allow syringes to be reused safely
103.x: BMW is treated before disposal mainly to prevent infection spread and protect human health (APPSC-GS 2025) - killing pathogens, stopping syringe reuse and cutting volume and toxicity. Raising calorific value is not the aim, composting is not the route, and treatment is meant to stop syringe reuse, not enable it.
103.tq: BMW treatment → kill pathogens, stop reuse, protect health.
xs: BMW is treated before disposal to **prevent infection spread and protect human health** — option **(2)** is correct (APPSC-GS 2025).
Treatment **kills pathogens**, **stops syringe reuse**, and cuts volume and toxicity — it is not for calorific value or compost.
xa: **White** bin: **sharps** — autoclave/dry heat, shredding, encapsulation.
Improper BMW/e-waste disposal releases **toxic substances into soil and water**.
BMW goes to **CBMWTFs** for incineration in AP.

103.s: Which of the following is NOT one of the four classic characteristics used to identify hazardous waste?
103.x: The four classic characteristics are ignitability, corrosivity, reactivity and toxicity. Biodegradability is not one of these four classic criteria.
103.tq: Reject a familiar environmental term that does not belong to the defined list.
xs: **Biodegradability** is not a hazardous-waste criterion — option **(3)** is the answer.
The four classic criteria are **ignitability, corrosivity, reactivity, toxicity**.
xa: Some notes add **explosive, infectious, radioactive**.
Examples: **lead, mercury, cadmium, chromium**, solvents, dyes, pesticides.
Forms: **solids, liquids, sludges, gases**.

103.s:
Hazardous waste may occur in which of the following forms?
1. Solids
2. Liquids
3. Sludges
4. Gases
103.x: Hazardous waste can occur as solids, liquids, sludges and gases. Hence, all four forms are included.
103.tq: Use the all-inclusive option after verifying every item in the classification.
xs: Hazardous waste occurs as **solids, liquids, sludges and gases** — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.
All four forms are listed, so options leaving any out are incomplete.
xa: Criteria: **ignitability, corrosivity, reactivity, toxicity**.
Household examples: **paints, batteries, fluorescent lamps**, aerosol cans, tyres.
AP: **2 CHWTSDFs** (**Anakapalli**, **SPSR Nellore**) for secure landfilling.

103.s: Which of the following is correctly matched as a household hazardous waste?
103.x: Paints and batteries are household examples of hazardous waste. The other options generally represent biodegradable or non-hazardous household wastes.
103.tq: Match a household item with its correct waste category.
xs: **Paints and batteries** are household hazardous waste — option **(1)** is correct.
**Peels**, **paper**, **cotton**, **garden leaves** are biodegradable, non-hazardous wastes.
xa: Other household hazardous items: **fluorescent lamps**, aerosol cans, tyres, fertilisers, pesticides.
Under **SWM Rules 2026**, these go to the **special care** bin (batteries, chemicals, paint cans, bulbs).
**HOWM Rules 2024**: household **Deposition Centres**.

103.s: Which one of the following best describes PFAS, often referred to as “forever chemicals”?
o: They are biodegradable chemicals used exclusively in cement production
They persist in the environment, occur in products such as food packaging, and may accumulate in animal bodies
They rapidly decompose in soil and water and do not accumulate in organisms
They are radioactive substances used mainly in fluorescent lamps
103.x: PFAS are persistent chemicals found in drinking water, food and food packaging. They do not break down easily and can accumulate in animal bodies.
103.tq: Use the option that combines the defining properties and common exposure pathways.
xs: **PFAS** persist, occur in **drinking water, food and food packaging**, and **accumulate in animal bodies** — option **(2)** is correct (UPSC 2024).
They **do not break down easily** — option (3) is wrong; they are not radioactive or biodegradable.
xa: PFAS are now listed under the **Stockholm** Convention.
Stockholm now covers **34 chemicals**, incl. **chlorpyrifos** and PFAS.

103.s: Fluorescent lamps and compact fluorescent lamps are treated as household hazardous waste primarily because they contain:
103.x: Fluorescent lamps and CFLs contain mercury. When broken, they can release mercury vapour into the surroundings.
103.tq: Identify the hazardous constituent associated with the specific consumer product.
xs: **Fluorescent lamps/CFLs** contain **mercury** — option **(2)** is correct.
Broken lamps release **mercury vapour**.
xa: Mercury-added products are being phased out under **Minamata**.
**Mercury** causes brain and kidney damage and **bioaccumulates in fish**.
Fluorescent lamps are listed among household hazardous waste.

103.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the legal control associated with mercury-added products?
o: They are exempt from international environmental agreements
They are being phased out under the Minamata Convention
They are being promoted under the Stockholm Convention
They are regulated exclusively under the Basel Convention
103.x: Mercury-added products are being phased out under the Minamata Convention, which addresses mercury pollution and its risks.
103.tq: Discriminate between international conventions by matching the pollutant with the correct treaty.
xs: Mercury-added products are being **phased out under the Minamata Convention** — option **(2)** is correct.
**Stockholm** = POPs; **Basel** = hazardous waste movement — options (3) and (4) are wrong.
xa: **Minamata (2013)**: dental amalgam phase-out by **2034**.
**Coal power plants** are a big mercury source.
**Fluorescent lamps/CFLs** contain mercury.

103.s:
With reference to the Hazardous and Other Wastes Rules, 2016, consider the following statements:
1. Imports and exports of hazardous waste follow the Basel Convention.
2. Import of hazardous waste for disposal is prohibited.
3. Co-processing is placed above prevention in the waste-management hierarchy.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
103.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because prevention is at the top of the hierarchy and co-processing occurs later, before safe disposal.
103.tq: Find the reversed hierarchy statement; the position of co-processing is the trap.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: imports/exports follow the **Basel** Convention — correct.
Statement 2: **import for disposal** is prohibited — correct.
Statement 3: wrong — **prevention** is at the top; **co-processing** comes just before **safe disposal**.
xa: Hierarchy: **prevention > minimisation > reuse > recycling > recovery > co-processing > safe disposal**.
**PIC** for import/export; **2024**: household **Deposition Centres**, simpler manifests.

103.s: The Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules, 2016 replaced which earlier rules?
o: The Hazardous Wastes (Management, Handling and Transboundary Movement) Rules, 2008
103.x: The 2016 Hazardous and Other Wastes Rules replaced the 2008 Rules.
103.tq: Separate closely related rule years by identifying the earlier framework that was replaced.
xs: The **HOWM Rules 2016** replaced the **2008 Rules** — option **(1)** is correct.
**BMW 1998** and **MSW 2000** were replaced by other 2016 rules.
xa: HOWM Rules amended **2019, 2020**.
**MSIHC Rules 1989** cover manufacture, storage, import of hazardous chemicals.
**Nodal body:** **HSMD**, MoEFCC.

103.s: In the context of transboundary movement of hazardous waste, PIC refers to:
103.x: PIC means Prior Informed Consent, a control associated with the import and export of hazardous waste.
103.tq: Break the abbreviation into its regulatory meaning before evaluating the options.
xs: **PIC** = **Prior Informed Consent** — option **(4)** is correct.
Under **HOWM Rules 2016**, imports/exports follow **Basel** with PIC.
xa: **Rotterdam** (in force **2004**) is the PIC convention for hazardous chemicals and pesticides; India acceded **2005**.
**Basel** in force **5 May 1992**; India ratified **June 1992**.

103.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: MSIHC Rules, 1989 — manufacture, storage and import of hazardous chemicals
CAEPPR Rules, 1996 — insurance compensation without fault
Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991 — constitution of crisis groups
Contaminated Sites Rules, 2025 — regulation of fluorescent lamp manufacture
103.x: The MSIHC Rules, 1989 address the manufacture, storage and import of hazardous chemicals. CAEPPR concerns crisis groups, while the Public Liability Insurance Act provides no-fault relief.
103.tq: Start with the sure pair and reject options that swap the functions of neighbouring legal instruments.
xs: **MSIHC Rules 1989** — **manufacture, storage, import of hazardous chemicals** — option **(1)** is correct.
The **Public Liability Insurance Act 1991** gives **no-fault insurance** — option (3) misassigns it.
**Contaminated Sites Rules 2025** deal with suspected contaminated sites, not lamp manufacture.
xa: **Contaminated Sites Rules 2025**: district half-yearly reports; **189** hazardous chemicals.
**EPA 1986** was enacted after **Bhopal**.

103.s: The principal purpose of the Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991 is to provide:
o: Compensation only after criminal conviction of the polluter
No-fault insurance cover and immediate relief to victims of hazardous-substance accidents
Insurance exclusively for transport of municipal waste
Long-term subsidies to industries using fly ash
103.x: The Act provides no-fault insurance cover intended to give immediate relief to victims of accidents involving hazardous substances.
103.tq: Identify the legal purpose by focusing on the beneficiary, liability basis and timing of relief.
xs: The **Public Liability Insurance Act 1991** gives **no-fault insurance** → **immediate relief** to victims of hazardous-substance accidents — option **(2)** is correct.
It does not wait for criminal conviction and is not about municipal transport or fly ash.
xa: **EPA 1986** — enacted after **Bhopal**.
**MSIHC Rules 1989** — hazardous chemicals.
**Bhopal (2-3 Dec 1984)**: **methyl isocyanate**, **5,400+** lives.

103.s: Under the Contaminated Sites Rules, 2025, which sequence correctly represents the time limits for assessment by the State Pollution Control Board?
o: Preliminary assessment in 30 days followed by a detailed survey in 60 days
Preliminary assessment in 90 days followed by a detailed survey in the next 90 days
Preliminary assessment in 180 days followed by a detailed survey in 30 days
Both preliminary assessment and detailed survey within 15 days
103.x: The SPCB is required to undertake a preliminary assessment within 90 days and a detailed survey in the subsequent 90 days.
103.tq: Track the sequential time periods and distinguish the first assessment from the follow-up survey.
xs: The SPCB does a **preliminary assessment in 90 days**, then a **detailed survey in the next 90 days** — option **(2)** is correct.
The 30, 60, 180 and 15-day limits in the other options are not in the Rules.
xa: **Contaminated Sites Rules 2025** are under **EPA 1986**.
District **half-yearly reports** on suspected sites; **189** hazardous chemicals listed.
EPA 1986 is the umbrella for **EIA, Hazardous Waste, CRZ and Contaminated Sites Rules**.

103.s: Which of the following correctly represents the complete hazardous-waste hierarchy given in the specified order?
o: Reuse, prevention, recovery, minimisation, recycling, disposal, co-processing
Minimisation, prevention, recycling, reuse, co-processing, recovery, disposal
Prevention, minimisation, reuse, recycling, recovery, co-processing, safe disposal
Prevention, recycling, minimisation, reuse, safe disposal, recovery, co-processing
103.x: The stated hierarchy is prevention, minimisation, reuse, recycling, recovery, co-processing and safe disposal.
103.tq: Recall the exact sequence in a graded management hierarchy.
xs: The hierarchy is **prevention, minimisation, reuse, recycling, recovery, co-processing, safe disposal** — option **(3)** is correct.
**Prevention** comes first and **safe disposal** last — the other options break this order.
xa: This hierarchy is in the **HOWM Rules 2016**.
AP: landfill = **last resort**; APPCB prefers **co-processing** in cement plants + **waste exchange**.

103.s: The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 was enacted in the aftermath of which event?
103.x: The EPA 1986 was enacted after the Bhopal gas tragedy (1984). The Stockholm Conference and Chernobyl are not the stated trigger, and Minamata gave its name to the 2013 mercury convention.
103.tq: Bhopal 1984 → EPA 1986 → PLI Act 1991.
xs: **EPA 1986** was enacted after the **Bhopal gas tragedy** — option **(1)** is correct.
Bhopal: **2-3 Dec 1984**, Union Carbide India Ltd, **methyl isocyanate**.
xa: SWM Rules 2026 and Contaminated Sites Rules 2025 are notified under **EPA 1986**.
**Public Liability Insurance Act 1991** — no-fault relief to accident victims.
Bhopal waste (early 2025): **337 t** incinerated → ~**900 t** toxic ash.

103.s: Which principle best describes the preferred approach to hazardous-waste disposal?
o: Landfilling is the first and preferred option for all hazardous waste
Hazardous waste should always be burned in open areas
Landfill is the last resort, while co-processing in cement plants and waste exchange are preferred where suitable
All hazardous waste must be discharged into surface water after dilution
103.x: Landfill is considered the last resort. APPCB prefers suitable co-processing as fuel in cement plants and exchange of waste between industries.
103.tq: Apply the waste hierarchy and reject options based on absolute or environmentally unsafe practices.
xs: **Landfill is the last resort**; **co-processing** in cement plants and **waste exchange** are preferred — option **(3)** is correct.
Open burning and discharge into water are not acceptable options.
xa: AP: **2 CHWTSDFs** (**Anakapalli**, **SPSR Nellore**) for secure landfilling; **6 pre-processing** facilities.
**APPCB** permitted **12 cement industries** to co-process waste.
**APEMC** tracks hazardous waste with **GPS**.

103.s: The two Common Hazardous Waste Treatment, Storage and Disposal Facilities (CHWTSDFs) in Andhra Pradesh are located at:
103.x: The two CHWTSDFs identified for Andhra Pradesh are located in Anakapalli and SPSR Nellore.
103.tq: Use location-based recall and distinguish the named facility sites from other Andhra Pradesh cities.
xs: AP's two **CHWTSDFs** are at **Anakapalli** and **SPSR Nellore** — option **(2)** is correct.
They are used for **secure landfilling** (2024-25).
xa: **6 pre-processing** facilities and **APEMC GPS tracking**.
AP **Circular Economy and Waste Recycling Policy 2025-30** targets industrial hazardous waste.
AP has **4,000+ industries** producing hazardous and non-hazardous waste (APPCB, 6 Feb 2026).

103.s: Which system is used by APEMC for tracking hazardous-waste movement in Andhra Pradesh?
o: Biometric tracking of every waste container
103.x: APEMC uses GPS tracking for monitoring hazardous-waste movement and management.
103.tq: Match the institution with the specific monitoring technology stated for it.
xs: **APEMC** uses **GPS tracking** of hazardous waste via GPS-fitted vehicles — option **(4)** is correct.
The **APEMC portal** tracks the movement in real time.
xa: **APCMMS** portal — real-time monitoring.
AP CHWTSDFs: **Anakapalli**, **SPSR Nellore**.
BMW Rules 2016 also use **GPS tracking** with **barcoding**.

103.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
103.x: The Bhopal disaster in December 1984 involved methyl isocyanate. The LG Polymers incident at Visakhapatnam in May 2020 involved styrene vapour.
103.tq: Use the location–date–chemical triplet to detect swapped disaster details.
xs: **Bhopal, 1984 — methyl isocyanate** is correctly matched — option **(2)**.
The Bhopal tragedy (**2-3 Dec 1984**) at **Union Carbide India Ltd** involved **methyl isocyanate**, not styrene.
xa: **5,400+** lives lost (TH).
**EPA 1986** was enacted after Bhopal.
SC asked victims' NGO to go to the **MP High Court** (Mar 2026).

103.s: The gas responsible for the Bhopal disaster of 2–3 December 1984 was:
103.x: The Bhopal disaster involving Union Carbide India Ltd was caused by methyl isocyanate. More than 5,400 lives were reported lost.
103.tq: Distinguish the Bhopal chemical from the Visakhapatnam chemical.
xs: The Bhopal gas was **methyl isocyanate** — option **(2)** is correct.
It leaked from **Union Carbide India Ltd** on **2-3 Dec 1984**; **5,400+** lives were lost.
xa: Bhopal waste (early 2025): **337 t** incinerated → ~**900 t** toxic residual ash.
**Public Liability Insurance Act 1991** gives no-fault relief for such accidents.
**MSIHC Rules 1989** regulate hazardous chemicals.

103.s:
With reference to the Bhopal waste cleanup reported in early 2025, consider the following statements:
1. About 337 tonnes of waste were incinerated.
2. Approximately 900 tonnes of toxic residual ash resulted.
3. The Supreme Court asked the victims’ NGO to approach the Madhya Pradesh High Court.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
103.x: All three statements are correct: 337 tonnes were incinerated, about 900 tonnes of toxic residual ash remained, and the Supreme Court directed the victims’ NGO to approach the Madhya Pradesh High Court.
103.tq: Check the quantities, procedural direction and court involved as separate facts.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: **337 t** incinerated — correct.
Statement 2: ~**900 t** toxic residual ash — correct.
Statement 3: SC asked the victims' NGO to approach the **MP High Court** (Mar 2026) — correct.
xa: Bhopal: **methyl isocyanate**, **2-3 Dec 1984**, **5,400+** lives.
**EPA 1986** enacted after Bhopal.

103.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Stockholm Convention currently includes 34 chemicals, including chlorpyrifos and PFAS.
2. The Minamata Convention concerns mercury.
3. Dental amalgam phase-out under the Minamata framework is associated with the year 2034.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
103.x: The current figure given for Stockholm is 34 chemicals, including chlorpyrifos and PFAS. Minamata concerns mercury, and dental amalgam phase-out is targeted by 2034.
103.tq: Test the treaty’s subject together with its current chemical count and target year.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: **Stockholm** now covers **34 chemicals** incl. **chlorpyrifos** and **PFAS** — correct (IYB still says 23).
Statement 2: **Minamata (2013)** concerns **mercury** — correct.
Statement 3: **dental amalgam** phase-out by **2034** — correct.
xa: ⚠ **Basel** = hazardous waste; **Rotterdam** = PIC; **Stockholm** = POPs; **Minamata** = mercury.
**Coal power plants** are a big mercury source.

103.s: The global issue involved in the transboundary movement of hazardous waste refers to:
o: exchange of agricultural seeds under biodiversity agreements
movement of only biodegradable waste between rural districts
transport of clean energy equipment to developed countries
physical transfer of hazardous waste for reprocessing or storage, often to developing countries
103.x: Transboundary hazardous-waste movement involves the physical transfer of hazardous waste for reprocessing or storage, frequently to developing countries.
103.tq: Use the operational meaning of the term rather than an unrelated environmental transfer.
xs: The issue is the **physical transfer of hazardous waste for reprocessing or storage**, often to **developing countries** — option **(4)** is correct (APPSC-G2 2025).
It is not about seeds, rural biodegradable waste or clean-energy equipment.
xa: Governed by the **Basel** Convention (1989; in force **5 May 1992**); India ratified **June 1992**.
HOWM Rules 2016 prohibit **import for disposal**.
China's **National Sword Policy (2018)** curbs plastic waste imports.

103.s: Which body functions as the nodal division for hazardous substances management in the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change?
103.x: The Hazardous Substances Management Division (HSMD) of MoEFCC is the nodal body for hazardous substances management.
103.tq: Match the function with the specialised administrative division.
xs: The **Hazardous Substances Management Division (HSMD)**, MoEFCC, is the nodal body — option **(4)** is correct.
The other bodies (CGWB, NBA, NDRF) do not handle hazardous substances management.
xa: Conventions it deals with: **Basel, Rotterdam, Stockholm, Minamata**.
Rotterdam DNAs sit in the **Chemicals & Fertilisers** and **Agriculture** ministries.

103.s:
Match List-I (Convention) with List-II (Subject):
a. Basel
b. Rotterdam
c. Stockholm
d. Minamata
i. Persistent Organic Pollutants
ii. Mercury
iii. Transboundary movement of hazardous wastes
iv. Prior Informed Consent for hazardous chemicals and pesticides in trade
Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
103.x: Basel (1989) covers transboundary movement of hazardous wastes, Rotterdam is the PIC convention for hazardous chemicals and pesticides, Stockholm (2001) covers POPs and Minamata (2013) covers mercury. The other codes swap Basel/Rotterdam, Stockholm/Minamata or Basel/Stockholm.
103.tq: Basel waste, Rotterdam PIC, Stockholm POPs, Minamata mercury.
xs: Correct matching is **a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii** — option **(1)**.
**Basel** (1989) — transboundary hazardous wastes; **Rotterdam** — **Prior Informed Consent**.
**Stockholm** (2001) — **POPs**; **Minamata** (2013) — **mercury**.
xa: Rotterdam in force **2004**; India acceded **2005**.
Stockholm now lists **34** chemicals incl. PFAS.

103.s: Surat is associated with which of the following applications of industrial waste?
o: A railway line constructed using plastic certificates
A dam constructed entirely using fly ash
A landfill constructed using PET resin
A road constructed using steel slag
103.x: Surat has a road made using steel slag, which is used as a road aggregate.
103.tq: Location-based recall with a material-use trap.
xs: **Surat** has a **road made with steel slag** — option **(4)** is correct.
Steel slag is used for **road base**, improving agricultural soil and cement production (UPSC 2020).
xa: **Fly ash** must be used for bricks, cement and roads within **300 km** of thermal plants.
**Red mud** (alumina refining) is being tried in cement/bricks.

103.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Industrial waste)
a. Fly ash
b. Steel slag
c. Red mud
d. Phosphogypsum

List-II (Source industry)
i. Alumina refining
 ii. Steel plants
 iii. Coal-based thermal power plants
 iv. Phosphoric acid or phosphatic fertiliser plants

Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
103.x: Fly ash comes from coal-based thermal power plants, steel slag from steel plants, red mud from alumina refining, and phosphogypsum from phosphoric acid or phosphatic fertiliser plants.
103.tq: Start from the sure source-industry pair and eliminate the codes that swap industrial processes.
xs: Correct matching is **a–iii, b–ii, c–i, d–iv** — option **(1)**.
**Fly ash** — coal thermal plants; **steel slag** — steel plants.
**Red mud** — alumina refining; **phosphogypsum** — phosphoric acid / phosphatic fertiliser plants.
xa: Phosphogypsum reuse: gypsum substitute in cement, **soil conditioner**.
**Chromium sludge** — tanneries, electroplating.

103.s: Which one of the following is a recognised reuse of mine tailings, overburden and waste rock?
o: Production of biogas by aerobic digestion
103.x: Mine tailings, overburden and waste rock can be reused for backfilling. Non-ferrous tailings may also carry heavy metals and cause acid or alkaline drainage.
103.tq: Identify the direct reuse associated with mining waste.
xs: Mine tailings, overburden and waste rock are reused for **backfilling** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Non-ferrous tailings** carry **heavy metals** and cause **acid/alkaline drainage**.
xa: **Fly ash** → bricks, cement, roads; **steel slag** → roads, soil, cement.
**Pharma sludge** comes from bulk-drug and pharmaceutical units.

103.s: The Fly Ash Utilisation Notification requires fly ash to be used for bricks, cement and road construction within what distance of thermal power plants?
103.x: The notification requires utilisation of fly ash for specified construction purposes within 300 km of thermal plants, helping prevent dumping on soil.
103.tq: Use the distance-based regulatory limit and distinguish it from nearer or broader alternatives.
xs: Fly ash must be used for bricks, cement and roads within **300 km** of thermal plants — option **(3)** is correct.
The rule stops fly ash being **dumped on soil**.
xa: Fly ash comes from **coal-based thermal power plants**.
It partly replaces **Portland cement** in concrete (UPSC 2015).

103.s: Which of the following is a recognised use of fly ash in construction?
o: Treating hazardous waste without any further processing
Replacing all aggregates in every type of concrete
Making building bricks and partly replacing Portland cement in concrete
103.x: Fly ash can be used to make building bricks and can partly replace Portland cement in concrete.
103.tq: Select the option that states practical uses without introducing an absolute or exclusive claim.
xs: Fly ash is used for **building bricks** and **partly replaces Portland cement** in concrete — option **(3)** is correct (UPSC 2015).
It is a **partial** replacement, not for all aggregates, and has nothing to do with mercury lamps.
xa: **Fly Ash Utilisation Notification (MoEFCC)**: bricks, cement, roads within **300 km**.
**Steel slag** is also used in **cement production**.

103.s:
Steel slag can be the material for which of the following?
1. Construction of base roads
2. Improvement of agricultural soil
3. Production of cement
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
103.x: All three uses are correct (UPSC 2020): steel slag is used as road base, to improve agricultural soil and in cement production; Surat has a steel-slag road. Options leaving out any use are incomplete.
103.tq: Steel slag → roads + soil + cement (all three).
xs: All three uses are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3** (UPSC 2020).
Steel slag serves as **road base**, **improves agricultural soil** and is used in **cement production**.
xa: **Surat** has a **steel-slag road**.
**Fly ash** — bricks, cement, roads within **300 km** of plants.

103.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The C&D Waste Management Rules, 2016 treat construction and demolition waste as a resource and provide for its collection, storage and reprocessing.
2. The Environment (C&D) Waste Management Rules, 2025 took effect from 1 October 2025.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
103.x: Statement 1 is correct: the 2016 Rules treat C&D waste as a resource (collection, storage, reprocessing). Statement 2 is wrong: the 2025 Rules took effect from 1 April 2026 (1 Oct 2025 was the date in the draft SWM Rules). So only 1 is correct; '2 only', 'Both' and 'Neither' are wrong.
103.tq: New waste rules of 2025-26 (SWM 2026, C&D 2025) both start 1 April 2026.
xs: Only statement 1 is correct — option **(1) 1 only**.
Statement 1: **C&D Rules 2016** treat C&D waste as a **'Resource'** — collection, transport, storage, re-processing — correct.
Statement 2: wrong — the **2025 Rules** took effect from **1 April 2026**; **1 Oct 2025** was the draft SWM Rules date.
xa: MoEFCC notified an **EPR framework for C&D waste** (2026).
India generates about **12 million tonnes** of C&D waste a year.

103.s: Which one of the following is NOT a recognised reuse of construction and demolition waste?
o: Use as a substitute for all hazardous chemical treatment
103.x: C&D waste can be reused as recycled aggregates and in bricks and tiles. It is not a substitute for hazardous chemical treatment.
103.tq: Find the option outside the stated reuse pathway by separating construction applications from hazardous-waste treatment.
xs: C&D waste is **not a substitute for hazardous chemical treatment** — option **(4)** is the answer.
Recognised reuses: **recycled aggregates, bricks, tiles**, re-processing.
xa: C&D waste is **mostly inert** — concrete, bricks, dirt, rocks, debris.
First C&D recycling plant: Delhi's **Burari**.

103.s: The Burari facility in Delhi is notable as:
o: India’s first fly-ash-based thermal power plant
India’s first secure landfill for hazardous waste
India’s first construction and demolition waste recycling plant
103.x: Delhi’s Burari plant is recognised as India’s first construction and demolition waste recycling plant.
103.tq: Match the named place with its distinctive facility rather than a neighbouring waste-management activity.
xs: Delhi's **Burari** plant is India's **first C&D waste recycling plant** — option **(4)** is correct.
It is not a mercury-recovery, fly-ash power or secure hazardous-waste landfill site.
xa: First **e-waste clinic**: **Bhopal**.
India generates about **12 million tonnes** of C&D waste a year (Jan 2026).
**C&D Rules 2025** in effect from **1 April 2026**.

103.s: Under the Construction and Demolition Waste Management Rules, 2016, which of the following activities falls within the scope of construction and demolition waste management?
o: Building, renovation, excavation, road, flyover, bridge and pipeline work
103.x: The 2016 Rules cover waste arising from building, renovation, excavation, road, flyover, bridge and pipeline activities.
103.tq: Prefer the comprehensive scope when the rule covers multiple related activities.
xs: The **C&D Rules 2016** cover **building, renovation, excavation, road, flyover, bridge and pipeline work** — option **(2)** is correct.
Scope is not limited to residential buildings, mining or household waste.
xa: They provide for **collection, transport, storage and re-processing**, with a **charge on bulk generators**.
C&D waste is treated as a **'Resource'**.
**C&D Rules 2025** in effect from **1 April 2026**.

103.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Construction and Demolition Waste Management Rules, 2016:
1. The Rules provide for collection, transport, storage and re-processing of C&D waste.
2. Bulk generators may be subject to charges.
3. Construction and demolition waste is treated as a resource.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
103.x: The 2016 framework covers collection, transport, storage and re-processing, permits charges on bulk generators and treats C&D waste as a resource.
103.tq: Test the rule through its management stages, economic provision and resource-oriented approach.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: the **C&D Rules 2016** cover **collection, transport, storage and re-processing** — correct.
Statement 2: a **charge on bulk generators** — correct.
Statement 3: C&D waste is treated as a **'Resource'** — correct.
xa: Scope: **building, renovation, excavation, road, flyover, bridge and pipeline** work.
**Environment (C&D Waste Management) Rules 2025** in effect **1 April 2026**.
First C&D recycling plant: Delhi's **Burari**.

103.s: Which new framework is associated with the Environment (Construction and Demolition Waste Management) Rules, 2025?
o: Extended Producer Responsibility for C&D waste
A national prohibition on using recycled aggregates
A complete ban on recycling construction waste
103.x: The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change has notified an Extended Producer Responsibility framework for C&D waste under the 2025 rules.
103.tq: Identify the policy instrument directly linked with the newer rules.
xs: MoEFCC notified an **EPR framework for C&D waste** (2026) with the **2025 Rules** — option **(2)** is correct.
The Rules promote reuse — **recycled aggregates, bricks, tiles** — so a ban on recycling is wrong.
xa: The **Environment (C&D Waste Management) Rules 2025** took effect on **1 April 2026** (3 Jan 2026).
India generates about **12 million tonnes** of C&D waste a year.
The **2016 Rules** already treated C&D waste as a **'Resource'**.

103.s: Operation Clean Sweep, launched in May 2026, is a campaign of the Municipal Administration Department for:
o: Scientific solid-waste management in Tier-1 and Tier-2 corporations
Only coastal plastic clean-up in villages
103.x: Operation Clean Sweep is the Municipal Administration Department’s campaign for scientific solid-waste management in Tier-1 and Tier-2 corporations.
103.tq: Link the campaign with its department, timing and operational scope.
xs: **Operation Clean Sweep** (May 2026) is the Municipal Administration department's drive for **scientific SWM in Tier-1/2 corporations** — option **(3)** is correct.
It covered all **123 ULBs**, **23 May-20 Jun 2026**, under **Swarna Andhra-Swachh Andhra**.
xa: **Swarna Andhra-Swachh Andhra** was launched in **January 2025**.
GVMC threatened to seal an apartment without **two segregation bins** (28 Aug 2026).
Guntur Commissioner studied **Indore's model** (24 Jun 2026).
