103.s: Which agency functions as the state agency running urban sanitation under SBM-U 2.0 in Andhra Pradesh?
o: Andhra Pradesh State Council of Higher Education
103.x: Swachha Andhra Corporation, or SAC, is the state agency running urban sanitation under SBM-U 2.0 in Andhra Pradesh.
103.tq: Identify the correct state agency from closely related institutional names.
xs: **Swachha Andhra Corporation (SAC)** runs urban sanitation under **SBM-U 2.0** in AP — option **(2)** is correct.
For SS 2026, SAC operationalised **Project Monitoring Units in 46 ULBs**, chosen on SS 2024 ranks.
xa: **CBMWTFs** handle biomedical waste — not the sanitation agency.
AP urban profile: **17 Municipal Corporations**, **113 Municipalities**, **7 Cantonment Boards**.
**Re Sustainability MoU** covers all **123 ULBs**; **ITC MoU** covers **30 ULBs**.

103.s: Which statement correctly describes the Re Sustainability MoU in Andhra Pradesh?
o: It covers all 123 ULBs for scientific e-waste collection, disposal and MRFs.
It covers only 30 ULBs for rural sanitation.
It operates only the state’s WtE plants.
It tracks hazardous waste through GPS-fitted vehicles.
103.x: The Re Sustainability MoU covers all 123 ULBs for scientific e-waste collection, disposal and material recovery facilities. The 30-ULB figure relates to the ITC MoU.
103.tq: Separate similar institutional agreements by coverage and function.
xs: The **Re Sustainability MoU** covers **all 123 ULBs** for scientific **e-waste collection, disposal and MRFs** — option **(1)** is correct.
The **30-ULB** figure belongs to the **ITC MoU**; GPS tracking is done by **APEMC**.
xa: AP collected **60,392 kg** of e-waste; MRFs in **101 ULBs** (SES 2025-26).
AP WtE plants: **Guntur** and **Visakhapatnam**.

103.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: APEMC portal — Swachh Survekshan ranking only
CBMWTF — GPS tracking of hazardous-waste vehicles
Re Sustainability MoU — monitoring only WtE electricity generation
103.x: Real-time monitoring is carried out on the APCMMS portal. The APEMC portal tracks hazardous waste using GPS-fitted vehicles, while BMW is sent to CBMWTFs.
103.tq: Match each portal or facility with its specific operational function.
xs: **APCMMS portal — real-time monitoring** is correctly matched — option **(1)**.
The **APEMC portal** tracks hazardous waste with **GPS-fitted vehicles**; **CBMWTFs** incinerate biomedical waste.
**Re Sustainability** handles e-waste collection, disposal and MRFs in **123 ULBs**.
xa: AP's **Circular Economy and Waste Recycling Policy 2025-30**: guidelines via **G.O. Ms. No. 26** (Feb 2026).
AP CHWTSDFs: **Anakapalli**, **SPSR Nellore**.

103.s: Clean Andhra Pradesh, popularly known as the CLAP programme, was launched on 2 October 2021 as:
103.x: CLAP was launched on 2 October 2021 under the name Jagananna Swachha Sankalpam. Swarna Andhra-Swachh Andhra is a later state drive launched in January 2025.
103.tq: Use the exact official name to distinguish related sanitation initiatives.
xs: **CLAP** was launched on **2 Oct 2021** as **Jagananna Swachha Sankalpam** — option **(3)** is correct.
**Swarna Andhra-Swachh Andhra** is the later State drive, launched **January 2025**.
xa: **Operation Clean Sweep** (May 2026) runs under Swarna Andhra-Swachh Andhra.
**SBM-U 2.0** was launched a day earlier, on **1 Oct 2021**.

103.s: Which one of the following correctly states the urban local-government set-up in Andhra Pradesh mentioned for waste management?
o: 17 Municipal Corporations, 113 municipalities and 7 cantonment boards
113 Municipal Corporations, 17 municipalities and 7 cantonment boards
7 Municipal Corporations, 113 municipalities and 17 cantonment boards
17 Municipal Corporations, 7 municipalities and 113 cantonment boards
103.x: The stated urban set-up consists of 17 Municipal Corporations, 113 municipalities and 7 cantonment boards.
103.tq: Keep the three administrative counts matched with their correct categories.
xs: AP has **17 Municipal Corporations, 113 Municipalities and 7 Cantonment Boards** (May 2026) — option **(1)** is correct.
The other options shuffle the figures **17**, **113** and **7**.
xa: **Operation Clean Sweep** covered all **123 ULBs** (23 May-20 Jun 2026).
**94.62%** of wards have full door-to-door coverage (SES 2025-26).

103.s: In Swachh Survekshan 2022, which of the following pairs of Andhra Pradesh cities and recognitions is correctly matched?
o: Visakhapatnam - 'Top Impact Creator'; Tirupati - first in 'Safai Mitra Surakshit Shehar'
Tirupati - 'Top Impact Creator'; Visakhapatnam - first in 'Safai Mitra Surakshit Shehar'
Vijayawada - 'Top Impact Creator'; Guntur - first in 'Safai Mitra Surakshit Shehar'
Visakhapatnam - cleanest city overall; Tirupati - 'Top Impact Creator'
103.x: In SS 2022, Visakhapatnam was 'Top Impact Creator' (million-plus) and Tirupati came first in 'Safai Mitra Surakshit Shehar' (APPSC-G1 2022 key). Option 2 swaps the two cities, option 3 names the wrong cities, and Visakhapatnam was not the overall cleanest city.
103.tq: SS 2022: Vizag = Top Impact Creator; Tirupati = Safai Mitra Surakshit Shehar.
xs: In **SS 2022**, **Visakhapatnam** was **'Top Impact Creator'** (million-plus) and **Tirupati** first in **'Safai Mitra Surakshit Shehar'** — option **(1)** is correct (APPSC-G1 2022 key).
Option (2) swaps the two cities; option (3) names the wrong cities; Visakhapatnam was not the overall cleanest.
xa: **Indore** was the cleanest city (10 lakh+) in the **2017 to 2022** editions.
**Vijayawada** "recognised well" last year; aiming for top rank (9 Apr 2026).

103.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
103.x: Anantapur is setting up a 170 tonnes-per-day waste-processing plant. Guthikondavaripalem yard in Ongole is associated with biomining.
103.tq: Use the location-action pair to distinguish two Andhra Pradesh waste projects.
xs: **Anantapur — 170 TPD** waste-processing plant is correctly matched — option **(1)**.
**Guthikondavaripalem** is **Ongole's** biomining yard, not Anantapur's or Surat's.
xa: Ongole: **1.76 lakh t** of **2.56 lakh t** legacy waste processed; **RDF** to cement plants.
**Surat** is known for a **steel-slag road**.

103.s: The Andhra Pradesh Pollution Control Board has permitted how many cement industries to co-process incinerable, plastic and municipal waste?
103.x: The APPCB permitted 12 cement industries to co-process incinerable, plastic and municipal waste.
103.tq: Recall the exact institutional count and distinguish it from nearby figures.
xs: **APPCB** permitted **12 cement industries** to co-process incinerable, plastic and municipal waste — option **(2)** is correct.
**6** is the number of **pre-processing facilities** that feed them; **46** is the number of ULBs with PMUs.
xa: APPCB prefers **co-processing** as fuel in cement plants + **waste exchange**; landfill is the **last resort**.
**RDF** is used in **cement kilns**.

103.s: Biomedical waste in Andhra Pradesh is sent to Common Bio-Medical Waste Treatment Facilities primarily for
o: Production of RDF for cement kilns only
103.x: Biomedical waste is sent to Common Bio-Medical Waste Treatment Facilities for incineration. It is not intended for open dumping or untreated agricultural composting.
103.tq: Identify the prescribed treatment route for a specialised waste stream.
xs: AP sends biomedical waste to **CBMWTFs** for **incineration** (2024-25) — option **(3)** is correct.
Open dumping and untreated composting are not permitted routes.
xa: **Yellow** category BMW → incineration / **plasma pyrolysis** / deep burial.
BMW Rules 2016 use **barcoding and GPS tracking**.
India (2024): **1.89 lakh** facilities generate **800+ tonnes/day**.

103.s: Which of the following correctly matches the Andhra Pradesh waste-management indicators?
o: 100% source segregation in wards — 49.32%; MRFs — 101 ULBs
100% source segregation in wards — 94.62%; MRFs — 30 ULBs
103.x: The cited figures are 49.32% of wards with 100% source segregation and MRFs in 101 ULBs.
103.tq: Start from the sure percentage and verify the associated institutional count.
xs: **49.32%** wards have **100% source segregation** and **MRFs** are in **101 ULBs** — option **(1)** is correct.
**94.62%** is the full **door-to-door coverage** figure, not segregation.
xa: AP collected **60,392 kg** of e-waste (SES 2025-26).
CM claim: **97%** door-to-door collection in municipalities (Feb 2026).

103.s: Which pair of Andhra Pradesh cities is associated with WtE plants?
103.x: The cited Andhra Pradesh WtE plants are located at Guntur and Visakhapatnam.
103.tq: Recall a location pair without substituting nearby urban centres.
xs: AP's **WtE plants** are at **Guntur** and **Visakhapatnam** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Ongole** is linked with biomining; **Nellore** with a CHWTSDF.
xa: India: **21 operational WtE plants**, **170+ MW** (Feb 2026).
**Anantapur** is setting up a **170 TPD** waste-processing plant.

103.s: In Andhra Pradesh, the ban on single-use plastic and carry bags applies to carry bags having thickness below:
103.x: Andhra Pradesh bans single-use plastic and carry bags below 120 microns, with enforcement involving the Revenue Department, Police and Pollution Control Board.
103.tq: Distinguish the precise statutory threshold from nearby thickness values.
xs: AP bans SUP and carry bags **under 120 microns** — option **(4)** is correct.
Enforcement involves **Revenue, Police, PCB**.
xa: National carry-bag limit is also **120 microns** from **31 Dec 2022**.
AP seizures: **5,505.06 kg** carry bags + **3,571.40 kg** SUP (SES 2025-26).
**100 microns** is the limit for banned **PVC banners**.

103.s:
With reference to the plastic curbs in Guntur, consider the following statements:
1. A complete ban was scheduled from 15 August 2026.
2. Fines could extend up to ₹5,000.
3. Fines were to be collected through the Swachh App.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
103.x: All three statements are correct: Guntur’s complete ban was scheduled from 15 August 2026, fines could reach ₹5,000, and the Swachh App was to be used for fines.
103.tq: Verify the date, monetary limit and enforcement mechanism separately.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: complete ban from **15 Aug 2026** — correct.
Statements 2-3: fines up to **₹5,000** via the **'Swachh App'** — correct.
xa: AP bans SUP and carry bags **under 120 microns**.
Guntur hosts one of AP's **WtE plants**.

103.s:
With reference to the Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026, consider the following statements:
1. They came into force on 1 April 2026.
2. Household hazardous waste has been recognised as a separate ‘special care’ stream.
3. They deal exclusively with industrial hazardous waste.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
103.x: The Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026 came into force on 1 April 2026 and recognise household hazardous waste as a separate ‘special care’ stream. They are not confined exclusively to industrial hazardous waste.
103.tq: Identify the statement that wrongly narrows the scope by using the word ‘exclusively’.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: in force **1 April 2026** — correct.
Statement 2: household hazardous waste is a separate **'special care'** stream — correct.
Statement 3: wrong — they cover **every generator**'s solid waste, not only industrial hazardous waste.
xa: Four streams: **wet, dry, sanitary, special care**.
National **IEC campaign** on the SWM Rules 2026.

103.s: The campaign associated with SBM-G in 2026 was:
o: Swachhata Ki Nayi Pehel - Badhayein Haath, Karein Safai Saath
103.x: The 2026 campaign of Swachh Bharat Mission-Grameen was titled “Swabhav Swachhata - Sanskaar Swachhata”. “Swachh Gaon, Surakshit Jalvayu” was the theme associated with June 2026.
103.tq: Separate the campaign title from the related monthly theme and state initiative.
xs: The **SBM-G 2026** campaign was **"Swabhav Swachhata - Sanskaar Swachhata"** — option **(3)** is correct.
**"Swachh Gaon, Surakshit Jalvayu"** was the **June 2026** theme; **Swarna Andhra-Swachh Andhra** is AP's State drive.
xa: **Swachhata Hi Seva**: fortnight shramdaan every year since **2017**.
Nearly **12 crore** rural toilets (Aug 2026).

103.s: The Supreme Court order of 18 August 2026 regarding responsibility for waste at the threshold held that:
o: Only Urban Local Bodies are responsible for such waste
Only sanitary workers are responsible for such waste
Responsibility begins only after waste reaches a landfill
Generators, and not only sanitary workers, are responsible for such waste
103.x: The Supreme Court held that generators, and not only sanitary workers, are responsible for waste at the threshold.
103.tq: Reject the exclusive responsibility claim by focusing on the phrase ‘not only’.
xs: The SC order of **18 Aug 2026** held that **generators**, not only sanitary workers, are responsible for waste at the threshold — option **(4)** is correct.
It was passed by the Bench of **Justice S.V.N. Bhatti**.
xa: SC pulled up Union and States for not institutionalising **SWM Rules 2026** (**1 Sep 2026**).
SC earlier gave pan-India directions; clean environment part of **Art. 21** (Feb 2026).

103.s: Which one of the following changes has been reported in the composition of rural waste?
o: A shift from municipal waste towards only industrial hazardous waste
A shift from biodegradable waste towards plastic, sanitary and other non-biodegradable waste
A complete disappearance of sanitary waste from rural areas
A shift from plastic waste towards exclusively biodegradable waste
103.x: Rural waste is shifting from predominantly biodegradable waste towards plastic, sanitary and other non-biodegradable waste.
103.tq: Identify the direction of change by comparing the earlier and emerging waste categories.
xs: Rural waste is shifting from **biodegradable** to **plastic, sanitary and other non-biodegradable** waste — option **(2)** is correct (5 Sep 2026).
Sanitary waste has grown, not disappeared, and the shift is away from biodegradable waste.
xa: Rural gaps: **Gram Panchayats lack capacity**; open dumping and burning continue.
Under **SWM Rules 2026**, **sanitary** waste (diapers, napkins) has its own bin.

103.s: Which of the following correctly describes the reported compliance position concerning Extended Producer Responsibility for plastic waste?
o: Fewer than 50% of producers comply with EPR targets
EPR targets have been withdrawn for producers
More than 90% of producers comply with EPR targets
Exactly 70% of producers comply with EPR targets
103.x: Fewer than 50% of producers were reported to comply with Extended Producer Responsibility targets, leading to criticism about enforceability.
103.tq: Distinguish the compliance percentage from the separate figure relating to informal recycling.
xs: **Fewer than 50%** of producers comply with EPR — option **(1)** is correct.
EPR has not been withdrawn; **90%** and **70%** are not the stated compliance figures.
xa: EPR collection targets are hard to enforce (6 Apr 2026).
CPCB EPR portal: **69,470 producers**, **4,402 recyclers** (29 Oct 2025).
2026 Amendment allows **carry-forward** up to **3 years**.

103.s:
With reference to plastic recycling and waste-pickers, consider the following statements:
1. More than 70% of recycled plastic is handled by informal workers.
2. The NAMASTE scheme aims to formalise informal workers.
3. About 15 lakh waste-pickers remain outside formal systems.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
103.x: All three statements are correct. More than 70% of recycled plastic is handled by informal workers, NAMASTE seeks to formalise them, and approximately 15 lakh waste-pickers remain outside formal systems.
103.tq: Keep distinct percentages, scheme objectives and population estimates separate while evaluating the statements.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: **70%+** of recycled plastic handled by informal workers — correct.
Statement 2: **NAMASTE** scheme (2024) aims to formalise them — correct.
Statement 3: ~**15 lakh** waste-pickers outside formal systems — correct.
xa: Segregation at source is **under 25%** (Oct 2025).
**78%** of e-waste is also processed informally.

103.s: Which of the following is an example of ‘invisible e-waste’ commonly discarded with regular waste?
o: Vapes, USB cables and LED accessories
Glass bottles, steel cans and paper cartons
Construction aggregates, fly ash and cement bags
Food scraps, garden leaves and crop residue
103.x: Vapes, USB cables and LED accessories are examples of ‘invisible e-waste’ that may be thrown into regular waste streams.
103.tq: Use the category clue and select the cluster of small electronic products.
xs: **Vapes, USB cables and LED accessories** are "invisible e-waste" — option **(1)** is correct (Jun 2026).
They are thrown into regular trash instead of reaching authorised recyclers.
xa: E-waste must **not be mixed** with other waste (E-waste Rules 2022).
Citizens should deposit old electronics with **authorised recyclers** after wiping data.

103.s: Which of the following correctly describes the criticism surrounding the Plastic Waste Management Amendment Rules, 2026?
o: They were criticised on the ground that compliance was eased.
They were criticised for abolishing Extended Producer Responsibility.
They were criticised for completely banning all plastic products.
They were criticised for transferring all plastic regulation to local bodies.
103.x: Critics argued that the Plastic Waste Management Amendment Rules, 2026 eased compliance requirements. The criticism did not amount to a complete ban or abolition of EPR.
103.tq: Reject extreme interpretations such as ‘completely’, ‘all’ and ‘abolishing’.
xs: Critics said the **PWM Amendment Rules 2026** **eased compliance** — option **(1)** is correct (4 Apr 2026).
They kept EPR (with **tradable certificates** and **carry-forward**) and did not ban all plastics.
xa: Recycled content in rigid plastics: **30% to 60% by 2028-29**.
**QR-code traceability** mandatory.

103.s: The Andhra Pradesh Circular Economy and Waste Recycling Policy 2025–30 particularly targets:
103.x: The Andhra Pradesh Circular Economy and Waste Recycling Policy 2025–30 targets industrial hazardous waste.
103.tq: Match the policy with its stated target instead of selecting an over-narrow category.
xs: The **AP Circular Economy and Waste Recycling Policy 2025-30** targets **industrial hazardous waste** — option **(1)** is correct (6 Feb 2026).
Guidelines were issued via **G.O. Ms. No. 26** (Feb 2026).
xa: AP has **4,000+ industries** (bulk drugs, chemicals, cement, steel) producing hazardous waste.
AP CHWTSDFs: **Anakapalli**, **SPSR Nellore**.

103.s: Which one of the following is NOT included among the legal frameworks for which the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 serves as an umbrella?
o: Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026 as the only framework
103.x: The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 serves as an umbrella for frameworks including the EIA, Hazardous Waste, Coastal Regulation Zone and Contaminated Sites Rules. It is not described as an umbrella exclusively for the Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026.
103.tq: Find the option that improperly uses an exclusive formulation and narrows a broader legal relationship.
xs: The odd one out is "**SWM Rules 2026 as the only framework**" — option **(1)**.
**EPA 1986** is the umbrella for **EIA, Hazardous Waste, CRZ and Contaminated Sites Rules** — not only for the SWM Rules.
xa: SWM Rules 2026 are themselves notified under **EPA 1986**.
EPA 1986 was enacted after **Bhopal**.

103.s: Which of the following best explains the major institutional concern raised in relation to the Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026?
o: Questions concerning federalism and administrative design
A proposal to eliminate all Urban Local Bodies
A proposal to replace all recycling with incineration
A decision to exempt rural areas from waste regulation
103.x: The Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026 have raised questions concerning federalism and administrative design. The other options do not represent the stated criticism.
103.tq: Identify the governance dimension of a policy debate rather than an unrelated operational claim.
xs: The SWM Rules 2026 raise **questions of federalism and administrative design** — option **(1)** is correct (12 May 2026).
No elimination of ULBs, replacement of recycling or exemption of rural areas is proposed.
xa: SC pulled up Union and States for not institutionalising the Rules (**1 Sep 2026**).
Only **68%** of ULBs had notified SWM by-laws.

104.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched with the footprint it measures?
o: Water footprint — only land required to absorb solid waste
Ecological footprint — only the volume of freshwater used in manufacturing
Carbon footprint — only direct emissions from owned sources
Carbon footprint — total greenhouse gases emitted by human activities, expressed in tonnes of CO2 equivalent per year
104.x: The carbon footprint measures total greenhouse-gas emissions from human activities in tonnes of CO2 equivalent per year. The other options describe ecological, water or Scope 1 concepts incorrectly.
104.tq: Match each footprint with its measured resource or emission category, not with a related sub-concept.
xs: **Carbon footprint** = **total GHGs emitted by human activities**, in **tonnes CO2e per year** — option **(4)** is correct (APPSC-GS 2025).
**Direct emissions from owned sources** are only **Scope 1**, not the whole carbon footprint — option (3) is wrong.
**Water footprint** = total **freshwater** used; **ecological footprint** = **land and water** needed — options (1) and (2) swap them.
xa: ⚠ **Carbon** = GHGs; **Ecological** = land and water; **Water** = blue, green, grey.
**1 carbon credit = 1 tonne CO2e** avoided or removed.

104.s: The ecological footprint represents the:
o: land and water needed to produce what people consume and absorb their waste
greenhouse gases emitted from purchased electricity alone
total freshwater used only for drinking purposes
104.x: The ecological footprint measures the land and water needed to produce consumed goods and absorb associated waste.
104.tq: Identify the broader resource-demand concept rather than a single emission category.
xs: The **ecological footprint** = **land and water** needed to produce what we consume and **absorb our waste** — option **(1)** is correct (APPSC-GS 2018).
**Purchased electricity** emissions are **Scope 2**; carbon stored in forests is a **sink** — not the ecological footprint.
xa: **Carbon footprint** = total GHGs, in **tonnes CO2e per year**.
**Water footprint** = total freshwater used: **blue, green and grey** water.

104.s: Which of the following correctly describes blue, green and grey water in the context of the water footprint?
o: They are three categories of carbon emissions from power plants.
They refer respectively to geological, ocean and terrestrial carbon storage.
They are three scopes of greenhouse-gas accounting.
They are categories included in the total freshwater used to produce goods and services.
104.x: The water footprint measures total freshwater used to produce goods and services and includes blue, green and grey water.
104.tq: Separate the water-footprint classification from carbon-storage and emissions classifications.
xs: **Blue, green and grey water** are parts of the **water footprint** — total **freshwater** used to produce goods and services — option **(4)** is correct.
**Geological, ocean, terrestrial** are types of **sequestration**; **Scope 1, 2, 3** are GHG-accounting scopes.
xa: ⚠ **Carbon** footprint = GHGs; **Ecological** = land and water; **Water** = blue, green, grey.
**Blue carbon** (mangroves, seagrass, salt marshes) is unrelated to "blue water".

104.s: A company's diesel generator emits greenhouse gases, its purchased electricity causes indirect emissions, and emissions occur in the manufacture and transport of its purchased inputs. These are respectively classified as:
104.x: Direct emissions from owned sources are Scope 1, emissions from purchased electricity or heat are Scope 2, and the remaining value-chain emissions are Scope 3.
104.tq: Classify the emissions by asking whether they are owned, purchased-energy or value-chain emissions.
xs: They are **Scope 1, Scope 2 and Scope 3** respectively — option **(1)** is correct.
Own **diesel generator** = **Scope 1** (direct, owned source); **purchased electricity** = **Scope 2**; **purchased inputs** = **Scope 3** (rest of value chain).
xa: **Net Zero Portal (MoEFCC, Sep 2026)**: **Scope 1 and 2 reporting encouraged; Scope 3 voluntary**.
**NAPCC Dashboard** launched with it (**17 Sep 2026**).

104.s:
According to the sector-wise distribution of India's greenhouse-gas emissions, which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
1. Cement — approximately 6%
2. Aluminium — approximately 2.8%
104.x: Cement accounts for approximately 6% and aluminium for approximately 2.8% of India's greenhouse-gas emissions.
104.tq: Use a comparison of sector shares and check both numerical values independently.
xs: Both are correct — option **(3) Both 1 and 2**.
**Cement ~6%** and **aluminium ~2.8%** of India's GHG emissions.
xa: **Waste sector**: **2.56%** of India's emissions (2020, BUR-4).
CCTS (Oct 2025) set emission-intensity targets for **aluminium, cement, chlor-alkali, pulp & paper**.
**DST** set up **five CCU testbeds** in the **cement sector**.

104.s: NITI Aayog's decarbonisation roadmaps for the cement, aluminium and MSME sectors rely on which combination of measures?
o: Round-the-clock renewable-energy power, nuclear power and CCUS
Hydropower, biofuels and ocean alkalinity enhancement only
Natural gas, nuclear disarmament and direct air capture only
Coal expansion, diesel generation and afforestation only
104.x: The roadmaps rely on renewable energy available round the clock, nuclear power and carbon capture, utilisation and storage.
104.tq: Identify the complete policy package rather than selecting a single decarbonisation measure.
xs: **NITI Aayog** roadmaps rely on **RE round-the-clock power, nuclear and CCUS** — option **(1)** is correct.
They cover **cement, aluminium and MSMEs**.
xa: **CCUS** captures CO2 and **uses** it or **stores** it permanently; supports **coal gasification and hydrogen**.
**Nuclear** supplies close to **one-third** of the world's low-carbon electricity.

104.s:
With reference to biomass co-firing in coal-based power plants, consider the following statements:
1. Coal plants are required to co-fire 5% biomass from FY 2024-25.
2. The requirement rises to 7% from FY 2025-26.
3. The SAMARTH mission monitors this requirement.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
104.x: All three statements are correct: the biomass co-firing requirement is 5% in FY 2024-25 and 7% from FY 2025-26, with monitoring by the SAMARTH mission.
104.tq: Check the two successive percentages and then identify the agency associated with monitoring.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: coal plants **co-fire 5% biomass** from **FY 2024-25** — correct.
Statement 2: rises to **7% from FY 2025-26** — correct.
Statement 3: monitored by the **SAMARTH** mission — correct.
xa: **BECCS** (bioenergy + CCS) → **net-negative** emissions.
**2035 NDC**: **60%** non-fossil power capacity.

104.s:
Consider the following statements about 'carbon bombs':
1. They are fossil-fuel projects that could emit over 1 Gt of CO2 in their lifetime.
2. The LINGO list of 425 carbon bombs is led by China, the USA, Russia and India.
3. The Gevra (Chhattisgarh) and Rajmahal (Jharkhand) coal mines are among the Indian carbon bombs.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
104.x: Statement 1 is correct: a carbon bomb is a fossil project that could emit over 1 Gt CO2 in its lifetime. Statement 2 is wrong: the LINGO list of 425 is led by China, USA, Russia and Saudi Arabia, not India. Statement 3 is correct: Gevra is in Chhattisgarh and Rajmahal in Jharkhand. So '1 and 3 only' is right; '1 only' misses 3, and options with 2 are wrong.
104.tq: Remember the four leaders: China, USA, Russia, Saudi Arabia - India is not among them.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 3 only**.
Statement 1: **carbon bombs** = fossil projects that could emit **over 1 Gt CO2** in their lifetime — correct.
Statement 2: wrong — the **LINGO list** of **425** is led by **China, USA, Russia, Saudi Arabia**, not India.
Statement 3: **Gevra** (Chhattisgarh) and **Rajmahal** (Jharkhand) coal mines — correct.
xa: India's **2035 NDC**: **47%** emission-intensity cut vs 2005.
Coal plants must co-fire **biomass** (5% → 7%).

104.s:
Consider the following statements about India's 2035 NDC:
1. It targets a 47% cut in emission intensity compared with 2005.
2. It targets 60% non-fossil power capacity.
3. It replaces the carbon-sink goal with a pledge to end coal use.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
104.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: 47% intensity cut vs 2005 and 60% non-fossil power capacity. Statement 3 is wrong: the NDC includes an extra sink of 3.5-4.0 bn t CO2e and no coal phase-out pledge is stated. So '1 only' is incomplete and options with 3 are wrong.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: **47%** intensity cut vs **2005** — correct.
Statement 2: **60%** non-fossil power capacity — correct.
Statement 3: wrong — the NDC keeps a sink goal: an extra sink of **3.5-4.0 bn t CO2e**.
xa: Earlier pledge: **33-35%** intensity cut by **2030**.
Indian carbon bombs: **Gevra** and **Rajmahal** coal mines.

104.s: Which of the following is NOT a natural carbon sink identified in the context of carbon sequestration?
104.x: Forests, soil and oceans are natural carbon sinks. Chlor-alkali plants are industrial entities covered by emission-intensity targets, not natural sinks.
104.tq: Find the odd category by separating natural systems from an industrial sector.
xs: **Chlor-alkali plants** are not a natural sink — option **(1)** is the answer.
**Natural sinks** are **forests, soil, oceans**; chlor-alkali is a **CCTS-covered industry**.
xa: **Blue carbon** is stored by **mangroves, seagrass and salt marshes**.
**Tropical peatlands** store more carbon per hectare than any other terrestrial ecosystem.

104.s: Blue carbon is primarily stored by which combination of ecosystems?
o: Tropical peatlands, deserts and alpine meadows
104.x: Blue carbon is stored in coastal ecosystems such as mangroves, seagrass beds and salt marshes.
104.tq: Associate blue carbon with the listed coastal and marine ecosystems.
xs: **Blue carbon** is stored by **mangroves, seagrass and salt marshes** — option **(2)** is correct.
Tropical peatlands are a terrestrial store, not blue carbon.
xa: Natural sinks: **forests, soil, oceans**.
**Ocean** storage is one type of **sequestration** (with geological and terrestrial).

104.s:
Consider the following statements about REDD+:
1. REDD+ stands for Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and Forest Degradation.
2. India does not take part in REDD+, and forest conservation under it cannot earn tradable credits.
3. The Green India Mission and the National Afforestation Programme raise India's carbon stock.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
104.x: Statement 1 is correct: that is the expansion of REDD+. Statement 2 is wrong: India takes part in REDD+ and forest conservation can earn tradable credits. Statement 3 is correct. Hence '1 and 3 only'; options with 2 are wrong and '1 only' misses 3.
104.tq: India participates in REDD+; conservation earns credits.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 3 only**.
Statement 1: **REDD+** = **Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and Forest Degradation** — correct.
Statement 2: wrong — **India takes part** and forest conservation **can earn tradable credits**.
Statement 3: **Green India Mission** + **National Afforestation Programme** raise carbon stock (UPSC) — correct.
xa: **IPCC carbon pools (5)**: above-ground biomass, below-ground biomass, dead wood, litter, soil organic carbon.
**1 carbon credit = 1 tonne CO2e**.

104.s: Which terrestrial ecosystem stores more carbon per hectare than any other terrestrial ecosystem?
104.x: Tropical peatlands store more carbon per hectare than any other terrestrial ecosystem.
104.tq: Identify the superlative comparison and avoid substituting a generally forested ecosystem.
xs: **Tropical peatlands** store **more carbon per hectare** than any other terrestrial ecosystem — option **(1)** is correct.
Grasslands, savannas and alpine forests are not given this record in the notes.
xa: **Blue carbon**: mangroves, seagrass, salt marshes.
**CO2 fertilisation** = **70%** of Earth's recent greening.

104.s: CO2 fertilisation is estimated to account for what proportion of the Earth’s recent greening?
104.x: CO2 fertilisation accounts for approximately 70% of the Earth’s recent greening.
104.tq: Distinguish the stated dominant contribution from rounded lower and higher estimates.
xs: **CO2 fertilisation** accounts for **70%** of Earth's recent greening — option **(3)** is correct.
**30%**, **50%** and **90%** are not the stated share.
xa: Natural sinks: **forests, soil, oceans**.
CO2-observing satellites: **OCO-2** (NASA), **GOSAT** (Japan).

104.s: The National Carbon Project is implemented under which programme?
o: India's National Action Plan on Climate Change only
104.x: The National Carbon Project is implemented under the ISRO Geosphere-Biosphere Programme.
104.tq: Identify the parent programme rather than a related climate or air-pollution initiative.
xs: The **National Carbon Project** runs under the **ISRO Geosphere-Biosphere Programme** — option **(3)** is correct.
It assesses **carbon pools, fluxes and the net carbon balance** of India's terrestrial biomes.
xa: APPSC-GS 2022 key: statements **I and III**.
Sub-projects: **vegetation carbon**, **soil carbon**, vegetation/soil-atmosphere fluxes.

104.s:
Which set of activities is associated with the National Carbon Project?
1. Assessment of carbon pools and carbon fluxes
2. Assessment of the net carbon balance of India's terrestrial biomes
3. Study of vegetation carbon, soil carbon and vegetation/soil–atmosphere fluxes
4. Measurement of only carbon emissions from coastal shipping
Select the correct answer using the code below.
104.x: The project assesses carbon pools, fluxes and the net carbon balance of terrestrial biomes, with sub-projects on vegetation carbon, soil carbon and related fluxes. Coastal shipping alone is not its stated scope.
104.tq: Select the three related project objectives and reject the unrelated narrow activity.
xs: Items 1, 2 and 3 are correct — option **(1) 1, 2 and 3 only**.
The project assesses **carbon pools and fluxes** and the **net carbon balance** of terrestrial biomes, with sub-projects on **vegetation carbon, soil carbon** and fluxes.
Item 4 is wrong — **coastal shipping** emissions are not its scope.
xa: It runs under the **ISRO Geosphere-Biosphere Programme**.
**IPCC carbon pools (5)**: above-ground, below-ground biomass, dead wood, litter, soil organic carbon.

104.s: Which one of the following is NOT included among the five IPCC carbon pools?
104.x: The five pools are above-ground biomass, below-ground biomass, dead wood, litter and soil organic carbon. Atmospheric oxygen is not one of them.
104.tq: Recall the five-member list and identify the item outside the classification.
xs: **Atmospheric oxygen** is not an IPCC carbon pool — option **(2)** is the answer.
The **five pools**: **above-ground biomass, below-ground biomass, dead wood, litter, soil organic carbon**.
xa: **National Carbon Project** assesses carbon pools and fluxes under **ISRO**.
**Green India Mission** raises carbon stock.

104.s: Which pair of satellites is correctly associated with CO2 observation?
104.x: NASA's OCO-2 and Japan's GOSAT are CO2-observing satellites.
104.tq: Match each satellite with its country or agency and avoid swapping the pair.
xs: **NASA's OCO-2** and **Japan's GOSAT** observe CO2 — option **(1)** is correct.
Option (2) swaps the agencies.
xa: **National Carbon Project** (ISRO) assesses India's **net carbon balance**.
Carbon pricing covers **29%** of global GHGs (World Bank 2026).

104.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: CCS — capture of CO2 at stationary sources and storage in geological or ocean formations
CCUS — removal of CO2 only from ambient air
Direct Air Capture — storage of carbon only in forests and soil
Ocean alkalinity enhancement — spreading basalt on land
104.x: CCS captures CO2 at stationary sources such as power plants and stores it in geological or ocean formations. Direct Air Capture removes CO2 from ambient air, while the other two descriptions are interchanged.
104.tq: Start with the sure definition and reject options that swap neighbouring carbon-removal terms.
xs: **CCS** = capturing CO2 at **stationary sources** (e.g. power plants) and storing it in **geological or ocean formations** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Direct Air Capture** pulls CO2 from **ambient air**; **ocean alkalinity enhancement** adds alkaline minerals to seawater; spreading **basalt** on land is **enhanced rock weathering**.
xa: ⚠ **CCS** = store only; **CCUS** = use or store.
**BECCS** → **net-negative** emissions.

104.s:
Consider the following statements about carbon capture, utilisation and storage (CCUS):
1. It captures CO2 and either uses it or stores it permanently.
2. It supports coal gasification and hydrogen.
3. It is restricted to the storage of atmospheric CO2 in forests.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
104.x: CCUS involves using captured CO2 or storing it permanently and can support coal gasification and hydrogen. It is not restricted to forest storage of atmospheric CO2.
104.tq: Reject the overly restrictive statement and retain the two functional features of CCUS.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: **CCUS** captures CO2 and **uses** it or **stores it permanently** — correct.
Statement 2: it supports **coal gasification and hydrogen** — correct.
Statement 3: wrong — forest storage is **terrestrial sequestration**, not CCUS.
xa: ⚠ **CCS** = store only; **CCUS** = use or store.
**DST**: **five CCU testbeds** in the cement sector.

104.s:
Which of the following is NOT a type or location of carbon sequestration identified in the context of carbon storage?
1. Geological storage in saline aquifers
2. Storage in depleted oil and gas fields
3. Ocean storage
4. Terrestrial storage in forests and soil
5. Atmospheric storage in the upper atmosphere
104.x: Geological, ocean and terrestrial storage are recognised forms of sequestration. Atmospheric storage in the upper atmosphere is not one of the listed forms.
104.tq: Find the option that does not belong to the recognised storage categories.
xs: **Atmospheric storage in the upper atmosphere** is not a sequestration type — option **(4) 5 only**.
Recognised types: **geological** (saline aquifers, depleted oil and gas fields), **ocean**, **terrestrial** (forests, soil).
xa: **APPSC-GS 2024 key**: "Captures and stores CO2 from industrial processes" = **carbon sequestration**.
**Direct Air Capture** pulls CO2 straight from ambient air.

104.s:
Consider the following pairs of carbon-removal methods and their meaning:
1. Direct Air Capture - pulls CO2 straight from ambient air
2. Enhanced rock weathering - injecting captured CO2 into saline aquifers
3. Ocean alkalinity enhancement - adding alkaline minerals to seawater so it absorbs more CO2
Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched?
104.x: Pair 1 is correct: DAC pulls CO2 from ambient air. Pair 2 is wrong: enhanced rock weathering spreads crushed silicate rock (e.g. basalt) on land to bind CO2 as carbonate; injection into saline aquifers is geological sequestration. Pair 3 is correct. Hence '1 and 3 only'; the other options either omit 3 or include the wrong pair 2.
104.tq: Rock weathering = rock on land (basalt to carbonate); ocean alkalinity = minerals into seawater.
xs: Pairs 1 and 3 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 3 only**.
Pair 1: **Direct Air Capture** pulls CO2 from **ambient air** — correct.
Pair 2: wrong — **enhanced rock weathering** spreads crushed **silicate rock (basalt)** on land to bind CO2 as **carbonate**; saline aquifers = **geological** sequestration.
Pair 3: **ocean alkalinity enhancement** — alkaline minerals added to seawater — correct.
xa: **BECCS** → net-negative emissions.
**CCS** stores CO2 in geological or ocean formations.

104.s: The DST's cement-sector initiative concerning carbon capture and utilisation consists of:
o: three CCU testbeds forming a regional demonstration network
seven DAC testbeds for urban transport
five CCU testbeds forming a first-of-its-kind research cluster
five CCS testbeds located only in coal mines
104.x: DST has established five Carbon Capture and Utilisation testbeds in the cement sector as a first-of-its-kind research cluster.
104.tq: Check both the number of testbeds and the technology abbreviation.
xs: **DST** set up **five CCU testbeds** in the **cement sector** — a **first-of-its-kind research cluster** — option **(3)** is correct.
They are **CCU** (utilisation), not CCS or DAC testbeds.
xa: Cement = **~6%** of India's GHG emissions.
**CCUS** supports coal gasification and hydrogen.

104.s:
Consider the following statements about NET Power's Allam-Fetvedt cycle plant:
1. It is located at La Porte, Texas.
2. It burns natural gas in air and uses steam as the working fluid.
3. It captures nearly all the CO2 it produces.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
104.x: Statement 1 is correct: the plant is at La Porte, Texas. Statement 2 is wrong: it burns gas in oxygen with supercritical CO2, not in air with steam. Statement 3 is correct: it captures nearly all CO2. Hence '1 and 3 only'; options including 2 are wrong and '1 only' misses 3.
104.tq: Allam cycle = oxy-combustion + supercritical CO2.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 3 only**.
Statement 1: **NET Power**'s **Allam-Fetvedt cycle** plant is at **La Porte, Texas** — correct.
Statement 2: wrong — it burns gas in **oxygen** with **supercritical CO2**, not in air with steam.
Statement 3: it **captures nearly all CO2** — correct.
xa: **Nuclear** supplies close to **one-third** of the world's low-carbon electricity.
**CCS** = store only; **CCUS** = use or store.

104.s: Which one of the following technologies is designed to produce net-negative emissions by combining bioenergy with carbon capture and storage?
104.x: BECCS means bioenergy with carbon capture and storage; it can generate net-negative emissions.
104.tq: Break the acronym into its component terms and identify the mitigation pathway.
xs: **BECCS** = **bioenergy with carbon capture and storage** → **net-negative** emissions — option **(1)** is correct.
**REDD+** is forest-emissions reduction; **VCS** is Verra's standard; **CBAM** is the EU carbon border levy.
xa: **Enhanced rock weathering** binds CO2 as **carbonate**.
**Direct Air Capture** pulls CO2 from ambient air.

104.s: Approximately what proportion of the world’s low-carbon electricity is supplied by nuclear power?
104.x: Nuclear power supplies close to one-third of the world’s low-carbon electricity.
104.tq: Distinguish the approximate fraction from the larger and smaller distractor shares.
xs: **Nuclear** supplies close to **one-third** of the world's low-carbon electricity — option **(2)** is correct.
One-tenth, one-half and two-thirds are not the stated figure.
xa: NITI Aayog decarbonisation roadmaps rely on **RE round-the-clock, nuclear and CCUS**.
**NET Power**'s Allam cycle plant captures nearly all CO2 from gas power.

104.s: The process of capturing carbon dioxide from industrial processes and storing it so that it does not enter the atmosphere is called:
104.x: Capturing and storing CO2 from industrial processes is carbon sequestration (APPSC-GS 2024 key; carbon capture was also accepted). CO2 fertilisation is plant greening from higher CO2, carbon leakage is emissions shifting abroad (the CBAM concern), and offsetting means using credits to balance emissions.
104.tq: Capture + store = sequestration.
xs: Capturing and storing CO2 from industrial processes = **carbon sequestration** — option **(1)** is correct (APPSC-GS 2024 key; carbon capture also allowed).
**CO2 fertilisation** = greening from higher CO2; **carbon leakage** = what **CBAM** tries to stop.
xa: Sequestration types: **geological**, **ocean**, **terrestrial**.
**CCS** stores CO2 from **stationary sources** such as power plants.

104.s:
Consider the following statements about carbon credits:
1. One carbon credit equals one tonne of CO2e avoided or removed.
2. Carbon credits originated with the Kyoto Protocol (1997).
3. The Clean Development Mechanism issues Verified Carbon Standard (VCS) units.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
104.x: Statement 1 is correct: 1 credit = 1 tonne CO2e. Statement 2 is correct: the Kyoto Protocol of 1997 is the origin. Statement 3 is wrong: the CDM issues Certified Emission Reductions (CERs); the VCS is run by Verra. Hence '1 and 2 only'.
104.tq: CDM gives CERs; Verra gives VCS.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: **1 carbon credit = 1 tonne CO2e** avoided or removed — correct.
Statement 2: origin — **Kyoto Protocol (1997)** — correct.
Statement 3: wrong — the **CDM** issues **CERs (Certified Emission Reductions)**; **VCS** is run by **Verra**.
xa: **Gold Standard** was founded by **WWF**.
India's **CCTS** trades **Indian Carbon Credits (ICCs)**.

104.s: Which of the following is correctly matched?
o: Gold Standard — Indian Carbon Credit administrator
CDM — voluntary standard founded by WWF
104.x: Verra runs the Verified Carbon Standard. BEE administers India’s CCTS, while CERs are issued under the CDM.
104.tq: Use the institution-function pairing to eliminate swapped authorities and standards.
xs: **Verra — Verified Carbon Standard** is correctly matched — option **(1)**.
**BEE** administers **CCTS**; the **CDM** issues **CERs**; **Gold Standard** was founded by **WWF**.
xa: **Maruti Suzuki** railway siding = world's first **modal-shift** project under Verra's VCS.
It expects about **1.7 lakh credits** over FY24-FY33 under **AM0090**.

104.s: Gold Standard, a voluntary carbon standard, was founded by which organisation?
104.x: Gold Standard was founded by WWF, the World Wide Fund for Nature.
104.tq: Identify the founding organisation rather than the administrator of a different carbon market.
xs: **Gold Standard** was founded by **WWF (World Wide Fund for Nature)** — option **(1)** is correct.
**BEE** administers India's CCTS — not a voluntary standard founder.
xa: **Verified Carbon Standard** is run by **Verra**.
Carbon credits began with the **Kyoto Protocol (1997)** → **CDM** → **CERs**.

104.s: Maruti Suzuki’s Gujarat in-plant railway siding has been described as the world’s first project of which type registered with Verra’s VCS?
104.x: The railway siding is the world’s first modal-shift project registered with Verra’s Verified Carbon Standard.
104.tq: Focus on the project’s defining activity—shifting freight movement to rail.
xs: Maruti Suzuki's Gujarat in-plant **railway siding** is the world's first **modal-shift project** under **Verra's VCS** — option **(3)** is correct.
It expects about **1.7 lakh credits** over **FY24-FY33** under CDM methodology **AM0090** (Feb 2026).
xa: **1 carbon credit = 1 tonne CO2e**.
**242 agri-food projects** registered (Dec 2025).

104.s: Which one of the following correctly describes India’s Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS)?
o: It is a voluntary farmer-only market trading CERs issued by the Kyoto Protocol.
It is India’s first mandatory compliance carbon market and trades Indian Carbon Credits.
It is an international market operated exclusively by Verra.
It is a forest conservation programme administered by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change.
104.x: The CCTS is India’s first mandatory compliance carbon market and trades Indian Carbon Credits. It is not a farmer-only or exclusively international voluntary market.
104.tq: Find the option that combines the correct nature of the scheme with its correct traded unit.
xs: **CCTS** is India's **first mandatory compliance carbon market** trading **Indian Carbon Credits (ICCs)** — option **(2)** is correct.
It is run by **BEE** (Ministry of Power), not Verra or MoEFCC, and is not a farmer-only market.
xa: Notified **June 2023** under **Sec. 14AA** of the **Energy Conservation Act, 2001**.
**282 obligated entities**; offset mechanism with **9 methodologies**.
World Bank 2026: **7 sectors**, ~**490 industries**, ~**477 Mt CO2e**.

104.s:
Under the CCTS, emission-intensity targets notified in October 2025 covered which sectors?
1. Aluminium
2. Cement
3. Chlor-alkali
4. Pulp and paper
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
104.x: The notified sectors were aluminium, cement, chlor-alkali, and pulp and paper.
104.tq: Treat each listed sector as an independent inclusion test before selecting the complete set.
xs: All four sectors were covered — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.
**Oct 2025** targets: **aluminium, cement, chlor-alkali, pulp & paper**; **282 obligated entities**.
xa: Only **China, EU and South Korea** cover more than India's CCTS (World Bank 2026).
Cement **~6%**, aluminium **~2.8%** of India's GHG emissions.

104.s: Which of the following correctly characterises the Budget 2026–27 carbon credit programme?
o: It follows the DST roadmap and is industrial in orientation, rather than being a farmer-only scheme.
It is a panchayat-level programme focused only on blue carbon.
It follows the Kyoto Protocol and is administered exclusively by WWF.
It is a voluntary scheme restricted to 282 agricultural entities.
104.x: The programme follows the DST roadmap and concerns industrial carbon credits; it is not a farmer-only scheme.
104.tq: Distinguish the policy’s target and institutional roadmap from attractive but incorrect sectoral labels.
xs: The **Budget 2026-27 carbon credit programme** follows the **DST roadmap** and is **industrial, not a farmer scheme** — option **(1)** is correct (Mar 2026).
**282** is the number of CCTS obligated entities, not agricultural entities.
xa: India could earn **$20-40 bn** from voluntary credits by 2030.
Agricultural credits face **measurement and credibility gaps** (Dec 2025).

104.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched with India’s voluntary carbon-credit potential and registered agri-food projects?
104.x: India could earn 20–40 billion dollars from voluntary credits by 2030, and 242 agri-food projects are registered.
104.tq: Match the monetary range with the project count instead of mixing figures from the compliance market.
xs: India could earn **$20-40 bn** from voluntary credits **by 2030**, with **242 agri-food projects** registered — option **(4)** is correct (Dec 2025).
**282**, **490** and **477** are CCTS figures (obligated entities, industries, Mt CO2e); **1.7** lakh is Maruti's expected credits.
xa: Agricultural credits face measurement and credibility gaps.
**1 carbon credit = 1 tonne CO2e** avoided or removed.

104.s: India's Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS), notified in June 2023, was issued under which provision, and which body administers it?
o: Section 3 of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986; CPCB
Section 14AA of the Energy Conservation Act, 2001; Bureau of Energy Efficiency
Section 16 of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986; MoEFCC
Section 14AA of the Energy Conservation Act, 2001; Verra
104.x: The CCTS was notified in June 2023 under Sec. 14AA of the Energy Conservation Act, 2001, and is administered by the BEE (Ministry of Power). The EPA sections are wrong legal bases, and Verra runs the voluntary VCS, not CCTS.
104.tq: CCTS = EC Act 2001 Sec 14AA + BEE; trades ICCs.
xs: **CCTS** was notified in **June 2023** under **Sec. 14AA of the Energy Conservation Act, 2001**, administered by **BEE** — option **(2)** is correct.
The **EPA** sections are wrong legal bases; **Verra** runs the voluntary **VCS**.
xa: **BEE** sits under the **Ministry of Power**.
Trades **Indian Carbon Credits (ICCs)**; **9 methodologies** for offsets.

104.s: Which pair correctly identifies the first country to propose and the first country to actually levy a livestock carbon tax?
104.x: New Zealand was the first country to propose a tax on agricultural emissions, while Denmark is to become the first to actually levy a livestock carbon tax from 2030.
104.tq: Distinguish a proposal from actual implementation and keep the countries in the correct order.
xs: **New Zealand** was first to **propose** an agri-emissions tax; **Denmark** first to **levy** a livestock carbon tax (from **2030**) — option **(2)** is correct.
Option (4) reverses them; the UK is not named.
xa: New Zealand fact = **APPSC-G1 2024** key.
⚠ **New Zealand** = propose; **Denmark** = levy (from 2030).

104.s:
Consider the following statements about the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM):
1. Its definitive phase started on 1 January 2026 after a transitional phase from 2023.
2. It covers iron and steel, aluminium, cement, fertilisers, hydrogen and electricity.
3. Importers buy CBAM certificates priced by the World Trade Organization.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
104.x: Statement 1 is correct: transitional phase 2023, definitive phase from 1 Jan 2026. Statement 2 is correct: these are the covered sectors (plus some downstream goods). Statement 3 is wrong: CBAM certificates are priced on the EU Emissions Trading System, not by the WTO. So '1 and 2 only'; '1 only' misses 2, and options with 3 are wrong.
104.tq: CBAM certificate price follows the EU ETS.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: transitional phase **2023**; **definitive phase 1 Jan 2026** — correct.
Statement 2: covers **iron and steel, aluminium, cement, fertilisers, hydrogen, electricity** — correct.
Statement 3: wrong — **CBAM certificates** are priced on the **EU ETS**, not by the WTO.
xa: CBAM aims to stop **carbon leakage**; also covers some downstream goods (**screws, bolts**).
⚠ **UK** CBAM starts **1 Jan 2027**.

104.s: What is the principal concern for Indian exporters arising from the EU CBAM?
o: CBAM applies only to India's domestic electricity consumption.
Decarbonisation costs may shift to exporters while the revenue remains in Europe.
CBAM removes the need for Indian industries to decarbonise.
Indian exporters receive all CBAM revenue directly from the EU.
104.x: CBAM can place decarbonisation costs on exporters, while the resulting revenue is retained in Europe.
104.tq: Apply the policy mechanism to the exporter–importer relationship rather than confusing it with a domestic tax.
xs: CBAM **shifts decarbonisation costs onto exporters** while **revenue stays in Europe** — option **(2)** is correct.
It does not remove the need to decarbonise or pay revenue to Indian exporters.
xa: **Art. 9** of the CBAM Regulation lets a carbon price already paid (e.g. **CCTS**) be deducted.
Critics see CBAM as a **climate-justice** issue — India risks being a "**rule-taker**".

104.s: Under Article 9 of the CBAM Regulation, which of the following may be deducted from the CBAM liability?
o: Voluntary forest plantation undertaken anywhere in the world
Only the importer's income tax paid in the EU
The entire value of the exported goods
A carbon price already paid in the exporting country, such as under the CCTS
104.x: Article 9 permits deduction of a carbon price already paid, including a price paid under India's Carbon Credit Trading Scheme, from the CBAM liability.
104.tq: Identify the legally recognised deduction and reject unrelated economic payments.
xs: **Art. 9** of the CBAM Regulation allows deduction of a **carbon price already paid**, such as under the **CCTS** — option **(4)** is correct (4 May 2026).
Forest plantations, EU income tax or goods value are not deductible.
xa: **UK** recognised CCTS as a **qualifying carbon price** (Sep 2026) → lowers CBAM liability.
EU CBAM definitive phase: **1 Jan 2026**.

104.s:
Consider the following statements about the UK CBAM:
1. It starts on 1 January 2027.
2. In September 2026 the UK recognised India's Carbon Credit Trading Scheme as a qualifying carbon price, which raises the CBAM liability on Indian exports.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
104.x: Statement 1 is correct: the UK CBAM starts on 1 Jan 2027. Statement 2 is wrong: recognition of CCTS as a qualifying carbon price lowers, not raises, the CBAM liability on Indian exports. Hence '1 only'; '2 only' and 'Both' include the false statement, and 'Neither' ignores the true one.
104.tq: Recognition of a carbon price already paid always reduces border-levy liability.
xs: Only statement 1 is correct — option **(1) 1 only**.
Statement 1: **UK CBAM** starts **1 Jan 2027** — correct.
Statement 2: wrong — recognising **CCTS** as a qualifying carbon price **lowers**, not raises, CBAM liability on Indian exports.
xa: ⚠ **EU** CBAM definitive = **1 Jan 2026**; **UK** = **1 Jan 2027**.
EU importers buy **CBAM certificates** priced on the **EU ETS**.

104.s: According to the World Bank's State and Trends of Carbon Pricing 2026, carbon pricing instruments covered approximately what share of global greenhouse-gas emissions?
104.x: Carbon pricing covered approximately 29% of global greenhouse-gas emissions.
104.tq: Retain the exact coverage percentage rather than rounding it to a nearby figure.
xs: Carbon pricing covers **29%** of global GHGs (World Bank, **State and Trends of Carbon Pricing 2026**) — option **(2)** is correct.
**19%**, **39%** and **49%** are not the stated share.
xa: Revenue passed **$107 bn** in 2025; **ETS coverage tripled** since 2016.
India's CCTS: ~**477 Mt CO2e** — only **China, EU, South Korea** cover more.

104.s: Palli village in Samba district was declared India’s first carbon-neutral panchayat in which year?
104.x: Palli in Samba, Jammu and Kashmir, was declared India’s first carbon-neutral panchayat in 2022.
104.tq: Combine the first-in-India claim with its exact year and location.
xs: **Palli** (Samba, J&K) became India's **first carbon-neutral panchayat** in **2022** — option **(3)** is correct.
2018, 2020 and 2024 are not the stated year.
xa: **Ladakh** is working to be a **carbon-neutral UT** (2026).
**CCTS** = India's **first mandatory compliance carbon market**.

104.s:
Which of the following measures is associated with Ladakh’s effort to become a carbon-neutral Union Territory?
1. Solar water lifting
2. Passive solar buildings
3. Geothermal heating
4. Electric vehicles
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
104.x: Ladakh’s carbon-neutral effort includes solar water lifting, passive solar buildings, geothermal heating and electric vehicles.
104.tq: Check whether all listed mitigation measures belong to the same regional strategy.
xs: All four are part of **Ladakh**'s carbon-neutral UT effort — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.
Measures: **solar water lifting, passive solar buildings, geothermal heating, e-vehicles** (2026).
xa: **Palli (Samba, J&K)** = first **carbon-neutral panchayat** (**2022**).
**Maruti Suzuki** railway siding = world's first **modal-shift** project under VCS.

104.s: The criticism that the CBAM may make India a “rule-taker” is primarily framed as an issue of what kind?
104.x: The criticism of CBAM as potentially placing India in a rule-taker position is framed as a climate-justice issue.
104.tq: Connect the quoted policy concern with its broader analytical category.
xs: The "rule-taker" criticism frames **CBAM** as a **climate justice** issue — option **(4)** is correct (May 2026).
It is not about biodiversity ownership, disaster compensation or nuclear safety.
xa: CBAM **shifts decarbonisation costs onto exporters**; revenue stays in Europe.
**UK** recognition of **CCTS** (Sep 2026) lowers CBAM liability on Indian exports.

104.s: Agricultural carbon credits face which principal concern identified in the carbon-market debate?
o: Inability to use any voluntary standard
104.x: Agricultural credits face measurement and credibility gaps, which affect the reliability of claimed reductions or removals.
104.tq: Select the specific implementation concern rather than an absolute claim about the market.
xs: Agricultural carbon credits face **measurement and credibility gaps** — option **(1)** is correct (Dec 2025).
Agri projects do exist — **242 agri-food projects** are registered — so option (2) is wrong.
xa: India could earn **$20-40 bn** from voluntary credits by 2030.
The **Budget 2026-27** carbon credit programme is **industrial**, not a farmer scheme.
Voluntary standards: **VCS** (Verra), **Gold Standard** (WWF).

104.s:
Which of the following developments is associated with carbon-market policy in the stated current context?
1. The United Kingdom recognised the CCTS for CBAM relief.
2. The definitive phase of the EU CBAM began on 1 January 2026.
3. A Net Zero Portal was noted in September 2026.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
104.x: All three developments are associated with the stated current carbon-market context: UK recognition, the EU CBAM definitive phase and the Net Zero Portal.
104.tq: Track the institution, policy milestone and date independently before selecting the combined answer.
xs: All three are current developments — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: **UK** recognised **CCTS** for CBAM relief (**Sep 2026**) — correct.
Statement 2: **EU CBAM** definitive phase from **1 Jan 2026** — correct.
Statement 3: **Net Zero Portal** (MoEFCC, **Sep 2026**) — correct.
xa: **UK CBAM** starts **1 Jan 2027**.
Net Zero Portal: **Scope 1 and 2** reporting encouraged, **Scope 3** voluntary; **NAPCC Dashboard** launched with it.

105.s:
Which of the following are examples of green technology in the cement industry?
1. Efficient kilns with precalciners and dry-process technology
2. Portland limestone cement (green cement)
3. Electrostatic precipitators fitted to kiln stacks
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
105.x: 1 is correct: efficient kilns (precalciners, dry process) are green technology. 2 is correct: Portland limestone cement is green cement. 3 is wrong: electrostatic precipitators are conventional end-of-pipe tools, not green technology. Hence '1 and 2 only'.
105.tq: Green technology changes the process or product; end-of-pipe tools only treat emissions.
xs: Items 1 and 2 are green technology — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
Item 1: **efficient kilns** (**precalciners, dry process**) — correct.
Item 2: **Portland limestone cement** = **green cement** — correct.
Item 3: wrong — **electrostatic precipitators** are **conventional end-of-pipe** tools.
xa: Green tech also uses **alternative fuels** — biomass, waste-derived fuel.
Other end-of-pipe tools: **scrubbers**, **selective catalytic reduction** (UPSC).

105.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Green technology may use biomass and waste-derived fuels as alternative fuels.
2. Carbon capture and storage captures carbon dioxide from point sources such as cement plants.
3. Carbon capture and storage is already universally deployed as a mature pollution-control technology.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
105.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. CCS remains largely at the research stage, so statement 3 is incorrect.
105.tq: Reject the extreme maturity claim and retain the statements describing actual functions.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: green tech uses **biomass and waste-derived fuels** — correct.
Statement 2: **CCS** captures CO2 from **point sources** like cement plants — correct.
Statement 3: wrong — CCS is **still largely at research stage**.
xa: **NITI Aayog** issued a report on a **CCUS policy framework (2022)**.
⚠ Trap: **incineration** = conventional; green tech, CCS, bioremediation = alternatives.

105.s:
Consider the following statements about bioremediation:
1. It uses microbes or plants to clean polluted water and soil.
2. It is cost-effective and faster than conventional methods.
3. Its results vary with local conditions.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
105.x: Statement 1 is correct: bioremediation uses microbes/plants on polluted water and soil. Statement 2 is wrong: it is eco-friendly and cost-effective but slower. Statement 3 is correct: results vary with conditions. Hence '1 and 3 only'.
105.tq: Bioremediation: cheap and green, but slow and condition-dependent.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 3 only**.
Statement 1: bioremediation uses **microbes/plants** to clean polluted **water and soil** — correct.
Statement 2: wrong — it is **cost-effective** but **slower**, not faster.
Statement 3: **results vary with conditions** — correct (UPSC).
xa: Bioremediation is **eco-friendly** — an alternative to conventional tools.
Conventional end-of-pipe tools: **ESPs, scrubbers, SCR**.

105.s: Incineration of waste is best classified as:
o: A conventional method of waste treatment
105.x: Incineration is a conventional waste-treatment method and is not classified as an alternative pollution-control approach in this context.
105.tq: Discriminate between a conventional pollution-control method and alternatives to it.
xs: **Incineration** is a **conventional** method of waste treatment, **NOT an alternative** (PYQ) — option **(2)** is correct.
It is not carbon storage, green cement or bioremediation.
xa: ⚠ Trap: incineration = conventional; **green tech, CCS, bioremediation** = alternatives.
**Green cement** = **Portland limestone cement**.

105.s: Which of the following is NOT a conventional end-of-pipe pollution-control tool?
105.x: Electrostatic precipitators, scrubbers and selective catalytic reduction are conventional end-of-pipe tools. Bioremediation is an alternative biological approach.
105.tq: Find the item belonging to an alternative category rather than the listed end-of-pipe group.
xs: **Bioremediation** is not an end-of-pipe tool — option **(1)** is the answer.
**Electrostatic precipitators, scrubbers and selective catalytic reduction** are the conventional end-of-pipe tools (UPSC).
xa: Bioremediation is an **alternative** — microbes/plants, **cost-effective** but **slower**.
Significance: move from **end-of-pipe control → prevention**.

105.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the relationship between CCS and CCUS initiatives in India?
o: CCS research has been completed for all industries, and the CCUS report was issued in 2016.
CCS research is ongoing for cement plants, while NITI Aayog issued a CCUS policy-framework report in 2022.
CCUS applies only to household cooking, while CCS applies only to beaches.
Neither CCS research nor policy work has been undertaken in India.
105.x: Research on CCS is ongoing for cement plants, and NITI Aayog published a report on a CCUS policy framework in 2022.
105.tq: Keep the technical research activity distinct from the policy-framework milestone.
xs: **CCS research is ongoing for cement plants**, and **NITI Aayog** issued a **CCUS policy framework** report in **2022** — option **(2)** is correct.
CCS is **still largely at research stage**, so "completed" and "nothing done" are both wrong.
xa: CCS captures CO2 from **point sources** and stores it.
Green technology also includes **efficient kilns** and **green cement**.

105.s:
Consider the following statements about the Jan Vishwas reforms to pollution laws:
1. The Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act, 2023 decriminalised minor offences under the Air Act and the Environment (Protection) Act.
2. The Water Act was amended likewise in 2024.
3. The reforms replaced monetary penalties with imprisonment for minor offences.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
105.x: Statement 1 is correct: the 2023 Act covered the Air Act and EP Act. Statement 2 is correct: the Water Act was amended likewise in 2024. Statement 3 is wrong: the reforms replaced jail with monetary penalties, not the reverse. Hence '1 and 2 only'.
105.tq: Decriminalisation = jail to fines.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: **Jan Vishwas Act 2023** decriminalised minor offences under the **Air Act** and **EP Act** — correct.
Statement 2: the **Water Act** was amended likewise in **2024** — correct.
Statement 3: wrong — **jail was replaced by monetary penalties**, not the reverse.
xa: Shift: "**command and control**" → **trust-based, technology-enabled** regulation.
Penalties go to the **Environmental (Protection) Fund** under **Sec 16 EPA**.

105.s: The regulatory approach associated with the Jan Vishwas reforms is described as a shift from:
o: Trust-based regulation to manual command-and-control regulation
Technology-enabled regulation to prohibition of digital systems
Command-and-control regulation to trust-based, technology-enabled regulation
Judicial regulation to complete self-regulation without technology
105.x: The reforms are described as moving regulation from a command-and-control model to trust-based, technology-enabled regulation.
105.tq: Identify the correctly oriented before-and-after comparison.
xs: The shift is from **command-and-control** to **trust-based, technology-enabled** regulation (2025-26) — option **(3)** is correct.
Option (1) reverses the direction; technology is used, not prohibited.
xa: **Jan Vishwas Act 2023** turned jail into **monetary penalties** for minor offences.
**CTO** now valid **till cancelled** (Jan 2026).
**PARIVESH 3.0**: single-window clearances + **compliance monitoring**.

105.s: Which of the following is NOT a stated use of the Environmental Protection Fund?
o: Providing universal subsidies for fossil-fuel consumption
Monitoring and remediation of contaminated sites
Laboratories and clean-technology research and development
105.x: The Fund may support monitoring, remediation of contaminated sites, laboratories and clean-technology R&D. Universal fossil-fuel subsidies are not a stated use.
105.tq: Eliminate the unrelated expenditure and retain the listed environmental purposes.
xs: **Universal fossil-fuel subsidies** are not a Fund use — option **(1)** is the answer.
Stated uses: **monitoring**, **remediation of contaminated sites**, **labs**, **clean-tech R&D**.
xa: Sharing: **75% States/UTs, 25% Centre**.
Audited by the **CAG**; Fund is under **Sec 16 EPA** (Public Account).

105.s: The accounts of the Environmental Protection Fund are to be audited by the:
o: Comptroller and Auditor General of India
105.x: The Environmental Protection Fund is subject to audit by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India.
105.tq: Identify the constitutional audit authority rather than a policy or adjudicatory body.
xs: The Environmental Protection Fund is audited by the **Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG)** — option **(2)** is correct.
NGT, Finance Commission and RBI are not named as auditors.
xa: Fund under **Sec 16 EPA**; **Environmental (Protection) Fund Rules, 2026**.
Sharing: **75%** States/UTs, **25%** Centre.

105.s: In August 2025, the Supreme Court upheld the power of Pollution Control Boards to impose environmental compensation under:
o: Section 33A of the Water Act and Section 31A of the Air Act
Section 16 of the Environment (Protection) Act alone
Section 33A of the Air Act and Section 31A of the Water Act
105.x: The Supreme Court upheld PCB power under Section 33A of the Water Act and Section 31A of the Air Act.
105.tq: Match each statutory section with the correct Act instead of swapping the pair.
xs: The SC (**Aug 2025**) upheld PCB power to impose **environmental compensation** under **Sec 33A Water Act** and **Sec 31A Air Act** — option **(1)** is correct.
Option (4) swaps the Acts; **Sec 16 EPA** is the **Environmental (Protection) Fund**, not compensation.
xa: ⚠ Water Act = **Sec 33A**; Air Act = **Sec 31A**; EPA Fund = **Sec 16**.
**Jan Vishwas Act, 2023** decriminalised minor offences under the **Air Act** + **EP Act**; the Water Act followed in **2024**.
**CTO** (**Jan 2026**): valid till cancelled.
Shift: "command and control" → **trust-based, technology-enabled** regulation (2025-26).

105.s: Which statement correctly describes the revised industrial categories?
o: The mandatory 33% green belt was retained without any change.
All industries were placed in one category based only on location.
A new Blue category was introduced, and the mandatory 33% green belt was replaced by pollution-potential norms.
The Blue category was abolished, and a mandatory 50% green belt was introduced.
105.x: The revised categories introduced a new Blue category, illustrated by compressed biogas, and replaced the mandatory 33% green belt requirement with pollution-potential norms.
105.tq: Test both halves of a regulatory change and reject reversed percentages or categories.
xs: A new **Blue** category was added and the mandatory **33% green belt** replaced by **pollution-potential norms** — option **(3)** is correct.
Example of the Blue category: **Compressed Biogas**.
xa: Critics: **relaxed green-belt norms** may weaken deterrence.
Online monitoring is compulsory for **17-category** highly polluting industries.

105.s: Under the Environmental Protection Fund Rules, 2026, the Fund is constituted under which provision, and how is it divided between the States/Union Territories and the Centre?
o: Section 33A of the Water Act; 75% and 25%
Section 31A of the Air Act; 25% and 75%
105.x: The Environmental Protection Fund Rules, 2026 place the Fund under Section 16 of the Environment (Protection) Act. Seventy-five per cent goes to States/UTs and 25 per cent to the Centre.
105.tq: Combine the enabling provision with the percentage split instead of treating them as separate figures.
xs: The Fund is under **Section 16 of the EPA; 75% and 25%** (States/UTs and Centre) — option **(2)** is correct.
Penalties go into the Fund, held in the **Public Account**.
**Sec 33A Water Act** and **Sec 31A Air Act** concern **environmental compensation**, not the Fund.
xa: The Fund is audited by the **CAG**.
Uses: monitoring, **remediation of contaminated sites**, labs, **clean-tech R&D**.
**Jan Vishwas Act, 2023**: jail → **monetary penalties** under the Air Act + EP Act.

105.s: PARIVESH 3.0 is primarily designed as a:
o: single-window portal for clearances and compliance monitoring
grant scheme for strengthening Pollution Control Boards
programme for replacing BS-IV vehicles with BS-VI vehicles
mobile application for publishing air-quality readings
105.x: PARIVESH 3.0 functions as a single-window portal for environmental clearances and compliance monitoring.
105.tq: Identify the precise institutional function rather than the associated environmental programme.
xs: **PARIVESH 3.0** is a **single-window portal for clearances** + **compliance monitoring** (2025-26) — option **(1)** is correct.
PCB grants come under **SAAP (1992)**; **BS-VI** is a vehicle norm.
xa: **CETPs** serve clusters of small industries.
AP's **BRAP** also streamlined clearances via **digitisation + single-window** systems.

105.s: Which one of the following is the appropriate application of Common Effluent Treatment Plants (CETPs)?
o: Issuing environmental clearances through a single window
Treatment of emissions from all thermal power stations
Monitoring of ambient air quality in major cities
Treatment of effluents generated by clusters of small industries
105.x: CETPs are intended for clusters of small industries, enabling common treatment of their effluents.
105.tq: Apply the facility to the industrial setting for which it is specifically intended.
xs: **CETPs** treat effluents from **clusters of small industries** — option **(4)** is correct.
Single-window clearance is **PARIVESH 3.0**; air monitoring is a separate tool.
xa: **SAAP (1992)**: grants to strengthen PCBs.
Online continuous monitoring compulsory for **17-category** industries.

105.s: The State Assistance for Abatement of Pollution (SAAP), introduced in 1992, provides grants primarily to:
o: finance Blue Flag certification of beaches
105.x: SAAP, dating from 1992, provides grants to strengthen Pollution Control Boards.
105.tq: Link the scheme with its year and the institution it supports.
xs: **SAAP (1992)** gives **grants to strengthen PCBs** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Blue Flag** is an **FEE** label; carbon credits are under CCTS.
xa: **PARIVESH 3.0**: single-window clearances.
**CETPs**: for clusters of small industries.

105.s: With regard to online continuous emission and effluent monitoring, which of the following statements is correct?
o: It is administered by the State Assistance for Abatement of Pollution without CPCB involvement.
It is voluntary for all industries but compulsory only for municipal bodies.
It applies exclusively to industries producing household solid waste.
It is compulsory for highly polluting industries belonging to the 17-category classification.
105.x: The CPCB made online continuous emission and effluent monitoring compulsory for highly polluting industries in the 17-category classification.
105.tq: Use the authority, target group and compulsory nature together to identify the correct statement.
xs: **Online continuous emission/effluent monitoring** is compulsory for highly polluting (**17-category**) industries by **CPCB** — option **(4)** is correct.
It is run by **CPCB**, not SAAP, and is not voluntary or limited to household waste.
xa: **APPCB** uses **computerised inspection allocation** by risk.
**PARIVESH 3.0** adds **compliance monitoring**.

105.s:
Consider the following statements about India's air-pollution programmes:
1. BS-VI emission norms came into force from 1 April 2020.
2. The National Ambient Air Quality Standards cover 12 pollutants.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
105.x: Both are correct: BS-VI applies from 1 April 2020, and NAAQS prescribe standards for 12 pollutants. NCAP, CAQM and GRAP are the other air programmes listed. So '1 only', '2 only' and 'Neither' are wrong.
105.tq: BS-VI 1 Apr 2020; NAAQS = 12 pollutants.
xs: Both statements are correct — option **(3) Both 1 and 2**.
Statement 1: **BS-VI** from **1 April 2020** — correct.
Statement 2: **NAAQS** for **12 pollutants** — correct.
xa: Other air programmes: **NCAP**, **CAQM**, **GRAP**.
Jan Vishwas Act 2023 decriminalised minor **Air Act** offences.

105.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: PM Ujjwala Yojana — 2016 — clean cooking and reduced indoor smoke
PM-KUSUM — 2016 — free LPG connections to poor households
PM E-DRIVE — 2019 — rooftop solar for households
PM Surya Ghar — 2024 — solar pumps exclusively for farmers
105.x: PM Ujjwala Yojana was launched in 2016 to provide free LPG connections to poor households, promoting clean cooking and reducing indoor smoke.
105.tq: Start with the sure scheme-year-objective combination and reject swapped objectives.
xs: **PM Ujjwala Yojana — 2016 — clean cooking, less indoor smoke** is correctly matched — option **(1)**.
**PM-KUSUM (2019)** is for **solar pumps and farm solar plants**; **PM E-DRIVE (2024)** is for **EVs and charging**.
xa: PMUY gives **free LPG connections** to poor households.
UNEP-CCAC "**Hidden Assets**" cites **PMUY** as a model clean-cooking programme.

105.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. PM-KUSUM was launched in 2019.
2. It promotes solar pumps and farm solar plants for farmers.
