Exam angle: "only GM crop cultivated" = **Bt cotton**.

111.s: Which State is the largest producer of Bt cotton in India?
111.x: Maharashtra is the largest Bt cotton producer (APPSC-G2 2017 key). Gujarat, Punjab and Andhra Pradesh grow Bt cotton but are not the largest producer.
111.tq: Bt cotton leader = Maharashtra.
xs: **Maharashtra** is the largest Bt cotton producer (APPSC-G2 **2017**) — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Punjab** is known for banning **glyphosate** sale in **2018**.
xa: Bt cotton covers ~**90%** of India's cotton area.
Bt cotton targets the **American bollworm**.
AP angle: **Pusa DST1** is an edited version of AP-bred **MTU1010**.

111.s: GM mustard DMH-11 (Dhara Mustard Hybrid-11) was developed by:
o: Delhi University (Centre for Genetic Manipulation of Crop Plants)
111.x: DMH-11 was developed at Delhi University's CGMCP (Deepak Pental). MAHYCO with UAS Dharwad and TNAU developed Bt brinjal; ICAR-IARI developed genome-edited Pusa Rice DST1.
111.tq: DMH-11 = Delhi University; Bt brinjal = Mahyco.
xs: **DMH-11** was developed by **Delhi University** (**CGMCP**, Deepak Pental) — so option **(2)** is correct.
**MAHYCO with UAS Dharwad** and **TNAU** developed **Bt brinjal**, not GM mustard.
xa: DMH-11 = **Dhara Mustard Hybrid-11**.
GEAC approved its environmental release in **Oct 2022**.
It is **under Supreme Court consideration**.

111.s: Which environmental concern has been associated with prolonged cultivation of Bt cotton?
o: Conversion of cotton into a non-flowering plant
Universal resistance of cotton to glyphosate
Development of resistance in pink bollworm
Permanent elimination of all soil microorganisms
111.x: Pink bollworm has developed resistance to Bt cotton, making resistance build-up an important environmental and agricultural concern.
111.tq: Identify the documented resistance problem rather than an extreme ecological claim.
xs: **Pink bollworm** has developed **resistance** to Bt toxins — so option **(3)** is correct.
Resistance build-up is a **listed environmental risk** of Bt cotton.
xa: Other problems: **non-adoption of refuge** practices, **sucking pests** (whitefly, mealybug).
**High input costs + seed dependency**.
Bt cotton targets the **American bollworm**.

111.s: Which of the following correctly represents the reported change in cotton yield associated with Bt cotton experience?
111.x: The reported yield increased from 190 kg/ha in 2002 to 480 kg/ha in 2023, although benefits varied by region.
111.tq: Check both endpoints and their direction before selecting the comparison.
xs: Cotton yield rose from **190 kg/ha in 2002** to **480 kg/ha in 2023** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Option (4) reverses the trend; (2) and (3) use wrong figures.
xa: Pesticide use fell **40-50%**.
Benefits **varied by region**.
Bt cotton covers ~**10.8 million ha**.

111.s: The rise of whitefly and mealybug in Bt cotton fields illustrates the problem of:
111.x: Whitefly and mealybug are examples of sucking or secondary pests that increased as a problem in Bt cotton cultivation.
111.tq: Classify the named pests under the correct agricultural category.
xs: **Whitefly and mealybug** illustrate the rise of **secondary or sucking pests** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Bt toxin targets bollworms, so pests outside its range have risen.
xa: **Pink bollworm** also overcame Bt toxins.
Other problems: **non-adoption of refuge**, **high input costs**, **seed dependency**.
Bt cotton cut pesticide use **40-50%**.

111.s: Which combination represents factors that contributed to difficulties associated with Bt cotton?
o: Pest resistance, non-adoption of refuges, high input costs and seed dependency
Absence of any pest resistance, free seed availability and zero input costs
Only improved soil fertility and increased landrace diversity
Exclusive control of fungal diseases through biofortification
111.x: The reported difficulties included pest resistance, failure to adopt refuges or recommended practices, high input costs and dependence on purchased seed.
111.tq: Select the option that combines the separate economic, ecological and management concerns.
xs: Bt cotton's difficulties: **pest resistance, non-adoption of refuges, high input costs and seed dependency** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The other options describe benefits never claimed (free seed, zero cost, fungal control).
xa: **Pink bollworm** developed resistance to Bt toxins.
Rise of **sucking/secondary pests** (whitefly, mealybug).
Yield still rose **190 → 480 kg/ha** (2002 to 2023).

111.s:
Which of the following are claimed environmental benefits or applications of genetically engineered crops?
1. Reduced pesticide use through Bt cotton
2. Herbicide tolerance
3. Drought tolerance
4. Stress tolerance through genome-edited crops
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
111.x: The claimed benefits include reduced pesticide use in Bt cotton, herbicide tolerance, drought tolerance and stress tolerance achieved through genome editing.
111.tq: Recognise that the broad benefits listed belong to different genetic-engineering or genome-editing approaches.
xs: All four are claimed benefits — so option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4** is correct.
Less pesticide via **Bt cotton**, plus **herbicide-tolerant** and **drought-tolerant** crops.
**Stress tolerance without transgenes**: genome-edited **Pusa Rice DST1**.
xa: Bt cotton cut pesticide use **40-50%**.
Pusa DST1 gives **10-30%** higher yield under stress.
Non-GMO route: **71 Trombay varieties** by mutation breeding.

111.s:
Consider the following statements about Pusa Rice DST1:
1. It is genome-edited for drought and salinity tolerance.
2. It gives about 10-30% higher yield under stress.
3. It is a transgenic variety carrying foreign genes.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
111.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: Pusa Rice DST1 is genome-edited for drought + salinity tolerance with 10-30% higher yield under stress. Statement 3 is wrong: it gives stress tolerance without transgenes (no foreign DNA). So 1 and 2 only.
111.tq: Genome-edited is not transgenic.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Pusa Rice DST1** is genome-edited for **drought + salinity** tolerance, with **10-30%** higher yield under stress.
Statement 3 wrong: it gives stress tolerance **without transgenes**.
xa: India is set to commercially launch it as its **first genome-edited rice** (1 Sep **2026**).
AP angle: it is an edited version of **MTU1010**, AP-bred at **Maruteru**.
**SDN-1** and **SDN-2** edits are **exempt** from GM rules (**2022**).

111.s: Which one of the following statements regarding mutation breeding is correct?
o: It is necessarily a transgenic technique involving foreign genes.
It is a non-GMO approach, and 71 Trombay varieties have been associated with climate resilience.
It is restricted to the production of GM mosquitoes.
It was used only for developing AquAdvantage salmon.
111.x: Mutation breeding is a non-GMO approach. Seventy-one Trombay varieties are associated with climate resilience.
111.tq: Discriminate between non-GMO mutation breeding and transgenic engineering.
xs: **Mutation breeding** is **non-GMO**, and **71 Trombay varieties** have climate resilience — so option **(2)** is correct.
It is not transgenic; **AquAdvantage** salmon and **GM mosquitoes** are transgenic examples.
xa: Genome-edited **Pusa Rice DST1** also gives stress tolerance **without transgenes**.
ICAR released **524 varieties** in the year, incl. **79 stress-tolerant**.

111.s: The principal nutritional objective of Golden Rice is to address deficiency of which substance?
111.x: Golden Rice produces beta-carotene, which is a precursor of Vitamin A and is intended to help combat Vitamin A deficiency and blindness.
111.tq: Use the application of the genetically modified product to identify its nutritional target.
xs: **Golden Rice** targets **Vitamin A** deficiency/blindness (APPSC **2025**) — so option **(3)** is correct.
It produces **beta-carotene**, the precursor of **Vitamin A**.
xa: Genes: **phytoene synthase from daffodil** + **crtI from Erwinia uredovora**.
Golden Rice **2** takes phytoene synthase from **maize**.
⚠ Golden Rice is **GM**; **biofortification** usually uses **conventional breeding**.

111.s: Which combination of genes is associated with the development of Golden Rice?
o: Phytoene synthase from daffodil and crtI from Erwinia uredovora
Cry1Ac from Bacillus thuringiensis and crtI from maize
Phytoene synthase from Erwinia uredovora and Cry2Ab from daffodil
Alpha-lactalbumin from cow and phytoene synthase from wheat
111.x: Golden Rice contains phytoene synthase derived from daffodil and crtI derived from the bacterium Erwinia uredovora. Golden Rice 2 used maize as the source of phytoene synthase.
111.tq: Start from the sure gene-source pair and distinguish closely related donor organisms.
xs: Golden Rice uses **phytoene synthase from daffodil** and **crtI from Erwinia uredovora** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Cry1Ac** and **Cry2Ab** are Bt genes; **alpha-lactalbumin** is from **Rosie** the cow.
xa: Golden Rice **2** uses **maize** phytoene synthase.
It produces **beta-carotene** (Vitamin A precursor).
It targets Vitamin A deficiency/**blindness** (APPSC **2025**).

111.s: The Flavr Savr tomato, developed by Calgene in the United States in 1994, was notable because it was the first commercially sold GM food and had which characteristic?
o: Resistance to the fruit and shoot borer
Delayed ripening and a longer shelf life
111.x: Flavr Savr was the first commercially sold genetically modified food. Its delayed ripening provided a longer shelf life.
111.tq: Combine the product's historical identity with its distinctive intended trait.
xs: **Flavr Savr** had **delayed ripening and a longer shelf life** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Beta-carotene** is Golden Rice; **fruit and shoot borer** resistance is Bt brinjal.
xa: It was made by **Calgene, USA**, in **1994** — the first commercially sold GM food.
First GMO: **1973**.
First transgenic cow: **Rosie (1997)**.

111.s:
Consider the following statements regarding transgenic animals:
1. Rosie was the first transgenic cow.
2. Rosie produced milk containing human alpha-lactalbumin.
3. Transgenic potatoes and bananas have been investigated for expressing antigens used in edible vaccines.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
111.x: Rosie, produced in 1997, was the first transgenic cow and produced milk containing human alpha-lactalbumin. Transgenic potato and banana have also been investigated for edible vaccines expressing cholera or hepatitis B antigens.
111.tq: Test a cluster of related applications through a coded combination.
xs: All three statements are correct — so option **(4) 1, 2 and 3** is correct.
**Rosie (1997)** was the first transgenic cow, with milk containing **human alpha-lactalbumin**.
**Edible vaccines**: transgenic **potato/banana** expressing **cholera or hepatitis B** antigens.
xa: **GM fish**: fast-growing **AquAdvantage** salmon.
**GM mosquitoes**: suppress populations or block **malaria/dengue/Zika**.

111.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes biofortification from genetic modification?
o: GM technology uses only conventional crossing, whereas biofortification uses viral vectors.
Biofortification usually raises nutrient levels through conventional breeding, whereas GM technology inserts foreign genes.
Biofortification always requires foreign genes, whereas GM technology never changes genes.
Both terms exclusively refer to pesticide resistance.
111.x: Biofortification generally increases nutritional value through conventional breeding, while GM crops involve insertion of foreign genes.
111.tq: Separate two look-alike concepts by their defining technological method.
xs: **Biofortification** raises nutrients usually by **conventional breeding**; **GM** inserts **foreign genes** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Options (1) and (3) reverse the two methods.
xa: Biofortification examples: **Dhanshakti** iron-rich pearl millet (**ICRISAT**); **high-lysine maize**.
ICAR released **524 varieties**, incl. **34 biofortified**.
**Golden Rice** is a GM route to more nutrients (beta-carotene).

111.s: Which of the following is correctly matched?
o: Pusa Rice DST1 — conventional biofortified millet
111.x: Dhanshakti is an iron-rich pearl millet variety associated with ICRISAT. High-lysine maize is another biofortification example, but the other matches are incorrect.
111.tq: Find the correctly matched pair among crop, trait and technology combinations.
xs: **Dhanshakti** = **iron-rich pearl millet** (**ICRISAT**) — so option **(2)** is correct.
**High-lysine maize** is a biofortified crop, not herbicide-tolerant cotton.
**Pusa Rice DST1** is **genome-edited rice** for drought + salinity, not a millet.
xa: Biofortification usually uses **conventional breeding**.
ICAR: **34 biofortified** + **79 stress-tolerant** varieties among **524** released.

111.s:
Consider the following statements about gene-drive mosquitoes:
1. A CRISPR-Cas9 gene drive copies itself onto the partner chromosome, so over 90% of offspring inherit it instead of the normal 50%.
2. Population suppression aims to make the mosquito unable to support parasite development, while population modification produces sterile females.
3. 'Transmission Zero' is a Tanzania-led project on GM mosquitoes.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
111.x: Statement 1 is correct: the drive copies itself onto the partner chromosome, giving over 90% inheritance. Statement 2 is wrong: it reverses the two types - suppression uses sterile females, modification stops the parasite developing. Statement 3 is correct. So 1 and 3 only; '1 only' misses 3, and options with 2 are wrong.
111.tq: Suppression = fewer mosquitoes (sterile females); modification = mosquitoes that cannot carry the parasite.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 correct: the drive copies itself onto the partner chromosome — **over 90%** inherit it (normal **50%**).
Statement 2 wrong: it reverses the types — **suppression** = **sterile females**; **modification** = **parasite cannot develop**.
Statement 3 correct: **"Transmission Zero"** is **Tanzania-led** (20 Apr **2026**).
xa: Gene drives give "**super-Mendelian**" inheritance.
Unlike pesticides, there is **no simple recall** (14 Jul **2026**).

111.s:
Genetically modified mosquitoes have primarily been developed with which of the following objectives?
1. Suppressing mosquito populations
2. Blocking transmission of malaria, dengue or Zika
3. Increasing the reproductive success of disease vectors
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
111.x: GM mosquitoes may be engineered either to suppress mosquito populations or to block transmission of diseases such as malaria, dengue and Zika. Increasing disease-vector reproduction is not an intended objective.
111.tq: Separate intended public-health applications from the reversed biological effect.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — so option **(3)** is correct.
GM mosquitoes are engineered to **suppress populations** or **block malaria/dengue/Zika transmission**.
Statement 3 wrong: increasing vector reproduction is the opposite of the aim.
xa: They raise **ecological + ethical concerns**.
Gene-drive types: **population suppression** vs **population modification**.
Tanzania-led project: **"Transmission Zero"**.

111.s: The term “super-Mendelian inheritance” in the context of gene drives refers to
o: inheritance in which all engineered genes are permanently deleted
inheritance restricted to only the male offspring
inheritance in which a trait spreads through a wild population at a rate greater than ordinary Mendelian inheritance
inheritance occurring only in laboratory microbes
111.x: A gene drive produces super-Mendelian inheritance, allowing an engineered trait to spread through a wild population more rapidly than ordinary Mendelian inheritance.
111.tq: Break the technical term into its defining population-genetics consequence.
xs: **"Super-Mendelian" inheritance** spreads a trait through a wild population **faster than ordinary Mendelian inheritance** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Over 90%** of offspring inherit the drive, against the normal **50%**.
xa: A **CRISPR-Cas9** system copies itself onto the **partner chromosome**.
Outcomes: **population collapse** or **malaria-resistant mosquitoes**.
Concern: **no simple recall**, unlike pesticides.

111.s: Which of the following is a distinctive concern associated with gene-drive mosquitoes?
o: The released trait can be recalled easily by stopping pesticide application.
The trait may spread through wild populations and there is no simple recall mechanism.
The technology is incapable of affecting mosquito populations.
The trait remains confined to the laboratory by definition.
111.x: Gene drives may spread a trait through wild populations, potentially causing population collapse or producing malaria-resistant mosquitoes. Unlike pesticide use, there is no simple recall mechanism.
111.tq: Test the practical implication of an irreversible or difficult-to-recall intervention.
xs: A gene-drive trait **spreads through wild populations** with **no simple recall** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Unlike pesticides, it cannot be stopped by ceasing application (14 Jul **2026**).
xa: Inheritance: **over 90%** of offspring (normal **50%**).
Types: **population suppression** (sterile females) vs **population modification**.
Tanzania-led **"Transmission Zero"** project.

111.s: The principal ecological concern regarding escape of AquAdvantage salmon is that they may
111.x: Escapees of fast-growing transgenic salmon may out-compete wild fish stocks, creating an ecological risk.
111.tq: Match the organism-specific risk with the relevant ecological interaction.
xs: Escaped **AquAdvantage** salmon may **out-compete wild fish stocks** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It is a **fast-growing transgenic salmon**; glyphosate and Bt pollen are unrelated.
xa: **GM mosquitoes** raise ecological + ethical concerns.
**Gene flow** can alter native gene pools and push endangered varieties towards extinction.
First transgenic cow: **Rosie (1997)**.

111.s:
Consider the following statements about CRISPR-Cas9:
1. It is derived from a natural defence of bacteria and archaea against viruses.
2. In this system, the guide RNA acts as the molecular scissors.
3. Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier demonstrated it in 2012 and received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2020.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
111.x: Statement 1 is correct: CRISPR originated as a bacterial/archaeal anti-viral defence. Statement 2 is wrong: Cas9 is the molecular scissors; guide RNA is the navigator. Statement 3 is correct. So 1 and 3 only.
111.tq: Cas9 cuts, guide RNA guides.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 correct: CRISPR is a natural **bacterial/archaeal defence** against viruses.
Statement 2 wrong: **Cas9 = molecular scissors**; **guide RNA = navigator**.
Statement 3 correct: **Doudna and Charpentier**, **2012**; **Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2020**.
xa: CRISPR is simpler, cheaper, more accurate than **ZFNs and TALENs**.
Personalised medicine built on genetic make-up = **CRISPR** (UKPSC **2025**).

111.s:
Consider the following statements about site-directed nuclease (SDN) categories of gene editing in India:
1. SDN-1 makes a small change without a template or foreign DNA and is exempt from GM rules under the 2022 guidelines.
2. SDN-2 uses a template and inserts foreign DNA.
3. SDN-3 inserts foreign DNA and is regulated as GM.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
111.x: Statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 is wrong: SDN-2 uses a template but introduces no foreign DNA, and is also exempt (2022). Statement 3 is correct: SDN-3 inserts foreign DNA and is regulated as GM. So 1 and 3 only; options with 2 are wrong and '1 only' misses 3.
111.tq: Only SDN-3 brings in foreign DNA - only SDN-3 is treated as GM.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — so option **(1)** is correct.
Statement 1 correct: **SDN-1** = small change, no template, no foreign DNA — **exempt** (**2022**).
Statement 2 wrong: **SDN-2** uses a template but adds **no foreign DNA**, and is **exempt**.
Statement 3 correct: **SDN-3** inserts foreign DNA and is regulated as **GM**.
xa: Criticism: **GE crops bypass GMO rules**.
**Pusa Rice DST1** is genome-edited without transgenes.

111.s: Which of the following is a smaller indigenous alternative to CRISPR-Cas9 developed by ICAR and considered easier to deliver?
111.x: TnpB is an indigenous, smaller alternative to CRISPR-Cas9 developed by ICAR and is considered easier to deliver.
111.tq: Match the institution and delivery advantage with the correct gene-editing tool.
xs: **TnpB** (**ICAR**) is an indigenous, **smaller alternative to CRISPR-Cas9**, easier to deliver — so option **(2)** is correct.
**DMH-11** is GM mustard; **Ti plasmid** is Agrobacterium's vector; **Cry2Ab** is a Bt gene.
xa: **CoE for CRISPR Innovation and Translation** to be set up in **Bengaluru**.
**Base editing** converts one base into another **without double-strand breaks**.
**ContactSeek** uses **AlphaFold3** to cut off-target edits.

111.s: Base editing differs from conventional double-strand-break editing because it:
o: Changes proteins without altering DNA bases
Converts one DNA base into another without creating double-strand breaks
Works exclusively by destroying the host cell
111.x: Base editing converts one DNA base into another without producing double-strand breaks in the DNA.
111.tq: Focus on the defining molecular distinction rather than the general purpose of gene editing.
xs: **Base editing** converts one DNA base into another **without double-strand breaks** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It does change DNA bases, so (1) is wrong; it does not insert chromosomes or destroy cells.
xa: Risk: a **6-year-old** in China died (March **2025**) after a first-of-its-kind **brain base-editing therapy**.
**ContactSeek** (27 Jul **2026**) cuts off-target edits.
Regulation: **CDSCO gene therapy rules 2023**.

111.s: ContactSeek is an AI tool associated with AlphaFold3 that is intended to:
111.x: ContactSeek uses AI with AlphaFold3 to help cut off-target edits, thereby improving the precision of gene editing.
111.tq: Match the named emerging tool with its specific biotechnology application.
xs: **ContactSeek** uses **AlphaFold3** to **cut off-target edits** — so option **(4)** is correct.
Bt toxin, **PCR** amplification and **T-DNA** transfer are unrelated tools.
xa: ContactSeek was reported on 27 Jul **2026**.
**Base editing** works **without double-strand breaks**.
**TnpB** (ICAR) is a smaller alternative to Cas9.

111.s: Personalised medicine built on an individual's genetic make-up is most directly associated with which technology?
111.x: Personalised medicine built on genetic make-up is associated with CRISPR (UKPSC 2025 key). PCR only amplifies DNA, mutation breeding is a crop method, and V-GURT makes sterile seeds.
111.tq: Personalised medicine = CRISPR.
xs: Personalised medicine built on genetic make-up = **CRISPR gene editing** (UKPSC **2025**) — so option **(1)** is correct.
**V-GURT** (Terminator) makes **sterile seeds**; **mutation breeding** is a non-GMO crop method.
xa: **Genetic medicines** correct/compensate for faulty genes, carried by **engineered viruses and lipid nanoparticles**.
**Mitochondrial replacement therapy** = "**three-parent baby**".
Regulation: **CDSCO gene therapy rules 2023**.

111.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. CRISPR-Cas9 is simpler, cheaper and more accurate than ZFNs and TALENs and can target many genes at once.
2. A Centre of Excellence for CRISPR Innovation and Translation (CoE-CIT) is to be set up in Bengaluru.
3. TnpB is larger than Cas9 and therefore harder to deliver.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
111.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: TnpB (ICAR) is a smaller alternative to CRISPR-Cas9 with easier delivery. So '1 and 2 only'; '1 only' misses the Bengaluru CoE, and options with 3 are wrong.
111.tq: CRISPR beats ZFN/TALEN; TnpB is smaller.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 correct: CRISPR-Cas9 is **simpler, cheaper, more accurate** than **ZFNs and TALENs** and targets many genes at once.
Statement 2 correct: **CoE-CIT** is to be set up in **Bengaluru**.
Statement 3 wrong: **TnpB** is **smaller** than Cas9, with **easier delivery**.
xa: CRISPR was demonstrated in **2012** by **Doudna and Charpentier**.
**SDN-1/SDN-2** edits are **exempt** from GM rules (**2022**).

111.s: Which of the following best describes the principal objective of genetic medicines?
o: To prevent the formation of mitochondrial DNA
To correct or compensate for faulty genes
To replace all normal cells with genetically modified cells
111.x: Genetic medicines are intended to correct or compensate for faulty genes. They do not aim to replace all normal cells or prevent mitochondrial DNA formation.
111.tq: Use the precise functional definition rather than choosing an extreme purpose.
xs: The principal objective of **genetic medicines** is **to correct or compensate for faulty genes** — so option **(2)** is correct.
They do not replace all normal cells, prevent **mitochondrial DNA** formation or produce antibiotic-resistant cells; the aim is gene correction.
xa: Carriers for genetic medicines are **engineered viruses** and **lipid nanoparticles** (UPSC **2026**: all statements correct).
Indian regulation: **CDSCO gene therapy rules 2023**.
⚠ Risk case: a 6-year-old in **China** died (March **2025**) after a first-of-its-kind **brain base-editing therapy**.

111.s: Which of the following can serve as carriers for delivering genetic medicines?
111.x: Engineered viruses and lipid nanoparticles are used as carriers for delivering genetic material in genetic medicine.
111.tq: Directly identify the correct delivery carriers from closely related biological alternatives.
xs: Genetic medicines are delivered by **engineered viruses and lipid nanoparticles** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Bacterial spores, blood cells or pollen are not the carriers named for genetic medicines.
xa: Genetic medicines **correct or compensate for faulty genes**.
**Recombinant vaccines**: **Hepatitis B**, **HPV**, **COVID-19**.
**Synthetic biology**: **insulin**, **artemisinin** made by microbes; **semaglutide** grown in **baker's yeast**.

111.s: Mitochondrial Replacement Therapy is popularly known as the ____ technique, and its main ethical concern relates to ____.
o: three-parent baby; germline editing and designer babies
three-parent baby; pollen sterility in crops
synthetic-embryo; germline editing and designer babies
111.x: MRT is the 'three-parent baby' technique and raises ethical issues of germline editing and designer babies (A). B has the wrong name and concern; C has the right name but a crop issue; D has the right concern but the wrong name.
111.tq: Three parents = nuclear DNA of two parents + donor mitochondria.
xs: **Mitochondrial replacement therapy** is the **"three-parent baby"** technique, and its ethical issue is **germline editing and designer babies** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Option (2) has the wrong name and concern; option (3) has the right name but a crop issue (pollen sterility); option (4) has the right concern but the wrong name.
xa: Genetic medicines aim to **correct/compensate for faulty genes**, carried by **engineered viruses** and **lipid nanoparticles**.
Gene therapy in India is regulated by the **CDSCO gene therapy rules 2023**.
⚠ **Sterile seeds** (crop issue) belong to **V-GURT (Terminator)** technology, not to human therapy.

111.s: The CDSCO gene therapy rules referred to in the context of genetic medicine were issued in:
111.x: The relevant CDSCO gene therapy rules were issued in 2023.
111.tq: Test the exact year using nearby-year distractors.
xs: The **CDSCO gene therapy rules** were issued in **2023** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**2022** is the year of India's genome-editing guidelines exempting **SDN-1** and **SDN-2** from GM rules — a confusable date.
xa: Genetic medicines' carriers: **engineered viruses** and **lipid nanoparticles**.
**Mitochondrial replacement therapy** = **"three-parent baby"** technique.
⚠ A child in **China** died (March **2025**) after a **brain base-editing therapy**.

111.s: Which one of the following combinations consists entirely of recombinant vaccines mentioned in the context of genetic medicine?
o: Hepatitis B, HPV and COVID-19 vaccines
Malaria, typhoid and yellow fever vaccines
111.x: The recombinant vaccines specifically mentioned are those for hepatitis B, HPV and COVID-19.
111.tq: Split the options and identify the combination containing only the stated examples.
xs: The recombinant vaccines listed are **Hepatitis B, HPV and COVID-19** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Recombinant vaccines are made by **rDNA technology**; the other sets are not the ones named in the notes.
xa: First human hormone by rDNA: **insulin**; human insulin marketed **1982** (**Humulin**).
**Edible vaccines**: transgenic **potato/banana** expressing **cholera** or **hepatitis B** antigens.
**Synthetic biology**: **artemisinin** by microbes; **semaglutide** grown in **baker's yeast**.

111.s:
Consider the following statements about synthetic biology:
1. Insulin and artemisinin have been produced by microbes.
2. Semaglutide has been grown in Bacillus thuringiensis.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
111.x: Statement 1 is correct: insulin and artemisinin are made by microbes. Statement 2 is wrong: semaglutide was grown in baker's yeast, not Bacillus thuringiensis (the Bt gene source). Hence 1 only.
111.tq: Semaglutide - baker's yeast.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **insulin** and **artemisinin** are produced by **microbes** — so **1 only**, option **(1)**.
Statement 2 is wrong: **semaglutide** is grown in **baker's yeast**, not in **Bacillus thuringiensis**.
**Bacillus thuringiensis** is the soil bacterium that is the source of the **Bt gene** (crystal **delta-endotoxins**).
xa: **Recombinant vaccines**: **Hepatitis B**, **HPV**, **COVID-19**.
First human hormone by rDNA = **insulin** (UKPSC **2024**); **Humulin** marketed **1982**.
**Genetic medicines** correct or compensate for faulty genes (carriers: **engineered viruses**, **lipid nanoparticles**).

111.s: Transfer of herbicide-tolerance from a GM crop into weedy relatives may result in:
o: Reduction in the number of plant genes
Immediate conversion of weeds into crops
Permanent loss of all soil microbes
111.x: Movement of herbicide-tolerance genes into weedy relatives can create invasive superweeds and increase weediness.
111.tq: Link the transferred trait with its most direct ecological consequence.
xs: Herbicide-tolerance moving into weedy relatives creates invasive **superweeds** with **increased weediness** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Gene flow does not reduce plant gene numbers, turn weeds into crops or wipe out all soil microbes.
xa: **Gene flow** (transgenes moving by **pollen**/cross-pollination) is the **primary environmental concern** of GM crops (PYQ).
Gene flow also **alters native gene pools** and can push **endangered varieties** of the same genus towards extinction.
Herbicide concern: HT crops encourage heavy **glyphosate** use; **Punjab banned glyphosate sale in 2018**.

111.s:
Consider the following statements about gene flow from GM crops:
1. The risk of transgene escape is highest in a crop's centre of origin or diversity, where many wild relatives occur.
2. India being a centre of diversity of wheat was a key argument against Bt brinjal.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
111.x: Statement 1 is correct: centres of origin/diversity hold many wild relatives, so risk is highest there. Statement 2 is wrong: the argument against Bt brinjal was that India is a centre of diversity of brinjal itself. Hence 1 only.
111.tq: Bt brinjal objection = India is brinjal's centre of diversity.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: risk of transgene escape is highest at a crop's **centre of origin/diversity**, with many **wild relatives** — so **1 only**, option **(1)**.
Statement 2 is wrong: India is the centre of diversity of **brinjal**, not wheat — that was the key argument against **Bt brinjal**.
xa: **Bt brinjal**: GEAC recommended release **2009**; **moratorium 2010** (**Jairam Ramesh**).
Bt brinjal was developed by **Mahyco + UAS Dharwad + TNAU** against **fruit and shoot borer**.
Gene flow can create **superweeds** and alter native gene pools.

111.s:
Which of the following may be adversely affected by Bt toxins or other engineered traits?
1. Pollinators
2. Natural enemies of pests
3. Soil nematodes and microbes
4. Aquatic organisms
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
111.x: Bt toxins or other engineered traits may affect beneficial insects such as pollinators and natural enemies, soil nematodes and microbes, and aquatic organisms.
111.tq: Use an all-inclusive option when each listed ecological group is affected by the same broad concern.
xs: Bt toxins or engineered traits may harm **pollinators, natural enemies, soil nematodes/microbes and aquatic organisms** — all four, option **(3)** (**1, 2, 3 and 4**).
This **non-target harm** is a listed environmental risk alongside **gene flow**.
xa: Bt gene source: **Bacillus thuringiensis**; protoxin activated in the **alkaline gut** of larvae, creates pores in midgut.
Bt proteins were feared to persist, but experiments show they **degrade in soil**.
**Pink bollworm** developed resistance to Bt toxins — resistance build-up is also a listed risk.

111.s: Which one of the following is regarded as the primary environmental concern about the cultivation of GM crops?
o: Transgenes moving by cross-pollination into non-GM crops and wild relatives
111.x: Gene flow, the movement of transgenes by pollen into non-GM crops and wild relatives, is the primary environmental concern (PYQ). It can create superweeds and alter native gene pools. The other options are not GM-crop concerns.
111.tq: GM crop main worry = gene flow by pollen.
xs: The primary environmental concern of GM crops is **gene flow**: **transgenes moving by cross-pollination into non-GM crops and wild relatives** — option **(1)** (PYQ).
Soil evaporation, ozone depletion and canal salinisation are not GM-crop concerns.
xa: Gene flow effects: invasive **superweeds**, raised **weediness**, altered **native gene pools**.
Risk is highest at a crop's **centre of origin/diversity**; India = centre of diversity of **brinjal**.
**Non-target harm**: pollinators, natural enemies, **soil nematodes/microbes**, aquatic organisms.

111.s: A soybean variety containing a Brazil-nut gene was not released commercially primarily because of concern regarding:
111.x: The Brazil-nut gene was intended to improve methionine content, but the resulting soybean raised allergy concerns and was therefore never released.
111.tq: Identify the risk that explains why a genetically modified product was withheld from release.
xs: The Brazil-nut-gene soybean was **never released** because of **allergenicity** — it triggered allergy in Brazil-nut-allergic people — option **(1)**.
The gene was added for **methionine**, so failure to produce methionine was not the issue.
xa: **Horizontal gene transfer**: genes moving between **unrelated organisms**.
**Antibiotic-resistance marker genes** raise fears of spreading resistance.
**Mon 863**: Monsanto's **pest-resistant maize** (against **corn rootworm**), in news over feeding-study safety.

111.s: Horizontal gene transfer in the biosafety context refers to:
o: Replacement of nuclear DNA by mitochondrial DNA in every cell
Movement of genes between unrelated organisms
Transmission of genes only from parent to offspring
Movement of pollen only within one flower
111.x: Horizontal gene transfer is the movement of genes between unrelated organisms. Antibiotic-resistance genes may potentially pass from environmental bacteria to human pathogens.
111.tq: Distinguish horizontal transfer from ordinary vertical inheritance.
xs: **Horizontal gene transfer** is the **movement of genes between unrelated organisms** — option **(2)** is correct.
Example: **antibiotic-resistance genes** can pass from soil/environment bacteria to **human pathogens**.
Parent-to-offspring transmission is vertical inheritance, not horizontal transfer.
xa: **Allergenicity**: **Brazil-nut** gene soybean caused allergy → **never released**.
**Mon 863** = GM **pest-resistant maize** (Monsanto; corn rootworm).
**Gene drives** spread a trait in a wild population — **over 90%** of offspring inherit it (normal **50%**).

111.s: The use of antibiotic-resistance marker genes in the construction of GM organisms raises concern primarily because such genes may:
111.x: Antibiotic-resistance marker genes may contribute to the spread of antibiotic resistance, which is a recognised biosafety concern.
111.tq: Link the marker gene with the specific public-health risk it may create.
xs: **Antibiotic-resistance marker genes** used in GM construction raise fears that they may **spread antibiotic resistance** — option **(4)** is correct.
"Antibiotic resistance" is listed among the **health risks** of GM organisms.
xa: **Plasmid** vectors carry **antibiotic-resistance genes** for selection.
**Horizontal gene transfer** can move resistance genes from environmental bacteria to **human pathogens**.
**Brazil-nut** soybean: **allergenicity** risk → never released.

111.s: Mon 863, which was in the news over the safety of feeding studies, was a genetically modified:
o: Vitamin-A enriched rice targeting night blindness
111.x: Mon 863 was a Monsanto genetically modified pest-resistant maize variety directed against corn rootworm and was discussed in connection with feeding-study safety.
111.tq: Use the crop-pest association to identify the correct GM variety.
xs: **Mon 863** was a **genetically modified pest-resistant maize** (Monsanto) **against corn rootworm** — option **(2)** is correct.
It was in the news over the **safety of feeding studies** (PYQ).
**Vitamin-A rice** is **Golden Rice**, not Mon 863.
xa: **Golden Rice** makes **beta-carotene**; genes: **phytoene synthase** from daffodil + **crtI** from **Erwinia uredovora**.
GEAC cleared confined trials of Bayer's **HT + insect-resistant GM maize** at **PAU**, Kharif **2025**.
**Brazil-nut** soybean → never released (allergenicity).

111.s: Which one of the following best explains genetic homogenisation in agriculture?
o: Cultivation of many locally adapted landraces in small farms
Increase in the number of unrelated crop species in a field
Exchange of seeds among farmers without commercial restrictions
Use of uniform engineered varieties over large areas, reducing agro-biodiversity
111.x: Genetic homogenisation results when uniform varieties are widely cultivated, reducing agro-biodiversity and increasing vulnerability to new pathogens and climate shocks.
111.tq: Choose the option that contains both the process and its defining consequence.
xs: **Genetic homogenisation** = **uniform engineered varieties over large areas**, **reducing agro-biodiversity** — option **(4)** is correct.
It raises vulnerability to **new pathogens** and **climate shocks**; growing many landraces is the opposite.
xa: **Monoculture** and a few patented seed firms displace **landraces** and farmer varieties.
Safeguards: **National Genebank** (**4,70,513** accessions, **2026**), **PPV&FR Act**, **National Gene Fund**.
PYQ: **genetic modification** is the technology flagged for impact on **biodiversity**.

111.s: Monoculture and the dominance of a few patented seed firms can lead to the displacement of:
111.x: Monoculture and concentration of seed production can displace traditional landraces and farmer varieties.
111.tq: Identify the specific agricultural genetic resources affected by monoculture.
xs: Monoculture and dominance of a few **patented seed firms** displace **landraces and farmer varieties** — option **(2)** is correct.
It is crop diversity that is lost — not pollinators, nitrogen or aquatic plants.
xa: **Genetic homogenisation**: uniform varieties over large areas → less **agro-biodiversity**.
The **PPV&FR Act** protects farmers' varieties, **landraces** and **wild relatives**.
**Terminator seeds** end **seed saving** → seed sovereignty and **corporate dependency** concerns.

111.s: Which technological development has been specifically flagged for its impact on biodiversity?
111.x: Genetic modification has been identified as the technology among these options that was flagged for its potential impact on biodiversity.
111.tq: Use the exclusion pattern to distinguish the biodiversity concern from unrelated technologies.
xs: **Genetic modification** is the technology flagged for its impact on **biodiversity** (PYQ) — option **(4)** is correct.
⚠ Trap: **solar panels**, **wind turbines** and **rainwater harvesting** are not the answer.
xa: GM risks to biodiversity: **gene flow**, **superweeds**, **genetic homogenisation**.
**Monoculture** displaces **landraces** and farmer varieties.
**National Genebank** holds **4,70,513** accessions (**2026**).

111.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched with a safeguard for crop genetic diversity?
o: National Gene Fund — prohibition of benefit sharing
PPV&FR Act — compulsory destruction of landraces
National Genebank — promotion of genetic homogenisation
111.x: The National Genebank conserves accessions. The PPV&FR Act protects farmers’ varieties, landraces and wild relatives, while the National Gene Fund relates to benefit sharing.
111.tq: Match each safeguard with its actual conservation or benefit-sharing function.
xs: The **National Genebank** conserves **accessions** (**4,70,513** in **2026**) — option **(4)** is correct.
The **National Gene Fund** is for **benefit sharing**, not its prohibition.
The **PPV&FR Act** protects **landraces**, farmers' varieties and wild relatives, not their destruction; the Genebank counters homogenisation.
xa: **V-GURT (Terminator)** is **banned in India under the PPV&FR Act (2001)**.
**Genetic homogenisation** reduces agro-biodiversity and raises vulnerability to pathogens and climate shocks.
**Mutation breeding** (non-GMO): **71 Trombay varieties** with climate resilience.

111.s: Which statement correctly distinguishes V-GURT from T-GURT?
o: V-GURT switches traits chemically, whereas T-GURT produces sterile seeds in every case.
V-GURT produces sterile seeds, whereas T-GURT switches a desired trait on or off through a proprietary chemical.
Both technologies are fully commercialised in India.
Both technologies refer only to antibiotic-resistance markers.
111.x: V-GURT, or terminator technology, makes the next generation of seeds non-viable. T-GURT controls expression of a desired trait using a proprietary chemical.
111.tq: Discriminate between two similar abbreviations by their mechanisms.
xs: **V-GURT** produces **sterile seeds**, while **T-GURT** switches a desired trait **on/off through a proprietary chemical** — option **(2)** is correct.
Option (1) swaps the two; neither is commercialised in India (**V-GURT is banned**; T-GURT is at **research stage**).
xa: V-GURT = **"Terminator"**; T-GURT = **"Traitor"**.
V-GURT is **not commercialised anywhere**; **banned in India under the PPV&FR Act (2001)**.
Farmer concern: seeds **incapable of forming viable seeds** → annual purchase forced.

111.s: Which of the following correctly describes the status of V-GURT in India and globally?
o: It is commercialised everywhere and compulsory in India.
It is not commercialised anywhere and is banned in India under the PPV&FR Act, 2001.
It is used only in public seed banks and encouraged under the PPV&FR Act.
It is research-stage technology with no legal status in India.
111.x: V-GURT has not been commercialised anywhere and is banned in India under the PPV&FR Act, 2001.
111.tq: Combine the technology’s global status with the specific Indian legal position.
xs: **V-GURT** is **not commercialised anywhere** and is **banned in India under the PPV&FR Act, 2001** — option **(2)** is correct.
"Research stage" describes **T-GURT (Traitor)**, not V-GURT.
xa: V-GURT (**Terminator**): plant produces **sterile seeds**; next generation cannot form viable seed.
T-GURT: trait switched on/off by a **proprietary chemical**.
Concern: ends **seed saving/replanting** → **seed sovereignty** and corporate dependency issues.

111.s: The principal concern of farmers regarding terminator technology is that it:
o: Allows farmers to reuse seed indefinitely without purchase
Increases the nutritional value of every seed
Makes all crops resistant to every insect
Prevents plants from forming viable seeds, ending normal seed saving and replanting
111.x: Terminator technology makes the next generation of seeds non-viable, preventing seed saving and replanting and potentially forcing annual purchases.
111.tq: Apply the mechanism to the farmer’s seed-saving decision.
xs: Terminator technology **prevents plants from forming viable seeds**, **ending seed saving and replanting** — option **(4)** is correct.
Farmers are forced into **annual purchase** of seed; it does not add nutrition or universal insect resistance.
xa: Terminator = **V-GURT**; **banned in India under the PPV&FR Act (2001)**; not commercialised anywhere.
**T-GURT (Traitor)**: trait controlled by a **proprietary chemical**; research stage.
Wider concerns: **seed sovereignty** and **corporate dependency**.

111.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched with Pusa Rice DST1?
o: Edited version of MTU1010 — rice bred at Maruteru in Andhra Pradesh
Transgenic version of AquAdvantage — salmon bred in Punjab
Bt version of IR8 — rice bred in Colombia
Gene-drive version of MTU1010 — mosquito bred in Maruteru
111.x: Pusa Rice DST1 is an edited version of MTU1010, an Andhra Pradesh-bred rice variety associated with Maruteru.
111.tq: Combine the crop identity, source variety and regional association in one precise match.
xs: **Pusa Rice DST1** is an **edited version of MTU1010**, an AP-bred rice from **Maruteru** — option **(1)** is correct.
It is **genome-edited**, not transgenic, Bt or gene-drive; **AquAdvantage** is a GM **salmon**.
xa: DST1 gives **drought + salinity** tolerance, **10-30%** higher yield under stress.
India set to commercially launch it as its **first genome-edited rice** (**1 Sep 2026**).
**SDN-1/SDN-2** edits (no foreign DNA) are **exempt** from GM rules (**2022** guidelines).

111.s:
Consider the following statements about the debate on genetic engineering:
1. Societies generally accept gene therapy but resist GM crops.
2. GM maize, soy, cotton and canola are grown and traded widely.
3. Genome-edited crops face stricter rules than GMOs.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
111.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct as stated in the debate. Statement 3 is wrong: the criticism is that genome-edited crops bypass GMO rules, not that they face stricter rules. So 1 and 2 only.
111.tq: Criticism of GE crops: they bypass GMO rules.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: societies **accept gene therapy but resist GM crops** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(2)**.
Statement 2 is correct: **GM maize, soy, cotton and canola** are grown and traded widely.
Statement 3 is wrong: the criticism is that genome-edited crops **bypass GMO rules**, not face stricter ones.
xa: **SDN-1** and **SDN-2** (no foreign DNA) are **exempt** from GM rules (**2022**); **SDN-3** inserts foreign DNA → regulated as GM.
**Pusa Rice DST1** = India's first genome-edited rice to be launched commercially.
**Bt cotton** (**2002**) remains the **first and only** GM crop commercially cultivated in India.

111.s:
With reference to the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety, consider the following statements:
1. It was adopted in 2000.
2. It entered into force in 2003.
3. It governs the transboundary movement of living modified organisms.
4. India is a party to it.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
111.x: The Cartagena Protocol was adopted in 2000, entered into force in 2003, governs transboundary movement of living modified organisms, and India is a party to it.
111.tq: Check each date, subject matter and membership statement before selecting the complete combination.
xs: All four are correct — option **(4)** (**1, 2, 3 and 4**).
The **Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety** was adopted in **2000** and came into force in **2003**.
It governs **transboundary movement of LMOs**, and **India is a party**.
xa: It is named after **Colombia**'s Cartagena.
In India, **GEAC** approves GM releases — e.g. **GM mustard DMH-11** (environmental release **Oct 2022**), now **under Supreme Court consideration**.
First GMO: **1973**; first GM food sold: **Flavr Savr tomato** (**1994**).

112.s: Which one of the following is the apex statutory body regulating genetically modified organisms in India?
o: Food Safety and Standards Authority of India
112.x: The Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee (GEAC) is the apex statutory body regulating GMOs in India. FSSAI, CPCB and ICAR are not the apex GMO regulator.
112.tq: Distinguish the correct regulatory authority from closely related bodies.
xs: The **Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee (GEAC)** is the **apex statutory body** that regulates GMOs in India — option **(2)** (APPSC-G2 **2023**).
⚠ Trap (PYQ): **FSSAI**, **CPCB** and **ICAR** are not the GMO regulator.
xa: GEAC is constituted in **MoEFCC** under the **Rules, 1989** of the **Environment (Protection) Act 1986**.
Chair: **Special/Additional Secretary, MoEFCC**; co-chair from **DBT**.
Renamed from "**Approval**" to "**Appraisal**" Committee in **2010**.

112.s: The Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee is chaired by:
o: The Special or Additional Secretary of the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
The Chairperson of the Central Pollution Control Board
The Director-General of the Indian Council of Agricultural Research
112.x: GEAC is chaired by a Special or Additional Secretary of MoEFCC. A senior officer from the Department of Biotechnology serves as co-chair.
112.tq: Apply the 'who would do this job?' method to identify the correct chairing authority.
xs: GEAC is chaired by the **Special/Additional Secretary of MoEFCC** — option **(1)** is correct.
The **Department of Biotechnology** provides only the **co-chair**, not the chair; CPCB and ICAR have no such role.
xa: GEAC sits in **MoEFCC** under the **Rules, 1989** (EPA **1986**).
It approves **field trials** and **commercial release** of GM crops.
**RCGM** (under **DBT**) monitors ongoing research and recommends to GEAC.

112.s: Which one of the following is NOT a function of the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee?
o: Approving field trials of genetically modified crops
Approving commercial release and cultivation of GM organisms
Approving large-scale use of hazardous microorganisms and recombinants
Fixing the maximum retail price of all commercial seeds
112.x: GEAC deals with field trials, environmental release, commercial cultivation and large-scale use of hazardous microorganisms and recombinants. Fixing the maximum retail price of all commercial seeds is not its function.
112.tq: Find the one unrelated function among powers of the same regulatory body.
xs: **Fixing the maximum retail price of commercial seeds** is not a GEAC function — option **(4)** is the answer.
GEAC approves **field trials and commercial release** of GM crops — option (1) is a function.
It approves **large-scale use, environmental release and commercial cultivation** of GMOs, and **large-scale use of hazardous microorganisms** and recombinants — options (2), (3).
xa: GEAC = **apex/statutory** GMO regulator, in **MoEFCC**.
Chair: **Special/Additional Secretary, MoEFCC**; co-chair: **DBT**.
⚠ Genome-edited **SDN-1/SDN-2** crops **skip GEAC** and need only **IBC** approval.

112.s: The Genetic Engineering Approval Committee was renamed the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee in:
112.x: The committee was renamed from Genetic Engineering Approval Committee to Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee in 2010.
112.tq: Use the exact year to distinguish a renamed institution from nearby biotechnology events.
xs: The **Genetic Engineering Approval Committee** was renamed the **Appraisal** Committee in **2010** — option **(3)** is correct.
**2002** is the year of **Bt cotton** approval; **2006** the PIL in the Supreme Court; **2014** the resumption of trials.
xa: **2010** also saw **Jairam Ramesh**'s **moratorium on Bt brinjal** and a mandatory **State NOC** for field trials.
GEAC is constituted under the **Rules, 1989** of the **EPA 1986**.
GEAC cleared **DMH-11** environmental release in **2022**.

112.s: The Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee (GEAC) is constituted under:
o: The Seeds Act, 1966, in the Ministry of Agriculture
The Rules, 1989 made under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, in MoEFCC
The Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, in the Ministry of Health
The Biological Diversity Act, 2002, in the Department of Biotechnology
112.x: GEAC is constituted in MoEFCC under the Rules, 1989 framed under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. The FSS Act 2006 governs GM food, the Biological Diversity Act 2002 is part of the wider biosafety framework, and the Seeds Act is not its basis.
112.tq: GEAC = MoEFCC + Rules 1989 + EPA 1986.
xs: GEAC is constituted in **MoEFCC** under **the Rules, 1989** made under the **Environment (Protection) Act, 1986** — option **(2)** is correct.
The **FSS Act 2006** is the legal basis for **GM food**, not GEAC.
The **Biological Diversity Act 2002** is part of the wider biosafety framework; the Seeds Act is not GEAC's basis.
xa: Other committees under the Rules 1989: **RDAC**, **IBSC**, **RCGM**, **SBCC**, **DLC**.
GEAC chair: **Special/Additional Secretary, MoEFCC**; co-chair from **DBT**.
Renamed "Appraisal" Committee in **2010**.

112.s:
Consider the following statements about the GMO regulatory bodies under the Rules, 1989:
1. RDAC, under DBT, is advisory and recommends safety regulations.
2. RCGM functions under MoEFCC and approves commercial release of GM crops.
3. IBSC is the first tier, functioning at the institutional level.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
112.x: Statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 is wrong: RCGM is under DBT and monitors ongoing research and advises GEAC; GEAC (MoEFCC) approves environmental release and commercial use. Statement 3 is correct. So 1 and 3 only.
112.tq: RCGM = DBT, advises; GEAC = MoEFCC, approves.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **RDAC** (DBT) is **advisory** and recommends safety regulations — so **1 and 3 only**, option **(2)**.
Statement 2 is wrong: **RCGM** is under **DBT** (Ministry of S&T); it monitors research and advises GEAC. **GEAC (MoEFCC)** approves commercial release.
Statement 3 is correct: **IBSC** is the **first tier**, at each institution.
xa: **SBCC** (State): powers to inspect, investigate and take **punitive action**.
**DLC** (District): field-level monitoring.
**IBSC** now clears **genome-edited crops** (Dec **2025**).

112.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: SBCC — State-level inspection, investigation and punitive action
DLC — Approval of all commercial GM releases
112.x: SBCC operates at the state level and has powers to inspect, investigate and take punitive action. DLC performs district-level monitoring, GEAC deals with environmental release and commercial use, and IBSC is institutional.
112.tq: Use the level of operation to reject swapped committee functions.
xs: **SBCC** is the **State-level** body with powers to **inspect, investigate and take punitive action** — option **(1)** is correct.
**DLC** does **district-level monitoring**, not commercial approvals; **GEAC** (MoEFCC) approves environmental release; **IBSC** is **institutional**, not international.
xa: Six tiers: **IBSC → RCGM → GEAC → SBCC → DLC** → expert committees.
**RCGM** under **DBT** monitors ongoing research.
Plus **rDNA Guidelines 2017**.

112.s:
Arrange the following bodies in the sequence of the six-tier biosafety system beginning with the institutional level:
A. GEAC
B. IBSC
C. DLC
D. RCGM
112.x: The sequence is IBSC, RCGM, GEAC, SBCC, DLC and expert committees. Among the listed bodies, the order is IBSC, RCGM, GEAC and DLC.
112.tq: Arrange administrative bodies by the stated regulatory progression.
xs: Order: **IBSC → RCGM → GEAC → DLC** (B, D, A, C) — option **(1)** is correct.
Full six-tier system: **IBSC → RCGM → GEAC → SBCC → DLC → expert committees**.
xa: **IBSC** = institution level, first tier; **RCGM** = **DBT**; **GEAC** = **MoEFCC**, apex.
**SBCC** = State (punitive action); **DLC** = District (field monitoring).
**RDAC** (DBT) is **advisory**, recommending safety regulations.

112.s: Which one of the following is NOT included among the broader instruments or features of the Indian biosafety framework described?
o: A separate enacted biosafety liability law
112.x: The framework includes the Biological Diversity Act, 2002 and the National Biosafety Framework, along with the rDNA Guidelines, 2017. Notably, there is no biosafety liability law.
112.tq: Identify the stated legal gap rather than a listed framework instrument.
xs: India has **no biosafety liability law** — so **a separate enacted biosafety liability law** is not part of the framework, option **(2)**.
The framework does include the **rDNA Guidelines 2017**, the **National Biosafety Framework** and the **Biological Diversity Act 2002**.
xa: Overlapping mandates (**DBT, GEAC, CDSCO, FSSAI, NBA**) → **7-10 years** for GM approval vs **3-5** globally.
National Biosafety Framework dates to **2009**.
The **BRAI Bill, 2013** (single regulator) **lapsed** with the **15th Lok Sabha**.

112.s:
Which sequence correctly represents the regulatory pathway for a confined biotechnology crop field trial?
A. Commercial clearance
B. Confined open-plot trials at agricultural universities or ICAR plots
C. Committees’ safety assessments
D. Assessment of superiority over non-GM varieties without ecological harm
112.x: The process begins with committees’ safety assessments, followed by confined open-plot trials, evaluation of superiority without ecological harm, and only then commercial clearance.
112.tq: Arrange the process from preliminary safety review to field testing, final evaluation and clearance.
xs: Order: **committees' safety assessments → confined open-plot trials → superiority test without ecological harm → commercial clearance** (C, B, D, A) — option **(1)**.
Trials run at **agricultural universities/ICAR plots** over several seasons and locations.
xa: Trials are **Biosafety Research Level** trials (**BRL-I**, **BRL-II**).
Field trials need the **State's NOC**; several States refuse them.
GEAC approves **field trials** and **commercial release**.

112.s: The field trials conducted before commercial clearance of GM crops are known as:
112.x: The trials are called Biosafety Research Level trials, comprising BRL-I and BRL-II stages.
112.tq: Expand the abbreviation precisely; similar-looking expansions are used as distractors.
xs: Pre-commercial field trials are **Biosafety Research Level** trials — **BRL-I** and **BRL-II** — option **(3)** is correct.
The other names are not used in the notes.
xa: They are **confined open-plot trials** at agricultural universities/**ICAR** plots.
Commercial clearance only if **superior to non-GM** varieties **without ecological harm**.
**State's NOC** is needed for field trials (made mandatory in **2010**).

112.s: Which of the following statements regarding commercial clearance of a GM crop is correct?
o: Clearance is granted only when the crop is superior to non-GM varieties and causes no ecological harm
Clearance follows automatically after one confined trial season
Clearance is possible even when ecological harm is established
Clearance depends exclusively on the market price of the crop
112.x: Commercial clearance is contemplated only when trials show superiority over non-GM varieties without ecological harm.
112.tq: Apply the stated approval condition to a practical clearance situation.
xs: Commercial clearance comes **only if the crop is superior to non-GM varieties and causes no ecological harm** — option **(1)** is correct.
It is not automatic after one season: trials run over **several seasons and locations**; market price is not the test.
xa: Sequence: safety assessments → **confined open-plot trials** → evaluation → clearance.
Trial levels: **BRL-I**, **BRL-II**.
**GEAC** grants environmental release and commercial use.

112.s: Which one of the following statements regarding field trials of GM crops is correct?
o: State-level approval is unnecessary when GEAC grants approval.
Field trials require the State's no-objection certificate, and several States have refused such permission.
Only the Department of Biotechnology can grant State-level permission.
State governments have no role in field trials.
112.x: Field trials require the State's NOC, and several States have refused to provide it. This creates an important element of State-level control.
112.tq: Apply the federal administrative condition to a field-trial scenario.
xs: Field trials **require the State's no-objection certificate**, and **several States have refused** — option **(2)** is correct.
So States do have a role; GEAC approval alone is not enough, and DBT does not issue State permission.
xa: The **State NOC** was made **mandatory in 2010**, with the **Bt brinjal** moratorium.
**SBCC** at State level can inspect, investigate and take **punitive action**.
Trials are **BRL-I/BRL-II** confined open-plot trials.

112.s: Under the Indian legal framework, import of genetically modified food requires:
o: Only a certificate from the exporting country
No approval if the food is commercially available abroad
Approval exclusively from a district-level committee
112.x: Import of GM food requires approval from the competent authority under Indian law. Foreign commercial availability does not remove this requirement.
112.tq: Apply the approval requirement to an import situation.
xs: GM food requires **approval of the competent authority** (**FSSAI GM food framework, 2024**) — option **(3)** is correct.
The law **prohibits GM food import without approval**; availability abroad or a foreign certificate does not suffice.
xa: Legal basis: **Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006**.
UPSC **2024** PYQ: India **does import** US apples (Statement-I wrong; Statement-II correct).
**BioE3 Policy (2024)** proposes **single-window clearance** + **regulatory sandboxes**.

112.s: The FSSAI GM food framework referred to for India is associated with the year:
112.x: The FSSAI GM food framework dates to 2024 and works under the Food Safety and Standards Act 2006. The other years belong to other things: 2002 is the Biological Diversity Act (and Bt cotton approval), 2009 the National Biosafety Framework, and 2017 the rDNA Guidelines.
112.tq: Distinguish the years of closely related regulatory instruments.
xs: The **FSSAI GM food framework** dates to **2024** — option **(4)** is correct.
**2002** = **Biological Diversity Act** and **Bt cotton**; **2009** = **National Biosafety Framework**; **2017** = **rDNA Guidelines**.
xa: It requires **approval of the competent authority** for GM food.
It works under the **FSS Act, 2006**.
**BioE3 Policy** is also of **2024**.

112.s: Regulation of genetically modified food, including its import, in India rests on which law?
o: Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001
112.x: GM food is governed by the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, with the FSSAI GM food framework of 2024; import of GM food without approval of the competent authority is prohibited. The EPA governs GMO release, the PPVFR Act plant varieties, and the Patents Act patents.
112.tq: GM food = FSS Act 2006 / FSSAI.
xs: GM food, including imports, rests on the **Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006** — option **(2)** is correct.
The **EPA 1986** governs GMO release (GEAC), the **PPVFR Act 2001** plant varieties, and the **Patents Act** patents.
xa: The law **prohibits GM food import without approval**.
**FSSAI GM food framework 2024**: approval of the **competent authority**.
July **2024**: SC **split verdict** on GM mustard; Centre told to frame a **national policy on GM crops**.

112.s: Which one of the following genetically modified crops was approved for commercial cultivation in India in March 2002?
112.x: Bt cotton was approved for commercial cultivation in March 2002. It remains the only genetically modified crop commercially cultivated in India.
112.tq: Use the date-and-crop association to distinguish the approved crop from proposed or trial crops.
xs: **Bt cotton** was approved in **March 2002** — option **(4)** is correct.
**DMH-11** got environmental-release clearance only in **2022**; genome-edited rice came later.
xa: Three **MAHYCO** hybrids, initially for **3** years; **only GM crop commercially cultivated**.
Area: **12.5 million ha**, **over 90%** of cotton area (older notes: **10.8** million ha).
Bt cotton genes: **Cry1Ac** (Bollgard I); **Cry1Ac + Cry2Ab** (Bollgard II).

112.s:
With reference to the commercial approval of Bt cotton in India, consider the following statements:
1. The initial approval covered three MAHYCO hybrids.
2. The approval was initially granted for three years.
3. Bt cotton remains the only GM crop commercially cultivated in India.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
112.x: All three statements are correct. Three MAHYCO hybrids were initially approved for three years, and Bt cotton remains the only GM crop commercially cultivated in India.
112.tq: Check each statement against the approval details before selecting the complete combination.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4)** (**1, 2 and 3**).
Statement 1: approval in **March 2002** covered **three MAHYCO hybrids**.
Statement 2: initially for **3 years**; Statement 3: Bt cotton is the **only GM crop commercially cultivated**.
xa: Leading State: **Maharashtra** (PYQ).
**Bollgard** = GM technology (PYQ); genes from **Bacillus thuringiensis**.
**DMH-11**'s commercial use is held up under **Supreme Court** review.

112.s: Which State is recognised as the leading Bt cotton-growing State in India?
112.x: Maharashtra is identified as the leading Bt cotton State.
112.tq: Test the crop-State association directly using a nearby cotton-growing State as the distractor.
xs: **Maharashtra** is the leading Bt cotton State (PYQ) — option **(3)** is correct.
Punjab, Gujarat and Telangana are not named as the leader in the notes.
xa: Bt cotton approved **March 2002**: three **MAHYCO** hybrids.
Area **12.5 million ha**, **over 90%** of cotton area.
Trait: **bollworm** resistance via **Cry1Ac**/**Cry2Ab**.

112.s:
Match List-I with List-II regarding genome-edited crop varieties released or developed in India.

List-I (Variety)
a. Pusa Rice DST1
b. Kamala (DRR Dhan 100)
c. CRISPR phosphate-uptake rice

List-II (Developer)
i. NIPGR
ii. ICAR-IARI, Delhi
iii. ICAR (IIRR, Hyderabad)

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
112.x: Pusa Rice DST1 was developed by ICAR-IARI, Delhi; Kamala by ICAR through IIRR, Hyderabad; and the CRISPR phosphate-uptake rice by NIPGR.
112.tq: Start from the sure developer-variety pair and eliminate codes containing a wrong pair.
xs: **Pusa Rice DST1 – ICAR-IARI, Delhi**; **Kamala – ICAR (IIRR Hyderabad)**; **phosphate-uptake rice – NIPGR** — option **(1)** (a–ii, b–iii, c–i).
**Kamala** is also called **DRR Dhan 100**: **SDN-1** edited, higher yield, early maturity.
xa: **Pusa DST1/Kamala** = first genome-edited rice.
NIPGR's CRISPR rice is **non-GMO** and could cut **fertiliser imports**.
**Rs 500 crore** (**2023-24**) earmarked for GE research.

112.s: Pusa Rice DST1 is associated with which of the following traits and editing features?
o: Insect resistance; insertion of a Bt toxin gene by SDN-2
Drought and salinity tolerance; DST gene knockout by SDN-1
Higher phosphate uptake; insertion of a foreign bacterial gene
Vitamin A enrichment; mitochondrial gene replacement
112.x: Pusa Rice DST1 is an edited form of MTU1010, designed for drought and salinity tolerance through DST gene knockout using SDN-1.
112.tq: Combine the crop, trait and technical method instead of relying on the variety name alone.
xs: **Pusa Rice DST1** gives **drought and salinity tolerance** by **DST gene knockout via SDN-1** — option **(2)** is correct.
It is a **CRISPR-Cas9** edit of **MTU1010**, with **no foreign DNA** — so not Bt insertion, foreign bacterial gene or vitamin A.
xa: Yield **10-30%** higher under stress; set for commercial launch (**1 Sep 2026**).
Developer: **ICAR-IARI, Delhi**.
**Phosphate uptake** rice is **NIPGR**'s; **vitamin A** rice is **Golden Rice**.

112.s: Which of the following correctly distinguishes SDN-1 and SDN-2 genome editing from SDN-3 editing?
o: All three categories are treated as conventional crops
SDN-1 alone is transgenic, while SDN-2 and SDN-3 are exempted
SDN-1 and SDN-2 introduce foreign DNA, whereas SDN-3 does not
SDN-1 and SDN-2 involve small edits without foreign DNA, whereas SDN-3 is transgenic
112.x: SDN-1 and SDN-2 involve small edits without foreign DNA and are exempted from GMO rules under the 2022 guidelines. SDN-3 is transgenic and remains under full regulatory control.
112.tq: Discriminate the paired categories by checking the presence or absence of foreign DNA.
xs: **SDN-1 and SDN-2** are **small edits without foreign DNA**, while **SDN-3 is transgenic** — option **(4)** is correct.
SDN-1/2 are **exempted** from GMO rules (**2022 guidelines**); SDN-3 stays under **full GM control** — so options (1)-(3) are wrong.
xa: Exempt GE crops **skip GEAC**; need only **IBC** approval.
Comparison: GMO = foreign gene, full **GEAC** route; SDN-1/2 = treated like **conventional crops**.
⚠ Criticism: the GE exemption is called a **"back door"**.

112.s: For genome-edited crops covered by the SDN-1 and SDN-2 exemption, which approval route is indicated?
o: IBC approval without the GEAC route
Only approval from the State Pollution Control Board
Approval from the Supreme Court after public consultation
112.x: Genome-edited crops covered by the SDN-1 and SDN-2 exemption can skip the GEAC route and require IBC approval.
112.tq: Ask which authority performs the relevant regulatory function instead of assuming every biotechnology product follows the GEAC route.
xs: Genome-edited crops under the SDN-1/SDN-2 exemption need only **IBC approval** and **skip the GEAC** route — option **(1)** is correct.
No State Pollution Board or Supreme Court route is involved.
xa: **IBSC** now clears **genome-edited crops** (Dec **2025**).
**2022 guidelines** exempt **SDN-1/SDN-2** (no foreign DNA).
**SDN-3** (transgenic) remains under full GM control.

112.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. NIPGR has developed a CRISPR rice with improved phosphate uptake.
2. The rice is described as non-GMO.
3. The innovation could help reduce fertiliser imports.
4. CRISPR mustard ‘Varuna’ is associated with improved oil quality.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
112.x: All four statements are correct. The NIPGR rice is non-GMO, improves phosphate uptake and may reduce fertiliser imports, while Varuna is a CRISPR mustard associated with oil quality.
112.tq: Combine several linked applications and institutional associations, watching for an omitted final statement.
xs: All four are correct — option **(3)** (**1, 2, 3 and 4**).
**NIPGR**'s CRISPR rice has **better phosphate uptake**, is **non-GMO**, and could **cut fertiliser imports** (1-3).
**CRISPR mustard 'Varuna'** targets **oil quality** (4).
xa: **Pusa Rice DST1** (IARI): **DST gene** knockout in **MTU1010**.
**Kamala** (DRR Dhan 100): SDN-1 edited rice.
GE research funding: **Rs 500 crore** (**2023-24**).

112.s: Which of the following is regarded as the primary environmental concern associated with genetically modified crops?
o: Cross-pollination and gene flow to non-GM crops
Reduction in soil mineral content in every cultivated field
Increase in atmospheric carbon dioxide from all crops
112.x: The primary environmental concern is cross-pollination or gene flow from GM crops to non-GM crops. The other effects are not identified as the primary concern.
112.tq: Select the precise environmental impact rather than a general ecological claim.
xs: The primary environmental concern is **cross-pollination/gene flow to non-GM crops** (APPSC-G2 **2023**) — option **(1)** is correct.
Groundwater, soil minerals and CO2 are not named concerns.
xa: Other environmental risks: **insect resistance build-up**, harm to **non-target organisms**, weediness in wild relatives, **genetic homogenisation**.
Health risks: **toxicity**, **allergenicity**, **antibiotic resistance**.
**Genetic modification** = technology raising **biodiversity concerns** (APPSC-GS **2023**).

112.s:
Consider the following:
1. Insect resistance build-up and harm to non-target organisms
2. Weediness in wild relatives and genetic homogenisation
3. Toxicity, allergenicity and antibiotic resistance
4. Ozone depletion
Which of the above are listed as environmental or health risks of GM crops?
112.x: 1 and 2 are listed environmental risks; 3 are listed health risks. Ozone depletion (4) is not a GM-crop risk. So 1, 2 and 3 only; options with 4 are wrong and '1 and 2 only' leaves out the health risks.
112.tq: GM risks: environment (resistance, non-target, weediness, homogenisation) + health (toxicity, allergy, antibiotic resistance).
xs: Items **1, 2 and 3** are listed risks; **ozone depletion** is not — option **(2)**.
1 and 2 are environmental risks: **insect resistance build-up**, **non-target harm**, **weediness**, **genetic homogenisation**.
3 are health risks: **toxicity**, **allergenicity**, **antibiotic resistance**.
xa: Primary environmental concern: **gene flow/cross-pollination**.
Reasons for resistance: **monoculture**, loss of diversity, control by **patent-holding seed companies**.
Herbicide-tolerance fears: **DMH-11** carries the **bar gene**.

112.s: Which of the following combinations correctly explains delays in approval of genetically modified products in India?
o: Overlapping mandates of DBT, GEAC, CDSCO, FSSAI and NBA, along with the absence of a biosafety liability law
Exclusive control of approval by ICAR and the presence of a comprehensive liability law
Absence of all environmental regulation and exclusive control by State governments
Only the high cost of imported seeds
112.x: Overlapping mandates among DBT, GEAC, CDSCO, FSSAI and NBA, together with the absence of a biosafety liability law, contribute to delays. Approval may take 7–10 years in India compared with 3–5 years globally.
112.tq: Combine the institutional and legal causes instead of selecting a single-factor explanation.
xs: Delays come from **overlapping mandates of DBT, GEAC, CDSCO, FSSAI and NBA** plus **no biosafety liability law** — option **(1)** is correct.
India takes **7-10 years** for GM approval vs **3-5** globally.
xa: ⚠ Criticism: multi-layered regulation **delays approvals yet lacks a liability law**.
**BioE3 Policy 2024**: **single-window clearance** + regulatory sandboxes.
**BRAI Bill 2013** (single regulator) **lapsed**.

112.s: Which one of the following technologies has been flagged for raising concerns about biodiversity?
112.x: Genetic modification is the technology flagged for biodiversity concerns (APPSC-GS 2023), through gene flow, monoculture and loss of diversity. Drip irrigation, solar panels and rainwater harvesting are not flagged this way.
112.tq: Biodiversity worry = genetic modification.
xs: **Genetic modification of crops** is flagged for **biodiversity concerns** (APPSC-GS **2023**) — option **(2)** is correct.
Drip irrigation, rooftop solar and rainwater harvesting are not flagged this way.
xa: Concerns: gene flow, **monoculture**, loss of diversity, **genetic homogenisation**.
Primary environmental concern: **cross-pollination** to non-GM crops.
Resistance also stems from control by **big seed companies** holding patents.

112.s:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
A. Introduction of Bt cotton
B. PIL against GM crops in the Supreme Court
C. Moratorium on Bt brinjal
D. GEAC clearance of trials of 11 crops and 21 varieties
112.x: Bt cotton was introduced in 2002, the PIL was filed in 2006, the Bt brinjal moratorium was imposed in 2010, and GEAC cleared trials in 2014.
112.tq: Use the first and last events, then place the intervening years in sequence.
xs: Order: **Bt cotton (2002) → SC PIL (2006) → Bt brinjal moratorium (2010) → trials of 11 crops/21 varieties (2014)** — option **(1)** (A, B, C, D).
The **2014** clearances came when **Veerappa Moily** resumed trials (Mar and Jul).
xa: **2009**: GEAC recommends **Bt brinjal** release.
**2012**: Parliamentary Standing Committee (**37th report**) — end all GM field trials.
**2022**: GEAC clears **DMH-11** environmental release.

112.s: The 2010 decision relating to Bt brinjal included which of the following additional measures?
o: A requirement that all GM seeds be branded by the State
A transfer of field-trial approval exclusively to FSSAI
A mandatory State no-objection certificate for field trials
A permanent ban on every GM crop in India
112.x: In 2010, a State NOC was made mandatory for field trials. The decision was not a permanent ban on every GM crop or a transfer of approval to FSSAI.
112.tq: Separate the specific administrative condition from exaggerated consequences.
xs: In **2010**, along with the **Bt brinjal moratorium**, a **State NOC was made mandatory** for field trials — option **(3)** is correct.
It was not a permanent ban on all GM crops (**Bt cotton** continued), nor a shift of approvals to FSSAI.
xa: Moratorium by Minister **Jairam Ramesh**: no scientific consensus, opposition of brinjal-growing States.
Bt brinjal targets **fruit and shoot borer**; by **Mahyco** with **UAS Dharwad** and **TNAU**.
GEAC recommended its release in **2009**.

112.s: Which report recommended ending all genetically modified crop field trials?
o: The report of the Central Pollution Control Board
The 37th Report of the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Agriculture
The annual report of the National Biodiversity Authority
The report of the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India
112.x: The 37th Report of the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Agriculture in 2012 recommended ending all GM field trials.
112.tq: Identify the report by matching the recommendation with the correct parliamentary body.
xs: The **37th Report of the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Agriculture** (**2012**) recommended ending all GM field trials — option **(2)** is correct.
CPCB, NBA and FSSAI reports are not the source.
xa: **2012-13**: SC-appointed **Technical Expert Committee** recommended a **10-year moratorium** on field trials.
Trials were put on hold (**Jayanthi Natarajan**); **Veerappa Moily** resumed them in **2014**.
**2006**: PIL against GM crops in the **Supreme Court**.

112.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Supreme Court-appointed Technical Expert Committee:
1. It recommended a 10-year moratorium on GM field trials.
2. Its recommendation amounted to a final Supreme Court verdict.
3. GM trials were halted during the relevant period.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
